```{r knitr_setup, include=FALSE}
# === GLOBAL KNITR OPTIONS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: sets the house rules for how every later block of code
# is turned into the finished HTML report -- whether the code itself is shown,
# whether R's background chatter is shown, and how large the figures come out.
# It runs no analysis and changes no number.
#
# WHY IT IS HERE AT ALL: these settings are made once, at the top, so that
# every section of the report looks and behaves the same way. Set chunk by
# chunk instead, they would drift, and one table would show its code while the
# next one hid it for no stated reason.
#
# echo = TRUE          -> show the code, not only its results. The code is part
#                         of what is being handed over. A reviewer should be
#                         able to see what produced every number in the report
#                         without opening the .Rmd source file.
# warning/message OFF  -> hide R's routine chatter. psych::alpha, psych::omega
#                         and lavaan talk while they work: key-direction notes,
#                         which say which way round an item is scored, and
#                         convergence chatter, which reports whether the
#                         routine fitting a model settled on a stable answer.
#                         Printed in full, that noise would bury the results a
#                         reader came for.
#                         WARNING: this hides CHATTER, not FAILURES. Every
#                         helper that can legitimately fail wraps its call in
#                         tryCatch() and hands back NA, which is R's marker for
#                         a missing value, and that NA then appears in the
#                         printed table where anyone can see it. Nothing that
#                         matters disappears.
# fig.width/height     -> the default figure size, in inches, for the forest
#                         plot, the scree plot and the heatmap. Individual
#                         chunks set a taller fig.height where a panel needs
#                         the extra room.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 7
)
```

# Overview

> ## CONFIRMATORY ANALYSIS -- FULL DATASET
>
> **This document runs the pre-registered confirmatory tests on the full
> dataset (`FullData_Values.csv`, 1,015 raw responses).** Pre-registered means
> the hypotheses and the tests were written down and filed before anyone saw
> the results, so nothing here was picked after the fact to make the numbers
> look good. Data collection is complete, so per pre-registration
> Section 4.4 -- "no hypotheses are tested before collection ends" -- these are
> the confirmatory results.
>
> **Realized N.** N is the number of people whose answers are actually
> analysed. The pre-registered exclusions (Section 6.2) retain **N = 948** of
> 1,015. Those 1,015 are the raw responses: every submission the survey
> recorded, before any exclusion. The stated target was 960 valid responses
> (Section 4.2), so the realized sample is **12 short of target (1.25%)**. The
> power consequence is negligible. Power is the chance of detecting a real
> effect when there is one. Losing 12 people barely moves it: the smallest
> detectable correlation moves from r ≈ .090 to r ≈ .091, and the smallest
> detectable group difference stays at d ≈ 0.19 (Section 4.3). The exclusion
> funnel in Phase 1.3 records where each excluded response drops out, so no
> response is removed without a stated reason a reader can check.

This document performs the **complete confirmatory analysis** for the
Retribution study. It ports `01_clean_and_score.R` and `02_basic_analysis.R`
into one knitting document, and extends them to the full pre-registered set
(H1–H21) plus the robustness variants the plan requires. A knitting document
is a single file that runs itself from top to bottom and writes out the
finished report. A robustness variant re-runs a test a second defensible way,
so a reader can see that the answer does not hang on one arbitrary choice.

## Pre-registered hypotheses

Everything below, the exploratory items included, was written down and filed
before the data were collected. For the moderators, the registration names the
two variables but no model; 9.18 sets out the models used. The wording here is deliberately short. The
phase that tests each one names the exact measures that go into it.

**Whole-sample replication of the Dark Side pattern**

Whole-sample means all 948 people rather than a subgroup. Replication means
checking whether a pattern reported in the earlier Dark Side study shows up
again in this one.

  - **H1** -- Punitiveness correlates positively with each of the 12 correlates:
    people who are more punitive also score higher on each of them (due
    process, uncertain evidence, hatred, anger, exclusion, degradation,
    suffering, prison violence, harsh conditions, revenge, crime rates, fear).
  - **H2** -- The hostile-aggression cluster correlates more strongly with
    punitiveness than the crime-concerns cluster does. The hostile-aggression
    cluster groups the hostile attitudes toward the offender; the
    crime-concerns cluster groups worry about crime itself. The comparison uses
    Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations, which asks whether
    one correlation is really larger than another when the two share a variable
    (here, punitiveness).
  - **H3** -- The correlates are mostly positively intercorrelated, meaning they
    rise and fall together: one punitiveness dimension runs through them.

**Construct validity of retribution**

Construct validity asks whether a measure really captures the idea it claims to
capture, rather than something else that happens to sit nearby.

  - **H4** -- Strict proportionality is not consistently endorsed. Agreement
    sits at or below the midpoint of the scale, and a sizeable share endorse
    punishment beyond it.
  - **H5** -- Support for punishment exceeding the crime is higher than support
    for punishment falling short of the harm.
  - **H6** -- Just deserts does not cohere. Just deserts is the idea that an
    offender deserves punishment and that the punishment should match the
    crime. Its desert and proportionality parts correlate weakly, do not form a
    reliable scale, and fail a one-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA),
    the model that asks whether a set of questions really measures one single
    thing.
  - **H7** -- Willingness to set aside the Kantian limits does not line up with
    just deserts and is positively related to revenge. The Kantian limits are
    the constraints on how punishment may be imposed: due process, reliable
    evidence, and judging without hatred or anger.
  - **H8** -- Willingness to set aside the limits correlates with punitiveness.
  - **H9** -- Support for just deserts exceeds support for revenge. The test is
    paired: each person's two scores are compared against each other.
  - **H10** -- Revenge correlates more strongly with punitiveness than just
    deserts does (Steiger's test again).

**Retributivists versus everyone else**

  - **H11** -- The H1–H10 relationships also hold inside the retributivist
    group, not only across the sample as a whole.
  - **H12** -- A sizeable share of retributivists endorse each hostile
    attitude, and each attitude correlates with punitiveness. The share is the
    proportion scoring above the midpoint of the scale, reported with CIs. A
    confidence interval (CI) is the range of values the data leave plausible.
  - **H13** -- Retributivists score higher on hostile aggression and on the
    wider correlate set.
  - **H14** -- Retributivists give longer sentences (standardized within
    vignette, so each person is compared with the others who read the same
    crime story).
  - **H15** -- Retributivists are more willing to put the shark to death
    (logistic regression, the model used when the outcome is a yes-or-no
    answer) and endorse a more painful death (t-test).
  - **H16** -- Stronger essentialism, the view that an offender is a certain
    kind of person rather than a product of circumstance. **H17** -- Crime is a
    choice. **H18** -- Side with the prosecution. **H19** -- Reject society's
    responsibility. **H20** -- Set aside due process and evidence limits.
    **H21** -- Higher punitiveness.

**Exploratory (reported briefly, not corrected as a confirmatory family)**

These are looked at, not staked on. They sit outside the confirmatory
family, so they are not folded into its multiple-testing correction, and they
should be read as leads worth following rather than as tested claims.

  - **E1** -- Personality differences (RWA, right-wing authoritarianism; SDO,
    social dominance orientation; violence proneness; racial resentment;
    cognitive reflection, scored as the number of correct answers on a short
    reasoning test).
  - **E2** -- Hostile solidarity versus Durkheimian solidarity (Steiger's
    test). The Durkheimian reading treats punishment as what binds the
    law-abiding together and restates shared norms; the hostile reading treats
    it as expelling the offender.
  - **Moderators** -- Political orientation and prosecution-defense leaning as
    moderators of the link between retributivism and punitiveness (prereg 6.6;
    section 9.18). A moderator is a variable that changes the strength of a
    relationship.

Directional predictions -- the ones that name which way the effect should go --
are tested **one-sided** in the predicted direction; the rest are tested
two-sided (prereg 6.8). A one-sided test spends its whole error allowance on
the predicted side; a two-sided test splits it across both sides. **Every test
reports an effect size and a confidence interval**, so a reader can see how
large the effect is and how precisely it was pinned down, not merely whether it
cleared a threshold.

## Phases

  1. **Phase 0** -- Setup, packages, helper functions
  2. **Phase 1** -- Load the Values export, exclusion funnel, vignette
     coalescing (folding the three vignette-specific columns into one)
  3. **Phase 2** -- Reverse coding, driven by a metadata table (`<item>_R`
     columns)
  4. **Phase 3** -- Within-vignette standardization of the sentence
  5. **Phase 4** -- Composites with Cronbach's α **and** McDonald's ω, two
     measures of how well a set of items hang together
  6. **Phase 5** -- The retributivist measures (categorical, continuous,
     behavioral)
  7. **Phase 6** -- Demographics and descriptives
  8. **Phase 7** -- H1–H3 (whole-sample replication)
  9. **Phase 8** -- H4–H10 (construct validity of retribution)
  10. **Phase 9** -- H11–H21 (retributivist contrasts) + continuous and
      sentencing-ratio robustness runs, E1, E2, the moderators (9.18), and
      the scorings the paper reports (9.19)
  11. **Phase 10** -- Export tables, figures, cleaned data

## Data note

The analysis reads the Qualtrics **Values** export (`FullData_Values.csv`,
1,015 raw responses), which is numeric: the attitude items come through as
numbers, 1–7. The **Labels** export is a codebook only. It writes the anchor
wording for the two end points but bare numbers for the middle scale points, so
a column read from it is part words and part digits and cannot be averaged. It
is **never** used for numeric work; it is loaded here (if present) purely to
print question wording. The instrument was identical throughout collection, so
the Labels file documents the decodes for every response.

`Data/` also holds an interim partial export (`Pilot_300_*`). Always read the
full file, `FullData_Values.csv`. Reading the partial file by mistake would
produce a complete-looking report resting on a fraction of the sample.

Three export quirks are handled explicitly, because each one quietly corrupts
the data if it is ignored:

  - The file has **three header rows** (names, question text, ImportId JSON),
    the last being the machine-readable line Qualtrics uses to re-import a
    survey. Names are therefore read from row 1 and the data with `skip = 3`.
    Read straight in, the two extra header rows would arrive as though they
    were participants.
  - The sentencing columns are **vignette-split**
    (`Sentence1_V1_1` / `_V2_1` / `_V3_1`, and likewise for `Sentence2` and the
    two open-ends). Each person saw only one of the three vignettes, so for any
    given row two of the three columns are empty. They are coalesced -- merged
    down into a single column -- using the embedded `Vignette` field, which
    records which version each person saw.
  - Slider exports carry a trailing `_1` (`CRT_1_1`, `age_1`, `Sentence1_V1_1`).
    The suffix carries no meaning: `age_1` is simply age.
  - The ranking explanation exports as **`Priorit_Explain`**; the
    pre-registration calls this item **Q333**.

Two scoring facts that are easy to get wrong:

  - `severity_1` is reverse-keyed **only** inside the just-deserts
    proportionality component. The standalone H4/H5 tests use the raw item.
    Using the reversed version there would report those two results backwards.
  - `punitiveness` (8 self-report items) versus `punitiveness_full` (adds the
    within-vignette z-scored sentence). CIRCULARITY HAZARD: the full index is
    **never** used where the sentence would enter on both sides -- that is,
    never with the sentencing ratio and never for H14. Doing so would correlate
    the sentence with itself and manufacture a finding out of nothing.

## Output organization

All outputs are written to subdirectories of the folder holding this file, so
the entire set of deliverables can be regenerated from scratch by deleting them
and re-knitting:

  - `output/tables/` -- CSV tables (every result table in this document)
  - `output/figures/` -- PNG figures (forest plot, heatmap, scree, histograms)
  - `data/cleaned/` -- the scored dataset (CSV + RDS) for downstream use

# PHASE 0: SETUP AND PACKAGE LOADING

Phase 0 gets the workspace ready and touches no data. It fixes where files are
read from and written to, loads the add-on packages the analysis needs, and
defines the helper functions that every later phase calls.

## 0.1 Path configuration

Where the data comes from and where the results go, decided once, in one place.

```{r phase0_paths}
# === PATH CONFIGURATION ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: fixes the two input paths and the three output
# directories, creates the output directories, and initialises the two
# collectors (TABLES, FIGURES) that every later phase appends to and that
# Phase 10 writes to disk. Nothing statistical happens here.
#
# WHY IT IS ALL IN ONE PLACE: suppose file locations were written into each
# chunk that needed one. Moving the data or renaming a folder would then mean
# hunting through the whole document for stragglers, and a missed one would go
# on reading a stale file without complaint. Setting the paths once, here,
# means one edit in one visible spot. It also lets a reader see at a glance
# every file this document reads and every place it writes.
#
# All paths are relative to this .Rmd file's folder:
#   Retribution/Analysis/Retribution R/   (the RStudio project)
# Data therefore sits two levels up, in Retribution/Data/. Each ".." below
# means "go up one folder".
# file.path() joins the pieces with whatever separator the current machine
# uses, rather than a hand-pasted "/", so the document also knits on Windows.

# THE analysis file: the full Values export (1,015 raw responses).
# "Values" = the numeric Qualtrics export: attitude items come through as 1-7
# integers, which is what any arithmetic needs. The parallel "Labels" export
# writes anchor TEXT for the endpoints but bare numbers for the middle scale
# points. A column taken from it is therefore half words and half digits, and
# can never be used for arithmetic. See LABELS_PATH below and the note in
# Phase 1.2.
# DANGER: Data/ also holds an interim partial export (Pilot_300_*). Always read
# the full file named here. Pointing this line at the partial file would yield
# a report that looks finished but rests on a fraction of the sample.
DATA_PATH   <- file.path("..", "..", "Data", "FullData_Values.csv")
# Codebook only, never used numerically: it supplies the question wording
# printed in Phase 1.2, so a reader can see what people were actually asked.
# The instrument was identical throughout collection, so its decodes describe
# every response in the full export even though the filename says Pilot_300.
LABELS_PATH <- file.path("..", "..", "Data", "Pilot_300_Labels.csv")

# Output roots. Every table, figure and dataset this document produces lands
# under one of these three, so the whole set of deliverables can be regenerated
# by deleting them and re-knitting -- and so nothing this document writes ever
# lands somewhere a reader would not think to look.
OUT_TABLES  <- file.path("output", "tables")
OUT_FIGURES <- file.path("output", "figures")
OUT_DATA    <- file.path("data", "cleaned")

# Create the folders before anything tries to write into them; writing to a
# folder that does not exist is an error that would stop the knit at Phase 10,
# after all the work.
# recursive = TRUE creates the intermediate levels too ("output/" before
# "output/tables/"); showWarnings = FALSE makes a re-knit a silent no-op
# instead of a wall of "directory already exists" warnings.
for (p in c(OUT_TABLES, OUT_FIGURES, OUT_DATA)) {
  dir.create(p, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}

cat("Output directories ready:\n")
cat("  Tables:  ", OUT_TABLES,  "\n")
cat("  Figures: ", OUT_FIGURES, "\n")
cat("  Cleaned: ", OUT_DATA,    "\n\n")
cat("Values export found: ", file.exists(DATA_PATH),   "\n")
cat("Labels codebook found: ", file.exists(LABELS_PATH), " (optional)\n")

# Collectors filled in as the document runs; written out in Phase 10. They
# exist so that results are gathered as they are produced rather than
# reconstructed at the end, where a table could easily be forgotten.
# TABLES is a NAMED list: TABLES[["H1_correlations"]] becomes the file
# output/tables/H1_correlations.csv in Phase 10.1, so the name chosen at the
# point of assignment IS the exported filename. Choose it carefully.
# FIGURES is a plain character vector (a simple run of values) holding the file
# paths that ggsave() or png() has already written; Phase 10.2 only lists them
# back. Both are assigned with <- at top level, outside any function, so
# ordinary scoping is enough -- no <<- is needed except inside
# compute_composite(), which writes to alpha_table from within a function.
TABLES  <- list()
FIGURES <- character(0)
```

## 0.2 Package loading

R on its own cannot do everything this plan requires, so a small set of add-on
packages is loaded here, all in one visible list.

```{r phase0_packages}
# === PACKAGE LOADING ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: attaches the add-on packages the analysis relies on and
# records which, if any, are missing.
#
# WHY: base R handles correlations and t-tests, but not factor analysis or the
# specialised effect-size intervals the pre-registration asks for. Those come
# from outside packages, listed here in one place so a reader can see exactly
# what outside code the published numbers depend on.
#
# WHAT WOULD GO WRONG OTHERWISE: packages loaded quietly halfway down the
# document would hide that dependency, and a machine without one would fail in
# the middle of an analysis with no explanation. Nothing is installed at knit
# time: missing packages are reported and only the analyses that need them are
# skipped, so the document still knits.
#
# Purpose of each package is annotated, in the comment beside its name in the
# list below. What those short notes mean, in plain terms:
#   alpha, omega   Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega: two numbers saying
#                  how well a set of questions hang together as one scale.
#   EFA            exploratory factor analysis: lets the data suggest how many
#                  underlying themes sit behind a set of items.
#   CFA            confirmatory factor analysis: a model that asks whether a
#                  set of questions really measures one single thing.
#   Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations: asks whether one
#                  correlation is really bigger than another when both share a
#                  variable.
#   Cohen's d      the size of a difference between two groups, measured in
#                  standard deviations. One-sample d compares one group against
#                  a fixed value, such as the midpoint of a scale.
#   confidence interval: the range of values the data leave plausible.
#   rotation       the step that turns raw factor-analysis output into a form a
#                  human can actually interpret.
#   kable          the function that prints a data frame (a table of rows and
#                  columns) as a tidy table in the report.

required_packages <- c(
  "tidyverse",    # dplyr / tidyr / ggplot2 / readr / tibble: data and plots
  "psych",        # alpha, omega, EFA, describe
  "cocor",        # Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations
  "lavaan",       # confirmatory factor analysis (H6)
  "effectsize",   # Cohen's d and one-sample d with confidence intervals
  "corrplot",     # correlation heatmap
  "GPArotation",  # rotation backend for psych::omega / psych::fa
  "knitr",        # kable tables
  "scales"        # axis formatting
)

# requireNamespace() TESTS for a package without attaching it, so this line can
# find out what is missing without erroring out. Note the deliberate design: a
# missing package must NOT stop the knit, because the confirmatory results
# (correlations, t-tests) come from base R and would still be valid. Only the
# analyses that genuinely need the missing package are skipped, each one
# guarded by HAVE() below, and the gap is announced rather than hidden.
missing_pkgs <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]
if (length(missing_pkgs)) {
  cat("MISSING PACKAGES (analyses that need them will be skipped):\n  ",
      paste(missing_pkgs, collapse = ", "), "\n")
}
# Attach only what is actually installed. character.only = TRUE because the
# names arrive as strings rather than as bare words; invisible() swallows the
# list of return values library() hands back, which nobody needs to see.
invisible(lapply(setdiff(required_packages, missing_pkgs),
                 library, character.only = TRUE))

# Availability flag used to guard optional analyses. Read HAVE("cocor") as
# "is the Steiger machinery available?" -- when it is FALSE the helper returns
# a row of NAs, R's marker for a missing value, instead of crashing, and that
# NA is plainly visible in the printed table. A skipped analysis should never
# look like an analysis that was run.
HAVE <- function(pkg) requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)

# scipen = 999 pushes R's threshold for switching to scientific notation
# effectively to never, so a small p-value prints as 0.000012 rather than
# 1.2e-05 in raw prints, which is far easier to read at a glance. It is a
# DISPLAY setting only and changes no computed value. (format_p() below is what
# actually formats p-values for the narrative text.)
options(scipen = 999)  # no scientific notation
# Significant digits -- how many meaningful digits R shows -- for bare prints
# such as print() and the cocor output. The formatted tables set their own
# precision through show_table(digits = 3) and the sprintf formats in the cat()
# lines, so this setting reaches only the unformatted printouts.
options(digits = 4)

cat("\nPackages loaded.\n")
```

## 0.3 Helper functions

The small, reusable pieces of code the rest of the document calls. Reading this
section once makes every later phase much shorter to follow.

```{r phase0_helpers}
# === HELPER FUNCTIONS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: defines the small functions used throughout, so that a
# rule such as "how a p-value is printed" or "how a composite score is built"
# is written down ONCE and then applied identically everywhere.
#
# WHY THAT MATTERS: the alternative is retyping the same handful of lines in
# every chunk that needs them. Then a correction made in one place silently
# disagrees with all the others, and two tables in the same report can round
# differently, score differently, or treat a skipped answer differently.
# Defining the rule once makes that whole class of error impossible.
#
# Conventions mirror the Dark Side / Punishment 2.1 pipeline (format_p,
# sig_stars, compute_composite, get_cor_ci, format_cor_table), extended here
# with the one-sided / effect-size machinery the Retribution pre-registration
# requires.
#
# Two conventions run through the whole set and are worth stating once:
#
#   1. EVERY test helper returns a ONE-ROW DATA FRAME with a fixed set of
#      columns. A data frame is a table with named columns. When the test
#      cannot be run at all, the helper returns that same one-row frame filled
#      with NA, R's marker for a missing value.
#      That fixed shape is what lets the hypothesis functions stack results
#      into a table with do.call(rbind, lapply(...)), never checking a return
#      value. It is also why a composite that failed to build shows up as a
#      visible NA row instead of stopping the knit. A result that could not be
#      computed must still be seen.
#   2. EVERY test helper carries BOTH p_two and p_dir. Prereg 6.8: predictions
#      that name a direction are tested one-sided in that direction, the rest
#      two-sided. For a directional hypothesis p_dir is therefore the
#      inferential number, the one the conclusion rests on, and p_two is
#      printed beside it for readers who want the undirected test. Confidence
#      intervals are always the two-sided 95% intervals. A confidence interval
#      is the range of values the data leave plausible. Holding every interval
#      to the same two-sided rule is what keeps a column of them comparable,
#      even in a table that mixes directional and non-directional rows.

#' Format a p-value for display
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  p  a single p-value; anything whose length is not exactly 1, or
#'               NA, gives back the text "NA".
#' RETURNS    a fragment that slots straight into a cat() sentence, so the text
#'            reads "p < .001" or "p = 0.032" and never doubles the equals sign.
#' USED BY    the narrative cat() lines throughout Phases 5 to 9.
#'
#' A p-value is the chance of seeing a result at least this extreme if there
#' were really no effect, so a small p-value is a surprising result. Below .001
#' the exact value carries no useful information, and "= 0.000" would be plainly
#' wrong, so the conventional "< .001" is substituted. Three decimals elsewhere:
#' the inference cutoff is alpha = .05 (prereg 6.8), and three decimals is
#' enough to see how far a test sits from it.
format_p <- function(p) {
  if (length(p) != 1 || is.na(p)) return("NA")
  if (p < .001) return("< .001")
  sprintf("= %.3f", p)
}

#' Convert p-values to significance stars
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  p  a vector (a simple run of values) of p-values.
#' RETURNS    a character vector of "", "*", "**" or "***", one entry per input
#'            value (the function is vectorised: it handles the whole run in one
#'            go rather than one value at a time).
#' USED BY    run_h1() on the BH-adjusted one-sided p, format_cor_table(), the
#'            H4-H10 summary table, and the side-by-side d table in Phase 9.12.
#'            BH is the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, which controls the false
#'            discovery rate. Testing many hypotheses at once throws up some
#'            false positives by chance, so BH raises the p-values to hold the
#'            expected share of false positives down.
#'
#' Thresholds are the conventional .05 / .01 / .001. CAREFUL: only the .05 star
#' carries inferential weight in this document -- that is the pre-registered
#' cutoff (prereg 6.8) -- and the finer two are reading aids, NOT a stronger
#' grade of evidence. NA maps to "" rather than to a star, so a test that could
#' not be computed never prints as though it were significant.
sig_stars <- function(p) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < .001 ~ "***",
    p < .01  ~ "**",
    p < .05  ~ "*",
    TRUE     ~ ""
  )
}

#' Reverse a 1-7 item so that higher = more of the named construct
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x  a numeric vector (a simple run of values) of 1-7 responses.
#' RETURNS    8 - x, i.e. 1<->7, 2<->6, 3<->5, with the midpoint 4 left alone.
#' USED BY    Phase 2.2, for severity_1_R and nothing else. Every other reversal
#'            runs through the reverse_spec metadata table, which carries a
#'            scale_max per item so the rule still holds if an item is ever
#'            added on some scale other than 1-7.
#'
#' Some questions are worded the other way round, so that agreeing with them
#' means LESS of the thing being measured. Those have to be flipped before they
#' can be averaged in with the rest, or they would cancel out the very items
#' they are meant to reinforce. 8 is (scale_max + 1) for a 1-7 scale.
#' HAZARD: applying this to an item that is ALREADY keyed in the high-is-more
#' direction silently inverts a construct without erroring. Nothing warns you;
#' the score simply comes out backwards. That is why the set of reversed items
#' lives in one auditable table (prereg 5.1) rather than being applied ad hoc.
rev7 <- function(x) 8 - x

#' Row-mean of z-scored columns, for aggregates that span different scales
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  ...  two or more numeric vectors (simple runs of values) of equal
#'                 length.
#' RETURNS    a numeric vector: each argument standardised across the whole
#'            sample, then averaged row by row with na.rm = TRUE.
#' USED BY    punitiveness_full (self-report scale + Sentence1_z), kant_core,
#'            kant_nonoverlap, hostile_agg, crime_concerns.
#'
#' A z-score restates a value as "how many standard deviations above or below
#' the sample mean this is", so 0 is exactly average and +1 is one SD high.
#' Standardising first is what makes the aggregate meaningful. Its constituents
#' live on different scales -- a 1-7 attitude mean alongside a z-scored sentence
#' in years, or five composites with different SDs -- so a raw row-mean would be
#' pulled around by whichever component happens to vary most, and the aggregate
#' would really be that one component under another name. After scale(), every
#' constituent contributes equally, which is the intent behind treating these as
#' clusters (prereg 5.2, 5.5, 5.6).
zmean <- function(...) {
  m <- scale(cbind(...))
  out <- rowMeans(m, na.rm = TRUE)
  # rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) on a row where every input is missing returns NaN
  # ("not a number"), not NA. R does count NaN as missing for is.na(), so
  # nothing downstream crashes over it. But NaN and NA are still two distinct
  # values, and the difference shows: NaN formats as the text "NaN" where NA
  # formats as "NA", and unique(), %in% and table() all keep the two apart, so
  # a table of counts gains a stray "NaN" category of its own. Converting here
  # means each composite carries exactly ONE marker for "no usable answer".
  out[is.nan(out)] <- NA_real_
  as.numeric(out)
}

#' Composite score with Cronbach's alpha AND McDonald's omega
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data            the working data frame (d, or a subset such as d_retrib).
#'   items           character vector (a simple run of values) of column names,
#'                   ALREADY reverse-coded where reverse_spec says so -- this
#'                   function reverses nothing. HAZARD: passing a raw item where
#'                   the "_R" version was meant produces a wrong composite with
#'                   no warning whatsoever.
#'   composite_name  the label used in the reliability table and the console
#'                   line. It is effectively the row key, so keep it unique.
#'   print_output    FALSE hides the console line but still records the row.
#' RETURNS  a numeric vector of length nrow(data): the composite score, one
#'          value per participant.
#' SIDE EFFECT  appends one row to the global `alpha_table` with <<-, the
#'              assignment that reaches out of a function to a variable living
#'              outside it. That table becomes the Phase 4.10 reliability table
#'              and is written to data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv in
#'              Phase 10.3. alpha_table must therefore exist before the first
#'              call (Phase 4.0 creates it), and the ORDER of the calls in
#'              Phase 4 is the order of the rows in the published table.
#' USED BY  every composite built in Phase 4, and so by everything downstream.
#'
#' SCORING RULE (prereg 5.1): a composite is the mean of its items after reverse
#' coding, computed for anyone who answered at least half of them. Half rounds
#' UP, so a 3-item scale needs 2 answers and a 7-item scale needs 4. Partial
#' responders are kept rather than listwise-deleted. Listwise deletion means
#' throwing away a person's entire record over a single skipped item. They are
#' kept instead because the items inside a block are near-parallel indicators
#' of one construct: several different questions that each track the same
#' underlying thing about equally well. A mean over 4 of 7 therefore estimates
#' the same quantity as a mean over all 7, just more noisily. Below half the
#' estimate is too unstable to trust, so the case is set to NA, R's marker for a
#' missing value, rather than being quietly averaged from one or two items and
#' presented as a real score.
#'
#' RELIABILITY asks whether the items in a scale agree with one another closely
#' enough to be averaged at all. Both coefficients are reported because they
#' answer different questions and the plan asks for both. Cronbach's alpha
#' assumes essential tau-equivalence, meaning equal loadings. A loading is how
#' strongly one item tracks the construct behind the scale, so the assumption is
#' that every item tracks it equally strongly. When loadings differ, alpha
#' understates reliability. McDonald's omega (omega.tot) is estimated from a
#' factor model that lets the loadings differ, so it does not make that
#' assumption. Where the two diverge sharply, the items are not equally good
#' indicators of the construct, which is itself worth seeing.
#'   k >= 2 for alpha: a one-item "scale" has no internal consistency to
#'                     estimate, since there is nothing for the item to agree
#'                     with.
#'   k >= 3 for omega: a single-factor model over two indicators is not
#'                     identified -- the data hold too little information to pin
#'                     the numbers down. Two items supply only 3 distinct
#'                     moments: two variances, i.e. how spread out each item is,
#'                     and one covariance, i.e. how the two move together. The
#'                     model needs four numbers, 2 loadings + 2 residual
#'                     variances (the spread in each item the factor does not
#'                     account for). So omega stays NA and prints as "-".
compute_composite <- function(data, items, composite_name, print_output = TRUE) {

  # as.data.frame() because psych::alpha and psych::omega both choke on a
  # tibble, the tidyverse's flavour of data frame; drop = FALSE keeps a
  # single-item selection two-dimensional, i.e. still a table with one column
  # rather than collapsing to a bare vector the code below cannot use.
  item_data    <- as.data.frame(data[, items, drop = FALSE])
  # ceiling() rounds up, which is what implements "at least half" when the
  # number of items is odd: half of 7 becomes 4, not 3.5.
  min_answered <- ceiling(length(items) / 2)
  # How many of this scale's items each person actually answered.
  n_answered   <- rowSums(!is.na(item_data))

  comp <- rowMeans(item_data, na.rm = TRUE)
  # Enforce the at-least-half rule AFTER the mean is taken: rowMeans with
  # na.rm = TRUE will happily average a single answered item, and that value
  # has to be thrown out here rather than never computed. Without this line,
  # somebody who answered one item of seven would carry a score that looks
  # exactly as solid as somebody who answered all seven.
  comp[n_answered < min_answered] <- NA_real_
  # A row where every item is missing gives NaN ("not a number") from rowMeans;
  # convert it to a real missing value, for the reason spelled out in zmean()
  # above -- one marker for "no answer", not two.
  comp[is.nan(comp)] <- NA_real_

  a <- o <- NA_real_
  if (length(items) >= 2) {
    # check.keys = FALSE is deliberate. DO NOT switch it on. With the default
    # TRUE, psych::alpha silently flips any negatively-loading item -- one that
    # runs the opposite way to the rest of its scale -- and then reports the
    # reliability of a scale that is NOT the one being scored.
    # Reversal is reverse_spec's job. A low or even negative alpha here is a
    # finding about the items -- it is the predicted outcome for H6 -- not
    # something to patch over. tryCatch keeps a failure from stopping the knit:
    # it catches the error and hands back NA, which is then visible in the
    # printed table instead of vanishing.
    a <- tryCatch(
      suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
        psych::alpha(item_data, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
      error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }
  if (length(items) >= 3) {
    # nfactors = 1 gives the single-factor omega total, the coefficient that
    # matches the one-dimensional composite actually being scored. Asking for
    # more factors would report the reliability of a richer model than the one
    # the published score comes from.
    # plot = FALSE stops psych drawing a diagram into the knitted document.
    o <- tryCatch(
      suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
        psych::omega(item_data, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)),
      error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }

  # <<- writes to the alpha_table created at top level in Phase 4.0. This is the
  # only place in the document that needs <<-, because it is the only collector
  # appended to from inside a function. A plain <- here would build a private
  # copy that vanishes the moment the function ends, and the published
  # reliability table would come out empty.
  alpha_table <<- rbind(
    alpha_table,
    data.frame(composite = composite_name, k = length(items),
               alpha = a, omega = o, mean = mean(comp, na.rm = TRUE),
               sd = sd(comp, na.rm = TRUE), n = sum(!is.na(comp)),
               items = paste(items, collapse = ", "),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE))

  if (print_output) {
    # A running console line, so the reliability of each scale is visible as it
    # is built rather than only at the end, when a bad one is easy to miss.
    # "  -  " marks a coefficient that is not defined at this number of items k.
    cat(sprintf("  %-34s k=%d  alpha=%s  omega=%s\n",
                composite_name, length(items),
                ifelse(is.na(a), "  -  ", sprintf("%.3f", a)),
                ifelse(is.na(o), "  -  ", sprintf("%.3f", o))))
  }
  comp
}

#' Correlation with a 95% CI, taking column NAMES plus the data frame
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x, y  column names as strings; data  the data frame (a data frame
#'            is R's word for a table: one row per participant, one column per
#'            measure).
#' RETURNS    a named numeric vector (a vector is a simple run of values):
#'            r, ci_lower, ci_upper, p, n.
#' USED BY    one-off correlations. cor_row() below is the tabular equivalent
#'            used by the hypothesis functions; it returns a one-row data frame
#'            and adds a directional p-value.
#'
#' WHAT A CORRELATION IS. r is one number for how strongly two measures move
#' together. It runs from -1 through 0 to +1. The 95% confidence interval is
#' the range of true values for r that the data are consistent with. Reporting
#' r on its own hides how firm it is: r = .30 from 30 people and r = .30 from
#' 900 people look identical until you see the interval. That is why prereg 6.1
#' asks for the interval with every association.
#'
#' complete.cases() over exactly these two columns is pairwise deletion: a
#' person counts here if they answered THESE two items, whatever else they
#' skipped. n is the number of people who answered both, and it is handed back
#' on purpose. Without it, a table could quietly rest some of its rows on far
#' fewer people than others and no reader would ever see it. cor.test() gives
#' the Fisher z-transformed 95% interval: r is squeezed together near -1 and
#' +1, so it is converted onto a stretched scale where the interval behaves
#' properly, and then converted back.
get_cor_ci <- function(x, y, data) {
  ok   <- stats::complete.cases(data[[x]], data[[y]])
  test <- stats::cor.test(data[[x]][ok], data[[y]][ok])
  c(r = unname(test$estimate),
    ci_lower = test$conf.int[1],
    ci_upper = test$conf.int[2],
    p = test$p.value,
    n = sum(ok))
}

#' One correlation as a table row: two-sided CI plus a directional p-value
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data              the data frame (whole sample, or d_retrib for H11).
#'   x, y              column names as strings.
#'   alternative       "two.sided", "greater" or "less" -- the DIRECTIONAL test.
#'   label_x, label_y  display names for the printed table; default to the raw
#'                     column names.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: x, y, n, r, ci_lower, ci_upper, p_two, p_dir,
#'          alternative. Every numeric field is NA when the test cannot be run.
#'          NA is R's marker for a missing value, and it is what shows up in
#'          the printed table. The row therefore always has the same shape, so
#'          do.call(rbind, lapply(...)) over a list of these always stacks them
#'          into one table.
#' USED BY  run_h1(), run_h6(), run_h7(), run_h8(), the Phase 5.5 convergence
#'          table and the H12 within-group correlations.
#'
#' Two p-values are carried on purpose. A p-value is the chance of seeing a
#' result at least this strong if there were really no relationship at all. A
#' two-sided p asks "is this different from zero in either direction?". A
#' one-sided, or directional, p asks only "is this in the direction we said in
#' advance?". Prereg 6.8 tests a prediction that names a direction one-sided in
#' that direction, and everything else two-sided. So p_dir is the inferential
#' quantity for a directional hypothesis: the number that hypothesis stands or
#' falls on. p_two sits beside it for readers who want the undirected test.
#'
#' The CONFIDENCE INTERVAL, though, is always the two-sided 95% interval. A
#' one-sided interval runs all the way out to +1 or -1 at one end. Put that in
#' the same column as ordinary two-sided intervals and the column can no longer
#' be read down the page. Neighbouring rows would no longer mean the same
#' thing. Tables here mix directional and non-directional rows, so the
#' intervals are kept on one footing.
#'
#' Guards, in the order they fire. First, a column that does not exist returns
#' the all-NA row: a composite that failed to build earlier leaves a visible NA
#' in the table instead of stopping the whole document from knitting. Second,
#' fewer than 4 complete pairs cannot give a Fisher interval. Third, a cor.test
#' error -- zero variance in either variable -- also returns the row. Variance
#' is how spread out a set of values is. Zero variance means everyone gave that
#' variable the same answer, so there is nothing for the other one to track.
cor_row <- function(data, x, y, alternative = "two.sided",
                    label_x = x, label_y = y) {
  out <- data.frame(x = label_x, y = label_y, n = NA_integer_, r = NA_real_,
                    ci_lower = NA_real_, ci_upper = NA_real_,
                    p_two = NA_real_, p_dir = NA_real_,
                    alternative = alternative, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(x, y) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(data[[x]], data[[y]])
  out$n <- sum(ok)
  if (sum(ok) < 4) return(out)
  # The plain two-sided call. Its estimate -- the r itself -- and its conf.int
  # are the numbers reported, whatever direction the prediction ran in.
  tt <- tryCatch(stats::cor.test(data[[x]][ok], data[[y]][ok]),
                 error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(tt)) return(out)
  out$r        <- unname(tt$estimate)
  out$ci_lower <- tt$conf.int[1]
  out$ci_upper <- tt$conf.int[2]
  out$p_two    <- tt$p.value
  # For a directional prediction, cor.test is run a second time with the
  # direction set. Running it again is safer than simply halving p_two. Halving
  # is only correct when r actually lands on the predicted side. When r lands
  # the OTHER way, halving would hand back a small p for a result that went
  # against the prediction. The refit returns a p above .5 instead, which is
  # the honest answer.
  out$p_dir    <- if (alternative == "two.sided") tt$p.value else
    tryCatch(stats::cor.test(data[[x]][ok], data[[y]][ok],
                             alternative = alternative)$p.value,
             error = function(e) NA_real_)
  out
}

#' Format a correlation matrix as text with significance stars
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  cor_matrix, p_matrix  square matrices of matching dimension and
#'            dimnames (a matrix is a grid of numbers; the dimnames are its row
#'            and column labels). One grid holds the correlations, the other
#'            holds the matching p-values, and the two must line up cell for
#'            cell. decimals  rounding for the printed r.
#' RETURNS    a character matrix with the same dimnames. Each off-diagonal cell
#'            is the rounded r with its stars stuck on the end, ready to print.
#'            The diagonal is overwritten, see below.
#'
#' WHY THIS EXISTS. A grid of correlations and a separate grid of p-values are
#' near impossible to read side by side. Merging them into single cells that
#' read "0.32**" is what a person can actually scan down a column.
#'
#' The as.vector()/matrix() round-trip is needed because sig_stars() is
#' vectorised over a plain vector. Vectorised means it takes a whole run of
#' values at once rather than one at a time, but it expects a plain run, not a
#' grid. So the grid is unrolled into one long vector, starred, and folded back
#' into a grid of exactly the same shape and labels.
#'
#' The diagonal is blanked to "-" deliberately. The diagonal is each variable
#' correlated with itself, which is always exactly 1. It carries no
#' information, and printing "1.00***" invites a reader into treating a
#' definition as a finding.
format_cor_table <- function(cor_matrix, p_matrix, decimals = 2) {
  r_formatted <- round(cor_matrix, decimals)
  stars_vec   <- sig_stars(as.vector(p_matrix))
  values_vec  <- paste0(format(as.vector(r_formatted), nsmall = decimals), stars_vec)
  result      <- matrix(values_vec, nrow = nrow(cor_matrix),
                        dimnames = dimnames(cor_matrix))
  diag(result) <- "-"
  result
}

#' Welch t-test + Cohen's d with a 95% CI for a two-level grouping
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data         the data frame.
#'   var          outcome column name.
#'   group        a two-level FACTOR column. A factor is R's type for a
#'                categorical variable: it holds the group labels in a fixed
#'                order, and that order matters here. Its FIRST level must be
#'                the more-retributive side. grp_rank, grp_med, grp_tert and
#'                grp_ratio are all constructed that way in Phase 5, so a
#'                positive t and a positive d both read as "the retributive
#'                group scores higher" everywhere in this document.
#'   alternative  "greater" for the directional H13-H21 predictions, "less" for
#'                cognitive reflection, "two.sided" for descriptive contrasts.
#'   label        display name for the outcome column of the result table.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: outcome, variable, n1, n2, M1, SD1, M2, SD2,
#'          t, df, p_two, p_dir, d, d_lower, d_upper, alternative. Subscript 1
#'          is the first factor level, i.e. the retributive group.
#' USED BY  run_contrast_set(), and so by H13-H21 and E1 under all four
#'          groupings; also the Phase 5.5 convergence checks and the H14
#'          raw-years and per-vignette runs.
#'
#' WHAT THIS ANSWERS. Two groups, one outcome. Do their averages differ, and by
#' how much? The t-test answers the first question. Cohen's d answers the
#' second: it is the gap between the two averages measured in standard
#' deviations, so d = 0.5 means the two groups sit half a standard deviation
#' apart. Its 95% confidence interval is the range of gaps the data are
#' consistent with. A small p-value on its own says only that the result is
#' hard to put down to chance. It says nothing at all about how big the
#' difference is. That is why prereg 6.8 requires the effect size and its
#' interval on every test.
#'
#' WELCH RATHER THAN STUDENT. The Welch t-test lets the two groups have
#' different variances; the older Student version assumes the variances are
#' equal. Variance is how spread out a group's answers are around its own
#' average. stats::t.test() defaults to var.equal = FALSE, which IS Welch, and
#' that default is kept deliberately. Retributivists are a minority of the
#' sample, so the two groups are markedly unequal in size. Unequal n combined
#' with unequal variance is precisely the case in which the pooled-variance
#' (Student) test has the wrong Type I error rate. The Type I error rate is how
#' often a test announces a difference when there is none. The pooled test does
#' not hold that rate where it claims to. Welch costs almost nothing when the
#' variances happen to be equal. In the printed tables its df -- degrees of
#' freedom -- comes out with a decimal part rather than as a whole number. That
#' is the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation, NOT a rounding error.
#'
#' COHEN'S d is computed with pooled_sd = FALSE for the same reason: the
#' denominator is the unpooled SD, matching the test that was actually run.
#' Pairing a Welch test with a pooled d would describe a comparison nobody
#' performed. effectsize::cohens_d supplies the noncentral-t 95% interval that
#' prereg 6.8 requires alongside every effect size. The fallback beneath it is
#' the root-mean-square of the two SDs: square them, average the two squares,
#' take the square root. It only fires when the effectsize package is not
#' installed. It gives a point estimate with no interval at all, and the table
#' shows that plainly.
welch_contrast <- function(data, var, group, alternative = "two.sided",
                           label = var) {
  out <- data.frame(outcome = label, variable = var,
                    n1 = NA_integer_, n2 = NA_integer_,
                    M1 = NA_real_, SD1 = NA_real_, M2 = NA_real_, SD2 = NA_real_,
                    t = NA_real_, df = NA_real_, p_two = NA_real_, p_dir = NA_real_,
                    d = NA_real_, d_lower = NA_real_, d_upper = NA_real_,
                    alternative = alternative, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(var, group) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  y <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[var]]))
  g <- data[[group]]
  # Casewise deletion, applied to THIS contrast only. A person is dropped here
  # if they are missing either the outcome or the grouping, and is still used
  # in other contrasts. So n1/n2 report exactly who contributed to this one
  # comparison, rather than to some sample defined elsewhere.
  ok <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(g)
  # droplevels() discards factor levels that no longer have anyone in them. A
  # level is one of the categories the grouping variable can take. droplevels()
  # is what makes the two-level check below work after the line above cuts the
  # data down. grp_tert, for instance, retains an unused "Middle third" level;
  # without it the grouping would still look three-level and the contrast would
  # be refused even though two levels are perfectly well populated.
  y <- y[ok]; g <- droplevels(factor(g[ok]))
  # Refuse the test rather than hand back a misleading one. Three conditions
  # trigger the refusal: not exactly two populated levels; a cell under 3
  # cases; or zero within-group variance in EITHER group. Zero variance there
  # means everyone in that group gave the identical answer, so the group says
  # nothing about how much answers vary. Returning the all-NA row here means
  # the table shows NA rather than a number nobody should trust.
  if (nlevels(g) != 2 || any(table(g) < 3) ||
      any(tapply(y, g, function(v) stats::sd(v, na.rm = TRUE)) %in% c(0, NA))) return(out)

  lv <- levels(g)
  tmp <- data.frame(y = y, g = g)
  # The y ~ g formula interface always subtracts level 2 from level 1. That is
  # why the factor levels were set retributive-first back in Phase 5. It makes
  # a positive result mean "the retributive group scored higher" in every table
  # in this document. There is no per-table sign convention to keep track of.
  tt  <- stats::t.test(y ~ g, data = tmp)                       # level1 - level2
  # Run the test again for the directional p rather than halving p_two. Same
  # reason as in cor_row(): halving is wrong whenever the difference came out
  # the way the prediction did NOT expect.
  pd  <- if (alternative == "two.sided") tt$p.value else
    stats::t.test(y ~ g, data = tmp, alternative = alternative)$p.value

  out$n1 <- sum(g == lv[1]); out$n2 <- sum(g == lv[2])
  out$M1 <- mean(y[g == lv[1]]); out$SD1 <- stats::sd(y[g == lv[1]])
  out$M2 <- mean(y[g == lv[2]]); out$SD2 <- stats::sd(y[g == lv[2]])
  out$t  <- unname(tt$statistic); out$df <- unname(tt$parameter)
  out$p_two <- tt$p.value; out$p_dir <- pd

  if (HAVE("effectsize")) {
    cd <- tryCatch(
      suppressWarnings(effectsize::cohens_d(y ~ g, data = tmp,
                                            pooled_sd = FALSE, ci = 0.95)),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(cd)) {
      out$d <- cd$Cohens_d; out$d_lower <- cd$CI_low; out$d_upper <- cd$CI_high
    }
  }
  # Fallback only, for when the effectsize package is absent or its call
  # failed. This is the unpooled d with NO interval attached. So d_lower and
  # d_upper stay NA, and the printed table shows the interval is missing rather
  # than pretending one was computed.
  if (is.na(out$d)) {
    s <- sqrt((out$SD1^2 + out$SD2^2) / 2)
    out$d <- (out$M1 - out$M2) / s
  }
  out
}

#' One-sample test against a fixed value -- here, the scale midpoint
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data, var    the data frame and the outcome column name.
#'   mu           the comparison value; 4 by default.
#'   alternative  "less" for H4, whose prediction is at or below the midpoint.
#'   label        display name.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: measure, variable, mu, n, mean, sd, t, df,
#'          p_two, p_dir, d, d_lower, d_upper, ci_lower, ci_upper, alternative.
#'          Note the two intervals do different jobs: ci_lower/ci_upper bound
#'          the MEAN, d_lower/d_upper bound the effect size. Reading one as the
#'          other will mis-state the result.
#' USED BY  run_h4(), on the whole sample in Phase 8.1 and inside the
#'          retributivist group in Phase 9.1.
#'
#' WHAT A ONE-SAMPLE TEST IS. There is no second group here. One group's
#' average is compared against a fixed number chosen in advance, mu.
#'
#' WHY mu = 4. The attitude items run 1 to 7 with 4 as the neutral anchor
#' (prereg 5.1), so 4 is the point at which a respondent neither agrees nor
#' disagrees. H4's claim that strict proportionality is not consistently
#' endorsed is exactly the claim that the mean sits at or below that neutral
#' point. So the test is one-sided in the "less" direction against 4. It is NOT
#' a test against zero, which on a 1-7 scale would be meaningless: nobody can
#' score zero, so beating zero would prove nothing.
#'
#' d here is the ONE-SAMPLE effect size, (mean - mu) / sd: how far the sample
#' mean sits from the midpoint measured in standard deviations. It answers "how
#' far from neutral", not "how far apart are two groups". It is therefore NOT
#' comparable to the between-group d's in the Phase 9 contrast tables, and the
#' two must never be lined up beside each other as though they were.
one_sample_mid <- function(data, var, mu = 4, alternative = "two.sided",
                           label = var) {
  out <- data.frame(measure = label, variable = var, mu = mu, n = NA_integer_,
                    mean = NA_real_, sd = NA_real_, t = NA_real_, df = NA_real_,
                    p_two = NA_real_, p_dir = NA_real_, d = NA_real_,
                    d_lower = NA_real_, d_upper = NA_real_,
                    ci_lower = NA_real_, ci_upper = NA_real_,
                    alternative = alternative, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!var %in% names(data)) return(out)
  y <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[var]]))
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  # Two ways this test cannot be run. Fewer than 3 answers is far too little to
  # work with. No variance at all -- every answer identical, no spread of any
  # kind -- leaves both t and d dividing by zero. Either way, hand back the
  # all-NA row rather than a number nobody should rely on.
  if (length(y) < 3 || stats::sd(y) == 0) return(out)
  tt <- stats::t.test(y, mu = mu)
  # Second run for the directional p, same rule as everywhere else in this file.
  pd <- if (alternative == "two.sided") tt$p.value else
    stats::t.test(y, mu = mu, alternative = alternative)$p.value
  out$n <- length(y); out$mean <- mean(y); out$sd <- stats::sd(y)
  out$t <- unname(tt$statistic); out$df <- unname(tt$parameter)
  out$p_two <- tt$p.value; out$p_dir <- pd
  # This interval brackets the MEAN itself, on whatever scale the outcome
  # column was measured in.
  out$ci_lower <- tt$conf.int[1]; out$ci_upper <- tt$conf.int[2]
  # The one-sample d: distance from the midpoint in standard deviations.
  out$d <- (mean(y) - mu) / stats::sd(y)
  if (HAVE("effectsize")) {
    # effectsize supplies the confidence interval AROUND d. Without the
    # package, d still prints and d_lower/d_upper stay NA.
    cd <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(effectsize::cohens_d(y, mu = mu, ci = 0.95)),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(cd)) { out$d_lower <- cd$CI_low; out$d_upper <- cd$CI_high }
  }
  out
}

#' Paired t-test with the paired Cohen's d and its CI
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data         the data frame.
#'   v1, v2       the two column names; the difference tested is v1 - v2.
#'   alternative  "greater" for H5 and H9, both of which name a direction.
#'   label        display name for the comparison.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: comparison, var1, var2, n, M1, M2, mean_diff,
#'          t, df, p_two, p_dir, d, d_lower, d_upper, ci_lower, ci_upper,
#'          alternative. ci_lower/ci_upper bound the MEAN DIFFERENCE, not
#'          either mean on its own.
#' USED BY  run_h5() (severity_1 vs severity_2) and run_h9() (just deserts vs
#'          revenge), each on the whole sample and inside the retributivist
#'          group for H11.
#'
#' PAIRED RATHER THAN INDEPENDENT, because both numbers come from the same
#' participant. The comparison is within-person: for each person we ask which
#' of the two items they backed more. An independent-samples test would carry
#' the between-person variance in its denominator. That is the variation from
#' one person to the next, and it is exactly the nuisance the pairing removes.
#' Some people simply agree with everything; pairing cancels that out, because
#' such a person's two answers rise together and their difference stays honest.
#'
#' complete.cases() enforces the pairing: a participant contributes only if
#' BOTH items were answered. Half a pair is not a pair, and filling the gap
#' with an average would invent a difference that person never expressed.
#'
#' d = mean(a - b) / sd(a - b) is the PAIRED d. It is standardised on the SD of
#' the DIFFERENCE scores, not on the SD of the raw answers. It is not on the
#' same footing as a between-group d. For the very same raw gap it comes out
#' larger whenever the two items are positively correlated. They are positively
#' correlated here, since both come from the same block of questions.
paired_test <- function(data, v1, v2, alternative = "two.sided",
                        label = paste(v1, "vs", v2)) {
  out <- data.frame(comparison = label, var1 = v1, var2 = v2, n = NA_integer_,
                    M1 = NA_real_, M2 = NA_real_, mean_diff = NA_real_,
                    t = NA_real_, df = NA_real_, p_two = NA_real_,
                    p_dir = NA_real_, d = NA_real_, d_lower = NA_real_,
                    d_upper = NA_real_, ci_lower = NA_real_, ci_upper = NA_real_,
                    alternative = alternative, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(v1, v2) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  # Keep only the people who answered both items, so every row entering the
  # test really is a matched pair from one participant.
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(data[[v1]], data[[v2]])
  a <- as.numeric(data[[v1]][ok]); b <- as.numeric(data[[v2]][ok])
  # sd(a - b) == 0 means every single participant gave the identical gap. The
  # difference scores then have zero variance, and the paired t divides by
  # exactly that. It looks like infinite precision and is in fact no test at
  # all, so refuse it. Fewer than 3 pairs is refused too: too little to work
  # with.
  if (length(a) < 3 || stats::sd(a - b) == 0) return(out)
  tt <- stats::t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE)
  # Second run for the directional p, never a halved two-sided p.
  pd <- if (alternative == "two.sided") tt$p.value else
    stats::t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE, alternative = alternative)$p.value
  out$n <- length(a); out$M1 <- mean(a); out$M2 <- mean(b)
  out$mean_diff <- mean(a - b)
  out$t <- unname(tt$statistic); out$df <- unname(tt$parameter)
  out$p_two <- tt$p.value; out$p_dir <- pd
  # Interval around the average difference, on the original scale.
  out$ci_lower <- tt$conf.int[1]; out$ci_upper <- tt$conf.int[2]
  # The paired d, standardised on the SD of the difference scores.
  out$d <- mean(a - b) / stats::sd(a - b)
  if (HAVE("effectsize")) {
    # The confidence interval around that d. Absent the package it stays NA.
    cd <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(
      effectsize::cohens_d(a, b, paired = TRUE, ci = 0.95)), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(cd)) { out$d_lower <- cd$CI_low; out$d_upper <- cd$CI_high }
  }
  out
}

#' Steiger's test for two DEPENDENT, OVERLAPPING correlations
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data         the data frame.
#'   j            the SHARED variable -- punitiveness in H2, H10 and E2.
#'   k, h         the two competing correlates. The hypothesis is always
#'                r(j,k) > r(j,h), so k is the predicted-stronger one.
#'   alternative  "greater", matching that directional prediction (prereg 6.8).
#'   label        the comparison string printed in the result table.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: comparison, r_jk, r_jh, r_kh, n, z, p, diff,
#'          diff_lower, diff_upper, alternative.
#' USED BY  run_h2() (hostile aggression vs crime concerns), run_h10() (revenge
#'          vs just deserts) and E2 (hostile vs Durkheimian solidarity) -- each
#'          on the whole sample and again inside the retributivist group.
#'
#' WHAT THE NAME MEANS. "Dependent" = the two correlations come from the SAME
#' people, not from two separate samples. "Overlapping" = the two correlations
#' share one variable, j. So the question is not "is r bigger than zero" but
#' "is one of these two correlations bigger than the other".
#'
#' WHY STEIGER. H2 and H10 each compare two correlations that share a variable
#' and are measured on the SAME people. Those two r's are not independent of
#' each other: how far apart they can drift by pure chance depends on r_kh, the
#' correlation between the two competing correlates themselves. A test that
#' treats them as coming from two independent samples -- Fisher's z on two
#' separate r's -- therefore uses the wrong null distribution. The null
#' distribution is the spread of gaps chance alone would produce if the two
#' correlations were really equal. Use the wrong one and the test OVERSTATES
#' the evidence whenever the two correlates are strongly related to each other.
#' That is exactly the situation here. Steiger (1980) is the standard
#' correction for the dependent-and-overlapping case, and it is what prereg 6.3
#' and 6.4 name.
#'
#' cocor is asked for two tests in one call. steiger1980 supplies z and p.
#' zou2007 supplies an asymmetric confidence interval for the DIFFERENCE,
#' r_jk - r_jh. The interval is the more important of the two here: prereg 6.8
#' requires an effect size with a confidence interval, and for this hypothesis
#' the gap between the two r's IS the effect size.
steiger_overlap <- function(data, j, k, h, alternative = "greater", label = "") {
  out <- data.frame(comparison = label, r_jk = NA_real_, r_jh = NA_real_,
                    r_kh = NA_real_, n = NA_integer_, z = NA_real_,
                    p = NA_real_, diff = NA_real_, diff_lower = NA_real_,
                    diff_upper = NA_real_, alternative = alternative,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(j, k, h) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  # complete.cases across ALL THREE columns is required, not a convenience. The
  # test takes r_jk, r_jh, r_kh and one single n as a description of one
  # covariance matrix. That is the grid of how these three variables vary
  # together. Computing each r on its own pairwise subset would build that grid
  # out of three different samples of people, and the test would no longer be
  # defined.
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(data[[j]], data[[k]], data[[h]])
  n  <- sum(ok)
  out$n <- n
  # Below n = 10 the asymptotic z is not usable, so the function returns here.
  # Asymptotic means the formula only becomes accurate as the sample grows.
  # NOTE what returning at this point does to the row: n is filled in, but
  # r_jk, r_jh, r_kh and diff all stay NA, because every line that computes
  # them sits below this one.
  # CAREFUL -- intent and behaviour disagree at this line. Further down, the
  # same function fills in diff before the cocor check so that the descriptive
  # comparison survives a missing package. This guard denies the descriptive
  # r's that same survival. Either the guard belongs below the three cor()
  # lines, or the descriptives were never meant to survive a small n. AUTHORS
  # TO DECIDE. Do not read the current behaviour as settled.
  if (n < 10) return(out)
  r_jk <- stats::cor(data[[j]][ok], data[[k]][ok])
  r_jh <- stats::cor(data[[j]][ok], data[[h]][ok])
  # r_kh is how strongly the two competing correlates relate to EACH OTHER.
  # That is the quantity that makes this a dependent-samples problem in the
  # first place. It is also what Steiger's formula needs beyond the two focal
  # correlations. Leave it out and there is no test, only a guess.
  r_kh <- stats::cor(data[[k]][ok], data[[h]][ok])
  out$r_jk <- r_jk; out$r_jh <- r_jh; out$r_kh <- r_kh
  # The raw difference is filled in even when cocor is unavailable, so the
  # descriptive comparison survives a missing package rather than vanishing.
  out$diff <- r_jk - r_jh
  if (!HAVE("cocor")) return(out)
  cc <- tryCatch(cocor::cocor.dep.groups.overlap(
    r.jk = r_jk, r.jh = r_jh, r.kh = r_kh, n = n,
    alternative = alternative, test = c("steiger1980", "zou2007")),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(cc)) return(out)
  # cocor returns an S4 object, a kind of R object whose parts are reached with
  # @ instead of $. The two requested tests come back as named slots.
  out$z <- cc@steiger1980$statistic
  out$p <- cc@steiger1980$p.value
  # Zou's confidence interval for the difference in r. It is asymmetric about
  # the point estimate: it reaches further one way than the other. That is not
  # a mistake. It is built on the Fisher z scale, where correlations are
  # stretched out, and then converted back.
  ci <- cc@zou2007$conf.int
  out$diff_lower <- ci[1]; out$diff_upper <- ci[2]
  out
}

#' Share of a 0/1 indicator with an exact (Clopper-Pearson) CI
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x  a 0/1 vector, typically an inequality evaluated at the scale
#'               midpoint such as as.integer(severity_1 > 4); label  display
#'               name for the measure column.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: measure, n (answered), k (endorsing), prop,
#'          ci_lower, ci_upper.
#' USED BY  run_h4() for the shares endorsing punishment beyond proportionality,
#'          and H12 for the share of retributivists above the midpoint on each
#'          hostile attitude.
#'
#' WHAT THIS ANSWERS. "What fraction of people said yes, and how sure are we of
#' that fraction?" A bare percentage from 900 people and the same percentage
#' from 40 people look the same on the page. The confidence interval is what
#' separates them.
#'
#' binom.test() gives the exact Clopper-Pearson interval rather than the normal
#' (Wald) approximation, the textbook percentage-plus-or-minus formula. That
#' matters because several of these proportions sit close to 0 or 1 --
#' endorsement of strict proportionality in particular. Near those edges the
#' Wald interval can run outside [0, 1], reporting a share above 100% or below
#' 0%. It also undercovers badly. Undercovering means an interval labelled 95%
#' catches the true share less often than 95% of the time. The exact interval
#' is conservative and always stays inside the unit interval, which is what
#' prereg 6.5 asks for when it requires these shares "with confidence
#' intervals".
prop_ci <- function(x, label = "") {
  # Drop non-responders first, so n is the number of people who answered the
  # item. Leaving them in would put non-answers in the denominator and quietly
  # push every reported share downward.
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  out <- data.frame(measure = label, n = length(x), k = NA_integer_,
                    prop = NA_real_, ci_lower = NA_real_, ci_upper = NA_real_,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (length(x) < 1) return(out)
  # "> 0" so that either a logical -- R's TRUE/FALSE type -- or a 0/1 integer
  # counts as an endorsement.
  k <- sum(as.numeric(x) > 0)
  bt <- stats::binom.test(k, length(x))
  out$k <- k; out$prop <- k / length(x)
  out$ci_lower <- bt$conf.int[1]; out$ci_upper <- bt$conf.int[2]
  out
}

#' Simple regression of a standardized outcome on a standardized predictor
#'
#' A regression asks a simple question: as the predictor goes up, how much does
#' the outcome move with it? Here both sides are first turned into z-scores. A
#' z-score restates a value as the number of standard deviations it sits above
#' or below the average of its own column.
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data                 the data frame (a table with one row per person and
#'                        one column per measure).
#'   outcome, predictor   column names.
#'   alternative          matched to the SAME directional prediction as the
#'                        group contrast this rerun mirrors, so the two tables
#'                        can be read side by side. A directional prediction
#'                        names which way the effect should go, not merely that
#'                        there is one.
#'   label                display name for the outcome.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: outcome, variable, predictor, n, beta,
#'          ci_lower, ci_upper, t, p_two, p_dir, r2, alternative.
#' USED BY  run_continuous_set(), i.e. Phases 9.9 and 9.10.
#'
#' WHY THIS EXISTS. Most tests in this document sort people into two groups,
#' retributivists and everyone else, and compare the groups. Prereg 6.5 requires
#' that every one of those group contrasts also be rerun with retributivism
#' entered CONTINUOUSLY -- using each person's actual score instead of a group
#' label -- "so the result does not depend on the split". This function is that
#' rerun. Without it, a reader could fairly ask whether a finding is real or is
#' just an artefact of where the line between the two groups was drawn.
#'
#' Both sides are z-scored before the fit, which makes beta the standardized
#' slope: how many standard deviations the outcome moves for each one standard
#' deviation of the predictor. That buys three things. In a model with a single
#' predictor it equals the Pearson r, the ordinary correlation running from -1
#' to +1. It is directly comparable across outcomes measured on different
#' scales, so a 1-7 rating and a sentence in years can be read on one ruler. And
#' it sits on the same footing as the Cohen's d -- a gap between two groups
#' expressed in standard deviations -- in the matching contrast table.
cont_reg <- function(data, outcome, predictor, alternative = "two.sided",
                     label = outcome) {
  out <- data.frame(outcome = label, variable = outcome, predictor = predictor,
                    n = NA_integer_, beta = NA_real_, ci_lower = NA_real_,
                    ci_upper = NA_real_, t = NA_real_, p_two = NA_real_,
                    p_dir = NA_real_, r2 = NA_real_, alternative = alternative,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(outcome, predictor) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(data[[outcome]], data[[predictor]])
  out$n <- sum(ok)
  # Fewer than 10 usable people is too thin to fit a slope on, so the row comes
  # back carrying its labels and the n, with NA (R's marker for a missing value)
  # in every result column. A beta printed from a handful of people would look
  # exactly as solid on the page as one from the whole sample.
  if (sum(ok) < 10) return(out)
  # Standardise AFTER the complete-case filter. Complete cases are the rows
  # where BOTH columns were answered, which is the set the model actually uses.
  # Centring and scaling on those rows means the average and the standard
  # deviation belong to the analysis sample. Standardising the whole column
  # first would fold in people who never enter the fit, and beta would no longer
  # be a clean "per one standard deviation" number.
  y <- as.numeric(scale(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[outcome]][ok]))))
  x <- as.numeric(scale(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[predictor]][ok]))))
  # scale() divides by the standard deviation, so it returns all-NaN when a
  # variable has zero variance -- when everyone gave the identical answer, so
  # the values are not spread out at all. NaN is R's marker for "not a number".
  # Catch that here, before a model is fitted to it.
  if (any(is.na(y)) || any(is.na(x))) return(out)
  m  <- stats::lm(y ~ x)
  sm <- summary(m)$coefficients
  # The slope row named "x" is missing from the coefficient table if the
  # predictor was aliased out of the fit, meaning R could not estimate it and
  # silently dropped it. Reaching for a row that is not there would stop the
  # whole document with an error, so check before reading.
  if (!"x" %in% rownames(sm)) return(out)
  ci <- stats::confint(m)["x", ]
  tval <- sm["x", "t value"]; pt2 <- sm["x", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  out$beta <- sm["x", "Estimate"]; out$ci_lower <- ci[1]; out$ci_upper <- ci[2]
  out$t <- tval; out$p_two <- pt2
  # The directional p -- the p value for a prediction that names a direction --
  # is recomputed from the t statistic rather than obtained by halving p_two. A
  # p value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were really
  # no effect. Halving is only correct when the estimate falls on the predicted
  # side. pt() with the appropriate tail is correct either way. It returns a p
  # above .5 when the slope runs the wrong direction, which is the honest
  # answer.
  out$p_dir <- switch(alternative,
    "two.sided" = pt2,
    "greater"   = stats::pt(tval, m$df.residual, lower.tail = FALSE),
    "less"      = stats::pt(tval, m$df.residual, lower.tail = TRUE))
  # r2 (R-squared) is the share of the outcome's variance -- how spread out its
  # values are -- that the predictor accounts for. With one standardized
  # predictor it is simply beta^2. It is carried anyway, so the tables state the
  # share of variance explained without the reader doing the algebra.
  out$r2 <- summary(m)$r.squared
  out
}

#' Logistic regression of a 0/1 outcome on one predictor
#'
#' A logistic regression is the form of regression used when the outcome is a
#' yes-or-no answer rather than a score on a scale. It models the chance of a
#' "yes" and, by construction, never lets that chance fall outside 0 to 1.
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data                 the data frame (rows are people, columns are
#'                        measures).
#'   outcome              a 0/1 column -- here always shark_kill.
#'   predictor            retributivist status, or one of the continuous
#'                        retributivism measures.
#'   alternative          "greater" for H15's directional prediction, i.e. the
#'                        registered guess that the effect runs one way.
#'   label                display name.
#' RETURNS  a one-row data frame: outcome, predictor, n, b, se, OR, OR_lower,
#'          OR_upper, z, p_two, p_dir, alternative. b is on the log-odds scale,
#'          the scale a logistic regression works on internally. OR is exp(b),
#'          the odds ratio, on which 1 means the predictor changes nothing.
#' USED BY  H15 in Phase 9.6 (retributivist status as predictor) and again in
#'          Phases 9.9 and 9.10 with the continuous measures.
#'
#' Prereg 6.5 names a logistic regression for the yes-or-no shark decision and a
#' t-test for the pain rating, and that split is honoured here. shark_kill is
#' binary, 0 or 1 with nothing in between, so an ordinary linear model would
#' produce two defects at once. It would give fitted probabilities outside
#' [0, 1], and a chance above 100% or below 0% means nothing. It would also give
#' residuals -- the gaps between what a person answered and what the model
#' predicts -- that are heteroscedastic by construction, meaning their spread
#' changes with the prediction. A linear model assumes that spread is steady, so
#' both defects undercut the arithmetic it rests on.
#'
#' The odds-ratio interval is the Wald interval exp(b +/- 1.96 * se). se is the
#' standard error: how far the estimate would move from one sample to another
#' sample of the same size. The interval is formed on the log-odds scale and
#' only then exponentiated. That keeps it positive and makes it asymmetric about
#' the OR, reaching further on one side than the other. 1.96 is the two-sided
#' normal 95% quantile: the number of standard errors spanning the middle 95% of
#' a normal curve. That is what makes this a 95% confidence interval, a range
#' built by a rule that captures the true value in 95% of samples. The
#' directional p uses pnorm() on z for the same reason cont_reg() uses pt().
logit_reg <- function(data, outcome, predictor, alternative = "two.sided",
                      label = outcome) {
  out <- data.frame(outcome = label, predictor = predictor, n = NA_integer_,
                    b = NA_real_, se = NA_real_, OR = NA_real_,
                    OR_lower = NA_real_, OR_upper = NA_real_, z = NA_real_,
                    p_two = NA_real_, p_dir = NA_real_, alternative = alternative,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  if (!all(c(outcome, predictor) %in% names(data))) return(out)
  ok <- stats::complete.cases(data[[outcome]], data[[predictor]])
  out$n <- sum(ok)
  # A higher floor than the linear helpers use. On very few cases, or with a
```
