```{r phase0_helpers}
  # rare outcome -- a yes-or-no answer almost everyone gives the same way -- a
  # logistic fit gives wildly unstable coefficients that can swing on one
  # person's answer. Reporting nothing beats reporting a number nobody should
  # believe.
  if (sum(ok) < 20) return(out)
  yy <- as.numeric(data[[outcome]][ok]); xx <- as.numeric(data[[predictor]][ok])
  # If everyone gave the same yes-or-no answer, or the predictor never varies,
  # there is nothing to relate to anything. R answers with complete separation
  # (a coefficient racing off toward infinity) or an aliased term (a predictor
  # it quietly drops), not with a usable model. Stop before that happens.
  if (length(unique(yy)) < 2 || stats::sd(xx) == 0) return(out)
  m <- tryCatch(stats::glm(yy ~ xx, family = stats::binomial()),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(out)
  sm <- summary(m)$coefficients
  if (!"xx" %in% rownames(sm)) return(out)
  # The four columns of the glm coefficient matrix, in order: the estimate, its
  # standard error (SE), the z statistic, and the two-sided p. They are pulled
  # by position, so this order is what the lines below depend on.
  b <- sm["xx", 1]; se <- sm["xx", 2]; z <- sm["xx", 3]; p2 <- sm["xx", 4]
  out$b <- b; out$se <- se; out$z <- z; out$p_two <- p2
  out$OR <- exp(b)
  # Build the interval on the log-odds scale and exponentiate, NEVER the other
  # way round. b +/- 1.96*se is symmetric, the same distance either side of b.
  # Exponentiating that is what keeps the odds-ratio interval positive and
  # correctly skewed, stretched further above the OR than below it. Adding and
  # subtracting on the odds-ratio scale instead can hand back a lower bound
  # below zero, and a negative odds ratio is impossible.
  out$OR_lower <- exp(b - 1.96 * se); out$OR_upper <- exp(b + 1.96 * se)
  # The one-sided p, read off the normal curve with pnorm() rather than obtained
  # by halving the two-sided p. Same reason cont_reg() uses pt(): halving is
  # only right when the estimate lands on the predicted side.
  out$p_dir <- switch(alternative,
    "two.sided" = p2,
    "greater"   = stats::pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE),
    "less"      = stats::pnorm(z, lower.tail = TRUE))
  out
}

#' kable wrapper used for every printed table
#'
#' kable is the knitr function that turns a data frame (a table of rows and
#' columns) into a formatted table in the knitted HTML report. Every table in
#' this document is printed through this one wrapper.
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x  a data frame; caption  the table caption; digits  rounding,
#'            3 unless a call overrides it.
#' RETURNS    a knitr_kable object; printing it is what places the table in the
#'            knitted document.
#'
#' Centralised for two reasons. Every table then rounds to the same number of
#' digits, so no table quietly shows more precision than its neighbour and
#' invites a reader to trust it further. And the caption -- which is where the
#' pre-registration section and how to read the table are recorded -- is part of
#' the call rather than an afterthought. row.names = FALSE because every result
#' frame in this document carries its labels in real columns; without it kable
#' would print a redundant integer index beside them, an unlabelled extra column
#' of row numbers 1, 2, 3.
show_table <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 3) {
  knitr::kable(x, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}

cat("Helper functions loaded:\n")
cat("  format_p(), sig_stars(), rev7(), zmean()\n")
cat("  compute_composite()  — composite + alpha + omega\n")
cat("  get_cor_ci(), cor_row(), format_cor_table()\n")
cat("  welch_contrast(), one_sample_mid(), paired_test()\n")
cat("  steiger_overlap(), prop_ci(), cont_reg(), logit_reg()\n")
cat("  show_table()\n")
```

# PHASE 1: DATA LOADING AND EXCLUSION FUNNEL

## 1.1 Load the Qualtrics Values export

```{r phase1_load}
# === LOAD THE VALUES EXPORT ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reads FullData_Values.csv into `raw_data`, one row per
# submitted response, before any exclusion has been applied. `raw_data` is the
# input to the exclusion funnel in 1.3 and is never analysed directly.
#
# THE EXPORT QUIRK: the Qualtrics CSV has THREE header rows, not one --
#   row 1 = variable names (Retribution_1, Sentence1_V2_1, ...)
#   row 2 = the full question text
#   row 3 = the ImportId JSON that Qualtrics uses for re-import
# A single read_csv() would take row 1 as the column names and then treat rows 2
# and 3 as DATA. Two things break at once. Every numeric column turns into
# character (text), because it now holds a sentence, and two junk
# "participants" join the sample with nobody the wiser. So the file is read
# TWICE. The first read uses n_max = 0, which reads no data rows at all and
# simply captures the names from row 1. The second uses skip = 3 to start at the
# first real response, and is handed those names explicitly.

if (!file.exists(DATA_PATH)) {
  # Hard stop rather than a warning. Everything below depends on this one file,
  # and a missing input should fail loudly here at the top, rather than knit a
  # document full of empty tables that looks finished and is worth nothing.
  stop("Values export not found at: ", normalizePath(DATA_PATH, mustWork = FALSE),
       "\nThe document cannot proceed without it.")
}

raw_names <- names(readr::read_csv(DATA_PATH, n_max = 0, show_col_types = FALSE))
# guess_max = 10000 is larger than the number of rows in the file, so readr
# decides each column's type by looking at the WHOLE file. readr's own default
# is to look at the first 1000 rows only, and that default would sink us here. A
# column can be blank for its first thousand rows, because each person saw only
# one of the three vignette blocks. Typed from those blanks alone, it would come
# back as logical (TRUE/FALSE), throwing away every real number further down.
raw_data  <- readr::read_csv(DATA_PATH, skip = 3, col_names = raw_names,
                             show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 10000)

# === PROVENANCE OF THE FILE JUST READ ===
# Fingerprint the export so any later run can prove it used the same data. The
# md5 is a hash: a short code computed from the file's contents, where changing
# one character anywhere in the file changes the code completely. A re-analysis
# that reproduces the numbers below but not this hash is working from a
# different download, and that is the single most likely cause of two runs
# disagreeing. The hash is printed here, written to output/tables/, and repeated
# in the session block at the end of the document.
data_provenance <- data.frame(
  file      = basename(DATA_PATH),
  bytes     = as.numeric(file.size(DATA_PATH)),
  md5       = unname(tools::md5sum(DATA_PATH)),
  raw_rows  = nrow(raw_data),
  raw_cols  = ncol(raw_data),
  read_on   = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
show_table(data_provenance, "Provenance of the analysed export")
TABLES[["data_provenance"]] <- data_provenance

# === RESPONSE AND PARTICIPANT UNIQUENESS ===
# One row per response and one response per participant are assumptions every
# later join relies on. A join is the step that matches rows from two tables by
# a shared identifier. Prolific IDs are typed in by participants themselves, so
# a repeated ID means either that somebody took part twice (which prereg 4.1
# excludes) or that two people typed the same string by accident. Either way it
# has to surface HERE. Left undetected, one person's answers would count twice
# in every test in this document.
n_dup_response <- sum(duplicated(raw_data$ResponseId))
pid_clean      <- trimws(as.character(raw_data$Prolific_ID))
pid_clean      <- pid_clean[!is.na(pid_clean) & nzchar(pid_clean)]
n_dup_prolific <- sum(duplicated(pid_clean))
cat(sprintf("Duplicate ResponseIds: %d | duplicate Prolific IDs: %d (of %d non-blank)\n",
            n_dup_response, n_dup_prolific, length(pid_clean)))
# stopifnot() halts the knit unless the count is zero. A repeated ResponseId
# would mean the export itself is malformed, and nothing computed below it
# could be trusted, so this one is a stop and not a printed note.
stopifnot(n_dup_response == 0)

# Expect 1,015 raw responses at this point; the funnel in 1.3 takes that number
# down to the analytic sample, the people whose answers are actually tested. The
# count is printed rather than assumed, so a reader can see for themselves what
# this export contained before anyone was excluded.
cat(sprintf("Raw data loaded: %d rows x %d columns\n",
            nrow(raw_data), ncol(raw_data)))
cat(sprintf("File: %s\n", DATA_PATH))
```

```{r phase1_codebook}
# === QUESTION-WORDING CODEBOOK ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `q_text`, a named character vector (a vector is a
# simple run of values, here pieces of text, each tagged with the column it
# belongs to) mapping column name -> question wording. It prints a few entries
# so a reader can see how an item was actually worded without opening Qualtrics.
# It produces no analysis object and alters no data.
#
# The Labels export is a CODEBOOK ONLY. Qualtrics writes the anchor TEXT for the
# two endpoints of a 1-7 scale but bare numbers for the middle five points, so a
# column read from it is a mixture of strings (text) and digits, and can NEVER
# be used for arithmetic. Every number analysed in this document comes from the
# Values export instead.
# The whole block is guarded with file.exists() so the document still knits when
# the codebook is missing: the wording is a convenience, not a dependency.
if (file.exists(LABELS_PATH)) {
  q_text <- tryCatch({
    # n_max = 2 reads only the header block instead of the whole file. read_csv
    # takes the file's first line as the column names, so what it hands back as
    # the first data row is the question-text row, which is the row wanted here.
    hdr <- readr::read_csv(LABELS_PATH, n_max = 2, show_col_types = FALSE,
                           col_names = TRUE)
    setNames(as.character(unlist(hdr[1, ])), names(hdr))
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(q_text)) {
    cat("Codebook loaded (question wording available for ",
        length(q_text), " columns). Example entries:\n\n", sep = "")
    # Four items whose exact wording matters most downstream: Retribution_4 is
    # one of the four "deserved" purpose items in H6; proportionality and
    # severity_1 carry H4 and H5; Shark_1 is the H15 decision. intersect() keeps
    # only the names that really are present, rather than indexing them
    # directly, so a renamed column drops quietly out of the printout instead of
    # stopping the knit.
    ex <- intersect(c("Retribution_4", "proportionality", "severity_1", "Shark_1"),
                    names(q_text))
    for (v in ex) cat(sprintf("  %-16s %s\n", v, substr(q_text[[v]], 1, 90)))
  }
} else {
  # No codebook file. Set q_text to NULL so anything that looks for it later
  # meets an explicit "not available" rather than a stale leftover object.
  q_text <- NULL
  cat("Labels codebook not found — skipping question-wording printout.\n")
}
```

## 1.2 Coerce the scale and numeric columns

```{r phase1_numeric}
# === TYPE COERCION ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: forces every scale and numeric column to be numeric, in
# place, and adds two convenience aliases (libcons, Q333). No rows are removed,
# no values are recoded, and nothing is reversed here.
#
# WHY: a column's "type" is R's idea of what kind of thing it holds -- numbers,
# or text. readr decides that from what it sees, so ONE stray non-numeric cell
# anywhere in a column makes the whole column character (text). A character
# column handed to rowMeans() inside compute_composite() would either stop with
# an error or, far worse, quietly push NA (R's marker for a missing value)
# through a composite score. Coercing on purpose here means any such problem
# shows itself immediately, as a column full of NA at a known point in the
# document, rather than as a baffling result in Phase 8.
#
# The three open-ended items (Sentence_OpenEnd1, Sentence_OpenEnd2,
# Priorit_Explain) are deliberately NOT in this list. They are written answers.
# They stay character, are carried through cleaning untouched, and are exported
# for the E3-E7 language pipeline in the companion document. Forcing them to
# numeric would turn every one of them into NA and destroy them.
num_cols <- c(
  paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3),
  paste0("Incapacitation_", 1:2), paste0("Rehabilitation_", 1:2),
  paste0("Solidarity_", 1:3), paste0("Prioritization_", 1:4),
  "punishmore_1", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1", "parsimony_2",
  "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2", "LWOP", "deathpenalty", "AttnCheck1",
  paste0("revenge_", 1:4), "proportionality", "severity_1", "severity_2",
  paste0("exclusion_", 1:3), paste0("essential_", 1:4),
  paste0("Society_", 1:3), paste0("choice_", 1:2), "AttnCheck2",
  paste0("dueprocess_", 1:3), paste0("uncertain_", 1:4),
  paste0("rates_", 1:2), paste0("fear_", 1:3),
  paste0("hate_", 1:3), paste0("anger_", 1:2),
  paste0("degrad_", 1:3), paste0("suffer_", 1:2), paste0("prisonvi_", 1:2),
  paste0("harsh_", 1:3), paste0("rwa_", 1:5), paste0("sdo_", 1:8),
  paste0("vprone_", 1:4), paste0("Raceresent_", 1:4),
  # SLIDER QUIRK: Qualtrics adds a trailing "_1" to the name of every slider
  # column, because internally it treats a slider as a matrix question that
  # happens to hold one statement. So CRT_1_1 is the answer to CRT item 1, NOT
  # "part 1 of CRT item 1"; the same goes for age_1 and all six Sentence*_V*_1
  # columns. Phase 1.4 strips the suffix and renames them to CRT_1, age and so
  # on. Read the suffix as a part number and you invent items that never exist.
  "CRT_1_1", "CRT_2_1", "CRT_3_1",
  # VIGNETTE-SPLIT QUIRK: each participant read ONE of three vignette blocks
  # (prereg 3.2), so Qualtrics wrote six sentencing columns and only two of them
  # hold anything for any given row; the other four sit empty. Phase 1.4
  # coalesces them, that is, collapses the six into two by taking from each row
  # the column belonging to the block that person actually saw.
  "Sentence1_V1_1", "Sentence2_V1_1", "Sentence1_V2_1", "Sentence2_V2_1",
  "Sentence1_V3_1", "Sentence2_V3_1",
  "Shark_1", "Shark_2", "Shark_3", "age_1", "gender", "race", "education",
  "lib/conserv", "PoliticalID", "leanPros_1", "leanPros_2",
  # Vignette is the embedded field -- a value Qualtrics stores alongside the
  # response instead of asking about it -- recording which block was shown
  # (1/2/3), and it is the key Phase 1.4 uses. Progress and Finished drive the
  # exclusion funnel in 1.3. All three have to be numeric for that work.
  "Vignette", "Progress", "Finished")

# intersect() keeps only the names that exist in this export, so a column that
# is absent is skipped instead of raising a subscript error -- R's complaint
# about being asked for a column that is not there. The list above names the
# full instrument, and the document should still run against a partial export.
num_cols <- intersect(num_cols, names(raw_data))
# suppressWarnings because as.numeric() prints a warning for every cell it
# cannot read as a number and turns into NA. That conversion is the whole point
# here, and the warnings would bury the console in noise. Nothing is being
# swept under the rug: the missing-data check in 1.5 is where the consequences
# of these conversions are inspected.
raw_data[num_cols] <- lapply(raw_data[num_cols],
                             function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))

cat(sprintf("Coerced %d columns to numeric.\n", length(num_cols)))

# `lib/conserv` has a slash in its name, so R demands backticks around it in
# every formula and every dplyr call, and one forgotten pair is an error. Alias
# it to the plain name libcons and use that everywhere downstream. The original
# column stays where it is, untouched.
if ("lib/conserv" %in% names(raw_data)) raw_data$libcons <- raw_data[["lib/conserv"]]

# NAMING QUIRK: the written explanation of the goal ranking comes out of
# Qualtrics as `Priorit_Explain`, while the pre-registration (5.15) calls the
# same item Q333. Rather than pick one, both names point at the single column
# from here on, so whichever name a reader arrives with will find it.
if ("Priorit_Explain" %in% names(raw_data)) raw_data$Q333 <- raw_data$Priorit_Explain
cat("Ranking explanation column present (Priorit_Explain / Q333): ",
    "Priorit_Explain" %in% names(raw_data), "\n", sep = "")
```

## 1.3 Exclusion funnel

The pre-registered exclusions (prereg 6.2). These decide whose answers are
analysed. Failing **either** attention check is enough to be dropped, since both
are easy for anyone who is genuinely reading. `AttnCheck1` is the
instructed-response item in the punitiveness block, an item that tells the
respondent which option to choose, and its correct answer is option **9**.
`AttnCheck2` is the arithmetic item in the due-process block, where the option
coded **4** is the answer "15" to 8 + 7; the 4 is that answer's position in the
list of options, not the sum itself. The n surviving each step is reported, so
anyone can audit the whole funnel from 1,015 responses down to the analytic
sample.

```{r phase1_funnel}
# === EXCLUSION FUNNEL (prereg 6.2) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: applies the four pre-registered exclusions in order,
# printing how many people survive each one, and produces `df` -- the analytic
# sample that every later phase builds on -- plus the table `exclusion_funnel`
# (exported as output/tables/exclusion_funnel.csv).
#
# WHY HERE, AND IN THIS ORDER. Exclusions are applied BEFORE any hypothesis is
# tested, as the plan requires. Deciding who counts after seeing how the tests
# come out is exactly how a null result gets talked into a finding. The steps
# are cumulative, each one working on whatever the step before it left behind,
# so the "excluded" figure on each row belongs to that criterion and to nothing
# else. Note that residency and Prolific approval (prereg 4.1) are enforced by
# the recruitment screener, not here.
n_raw <- nrow(raw_data)
cat("=== EXCLUSION FUNNEL ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("Starting N (raw responses):        %d\n", n_raw))

# Step 1: Qualtrics marks Finished == 1 when a respondent reached the end of the
# survey. !is.na() has to come FIRST, because a partial response can leave the
# flag empty, and in R `NA == 1` is NA rather than FALSE. Selecting rows on NA
# does not drop them; it inserts a phantom row of NA values into `df`. Testing
# for NA first is what stops that.
df <- raw_data[!is.na(raw_data$Finished) & raw_data$Finished == 1, ]
n_fin <- nrow(df)
cat(sprintf("After Finished == 1:               %d  (excluded %d)\n",
            n_fin, n_raw - n_fin))

# Step 2: Progress is the percentage of the instrument completed. It is a
# belt-and-braces check on Finished, because a response can be flagged finished
# after a timeout without ever reaching 100. It normally removes nobody, and
# that is fine. It is here for the occasion when it does.
df <- df[!is.na(df$Progress) & df$Progress == 100, ]
n_prog <- nrow(df)
cat(sprintf("After Progress == 100:             %d  (excluded %d)\n",
            n_prog, n_fin - n_prog))

# Step 3: AttnCheck1, the instructed-response item. It names one specific option
# and asks the respondent to pick it, so the only thing it measures is whether
# they read the item. 9 is that option's code in the Values export, so anything
# other than 9 is a failure, however plausible it might look as an opinion.
df <- df[!is.na(df$AttnCheck1) & df$AttnCheck1 == 9, ]
n_a1 <- nrow(df)
cat(sprintf("After AttnCheck1 == 9:             %d  (excluded %d)\n",
            n_a1, n_prog - n_a1))

# Step 4: AttnCheck2, the arithmetic item (prereg 5.14: "8 plus 7 is 15"). The
# answers were offered as a list of options, and "15" sits fourth in that list,
# so 4 is the code stored for a correct answer -- a position, NOT the sum.
# CAREFUL: "correcting" this line to == 15 filters on the sum rather than on the
# option code, which is not what this column holds. Reading the code as the
# answer is the easiest way to break this line.
df <- df[!is.na(df$AttnCheck2) & df$AttnCheck2 == 4, ]
n_a2 <- nrow(df)
cat(sprintf("After AttnCheck2 == 4:             %d  (excluded %d)\n",
            n_a2, n_a1 - n_a2))

cat(sprintf("\n*** ANALYTIC SAMPLE: N = %d ***\n", nrow(df)))
cat(sprintf("Total excluded: %d (%.1f%%)\n\n",
            n_raw - nrow(df), 100 * (n_raw - nrow(df)) / n_raw))

# The same funnel as a table, so the audit trail is exported alongside the
# results instead of living only in the console output above. Anyone can then
# check the arithmetic without rerunning anything. The first row's n_excluded is
# NA (R's marker for a missing value) because nothing has been excluded at the
# point of loading; a 0 there would suggest a step ran and removed nobody.
exclusion_funnel <- data.frame(
  step = c("Loaded (raw)", "Finished == 1", "Progress == 100",
           "AttnCheck1 == 9", "AttnCheck2 == 4"),
  n_remaining = c(n_raw, n_fin, n_prog, n_a1, n_a2),
  n_excluded  = c(NA, n_raw - n_fin, n_fin - n_prog, n_prog - n_a1, n_a1 - n_a2),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["exclusion_funnel"]] <- exclusion_funnel
show_table(exclusion_funnel, "Exclusion funnel (prereg 6.2)")

# === PARTICIPANT UNIQUENESS IN THE ANALYSED SAMPLE ===
# Phase 1.1 counted repeated Prolific IDs across the whole raw export. The count
# that matters for the conclusions is this one: does any participant appear
# twice among the responses actually analysed? Prereg 4.1 requires that nobody
# took part more than once, so a duplicate that survived the funnel would mean
# one person's views carrying double weight through every test below.
pid_kept <- trimws(as.character(df$Prolific_ID))
pid_kept <- pid_kept[!is.na(pid_kept) & nzchar(pid_kept)]
n_dup_kept <- sum(duplicated(pid_kept))
cat(sprintf("Duplicate Prolific IDs among the %d analysed responses: %d\n",
            nrow(df), n_dup_kept))
if (n_dup_kept == 0) {
  cat("Every analysed response comes from a distinct participant.\n")
} else {
  cat("NOTE: a repeated ID survived the funnel; resolve before interpreting.\n")
}
```

```{r phase1_response_quality}
# === RESPONSE-QUALITY DIAGNOSTICS (reported, never applied) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: describes completion time and straightlining in the
# analytic sample. Completion time is how long a person took; straightlining is
# giving the same answer over and over down a run of items. It creates no
# analysis variable and it removes nobody.
#
# WHY REPORT THEM AND NOT ACT ON THEM. Prereg 6.2 is explicit that these are
# examined and reported but that "neither on its own removes a participant from
# the confirmatory analyses". Both are ambiguous signals. A fast respondent may
# simply be a fast reader, and a long run of identical answers is expected on a
# block of similarly-keyed items -- items worded so that agreeing with one means
# agreeing with the rest -- for someone with a consistent view. Turning either
# one into an exclusion after seeing the data would be an unregistered
# researcher degree of freedom. That means a choice made with the results
# already in view, which is how a sample gets quietly shaped to fit the story.
# So they are printed for the reader to weigh, and nothing more.
#
# HAZARD: DO NOT "improve" this chunk by filtering df. Every N reported anywhere
# downstream assumes the sample fixed by the funnel above. Remove people here
# and every table in the document silently describes a different sample from the
# one the pre-registration named.

# Qualtrics names the timing column "Duration (in seconds)". Match on the stem
# with grep rather than typing the full name, so a change to the wording inside
# the parentheses does not break the lookup. [1] takes the first match, and
# yields NA when there is no match at all, which the guard below catches instead
# of letting it fail further down.
dur_col <- grep("^Duration", names(df), value = TRUE)[1]
if (!is.na(dur_col)) {
  # Divide by 60 to turn seconds into minutes. Cosmetic only: nothing is tested
  # on this number, it just makes the printed summary readable at a glance.
  dur <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[dur_col]])) / 60
  # The median is the middle value and the IQR (interquartile range) is the span
  # covering the middle half of people, from the 25th to the 75th percentile.
  # Both are reported instead of the mean because a handful of very long
  # durations would drag a mean upward and describe nobody.
  cat(sprintf("Completion time (minutes): median %.1f, IQR %.1f-%.1f, range %.1f-%.1f\n",
              median(dur, na.rm = TRUE), quantile(dur, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
              quantile(dur, .75, na.rm = TRUE), min(dur, na.rm = TRUE),
              max(dur, na.rm = TRUE)))
  # The 5-minute mark is a reporting flag and nothing else. Nobody is removed
  # for falling under it; the count is printed so the reader can judge it.
  cat(sprintf("  under 5 minutes: %d participants (flagged, not excluded)\n",
              sum(dur < 5, na.rm = TRUE)))
}

# Straightlining: the longest run of identical CONSECUTIVE answers across a
# 28-item stretch of 1-7 attitude items drawn from the six different blocks
# listed below. Items from several blocks rather than one, on purpose. A long
# run inside a single similarly-keyed block is ordinary agreement. A run that
# survives a change of topic is the signal of interest.
attitude_items <- intersect(
  c(paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), paste0("revenge_", 1:4), paste0("hate_", 1:3),
    paste0("degrad_", 1:3), paste0("harsh_", 1:3), paste0("sdo_", 1:8)),
  names(df))
longest_run <- apply(as.matrix(df[, attitude_items]), 1, function(r) {
  r <- r[!is.na(r)]
  # Somebody who answered none of these items has no run to measure, so return
  # NA rather than a made-up 0 that would look like a real, very short run.
  if (!length(r)) return(NA_integer_)
  # rle() is run-length encoding: it walks along the row and reports each
  # stretch of repeated values together with how long that stretch ran. The
  # longest of those lengths is this person's straightlining index. Skipped
  # items were dropped just above, so an unanswered item in the middle does not
  # split one long run into two short ones and hide it.
  max(rle(as.numeric(r))$lengths)
})
# The >= 15 threshold below is a reporting marker only: roughly half of these 28
# items answered identically, one straight after the other. It carries NO
# exclusion, and nobody is removed for crossing it.
cat(sprintf("Longest identical-answer run: median %.0f, max %.0f; %d participants with a run >= 15\n",
            median(longest_run, na.rm = TRUE), max(longest_run, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(longest_run >= 15, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat("(Reported for transparency; neither removes a participant.)\n")
```

## 1.4 Coalesce the vignette-split sentencing columns

Each participant read **one** of three vignettes (short crime stories), so
Qualtrics wrote the sentencing answers into three separate sets of columns. On
any one person's row, two of those three sets are empty. This section coalesces
them, which means collapsing each three-way split down to a single column that
holds whatever that person actually answered. The key that says which story
someone saw is the embedded `Vignette` field (1/2/3). An embedded field is a
value Qualtrics stores alongside the response rather than asking about it. One
export quirk matters here: the slider questions arrive with a trailing `_1` on
their column names, and the typed-in answers do not.

```{r phase1_coalesce}
# === COALESCE THE VIGNETTE-SPLIT COLUMNS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: collapses the twelve vignette-split sentencing columns
# into four (Sentence1, Sentence2, Sentence_OpenEnd1, Sentence_OpenEnd2), and
# strips the slider "_1" suffix (ending) from CRT_1_1..CRT_3_1 and age_1.
# Everything after this point uses the coalesced names.
#
# WHY IT MATTERS: until this runs there is no single column meaning "the
# sentence this person gave". Sentence1 and Sentence2 are what the
# within-vignette standardizing in Phase 3, the punitiveness index and the H14
# test of the sentence all read. The two open-end columns are not analysed
# here; they are carried through for the language pipeline noted below.
#
# THE QUIRK: a randomizer assigned each participant ONE of three vignette blocks
# (prereg 3.2), all describing the same charge but differing in circumstance.
# Qualtrics writes a separate column per block, so for any given row two of the
# three are empty. The embedded field `Vignette` (1, 2 or 3) records which block
# was shown and is the key used to pick the populated one -- the one that was
# actually filled in.

#' Pick the populated vignette column for each participant
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the data frame (the table of responses, one row per
#'            participant); stem  the column stem, meaning the start of the name
#'            without the block suffix ("Sentence1", "Sentence_OpenEnd2", ...);
#'            slider  TRUE for the numeric slider columns, whose export names
#'            carry a trailing "_1", FALSE for the character (text) open-ends,
#'            which do not.
#' RETURNS    one vector (a simple run of values) of length nrow(data), so one
#'            entry per participant: numeric when slider = TRUE and character
#'            otherwise.
pick_vig <- function(data, stem, slider = FALSE) {
  # SLIDER QUIRK: only the slider exports carry the trailing "_1", so
  # Sentence1_V2_1 is a slider column while Sentence_OpenEnd1_V2 is not. Get
  # this backwards and the name built below matches nothing in the export.
  suffix <- if (slider) "_1" else ""
  # The three names to look for, one per block: the stem plus the block suffix
  # "_V1", "_V2" or "_V3", plus the slider suffix when there is one.
  cols   <- paste0(stem, "_V", 1:3, suffix)
  if (!all(cols %in% names(data))) {
    # A warning rather than a stop: a missing block leaves an all-NA column (NA
    # is R's marker for a missing value) that is visible in the per-vignette
    # counts printed below. Halting here instead would hide every other check
    # further down the document.
    warning("Missing vignette columns for stem: ", stem)
    return(rep(NA, nrow(data)))
  }
  # Pre-allocate with the right TYPE: NA_real_ is a missing NUMBER, and
  # NA_character_ is missing TEXT. Starting from a plain NA vector, which R
  # treats as logical, would let the first assignment decide the type, and a
  # character sentence column would then silently break every numeric operation
  # downstream.
  #
  # NOTE: the early return above hands back rep(NA, nrow(data)), which is a
  # plain logical NA vector -- exactly what this line refuses to start from. So
  # the missing-column path does not follow the typing rule stated here. The
  # comment and the code disagree on that path, and the authors should decide
  # which of the two to change.
  out <- if (slider) rep(NA_real_, nrow(data)) else rep(NA_character_, nrow(data))
  for (v in 1:3) {
    # Take from block v only the rows whose Vignette field says they saw block
    # v. The !is.na() guard comes first because NA == v is itself NA, which does
    # not pick out a row cleanly. A participant with a missing Vignette field is
    # never selected and keeps NA, which is the honest result -- their sentence
    # cannot be attributed to any story.
    sel <- !is.na(data$Vignette) & data$Vignette == v
    vals <- data[[cols[v]]][sel]
    # Slider answers are forced to numbers; suppressWarnings() because a blank
    # entry turns into NA and R would otherwise warn once per block about it.
    # Open-ends stay character, exactly as the participant typed them.
    out[sel] <- if (slider) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(vals)) else as.character(vals)
  }
  out
}

# Sentence1 = the sentence set after the vignette; Sentence2 = the sentence set
# after the added facts remove the forward-looking reasons (prereg 5.11) --
# forward-looking meaning the reasons that look ahead to future benefit, such as
# deterring others, rather than back at what the defendant did.
df$Sentence1         <- pick_vig(df, "Sentence1", slider = TRUE)
df$Sentence2         <- pick_vig(df, "Sentence2", slider = TRUE)
# The two open-ends, the free-text boxes where people answered in their own
# words, stay character (text) and are not analysed here; they are carried
# through cleaning and exported for the E3-E7 language pipeline (prereg 5.15).
df$Sentence_OpenEnd1 <- pick_vig(df, "Sentence_OpenEnd1")
df$Sentence_OpenEnd2 <- pick_vig(df, "Sentence_OpenEnd2")

# Drop the slider "_1" from the remaining slider exports. Qualtrics exports a
# slider one statement at a time and numbers them, and each of these sliders
# holds a single statement. CRT_1_1 is therefore the answer to CRT item 1, not
# part 1 of item 1, and age_1 is age; the suffix carries no meaning and only
# invites misreading.
df$CRT_1 <- df$CRT_1_1; df$CRT_2 <- df$CRT_2_1; df$CRT_3 <- df$CRT_3_1
df$age   <- df$age_1

# Verification: each vignette group should have a non-missing Sentence1 for
# essentially everyone, and the three group sizes should be close to equal since
# assignment was randomized with even weights. A group with far fewer sentences
# than participants is the sign that the wrong column was picked, or that a
# block name changed in the export.
cat("Coalesced sentencing columns by the embedded Vignette field:\n\n")
print(as.data.frame(
  df %>% dplyr::group_by(Vignette) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     n_Sentence1 = sum(!is.na(Sentence1)),
                     n_Sentence2 = sum(!is.na(Sentence2)),
                     n_OpenEnd1  = sum(!is.na(Sentence_OpenEnd1) &
                                       nchar(trimws(Sentence_OpenEnd1)) > 0),
                     .groups = "drop")), row.names = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("\nSentence1 missing overall: %d; Sentence2 missing overall: %d\n",
            sum(is.na(df$Sentence1)), sum(is.na(df$Sentence2))))
```

## 1.5 Missing-data check

A count of how many `NA` values (R's marker for a missing value) sit in one
representative item from each part of the survey. This is a check on the work
Phase 1 has just done, not an analysis. A surprising count points at a naming
or coalescing mistake upstream rather than at people skipping questions.

```{r phase1_missing}
# === MISSING-DATA CHECK ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: counts NAs (R's marker for a missing value) on one
# representative item per block, as a check that Phase 1's coercion (forcing a
# column into the type it should have) and coalescing did what they were meant
# to. It produces no analysis variable.
#
# These are chosen to cover every part of the instrument that a later phase
# depends on: the two sentences and the vignette key (Phase 3), one punitiveness
# item, one emotion and one revenge item, the three proportionality/severity
# items behind H4-H6, the ranking that defines retributivists (Phase 5.1), two
# shark items (H15), one item from each of two personality scales, and the first
# CRT item. A surprising count here means a coalescing or naming problem
# upstream, not participant non-response. A column that comes back entirely
# missing means something above renamed it or picked the wrong vignette block.
#
# intersect() keeps only the names that really exist in `df`, so the checklist
# adapts to what the export actually contains. Without it, a renamed column
# would still get a row in the table below, and that row would read zero:
# df[["oldname"]] returns NULL, is.na(NULL) is empty, and summing nothing gives
# 0. A column that had vanished would be reported as fully answered. With
# intersect() it drops off the list instead, so a name you expect and cannot
# find in the printed table is itself worth chasing.
key_vars <- intersect(
  c("Sentence1", "Sentence2", "Vignette", "punishmore_1", "punishmore_2",
    "hate_1", "revenge_1", "proportionality", "severity_1", "severity_2",
    "Prioritization_1", "Shark_1", "Shark_3", "rwa_1", "sdo_1", "CRT_1"),
  names(df))

# One row per checked variable: its name, and how many participants are missing
# it. vapply() with integer(1) insists on exactly one whole number back per
# variable, so anything unexpected errors here rather than producing a mangled
# table.
missing_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable  = key_vars,
  N_Missing = vapply(key_vars, function(v) sum(is.na(df[[v]])), integer(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

cat("=== MISSING DATA CHECK (key variables) ===\n\n")
print(missing_summary, row.names = FALSE)
```

# PHASE 2: REVERSE CODING

Some questions are worded the opposite way round from the rest. Agreeing that
"punishments should be as light as possible" makes someone LESS punitive, while
agreeing with most of the other items makes them more punitive. Averaging the
two directions together would cancel real differences out, so those items are
reverse-coded: their answers are flipped end for end first. After the flip,
**higher values always mean more of the named construct** (more punitive, more
hostile, more willing to set a limit aside).

The logic lives in one metadata table, `reverse_spec` -- metadata being data
that describes the data. It lists every reversed item with the scale it sits on
and the reason, and is printed below so the keying can be checked against prereg
Appendix A without reading any code. Each item `X` becomes a **new** column
`X_R = 8 − X`; the original column is preserved, so nothing is thrown away.

**Note on `severity_1`.** It is reverse-keyed *only* inside the just-deserts
proportionality component (wanting punishment greater than the crime lowers
proportionality). The standalone H4/H5 tests use the raw, unflipped item, so
`severity_1_R` is created separately and flagged in the table below.

## 2.1 Reverse-coding metadata

```{r phase2_metadata}
# === REVERSE-CODING METADATA ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: declares `reverse_spec`, the single table listing every
# item to be reversed, the scale it lives on, the construct it belongs to, and
# the reason. Phase 2.2 applies it mechanically. It computes nothing itself, and
# it is printed into the document so the keying can be checked against prereg
# Appendix A without reading any code.
#
# WHY A TABLE RATHER THAN A LIST OF ASSIGNMENTS. Reverse coding is the easiest
# step in the pipeline to get silently wrong: reversing an item twice, or
# reversing one that was already keyed correctly, produces a composite that
# still looks entirely plausible. Nothing errors and no impossible number
# appears. Putting the rule in data rather than in code means the full set is
# visible in one place and its rationale travels with it.
#
# HAZARD: Retribution_6 and Retribution_7 are worded negatively in the
# instrument but arrive from Qualtrics ALREADY recoded to the 1-7
# high-is-more-retributive direction. They are correctly absent from this table.
# DO NOT ADD THEM. Adding them would flip them a second time and quietly corrupt
# the retribution subscale, which feeds the definition of a retributivist in
# Phase 5.
#
# `scale_max` is the highest answer an item's scale allows. It is carried per
# item rather than assumed, so the rule below reads (scale_max + 1) - x and
# stays correct if an item on some other scale is ever added. Every item here is
# on the standard 1-7 agree-disagree scale (prereg 5.1), so every reversal is
# 8 - x: a 1 becomes a 7, a 2 becomes a 6, and the midpoint 4 stays where it is.
reverse_spec <- tibble::tribble(
  ~item,          ~scale_max, ~construct,               ~rationale,

  # --- Punitiveness ---
  "punishmore_1",  7, "Punitiveness",        "'Current punishment is too high' — agreeing = LESS punitive",
  "parsimony_1",   7, "Punitiveness",        "'Punishments as light as possible' — agreeing = LESS punitive",
  "parsimony_2",   7, "Punitiveness",        "'Should not punish more than necessary' — agreeing = LESS punitive",

  # --- Revenge / proportionality ---
  # severity_2 asks whether punishment should fall SHORT of the harm. Just
  # deserts is the idea that the punishment should match what was done, no more
  # and no less, so wanting punishment either greater OR less than the crime is
  # a departure from proportionality (prereg 5.4). Agreement therefore lowers
  # the proportionality component, which is why the item is reversed into it.
  # Its partner severity_1 is handled separately in Phase 2.2 -- see the note
  # there.
  "severity_2",    7, "Proportionality (JD)","'Punishment less severe than the harm' — agreeing = LOWER proportionality",

  # --- Kantian limits ---
  # The Kantian limits are the restraints on how punishment may be pursued: fair
  # process, reliable evidence, and judgment free of passion. They are scored
  # throughout as WILLINGNESS TO SET THE LIMIT ASIDE, so that higher always
  # means less restrained (prereg 5.5). An item worded as protecting the limit
  # therefore has to be reversed to join that direction, or it would pull
  # against the rest of its own scale.
  "dueprocess_2",  7, "Due process",         "'Every defendant deserves due process' — agreeing = NOT permissive",

  # --- Emotions ---
  "hate_2",        7, "Hatred",              "'I am sympathetic towards criminals' — sympathy is the opposite of hatred",

  # --- Harshness / hostile aggression ---
  "degrad_1",      7, "Degradation",         "'Prisoners deserve dignity and respect' — agreeing = LOW degradation",
  "prisonvi_1",    7, "Prison violence",     "'I feel bad when a prisoner is assaulted' — feeling bad = NOT tolerating",
  "prisonvi_2",    7, "Prison violence",     "'Sexual assault of prisoners is serious' — seeing it as serious = NOT tolerating",
  "harsh_2",       7, "Harsh conditions",    "'Prisoners deserve decent living conditions' — agreeing = LOW harshness",

  # --- Crime concerns ---
  "fear_1",        7, "Fear of crime",       "'How safe do you feel walking at night' — feeling safe = LOW fear",

  # --- Exclusion / essentialism / society ---
  "essential_3",   7, "Essentialism",        "'Crime comes from tough life circumstances' — agreeing = LOW essentialism",
  "Society_1",     7, "Society (rejection)", "'Crime is also society's failure' — agreeing = ACCEPTS society's responsibility",
  "Society_2",     7, "Society (rejection)", "'State should take better care of people' — agreeing = ACCEPTS responsibility",
  "Society_3",     7, "Society (rejection)", "'Society should embrace all members' — agreeing = ACCEPTS responsibility",

  # --- Personality ---
  "rwa_3",         7, "RWA",                 "'Nothing wrong with premarital sex' — disagreeing = HIGH authoritarianism",
  "sdo_3",         7, "SDO",                 "'No one group should dominate' — agreeing = LOW SDO",
  "sdo_4",         7, "SDO",                 "'Bottom groups just as deserving' — agreeing = LOW SDO",
  "sdo_7",         7, "SDO",                 "'Should equalize conditions' — agreeing = LOW SDO",
  "sdo_8",         7, "SDO",                 "'All groups an equal chance' — agreeing = LOW SDO",
  "Raceresent_1",  7, "Racial resentment",   "'Slavery created difficult conditions' — agreeing = LOW resentment",
  "Raceresent_4",  7, "Racial resentment",   "'Blacks have gotten less than they deserve' — agreeing = LOW resentment"
)

# Print the plan into the report. show_table() renders it through kable, knitr's
# table formatter, so a reader can check every reversal against prereg
# Appendix A without opening the code.
cat("=== REVERSE-CODING PLAN ===\n")
cat(sprintf("%d items are reverse-coded as X_R = (scale_max + 1) - X.\n\n",
            nrow(reverse_spec)))
show_table(as.data.frame(reverse_spec[, c("item", "construct", "rationale")]),
           "Reverse-coded items (prereg Appendix A)")
```

## 2.2 Apply reverse coding

```{r phase2_apply}
# === APPLY REVERSE CODING ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: walks reverse_spec and creates one NEW column X_R per
# listed item, plus severity_1_R. It produces `d`, the scored working data frame
# (the working table of participants) that every phase from here to the export
# uses.
#
# `d` is a copy of `df` rather than an in-place edit, so the post-exclusion,
# pre-scoring frame stays available for comparison. If a scored column ever
# looks wrong, the untouched original is still sitting there to check against.
d <- df

for (i in seq_len(nrow(reverse_spec))) {
  # Read the item name and the top of its scale straight out of the table above,
  # so the loop never hard-codes either one.
  it  <- reverse_spec$item[i]
  mx  <- reverse_spec$scale_max[i]
  # A named item that is not in the export is reported and skipped, so a
  # renamed column surfaces as a warning plus a missing composite rather than as
  # a silently mis-scored one.
  if (!it %in% names(d)) { warning("Reverse item not found: ", it); next }
  # A NEW column, never an overwrite. Keeping the original alongside means the
  # raw item is still available where the analysis wants it -- H4 and H5 use
  # raw severity_1 -- and it makes the sanity check in 2.3 possible at all.
  # Overwrite the original and there is nothing left to check the flip against.
  d[[paste0(it, "_R")]] <- (mx + 1) - d[[it]]
}

# severity_1 asks whether punishment should EXCEED the seriousness of the crime.
# It is reverse-keyed ONLY inside the just-deserts proportionality component,
# where wanting more than the crime deserves is a departure from proportionality
# (prereg 5.4). That is why it sits here rather than in reverse_spec: the table
# is the list of items reversed everywhere, and this one is not.
#
# HAZARD: H4 and H5 test severity_1 in its own right -- "a sizeable share
# endorse punishment beyond the crime" -- and both use the RAW item. Swapping
# severity_1_R into either would reverse the sign of the reported finding: the
# test would then count the people who want LESS than the crime deserves.
d$severity_1_R <- rev7(d$severity_1)

cat(sprintf("Reverse coding complete: %d '_R' columns from the metadata table,\n",
            nrow(reverse_spec)))
cat("plus severity_1_R, created separately for the just-deserts component only.\n")
cat("Original columns are preserved unchanged.\n")
```

## 2.3 Sanity check

```{r phase2_sanity}
# === REVERSE-CODING SANITY CHECK ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: two checks on the columns just created. Nothing is
# modified.
#
# Check 1 is a full crosstab of one item against its reversed twin. A crosstab
# is a count of how often each pair of values occurs together. Every row must
# satisfy 8 - original = reversed, and the crosstab shows all seven pairs at
# once. An off-by-one or a wrong scale_max is therefore visible on its face.
# Checking a mean instead would hide it, because a wrongly flipped item still
# averages out to an ordinary-looking number.
cat("Sanity check (punishmore_1 -> punishmore_1_R):\n\n")
sanity <- as.data.frame(
  d %>% dplyr::count(punishmore_1, punishmore_1_R) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(check = paste0("8 - ", punishmore_1, " = ", punishmore_1_R)))
print(sanity, row.names = FALSE)

# Check 2 covers every reversed column at once. Since all of them come from 1-7
# items, the smallest value found across all _R columns must be 1 and the
# largest 7. Anything outside that range means an item was not on the scale
# reverse_spec claims, and the composite built from it would be on the wrong
# metric -- mixing, say, a 1-5 item into an average of 1-7 items.
cat("\nRange check on every _R column (all should be 1-7):\n")
# grep() collects the names of every column ending in "_R", so the check covers
# whatever Phase 2.2 actually made rather than a hand-typed list that could fall
# out of date.
r_cols <- grep("_R$", names(d), value = TRUE)
# One row per reversed column, holding its smallest and largest observed value.
# na.rm = TRUE ignores missing answers, which would otherwise swallow both ends.
rng <- data.frame(
  column = r_cols,
  min = vapply(r_cols, function(v) min(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  max = vapply(r_cols, function(v) max(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("  %d reversed columns; min = %g, max = %g across all of them.\n",
            nrow(rng), min(rng$min), max(rng$max)))
```

# PHASE 3: WITHIN-VIGNETTE STANDARDIZATION OF THE SENTENCE

The three vignettes describe the same charge but differ in circumstance, and
they draw different sentences as a result. The *absolute* sentence is therefore
not comparable across them: fifteen years in the mildest story is a harsher
response than fifteen years in the harshest one. `Sentence1` is accordingly
**z-scored within vignette** (prereg 5.11) before it is pooled or added to the
punitiveness index. A z-score restates an answer as how far it sits above or
below the average, measured in standard deviations. Doing that separately inside
each vignette leaves a score that means "how severe was this person compared
with the others who read the SAME story".

## 3.1 Raw sentence by vignette

```{r phase3_raw}
# === RAW SENTENCES BY VIGNETTE ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: describes Sentence1 and Sentence2 in years within each
# vignette, and produces the table `sentence_by_vignette` (exported as
# output/tables/sentence_by_vignette.csv).
#
# The table carries the group size, then the mean (average) and the SD
# (standard deviation, the typical distance from that average) for each of the
# two sentences. It adds the median (the middle value) for Sentence1 only.
#
# This is the evidence for the standardization in 3.2: if the three vignettes
# elicit different sentence distributions, pooling raw years would confound the
# sentence with the block a participant happened to be assigned. A big number
# would then be ambiguous -- a harsh person, or merely the harshest story.
raw_sentence <- as.data.frame(
  d %>% dplyr::group_by(Vignette) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     mean_S1 = mean(Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     sd_S1   = sd(Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     median_S1 = median(Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
                     mean_S2 = mean(Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
                     sd_S2   = sd(Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE),
                     .groups = "drop"))
# Park the table in the TABLES collector so Phase 10 writes it out with all the
# others, then print it here through show_table(), which formats it with kable
# so it appears as a real table in the knitted report.
TABLES[["sentence_by_vignette"]] <- raw_sentence
show_table(raw_sentence, "Raw sentences (years) by vignette, before standardizing")

# NO OUTLIER RULE. The slider is bounded at 0 and 50 years by design, where 50
# stands for life (prereg 5.11), so an extreme value is a real, available
# response and not a data-entry error. Prereg 6.2 sets no separate outlier rule
# for the composites and does not trim the sentence, and none is applied here.
# A 50 is the top of the scale, not a point to be Winsorized away -- Winsorizing
# means pulling extreme values in to a less extreme number, and here that would
# erase the very harshest answers the study set out to measure.
cat(sprintf("\nSentence1 range: %g to %g; Sentence2 range: %g to %g (slider bounds 0-50, untrimmed).\n",
            min(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE), max(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
            min(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE), max(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE)))

# --- HOW MANY PEOPLE SAT AT THE TOP OF THE SCALE ---------------------------
# The note above says a 50 is a real answer and not an outlier. How MANY people
# gave one is what tells a reader how much of the sentence's range the bound
# took away, and it is the number any comparison with another sentencing study
# needs. prop_ci() gives the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval, the same one H4
# and H12 use for every other share in this document, so the interval is
# computed the same way here as everywhere else.
sentence_ceiling <- prop_ci(as.integer(d$Sentence1 == 50),
                            "Gave the maximum sentence (50 years)")
TABLES[["sentence_ceiling_share"]] <- sentence_ceiling
show_table(sentence_ceiling,
           "3.1: share of participants at the top of the sentencing scale")

# --- ROUND-NUMBER ANSWERING ------------------------------------------------
# Sentences pile up on round numbers. The six most-used values are worked out
# FROM THE DATA rather than named by hand, so the printed sentence cannot go
# stale if the data or the exclusions ever change.
sentence_top6 <- sort(table(d$Sentence1[!is.na(d$Sentence1)]),
                      decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]
sentence_top6_share <- prop_ci(
  as.integer(d$Sentence1 %in% as.numeric(names(sentence_top6))),
  paste0("Gave one of the six most common values (",
         paste(names(sentence_top6), collapse = ", "), ")"))
TABLES[["sentence_modal_values"]] <- data.frame(
  value = as.numeric(names(sentence_top6)),
  n = as.integer(sentence_top6), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["sentence_modal_share"]] <- sentence_top6_share
show_table(TABLES[["sentence_modal_values"]], "3.1: the six most common sentences")
show_table(sentence_top6_share,
           "3.1: share of participants giving one of those six values")
# The SHAPE of the distribution is reported once, in 6.2, which computes skew
# for every variable in the study. It is deliberately not recomputed here: a
# second copy of a number is a second place for it to drift.
```

## 3.2 Z-score within vignette

```{r phase3_zscore}
# === WITHIN-VIGNETTE STANDARDIZATION OF THE SENTENCE (prereg 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: creates `Sentence1_z`, the first sentence expressed as a
# z-score -- how many SDs (standard deviations, the typical distance from the
# average) it sits above or below the mean OF ITS OWN VIGNETTE. This is the
# sentence variable used for H14 and for the full punitiveness index; raw years
# are reported alongside but never pooled across vignettes.
#
# WHY. All three vignettes charge second-degree murder against the same
# defendant and victim, but they differ in circumstance -- a robbery that turns
# deadly, intimate-partner violence, a killing inside a criminal operation --
# and 3.1 shows that the resulting sentences differ in level. Fifteen years in
# the mildest vignette is a harsher response than fifteen years in the harshest
# one. Standardizing within vignette makes the score "how severe was this person
# relative to others who read the same facts", which is comparable across blocks
# and is what the hypotheses are about. Assignment was randomized (prereg 3.2),
# so within-group centring removes the vignette effect without removing any
# systematic person-level variance. Variance is how spread out the values are,
# and the person-to-person spread is the part that has to survive. The three
# groups differ only by chance in who ended up in them.
#
# group_by() before mutate() is what makes it WITHIN vignette: scale() is then
# applied to each group's values separately, using that group's own mean and SD.
# Dropping the group_by would standardize on the pooled distribution and quietly
# reintroduce the between-vignette differences this step exists to remove.
# ungroup() immediately, so no later verb inherits the grouping and computes
# something per-vignette by accident.
d <- d %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Vignette) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Sentence1_z = as.numeric(scale(Sentence1))) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

# Verification: by construction each vignette's z-scores must have mean 0 and
# SD 1. Anything else means the grouping did not take effect, and the table
# printed below is where that would show up.
check_z <- as.data.frame(
  d %>% dplyr::group_by(Vignette) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     mean_z = mean(Sentence1_z, na.rm = TRUE),
                     sd_z   = sd(Sentence1_z, na.rm = TRUE),
                     .groups = "drop"))
cat("Verification — within-vignette means should be ~0 and SDs ~1:\n\n")
print(check_z, row.names = FALSE)
```

# PHASE 4: COMPOSITES WITH CRONBACH'S ALPHA AND MCDONALD'S OMEGA

A composite is one score built by averaging several questions that are meant to
measure the same thing. Each composite here is the mean of its items after
reverse coding, computed for anyone who answered at least half of them
(prereg 5.1).

**Both** Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω are reported, as the plan requires. Both
are reliability coefficients. They ask how consistently a set of items moves
together, and a higher value means the items behave more like repeated readings
of one single thing. Cronbach's α assumes every item is an equally good
indicator; McDonald's ω comes from a factor model and does not assume that. A
single-factor ω is not identified for two-item composites -- the model asks for
more unknowns than two items can pin down -- so ω is reported for k ≥ 3, where
k is the number of items in the composite.

```{r phase4_init}
# Create the empty collector that compute_composite() appends to with <<-. That
# operator writes to a variable OUTSIDE the function, which is how each
# composite adds its own reliability row as it is built. Two consequences
# follow. The collector must exist before the first call, or every call fails.
# And the order in which Phase 4 builds composites becomes the row order of the
# reliability table in 4.10.
alpha_table <- data.frame()   # filled by compute_composite()
cat("Composites (alpha / omega):\n\n")
```

## 4.1 Goals of punishment

```{r phase4_goals}
# === THE FOUR GOALS OF PUNISHMENT + SOLIDARITY (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the goal subscales, each as the mean of its own
# items. The four goals are retribution (punishment is deserved for what was
# done), deterrence (punishment discourages future offending), incapacitation
# (someone who is locked up cannot offend) and rehabilitation (punishment
# should leave the offender better able to live within the law).
#
# `retribution` is the one that matters most downstream: Phase 5.2 turns it into
# the relative retribution subscale, which is the primary CONTINUOUS definition
# of a retributivist and the predictor in every prereg 6.5 rerun. An error here
# would travel into every retributivist result in the document.
d$retribution    <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Retribution_", 1:7), "retribution (7 items)")
d$deterrence     <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3), "deterrence")
d$incapacitation <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Incapacitation_", 1:2), "incapacitation")
d$rehabilitation <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Rehabilitation_", 1:2), "rehabilitation")

# All seven retribution items enter the subscale in the same direction.
# Retribution_6 and _7 are worded negatively but arrive already recoded 1-7 by
# Qualtrics, which is why they are absent from reverse_spec: reversing them here
# would flip two of seven items and drag the subscale toward zero.

# E2 reads the solidarity items two ways. The DURKHEIMIAN reading -- punishment
# as something that binds the law-abiding together and states shared norms -- is
# Solidarity_2 and _3 only. Solidarity_1 ("removing criminals from society helps
# society cleanse itself") is dropped because it reads as exclusionary rather
# than Durkheimian (prereg 5.3), and including it would blunt exactly the
# contrast E2 is built to draw. The hostile reading is the exclusion items,
# assigned in 4.9.
d$solidarity_durk <- compute_composite(d, c("Solidarity_2", "Solidarity_3"),
                                       "solidarity (Durkheimian)")
```

## 4.2 Punitiveness

```{r phase4_punitiveness}
# === PUNITIVENESS: THE TWO VERSIONS (prereg 5.2) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds both versions of the punitiveness measure and
# records how reliable each one is. Punitiveness -- how much punishment a
# person wants -- is the central variable of the study. It is the shared term
# in H1, H2, H8, H10, H12 and E2, and it is the outcome in H21. If it is built
# wrong here, every one of those tests is built wrong too.
#
# THE SELF-REPORT SCALE: 8 items, and NO sentence. The items are support for
# more punishment (punishmore_1 reversed, punishmore_2), rejection of
# parsimony (both parsimony items reversed), three strikes, life without
# parole, and the death penalty. Parsimony is the principle that punishment
# should be no heavier than it has to be, so rejecting it is the punitive
# answer. Averaging the eight gives one number for how punitive a person is.
# All eight are general attitude questions, so no part of the sentence the
# participant handed down enters this version. The hazard note below is why
# that matters.
#
# HAZARD -- WHICH VERSION TO USE. `punitiveness_full` has Sentence1_z built
# into it, so NEVER use it where the sentence also sits on the other side of
# the analysis. The sentence would then be counted twice, and the output would
# look like a relationship between two measures when it is really the sentence
# agreeing with itself. That rules the full index out for the sentencing ratio
# (which is built from Sentence1) and for H14 (whose outcome IS the sentence).
# Prereg 5.11 forbids exactly that, so this document uses the 8-item
# self-report scale in every such place. The full index appears only as a
# labelled robustness row.
punit_items <- c("punishmore_1_R", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1_R", "parsimony_2_R",
                 "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2", "LWOP", "deathpenalty")
d$punitiveness <- compute_composite(d, punit_items, "punitiveness (self-report, 8)")

# THE FULL INDEX: the 8-item self-report scale and the sentence, each
# standardized and then averaged. The sentence used is Sentence1_z, the
# within-vignette z-score. A z-score restates a value as how many standard
# deviations it sits above or below the average. The average here is the
# average of the SAME crime story. So a high Sentence1_z means this person was
# harsher than most of the others who read the same facts.
#
# zmean() is used rather than rowMeans() because zmean() standardizes each
# part before averaging. The two parts live on different metrics: a 1-7
# attitude mean on one side, a z-score on the other. A raw average of parts on
# different metrics hands the larger share of the result to whichever part
# happens to vary more. Which part that is depends on the response scales, not
# on any decision anyone made. Standardizing first makes the scale and the
# sentence count equally, which is what calling this an index is meant to
# mean.
d$punitiveness_full <- zmean(d$punitiveness, d$Sentence1_z)

# RELIABILITY OF THE FULL INDEX, treated as a 9-part scale. Reliability asks
# whether the parts of a scale behave as though they are measuring one thing.
# Two coefficients are reported. Cronbach's alpha is the standard measure of
# how consistently a set of items hangs together. McDonald's omega asks the
# same question through a factor model, a model that supposes one hidden
# attitude sits behind all the answers and checks how well that fits.
#
# The 8 items are z-scored here so that they sit on the same footing as
# Sentence1_z, which is already standardized. Skip that step and alpha would
# be computed over a set whose ninth element has a wildly different variance
# from the other eight. Variance is how spread out a set of values is. Alpha
# is built from the covariances between the parts, so the parts that vary most
# carry the most weight in it.
#
# This block does not call compute_composite(), because that function scores a
# row-mean of raw items and the index here is the zmean() built just above.
# The alpha_table row is therefore assembled by hand, so that the published
# reliability table in 4.10 still carries a line for the full index instead of
# silently leaving it out.
punit9 <- data.frame(scale(d[, punit_items]), Sentence1_z = d$Sentence1_z)
# tryCatch stops a failed coefficient from halting the knit. On failure the
# value becomes NA, R's marker for a missing value, which then shows up in the
# printed table where a reader can see it, rather than an error page.
a9 <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::alpha(punit9, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)
o9 <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::omega(punit9, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)
# One row appended to the running reliability table, in the same shape
# compute_composite() writes for every other composite, so 4.10 can print them
# all together without special-casing this one.
alpha_table <- rbind(alpha_table, data.frame(
  composite = "punitiveness (full index, + sentence)", k = 9,
  alpha = a9, omega = o9,
  mean = mean(d$punitiveness_full, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd = sd(d$punitiveness_full, na.rm = TRUE),
  n = sum(!is.na(d$punitiveness_full)),
  items = paste(c(punit_items, "Sentence1_z"), collapse = ", "),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
# A running console line as the index is built, matching the lines
# compute_composite() prints for the other composites, so the reliability of
# every scale is visible in order as Phase 4 runs. "  -  " marks a coefficient
# that could not be computed.
cat(sprintf("  %-34s k=9  alpha=%.3f  omega=%s\n",
            "punitiveness (full index)", a9,
            ifelse(is.na(o9), "  -  ", sprintf("%.3f", o9))))
```

## 4.3 Revenge, proportionality, and just deserts

```{r phase4_justdeserts}
# === REVENGE, PROPORTIONALITY, JUST DESERTS (prereg 5.4) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the four variables that carry H6, H7, H9 and
# H10.
#
# WHY THE SPLIT MATTERS. Just deserts is scored in two separate pieces here,
# and that is the analytic point of the whole section. The study asks whether
# "punishment is DESERVED" and "punishment should be PROPORTIONATE" are one
# idea or two. That question can only be asked if the two are scored apart
# first. Merge them at the start and the question disappears, because there is
# nothing left to compare.

# REVENGE: four items on society's right to get back at offenders. It is the
# rival construct in H10 and the criterion in H7. A construct is the
# underlying thing a set of items is meant to measure. A criterion is the
# measure a hypothesis asks the other measures to line up with.
d$revenge <- compute_composite(d, paste0("revenge_", 1:4), "revenge")

# THE PROPORTIONALITY PART of just deserts: the direct proportionality item
# plus BOTH severity items reverse-keyed, meaning their answers are flipped so
# that a high number means the same thing on every item.
#
# Reversing both is what makes this a two-sided constraint. Wanting punishment
# greater than the crime (severity_1) and wanting it to fall short of the harm
# (severity_2) both count as departures from proportionality, and each one
# lowers this score by the same amount. Reverse only one of the two and the
# measure stops being about the constraint: it would then reward a departure
# in one direction and penalise a departure in the other.
#
# This composite is one of only two places in the document that uses
# severity_1_R. The other is the item-level confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)
# inside run_h6(), a model that asks whether a set of questions really
# measures one single thing, and which takes this composite apart again.
# Everywhere else uses severity_1 raw, unreversed.
d$proportionality_jd <- compute_composite(
  d, c("proportionality", "severity_1_R", "severity_2_R"),
  "proportionality (just-deserts)")

# THE 'DESERVED' PART: the four purpose items, Retribution_1 to _4, each of
# which says that punishment is deserved because of what the offender did.
# Only the first four of the seven retribution items are used here. The other
# three are not desert claims, and prereg 5.4 names 1 to 4 specifically.
# Sweeping in all seven would put items about a DUTY to punish, and about WHY
# desert might hold, into a measure meant to capture desert alone.
d$deserved <- compute_composite(d, paste0("Retribution_", 1:4),
                                "deserved (purpose R1-R4)")

# THE COMBINED JUST-DESERTS SCORE: the unweighted mean of the two parts -- a
# plain average, in which each part counts equally and neither is given more
# say. H9 and H10 use it as "self-reported support for just
# deserts". H6 is what gives permission to read it as ONE thing, because H6 is
# the test of whether the two parts hold together. If they do not, this
# average is reported as exactly what it is -- an average of two different
# things -- and prereg 5.4 says so ("if they do not, we report that instead of
# forcing them into one score").
d$just_deserts <- rowMeans(cbind(d$deserved, d$proportionality_jd), na.rm = TRUE)
# For a participant missing BOTH parts, rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) has nothing
# left to average and returns NaN, R's "not a number" marker for an undefined
# piece of arithmetic. R already counts NaN as missing, so this line is not
# repairing a broken check. It is making one state carry one marker. NaN and
# NA PRINT DIFFERENTLY: without this line, that participant shows as "NaN" in
# the knitted tables while every other missing value on the page shows as
# "NA". The .rds export in 10.3 keeps the two apart as well. Two labels for
# "this person could not be scored" is one label too many.
d$just_deserts[is.nan(d$just_deserts)] <- NA_real_

# === THE SEPARATED PROPORTIONALITY AND SEVERITY MEASURES ===
# The three-item component above answers one question: does this participant
# hold punishment to the size of the offense? It treats a wish for MORE
# punishment and a wish for LESS as the same kind of departure. That is what
# prereg 5.4 registers, and it is kept exactly as registered.
#
# It also merges two questions that a retributive theory keeps apart. Whether
# punishment SHOULD FIT the crime is a claim about the principle. Whether
# punishment should RUN BEYOND the crime is a claim about which direction
# people depart in. A defensible retributivism endorses the first and says
# nothing about the second. Those two claims therefore have to sit in separate
# measures, or that expectation cannot be tested at all.
#
# DEVIATION FROM THE REGISTRATION. Prereg 5.4 scores proportionality as one
# three-item component. The two measures below are ADDITIONAL, not
# replacements. Every registered test still runs on `proportionality_jd`, and
# these two appear beside it, never in place of it. Section 8.3b reports both.

# THE PRINCIPLE ON ITS OWN: the single proportionality item, not averaged with
# anything and not reversed. High = punishment should fit the crime, no more
# and no less.
d$proportionality_principle <- d$proportionality

# THE DIRECTION OF DEPARTURE. severity_1 asks for punishment greater than the
# seriousness of the crime, and enters exactly as it was answered. severity_2
# asks for punishment below the harm, and is reversed, so that REJECTING
# leniency also pushes the score up. Both items therefore point the same way.
# High = punishment should run beyond what the offense warrants.
d$severity_index <- rowMeans(cbind(d$severity_1, d$severity_2_R), na.rm = TRUE)
# The same NaN-to-NA cleanup as above, for anyone who answered neither item.
d$severity_index[is.nan(d$severity_index)] <- NA_real_

# WHY NO CRONBACH'S ALPHA IS REPORTED FOR severity_index. The two items
# correlate at only about .06, so alpha would come out near zero. Printing
# that number would announce a failure that has not happened.
#
# Cronbach's alpha assumes a REFLECTIVE scale: one where the items are
# exchangeable symptoms of one latent trait, so that anyone high on the trait
# answers all of them much the same way. Latent means the trait is never
# observed directly and is only inferred from the answers. This index is
# FORMATIVE instead. Wanting punishment above the crime and refusing
# punishment below the harm are two DIFFERENT ways of departing upward, and a
# participant can do either one without the other. The composite is the union
# of two behaviours, not two readings of one, so weak agreement between the
# items is what should be expected and is not a defect. It is also why the
# index correlates more strongly with every criterion than either item does
# alone.
#
# Because the two items are not interchangeable, both are carried separately
# and reported item by item wherever this index is reported.
#
# The SECOND of the two console lines below prints the correlation between the
# two items. The figure quoted here can therefore be checked against the
# output rather than taken on trust. The first line prints only the mean and
# standard deviation of the proportionality principle.
cat(sprintf("  %-34s M = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n", "proportionality (principle)",
            mean(d$proportionality_principle, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$proportionality_principle, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("  %-34s M = %.2f (SD %.2f), inter-item r = %.3f (formative; no alpha)\n",
            "severity index", mean(d$severity_index, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$severity_index, na.rm = TRUE),
            cor(d$severity_1, d$severity_2_R, use = "complete.obs")))
```

## 4.3b The retribution scale in three tiers

Writing on retribution splits the theory in two. The **negative** form says
that desert makes punishment *permissible*: an offender MAY be punished. The
**positive** form says that desert makes punishment *obligatory*: an offender
MUST be punished, and the state fails in a duty if it lets the offense pass.
Practically every retributivist accepts the negative form. The positive form is
the Kantian position, and most present-day defenders of the theory reject it.
Scoring all seven items as one thing therefore invites an objection: that the
scale measures a demanding position few retributivists actually hold.

This subsection scores the same items a second time, in tiers, so that the tier
an objector accepts can be read on its own page. It is a **robustness check,
not a second finding**. The soft tier shares most of its items with the
registered `deserved` composite, the two correlate near the top of the scale,
and the tier version therefore returns very nearly the registered answer by
construction. That the answer survives is the result. Nothing registered is
displaced.

```{r phase4_retribution_tiers}
# === THE RETRIBUTION SCALE IN THREE TIERS (beside prereg 5.3 and 5.4) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the seven retribution items a second time, as
# smaller composites. The split separates a claim that society has a RIGHT to
# punish from a claim that it has a DUTY to punish, and separates both of
# those from the two items that give REASONS why desert might hold rather than
# saying that punishment is deserved.
#
# NOTHING REGISTERED CHANGES HERE. `retribution` (all seven items, prereg 5.3)
# and `deserved` (Retribution_1 to _4, prereg 5.4) are built in 4.1 and 4.3,
# and nothing below touches, rescores or renames them. The composites here are
# additional, not replacements: they carry names of their own, and every
# registered test goes on running against the registered composites. This
# subsection is a deviation from the registration in exactly the sense 8.3b
# is: something extra reported BESIDE the registered scoring, never instead of
# it.
#
# THIS CHUNK MUST STAY AHEAD OF 4.10. compute_composite() appends its row to
# the global `alpha_table` with <<-, and 4.10 COPIES alpha_table into
# `alpha_table_out` and into TABLES by value. A composite built after 4.10 has
# already run would still score correctly and would still never reach the
# exported reliability table. No error would be raised anywhere, so the
# omission would be completely silent. Sitting between 4.3 and 4.4 is what
# keeps the four composites below in that table. DO NOT move this chunk later
# in the file.
#
# WHY THE SPLIT EXISTS.
#   NEGATIVE retributivism says desert makes punishment PERMISSIBLE. An
#     offender MAY be punished, and only up to what the offense warrants.
#     Practically every retributivist accepts this much.
#   POSITIVE retributivism says desert makes punishment OBLIGATORY. The
#     offender MUST be punished, and the state fails in a duty if it lets the
#     offense pass. This is the Kantian position, and it is the one most
#     present-day retributivists reject.
# Treating all seven items as one thing called "retribution" invites an
# objection: that the scale measures a demanding position few defenders of the
# theory actually hold, so any failure reported here is a failure of the
# questionnaire rather than of retribution. Scoring the tiers separately meets
# that objection with numbers instead of argument.
#
# THE ITEMS, in the wording participants saw. The codebook chunk under Phase
# 1.1 reads this text into `q_text` from the Labels export, but it prints four
# example items only and cuts each one off at 90 characters. The seven stems
# are therefore set out in full here rather than pointed at.
#   R1  Society has a moral right to punish criminals
#   R2  Justice requires that crimes be punished
#   R3  Justice is restored when criminals are punished
#   R4  Punishment is justified because criminals deserve to be punished
#   R5  The state has a duty to punish its criminals
#   R6  Criminal punishment is a good way to get criminals to repay their debt
#       to society
#   R7  Punishment negates the unfair advantage that criminals gain over
#       law-abiding citizens
#
# THE TIERS are named for what their items SAY rather than for the
# philosophical labels, because the fit between the two is not exact (see the
# note on R3 below).
#   SOFT CORE     R1 a moral right to punish
#                 R3 justice restored by punishment
#                 R4 punishment deserved
#   OBLIGATION    R2 justice requires that crimes be punished
#                 R5 the state has a duty to punish
#   RATIONALES    R6 punishment as a debt repaid
#                 R7 punishment as an unfair advantage cancelled
#
# R3 IS AN OPEN QUESTION AND IS THEREFORE SCORED BOTH WAYS. R1 and R4 are
# permissibility claims and belong in the soft core without argument. R3 is
# not a permissibility claim: "justice is restored when criminals are
# punished" says that punishment ACHIEVES something, which is the
# positive-retributive position the split exists to quarantine. An objector to
# the scale is precisely the reader who would target R3, so putting it in the
# tier built to answer that objector is a substantive choice and not a
# clerical one. The authors should settle where it belongs. Until they do, the
# soft core is scored twice -- once with R3 and once without -- and both are
# reported, so that no conclusion in this subsection rests on the placement.
#
# R6 AND R7 are held apart from the other two tiers because neither one says
# that punishment is deserved. Each offers a REASON why desert might hold, one
# in the vocabulary of a debt owed and one in the vocabulary of an unfair
# advantage cancelled. A participant can accept that punishment is deserved
# while rejecting either account of why, so these two items answer a different
# question from the other five.
#
# WARNING: R2 SITS IN TWO COMPOSITES AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. Retribution_2 is
# one of the four items in the registered `deserved` composite, because prereg
# 5.4 names R1 to R4, and it is also one of the two items in
# `retribution_hard`. This is NOT a typo and it must NOT be tidied up by
# dropping the item from either place. The registered composite is frozen and
# keeps all four of its items at their registered values. The tier split reads
# the same item a second way, because "justice requires that crimes be
# punished" is an obligation claim wherever it appears.
#
# THE THREE TIERS DO NOT OVERLAP EACH OTHER. R1,R3,R4 / R2,R5 / R6,R7 uses
# each of the seven items exactly once. That is what keeps the three
# correlations among the tiers in the next chunk clean: no item appears on
# both sides of any of them, so no number there is inflated by an item
# correlating with itself.
```
