```{r phase4_retribution_tiers}
#   `deserved_soft_strict` is NOT a fourth tier. It is the soft core with R3
#   removed, so it is CONTAINED IN the soft core, and the two are never
#   correlated with each other. It appears only where the soft core does, as
#   the same comparison run under the other placement of R3.
#
# THE TIERS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT OF THE REGISTERED COMPOSITE, AND MUST NOT BE
# READ AS THOUGH THEY WERE. `deserved_soft` shares three of the four items in
# `deserved`, and `deserved_soft_strict` shares two of them. Each will
# therefore correlate with `deserved` near the top of the scale, and each will
# reproduce the registered correlations to within a rounding error. THAT is
# what makes this a robustness demonstration: the registered finding survives
# an objection to the scale's contents. It is NOT a second, independent test
# of the same claim, and nothing here should be written up as one. The overlap
# is measured and labelled part-whole -- a part of a scale correlated against
# the whole scale it sits inside -- in the next chunk.
#
# REVERSE CODING, restated here because this is the point in the file where
# getting it wrong is easiest. Retribution_6 and _7 are worded negatively in
# the instrument, but they arrive from Qualtrics ALREADY scored 1-7 in the
# high-is-more-retributive direction. That is why they are correctly absent
# from reverse_spec in Phase 2.1. Feeding reversed versions into
# retribution_rationale would flip both of its items and turn that composite
# upside down, with no warning printed anywhere.
#
# EXPECT THE TIERS TO CORRELATE HIGHLY, AND DO NOT READ THAT AS A PROBLEM. The
# full seven-item scale has a Cronbach's alpha (a measure of how consistently
# a set of questions behaves as one scale) of about .90, printed in 4.10. The
# seven items already behave as one tightly-related set: someone who agrees
# with one tends to agree with all of them. The split is not a claim that
# these are three different constructs, and the tables below are not offered
# as evidence that they are. It is a precaution, so that a reader who objects
# to the obligation items being in the scale at all can be shown the soft core
# standing on its own.
#
# MISSINGNESS IS RESOLVED PER COMPOSITE. compute_composite() keeps a
# participant who answered at least half the items of THAT composite. So the
# threshold is 2 of 3 for the soft core, 1 of 2 for the two-item composites,
# and 2 of 4 for the registered `deserved`. A participant who skipped items
# can therefore be scored on one composite and not on another. Any such
# difference shows up as a difference in the n column of the tables below, and
# it is a difference in WHO IS INCLUDED rather than in the arithmetic.
#
# WHY THE NAMES ARE NOT PARALLEL. `deserved_soft` is named after the
# registered `deserved` because it IS that composite minus its obligation
# item, and a reader comparing the two should see the family resemblance in
# the name. The other two take the `retribution_` prefix because they are cuts
# of the seven-item retribution scale rather than of the desert composite.
# Renaming any of them for tidiness would break that correspondence, and it
# would also rename the columns in the exported dataset,
# retribution_scored.csv/.rds from 10.3.

# THE SOFT CORE. k = 3, meaning three items, so both coefficients are defined:
# Cronbach's alpha, and McDonald's omega, which comes from a factor model (a
# model asking whether one underlying attitude explains the answers to all
# three questions).
d$deserved_soft <- compute_composite(
  d, paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 3, 4)),
  "retribution: soft core (R1,R3,R4)")

# THE SOFT CORE WITHOUT R3: the other placement of the contested item, scored
# so that no conclusion below can depend on where R3 was put. k = 2.
d$deserved_soft_strict <- compute_composite(
  d, paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 4)),
  "retribution: soft core strict (R1,R4)")

# THE OBLIGATION TIER. k = 2 here, as it is for the strict soft core above and
# for the rationales below, so Cronbach's alpha is reported and McDonald's
# omega stays NA (R's marker for a missing value). A single-factor model over
# two items cannot be estimated -- it asks for more quantities than two items
# can supply -- so the missing omega is a property of ANY two-item scale, not
# a failure of these particular items. The running console line from
# compute_composite() shows an undefined coefficient as "-"; the 4.10 table
# shows it as NA. If any two-item alpha lands below the .60 line that 4.10
# flags, that is a fact about how closely the pair hangs together and is
# reported as such. Nothing is dropped for it, and 4.10 sets no exclusion
# rule.
d$retribution_hard <- compute_composite(
  d, paste0("Retribution_", c(2, 5)),
  "retribution: obligation (R2,R5)")

# THE RATIONALES: R6 and R7, the two items that give a reason why desert might
# hold rather than asserting that punishment is deserved. k = 2, so again
# alpha is reported and omega stays NA.
d$retribution_rationale <- compute_composite(
  d, paste0("Retribution_", c(6, 7)),
  "retribution: rationales (R6,R7)")
```

```{r phase4_retribution_tiers_relate}
# === WHERE THE THREE TIERS POINT ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: three tables.
#   1. How the three tiers relate to one another.
#   2. Each tier, plus the contested item R3 on its own, set against the three
#      criteria the rest of the document turns on -- punitiveness, the
#      proportionality principle and the severity index -- with the two
#      registered composites listed underneath as the yardstick.
#   3. Whether dropping an item from the registered desert composite changes
#      what desert tracks.
# Produces `retribution_tiers_intercorrelations`, `retribution_tiers_criteria`
# and `retribution_tiers_overlap_steiger`.
# PREREG: outside every registered family. No multiplicity correction is
#         applied and none is implied.
#         A multiplicity correction is an adjustment made when many tests are
#         read together. It raises the evidence each single test needs before
#         its result is called real. The p-value after that adjustment is the
#         ADJUSTED p-value. The correction the registered families use is FDR,
#         the false discovery rate. FDR caps the expected share of false
#         claims among the results called significant.
#         These rows are descriptive. Folding them into the H1 family would
#         move the adjusted p-value of every registered correlate in that
#         table, because adding tests to a family changes the answers for the
#         tests already in it. That is the same reason 7.1 keeps its companion
#         table separate rather than adding rows to H1.
# CONSUMES: deserved_soft, deserved_soft_strict, retribution_hard,
#           retribution_rationale (previous chunk); punitiveness (4.2);
#           proportionality_principle and severity_index (4.3); deserved (4.3)
#           and retribution (4.1); the raw item Retribution_3, coerced in 1.2.
#
# EVERY ROW IS TWO-SIDED. A two-sided test asks whether there is any
# relationship at all, in either direction. The tier split was not registered
# and names no predicted direction, so picking a side now would mean picking
# it after seeing the data, which makes a result easier to get than it should
# be. Prereg 6.8 reserves the one-sided test for predictions made in advance.

# --- Table 1: the tiers against each other -------------------------------
# Three rows, because three tiers make three pairs. Each row uses disjoint
# items -- disjoint meaning the two sides have no item in common -- so no row
# is inflated by an item that sits on both sides and therefore correlates with
# itself.
# `deserved_soft_strict` is absent here by design. It is contained inside the
# soft core, so correlating the two would be part-whole -- a part of a scale
# against the whole scale it belongs to -- which comes out high no matter what
# participants think. It appears instead in Table 2 and in the Steiger table,
# where its job is to show that the placement of R3 carries no conclusion.
tier_inter <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cor_row(d, "deserved_soft", "retribution_hard",
          label_x = "Soft core R1,R3,R4",
          label_y = "Obligation R2,R5"),
  cor_row(d, "deserved_soft", "retribution_rationale",
          label_x = "Soft core R1,R3,R4",
          label_y = "Rationales R6,R7"),
  cor_row(d, "retribution_hard", "retribution_rationale",
          label_x = "Obligation R2,R5",
          label_y = "Rationales R6,R7")
))
TABLES[["retribution_tiers_intercorrelations"]] <- tier_inter

# The columns worth printing from a cor_row() frame: the two labels, the
# number of participants who answered both measures, the correlation with its
# 95% confidence interval, and the two-sided p. A confidence interval is the
# range of values the data leave plausible for the correlation.
# The directional p and the `alternative` column are left out of the printout,
# because every row here is two-sided. Those two columns would simply repeat
# p_two and the word "two.sided" all the way down the page. Both are still in
# the exported CSV, because TABLES holds the full frame rather than the
# trimmed one.
tier_print_cols <- c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")
show_table(tier_inter[, tier_print_cols],
           "4.3b: the three tiers against each other; no item appears on both sides of any row.")

# --- Table 2: each tier against the three criteria ------------------------
# The labels are held in a NAMED vector. A vector is a simple run of values,
# and a named one attaches a name to each value, so a display label can never
# drift out of order relative to the variable it names. This is the same
# arrangement used for the H1 correlate labels in 7.0, and it exists for the
# same reason: two plain parallel vectors are one careless insertion away from
# mislabelling an entire table, and nothing would flag the mistake.
#
# The two registered composites are listed last and marked REGISTERED. They
# are in the table so the tiers can be read against the preregistered scoring
# on the same page, in the same sample, with the same criteria. Their
# correlations ARE computed here, by the same cor_row() call as every other
# row. What is not touched is the columns themselves: they arrive from 4.1 and
# 4.3 exactly as those chunks left them. cor_row() uses pairwise deletion ON
# THE SAME TWO COLUMNS wherever it is called. Pairwise deletion means it keeps
# whoever answered both of the two columns being correlated and nobody else.
# The same two columns therefore leave the same people standing here as they
# do in 8.3b. That is why the two rows this table shares with 8.3b (desert
# against the principle, and desert against the severity index) reproduce the
# 8.3b figures rather than merely resembling them.
#
# Retribution_3 is carried as a row of its own, and it is the one row here
# that is a single ITEM rather than a composite. It is here because the
# placement of R3 is the open question flagged in the previous chunk. A reader
# deciding where the item belongs needs to see what it does against these
# criteria by itself, not only what the soft core does with it and without it.
# Its row is not part-whole, because none of the three criteria contains a
# retribution item.
tier_row_labels <- c(
  deserved_soft         = "Soft core R1,R3,R4 (right, restored, deserved)",
  deserved_soft_strict  = "Soft strict R1,R4 (right, deserved)",
  Retribution_3         = "  R3 alone (justice restored) -- single item",
  retribution_hard      = "Obligation R2,R5 (justice requires, state duty)",
  retribution_rationale = "Rationales R6,R7 (debt, unfair advantage)",
  deserved              = "REGISTERED deserved R1-R4 (prereg 5.4)",
  retribution           = "REGISTERED retribution, 7 items (prereg 5.3)")

# The three criteria. Punitiveness here is the 8-item self-report scale, never
# punitiveness_full: the full index has the sentence built into it, and
# prereg 5.11 keeps the sentence off both sides of an analysis at once.
# Nothing in this table involves the sentence, but the 8-item scale is the
# document's default, and using it keeps these rows directly comparable with
# the H1 family and with 8.3b.
#
# None of the three criteria shares an item with any retribution tier, so no
# row of this table is part-whole.
#
# The two proportionality measures ask different questions, and 4.3 explains
# why they are carried apart: the PRINCIPLE is whether punishment should fit
# the offense, the SEVERITY INDEX is whether it should run past it.
tier_criterion_labels <- c(
  punitiveness              = "Punitiveness (8-item self-report)",
  proportionality_principle = "Proportionality principle (FIT the crime)",
  severity_index            = "Severity index (EXCEED the crime)")

# Every tier crossed with every criterion. The outer lapply walks the tiers,
# the inner one walks the criteria, and the two rbinds stack the one-row data
# frames that cor_row() returns into a single table. Row order follows the
# order of the two label vectors above, so the table can be rearranged simply
# by rearranging them, with no risk of a label parting company from its
# numbers.
tier_crit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tier_row_labels), function(tier_var)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tier_criterion_labels), function(crit_var)
    cor_row(d, tier_var, crit_var,
            label_x = unname(tier_row_labels[tier_var]),
            label_y = unname(tier_criterion_labels[crit_var]))))))
TABLES[["retribution_tiers_criteria"]] <- tier_crit
show_table(tier_crit[, tier_print_cols],
           "4.3b: each tier against the three criteria, registered composites beneath; descriptive and two-sided, outside the registered FDR family.")

# WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT FROM THE TWO CORRELATION TABLES. No tier is
# correlated with `deserved` or with `retribution` in either of them, because
# every tier is built out of items that already sit inside those two
# composites. Such a correlation is part-whole -- the items correlated against
# themselves -- so it measures how large a share of the parent scale the tier
# makes up, and it comes out high whatever the participants think. The overlap
# IS reported, once, beneath the Steiger table below and labelled part-whole
# there. That is the same reasoning that makes 8.3b print its contaminated
# figure: it is the number a reader needs in order to see that the tier
# version is a rerun of the registered test rather than a fresh one.

# A lookup by name rather than by row number. Row numbers would keep working
# and would quietly point at the wrong row if a tier or a criterion were ever
# added to the vectors above. A label that matches nothing returns NA rather
# than raising an error, which is the same convention cor_row() follows, and
# the guards further down refuse to draw a conclusion from an NA.
tier_pick_r <- function(tier_var, crit_var) {
  hit <- tier_crit$x == unname(tier_row_labels[tier_var]) &
         tier_crit$y == unname(tier_criterion_labels[crit_var])
  if (!any(hit)) return(NA_real_)
  tier_crit$r[hit][1]
}

# WHAT THE THEORY PREDICTS, stated before any number is printed, so that the
# prediction cannot be quietly reshaped to fit the output. A retributivism
# that BOUNDED punishment -- one that held punishment to the size of the
# offense -- would tie desert to the principle of fitting the crime more
# closely than to the wish to exceed it. The FIT column would then be the
# larger of the two in every row. The tiers are printed without a verdict
# attached: the confidence intervals in the table above carry the inference.
cat("\nEach tier against the two proportionality measures.\n")
cat("A retributivism that bounded punishment would show FIT above EXCEED.\n\n")
cat(sprintf("  %-48s %6s  %8s\n", "MEASURE", "fit r", "exceed r"))
for (tier_var in names(tier_row_labels)) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-48s %+6.3f  %+8.3f\n",
              unname(tier_row_labels[tier_var]),
              tier_pick_r(tier_var, "proportionality_principle"),
              tier_pick_r(tier_var, "severity_index")))
}

# --- Table 3: does dropping an item change what desert tracks? -------------
# The question the split was built to answer, put as a test rather than as an
# eyeball comparison of two numbers. r(deserved, criterion) and
# r(deserved_soft, criterion) share the criterion AND are measured on the same
# participants, so the two correlations are dependent and overlapping in
# exactly the sense steiger_overlap() exists for. Dependent means the two r's
# are computed on the same people; overlapping means they share a variable.
# How far apart the two can fall by chance depends on how strongly the two
# desert composites correlate with EACH OTHER, which here is very strongly
# indeed. A test that ignored that would overstate the evidence.
#
# j is the shared variable (the criterion), k is the registered composite and
# h is the tier, so `diff` = r(registered) - r(tier) reads as the amount that
# dropping the item moves the correlation. Two-sided, because nothing here was
# registered and no direction was named in advance.
#
# READ THE SIZE OF THE CHANGE, NOT THE p-VALUE. With N = 948 and two
# composites that correlate above .95 because they share most of their items,
# this test has enough power that a change in r in the second decimal place
# can come back at p < .05. Statistical significance here is NOT evidence that
# the objection to the scale has any bite. Only a change large enough to alter
# how a correlation would be described in a sentence would count as that. The
# `diff` column with its zou2007 confidence interval is the quantity to read.
# The p-value is printed because the test produces it, not because it settles
# anything.
#
# DELETION RULE, which differs from the tables above and must not be confused
# with them. steiger_overlap() takes complete cases across all three columns
# at once. It has to: the test treats r_jk, r_jh, r_kh and one n as a
# description of a single covariance matrix -- one table of how each pair of
# the three variables moves together, in one sample. Mixing three different
# subsamples would leave the test undefined. cor_row() above instead uses
# pairwise deletion on two columns.
# The r's printed below are therefore taken from THIS frame, not
# from Table 2, so that the numbers quoted and the test applied to them come
# from one source and cannot drift apart. Where a participant is missing on a
# criterion the two n's will differ, and so, in the third decimal, will the
# two r's.
#
# The spec below carries each row's display label alongside the pair of
# variables it describes, so a row can be added or reordered without any
# lookup further down depending on where that row happens to land.
tier_overlap_spec <- list(
  list(var = "deserved_soft",        crit = "severity_index",
       label = "Severity: registered R1-R4 vs soft R1,R3,R4"),
  list(var = "deserved_soft",        crit = "proportionality_principle",
       label = "Principle: registered R1-R4 vs soft R1,R3,R4"),
  list(var = "deserved_soft_strict", crit = "severity_index",
       label = "Severity: registered R1-R4 vs strict R1,R4"),
  list(var = "deserved_soft_strict", crit = "proportionality_principle",
       label = "Principle: registered R1-R4 vs strict R1,R4"))

tier_overlap <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tier_overlap_spec, function(s)
  steiger_overlap(d, s$crit, "deserved", s$var,
                  alternative = "two.sided", label = s$label)))
# The variant name is carried along so the part-whole line below can be looked
# up by name rather than by row position, which would break the moment a row
# was added or reordered.
tier_overlap$variant <- vapply(tier_overlap_spec, function(s) s$var,
                               character(1))
TABLES[["retribution_tiers_overlap_steiger"]] <- tier_overlap
show_table(tier_overlap,
           "4.3b: Steiger's test for whether dropping an item from the registered desert composite changes what desert tracks.")

# THE PART-WHOLE FIGURE, printed in order to be disarmed. r_kh is the
# correlation between the registered `deserved` and the tier, and the tier is
# made out of `deserved`'s own items, so this is not a finding about
# participants at all. It is a measure of how much of the registered composite
# each tier reproduces. It is printed because a reader who does not see it may
# take the rows above as a second, independent test of the registered claim,
# which they are not.
cat("\nOverlap with the registered `deserved` composite (PART-WHOLE, do not\n")
cat("interpret as a relationship between two measures):\n\n")
for (v in unique(tier_overlap$variant)) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-48s r = %+.3f\n", unname(tier_row_labels[v]),
              tier_overlap$r_kh[tier_overlap$variant == v][1]))
}

# The shifts themselves. An NA anywhere in a row prints as the characters "NA"
# and breaks the column alignment. That is deliberate: a failed test should be
# conspicuous rather than tidy, because a tidy failure is one a reader skims
# past.
cat("\nDropping an item from the registered desert composite moves its tie\n")
cat("to each criterion by:\n\n")
for (i in seq_len(nrow(tier_overlap))) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-45s %+.3f -> %+.3f  change %+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]\n",
              tier_overlap$comparison[i], tier_overlap$r_jk[i],
              tier_overlap$r_jh[i], tier_overlap$diff[i],
              tier_overlap$diff_lower[i], tier_overlap$diff_upper[i]))
}

# THE INTERPRETIVE LINE, guarded on the numbers rather than simply asserted,
# the way 8.3b guards its own. .05 in r is used as the reporting threshold,
# because it is the smallest change that would alter how any correlation in
# the tables above would be described in a sentence. It is a threshold chosen
# here for reading the output and it is NOT a test, which is why the sentence
# below reports the largest observed shift alongside it. If any of the four
# tests failed to return a difference, nothing is concluded at all -- an
# unavailable number is never treated as a passing one.
tier_shift <- abs(tier_overlap$diff)
if (all(!is.na(tier_shift))) {
  if (max(tier_shift) < .05) {
    cat(sprintf(
      "\nThe largest of the four shifts is %.3f in r, under the .05 mark, so\n",
      max(tier_shift)))
    cat("on these criteria the tier an objector accepts carries what the\n")
    cat("registered composite carries, and the placement of R3 does not\n")
    cat("change that. The registered result survives the objection. It is\n")
    cat("not confirmed a second time by an independent measure.\n")
  } else {
    cat(sprintf(
      "\nThe largest of the four shifts is %.3f in r, past the .05 mark, so\n",
      max(tier_shift)))
    cat("at least one registered correlation depends on which items are in\n")
    cat("the desert composite. Read the rows above one at a time.\n")
  }
}
```


## 4.3c The direction of departure

`disproportionality` is the second of the two measures that 4.3 separates out of
the registered proportionality component. It is the mean of two items.
`severity_1` asks whether punishment should exceed the seriousness of the crime,
and it enters as scored, so agreeing raises the score. `severity_2_R` asks
whether punishment should fall short of the harm, and it is reversed, so
rejecting leniency also raises the score. Both halves are keyed the same way,
which is up. Keyed means which answer counts as a high score. The two-sided
version of the same idea is the registered `proportionality_jd`, which reverses
**both** severity items and therefore counts wanting too much and wanting too
little as the same departure.

**The high end is a mixture, and the name overstates it.** About two fifths of
the participants who sit at or above the scale midpoint disagree that punishment
should exceed the crime. Their score is carried by the second item on its own.
What they are doing is refusing punishment below the harm rather than asking for
punishment above it. A high score therefore supports "wants punishment at or
above what the offense warrants, never below", which is a weaker claim than the
word "disproportionality" suggests when it is read cold. The chunk prints the
breakdown so that the reading is checked against the sample rather than assumed
from the name.

The low end carries no such ambiguity. Reaching it takes both answers at once,
disagreeing that punishment should exceed the crime and agreeing that it may
fall below the harm, which is the systematically lenient participant. Someone
who holds punishment to exactly the size of the offense sits near the middle
instead, because refusing sub-proportional punishment, meaning punishment
smaller than the offense, puts them high on the second item.

The scored dataset exported in Phase 10.3 carries this quantity under two column
names, `disproportionality` and `severity_index`, with identical values in every
row.

```{r phase4_disproportionality}
# === THE DIRECTION OF DEPARTURE (prereg 5.4, a deviation) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: writes the direction-of-departure measure under the name
# `disproportionality`, checks it against the column 4.3 builds from the same
# two items, and prints what the high end of the scale is made of.
# WHY IT MATTERS: the name of this measure promises more than the arithmetic
# delivers. The chunk builds the measure AND shows the reader its limits, so
# that nobody reports it as something it is not.

# ================= READ THIS BEFORE USING THE NAME =================
# WARNING ABOUT THE WORD ITSELF. "Disproportionality" sounds two-sided. In
# ordinary use a punishment is disproportionate if it is too big OR too small,
# and a reader meeting the word cold will assume this measure captures both.
# IT DOES NOT. The measure is one-sided by construction:
#
#     disproportionality = rowMeans(severity_1, severity_2_R)
#
#   severity_1    "punishment should EXCEED the seriousness of the crime",
#                 entered as scored, so AGREEING raises the score.
#   severity_2_R  "punishment should be LESS severe than the harm", reversed,
#                 so REJECTING leniency raises the score.
#
# Both halves point up, but they are not the same claim, and the high end of
# the scale therefore holds two kinds of participant. One wants punishment above
# the crime. The other refuses punishment below the harm and is silent about, or
# opposed to, punishment above it. The second kind can be numerous: severity_2_R
# has the higher mean of the pair, so a score above the midpoint is not on its
# own evidence of wanting excess. The breakdown printed below counts the two
# kinds, so the mixture is read off the sample rather than guessed at.
#
# WHAT A HIGH SCORE SUPPORTS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It supports "wants
# punishment at or above what the offense warrants, never below". It does NOT
# support "wants punishment beyond the offense", which a large share of the high
# scorers reject outright on severity_1. LBL_DISPROP below holds the defensible
# wording. Defining it once means the gloss that travels with this measure is
# one object rather than a phrase retyped, and drifting, at each site.
#
# THE TWO-SIDED MEASURE IS A DIFFERENT VARIABLE. It is `proportionality_jd`, the
# registered three-item component built in 4.3, which reverses BOTH severity
# items and therefore counts wanting-too-much and wanting-too-little as the same
# departure. Collapsing the two directions is what makes that component hard to
# interpret, and pulling the direction of departure out into its own measure is
# why 4.3 builds them apart. A table or a sentence that reads this measure as
# two-sided puts that collapse back in.
# ===================================================================

# THE DEFINITION, written out from the raw items rather than pointed at. Two
# reasons for spelling it out. First, it makes this subsection readable on its
# own, so a reader looking the measure up lands on the arithmetic rather than on
# a pointer to somewhere else. Second, it makes the equality check below a real
# test rather than a tautology, meaning a check that could never fail: the two
# columns are computed independently, so if anything upstream ever changes how
# severity_1 or severity_2_R are built, they come apart here and the knit stops.
# Without that, two different numbers would circulate under two names for what
# is supposed to be one measure.
#
# severity_1 enters RAW, never as severity_1_R. The reversed version exists for
# exactly one purpose, the just-deserts proportionality component in 4.3, where
# wanting more than the crime counts as a departure and therefore lowers the
# score. Substituting severity_1_R here would flip the meaning of this measure
# end for end and reverse the sign of every result that uses it.
d$disproportionality <- rowMeans(cbind(d$severity_1, d$severity_2_R),
                                 na.rm = TRUE)
# rowMeans() with na.rm = TRUE returns NaN, not NA, for a participant who
# answered neither item. NaN means "not a number" and NA is R's marker for a
# missing value, and R holds them apart: identical(), which the equality guard
# below runs, reads NaN and NA as different values. Section 4.3 does convert,
# so skipping the conversion here would put the two columns out of agreement
# and stop the knit at that guard. Convert it so missing values behave like
# missing values everywhere downstream. This is the same two-line pattern used
# in 4.3.
d$disproportionality[is.nan(d$disproportionality)] <- NA_real_

# EQUALITY GUARD, AND ITS POSITION. Section 4.3 builds this same quantity from
# the same two items under the name `severity_index`. identical() is the strict
# form of the comparison: same storage type, same length, same values, and the
# missing values, which print as NA, in the same positions. It runs BEFORE the
# assignment below, and that order is load-bearing. After that assignment the
# two columns hold equal values by construction, so the same call would be
# comparing a column with a copy of itself and could never fail.
# The `%in% names(d)` wrapper covers the one case where there is nothing to
# compare against, which is this chunk running without 4.3 ahead of it.
if ("severity_index" %in% names(d)) {
  if (!identical(d$disproportionality, d$severity_index)) {
    stop("disproportionality does not match the severity_index built in 4.3. ",
         "One of the two definitions has drifted. They have to agree before ",
         "anything downstream reads either name.")
  }
}

# THE SECOND COLUMN NAME. Around a dozen lines in this document read this
# quantity as `severity_index`, and the dataset exported in Phase 10.3 goes out
# carrying both names. R copies on assignment, so this line produces a second
# column holding equal values, not a second name for one column: a later change
# to either one does not follow through to the other. The guard above is what
# makes them equal, and it is the only thing that does.
# The absence of a name is not loud here. Ask cor_row() for a column it cannot
# find and it hands back a row of NA, R's marker for a missing value, rather
# than raising an error. The line that does it is
# `if (!all(c(x, y) %in% names(data))) return(out)`, in its definition in Phase
# 0.3. That row then prints into a table looking like a missing finding rather
# than like the mistake it actually is.
d$severity_index <- d$disproportionality

# The display gloss, defined once and used below, so that every place naming
# this measure can state what it is without anyone having to remember to. The
# wording is what the arithmetic supports: at or above, never below.
LBL_DISPROP <- paste("Disproportionality",
                     "(punishment at or above the offense, never below)")

# WHY NO ALPHA IS REPORTED. Cronbach's alpha is a number for how consistently a
# set of items measures one single thing. The two items here correlate at about
# .06. Alpha would come out near zero, and reporting it would announce a failure
# that has not happened. Alpha assumes a REFLECTIVE scale, meaning one where the
# items are interchangeable symptoms of a single underlying trait, so that a low
# value is evidence the trait is not there. This index is FORMATIVE instead:
# wanting punishment above the crime and refusing punishment below the harm are
# two distinct ways of departing upward, and a participant can do either one
# without the other. The composite is the union of two behaviours rather than
# two readings of one behaviour, which is why it correlates more strongly with
# punitiveness, and with desert, than either item does alone. CONSEQUENCE FOR
# REPORTING: both items are shown individually wherever the index is shown, and
# the index is never sent through compute_composite(), which would append a
# meaningless alpha to the reliability table.

# WHAT THE HIGH END IS MADE OF. On a 1-7 agreement scale the midpoint is 4, the
# same threshold H4 reads severity_1 against, and a participant at or above it
# on the index would ordinarily be taken to endorse what the name asserts.
# severity_1 is the item that puts that question directly, so it is read on its
# own within that group: 1 to 3 is disagreement that punishment should exceed
# the crime, 4 is neutral, 5 to 7 is agreement. A large disagreeing block means
# the index is carrying people the bare name misdescribes.
# hi_index is a logical vector, one TRUE or FALSE per participant. A vector is
# just a run of values kept in order. It is TRUE for everyone who has an index
# score at all and whose score is 4 or more. sev1_hi pulls that group's
# severity_1 answers out, and n_hi counts the group.
hi_index <- !is.na(d$disproportionality) & d$disproportionality >= 4
sev1_hi  <- d$severity_1[hi_index]
n_hi     <- sum(hi_index)
# A participant in that group who skipped severity_1 falls into none of the
# three categories, so the shares are taken over those with an answer rather
# than over the whole group and cannot silently fail to add up. Divide by n_hi
# instead and the three percentages would quietly stop adding to 100 as soon as
# anyone in the group had skipped the item.
n_hi_ans  <- sum(!is.na(sev1_hi))
n_reject  <- sum(sev1_hi <= 3, na.rm = TRUE)
n_neutral <- sum(sev1_hi == 4, na.rm = TRUE)
n_endorse <- sum(sev1_hi >  4, na.rm = TRUE)

# The printed panel: the defensible wording for the measure, then each of the
# two items on its own with its mean and standard deviation, then the make-up
# of the high end. The items are shown separately because the index is
# formative, so neither item stands in for the other.
cat("=== DISPROPORTIONALITY ===\n\n")
cat(sprintf("  %s\n", LBL_DISPROP))
cat(sprintf("  %-40s M = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n",
            "severity_1: punish MORE than the crime",
            mean(d$severity_1, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$severity_1, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("  %-40s M = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n",
            "severity_2_R: reject punishing LESS",
            mean(d$severity_2_R, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$severity_2_R, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("  At or above the midpoint of 4: n = %d of %d. On severity_1:\n",
            n_hi, sum(!is.na(d$disproportionality))))
# The three shares only exist if somebody in the high group answered severity_1.
# Without the guard the divisor would be zero, and all three lines would print
# " NaN%" into the table.
if (n_hi_ans > 0) {
  cat(sprintf("    %-38s n = %3d (%4.1f%%)\n",
              "disagree punishment should exceed",
              n_reject, 100 * n_reject / n_hi_ans))
  cat(sprintf("    %-38s n = %3d (%4.1f%%)\n",
              "neutral on punishment exceeding",
              n_neutral, 100 * n_neutral / n_hi_ans))
  cat(sprintf("    %-38s n = %3d (%4.1f%%)\n",
              "agree punishment should exceed",
              n_endorse, 100 * n_endorse / n_hi_ans))
}
# The one-line reading of that breakdown, printed from the counts rather than
# asserted ahead of them, so it stays true whichever way they fall. A sentence
# hard-coded to say "mostly refusing leniency" would become a false statement
# the first time the data moved.
# NOTE FOR THE AUTHORS: there are two branches for three possible outcomes. On
# an exact tie, n_reject == n_endorse, the second branch runs and prints "More
# of the high end is asking for punishment above the crime", which a tie does
# not support. The counts printed above it are correct either way. Whether a
# tie should get its own line is a decision to make, not something to read off
# the code.
if (n_hi_ans > 0 && n_reject > n_endorse) {
  cat("  More of the high end is refusing punishment below the harm than is\n",
      "  asking for punishment above the crime.\n", sep = "")
} else if (n_hi_ans > 0) {
  cat("  More of the high end is asking for punishment above the crime than\n",
      "  is refusing punishment below the harm.\n", sep = "")
}
# A last line in the output confirming that the second column name carries the
# same numbers, so nobody goes hunting for a difference between the two.
cat("  severity_index holds the same values, column for column.\n")
```

## 4.4 The Kantian limits

```{r phase4_kant}
# === THE KANTIAN LIMITS (prereg 5.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the two limit components that are not shared with
# any other composite. The two aggregate limit measures themselves are assembled
# in 4.5, once the emotion composites they need exist.
#
# WHAT A LIMIT IS. The Kantian limits are the restraints that are supposed to
# hold even against someone who is guilty: give the defendant due process,
# convict only on reliable evidence, and judge without hatred or anger. That
# last one is what dispassion means below. The limits are the brakes on
# punishment, not the reasons for it.
#
# WHAT compute_composite() DOES, since every line below calls it. It averages
# the named items for anyone who answered at least half of them, and returns
# that score. It also adds one row to the reliability table. That row carries
# Cronbach's alpha, a number for how consistently a set of items measures one
# single thing, whenever the scale has at least two items. It carries
# McDonald's omega, the same idea estimated from a factor model that does not
# assume every item is an equally good indicator of the thing being measured,
# only when the scale has at least three. A two-item scale therefore gets no
# omega, and the running console line prints a dash where the number would go.
#
# KEYING. Keying is which direction of answer counts as a high score. Every
# limit is scored as WILLINGNESS TO SET THE LIMIT ASIDE, so higher always means
# less restrained and more punitive. That is why dueprocess_2 ("every defendant
# deserves due process") is reversed into the composite while its two permissive
# siblings are not. Read the resulting scale as "how far this person will go",
# not "how much this person values due process" -- H7 and H8's predicted
# directions depend on that reading, and rekeying the limits would flip the sign
# of both.
d$dueprocess <- compute_composite(d, c("dueprocess_1", "dueprocess_2_R", "dueprocess_3"),
                                  "due process (permissive)")
# Reliable evidence, scored as willingness to convict on weak or improper proof.
# Same keying rule as due process: higher means readier to convict anyway.
d$uncertain  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("uncertain_", 1:4), "uncertain evidence")

# THE OVERLAP PROBLEM. Degradation, suffering and prison-violence tolerance are
# limit components AND hostile-aggression constituents, in the same direction.
# Entering them on both sides of one analysis double-counts them: the very same
# answers would sit on both sides, so part of any relationship between the two
# would be those answers agreeing with themselves. So prereg 5.5 restricts the
# limits measure to its non-overlapping parts -- due process, reliable
# evidence, and dispassion -- wherever hostile aggression is also in play. Two
# aggregates are therefore carried, and 4.5 builds both:
#   kant_core       = due process + evidence + dispassion (hatred AND anger)
#   kant_nonoverlap = due process + evidence + anger, dropping hatred, which is
#                     itself one of the five hostile-aggression constituents
# H7, H8 and H20 report both, so the reader can see whether a result survives
# the stricter, non-overlapping definition. A result that showed up only under
# the looser one would be carried by the shared component, hatred, rather than
# by permissiveness about process and evidence.
```

## 4.5 Emotions and harshness

```{r phase4_emotions_harsh}
# === EMOTIONS AND HARSHNESS (prereg 5.7, 5.8) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the six composites that make up most of the
# hostile-aggression cluster, then assembles the two Kantian-limits aggregates
# that need them.
# WHY THE ASSEMBLY WAITS UNTIL HERE: the limits aggregates described in 4.4
# need hatred and anger, and hatred and anger are built in this chunk. Build
# them in 4.4 and `d$hatred` is not there yet. R calls a missing column NULL,
# and cbind() inside zmean() drops a NULL without complaining, so the aggregate
# would be quietly built from the constituents that did exist.

# Hatred does double duty: it is a hostile-aggression constituent AND, reversed,
# it stands in for dispassion among the Kantian limits (prereg 5.7). Judging
# without hatred is the limit, so scoring high on hatred is failing to keep it.
# That double role is precisely why kant_nonoverlap exists.
d$hatred <- compute_composite(d, c("hate_1", "hate_2_R", "hate_3"), "hatred")
# Anger is the other half of dispassion, and the half kant_nonoverlap keeps.
# It can stay because anger is NOT one of the five hostile-aggression
# constituents, which are hatred, revenge, degradation, suffering and
# prison-violence tolerance. Dropping hatred and keeping anger is therefore
# what removes the double count while leaving the limits measure a dispassion
# component to stand on.
d$anger  <- compute_composite(d, paste0("anger_", 1:2), "anger")

# Degradation, suffering and prison-violence tolerance are the three composites
# that belong to both the limits and the hostile-aggression cluster. Each is
# keyed so higher = more willing to see it happen: hence degrad_1 ("prisoners
# deserve dignity") and BOTH prisonvi items are reversed in. Reversed means the
# answer is flipped before averaging, so agreeing that prisoners deserve dignity
# lowers the score. Leave an item pointing the other way and it pulls against
# the rest, so the average runs two opposite meanings together.
d$degradation <- compute_composite(d, c("degrad_1_R", "degrad_2", "degrad_3"), "degradation")
d$suffering   <- compute_composite(d, paste0("suffer_", 1:2), "infliction of suffering")
d$prisonviol  <- compute_composite(d, c("prisonvi_1_R", "prisonvi_2_R"),
                                   "prison-violence tolerance")
# Harsh conditions is an H1 correlate but NOT a hostile-aggression constituent
# (prereg 5.8 lists only degradation, suffering and prison violence there), so
# it stays out of the cluster built in 4.9. Slipping it into that cluster would
# change what H2 tests, which is why 4.9b builds a separate six-part version
# under its own name instead of quietly widening the registered one.
d$harsh       <- compute_composite(d, c("harsh_1", "harsh_2_R", "harsh_3"),
                                   "harsh prison conditions")

# The two limits aggregates, built here rather than in 4.4 because they need the
# emotion composites above. zmean() turns each constituent into a z-score first
# and then averages. A z-score restates a value as how many standard deviations
# it sits above or below the mean of its own column. Doing that first is what
# lets four (or three) composites with different SDs each contribute equally,
# rather than the widest-spread one dominating.
# Note that neither aggregate is passed through compute_composite(), so neither
# appears in the reliability table. They are z-score aggregates across whole
# scales rather than item-level scales, and a Cronbach's alpha over them would
# not mean what alpha usually means.
d$kant_core       <- zmean(d$dueprocess, d$uncertain, d$hatred, d$anger)
d$kant_nonoverlap <- zmean(d$dueprocess, d$uncertain, d$anger)
```

## 4.6 Crime concerns

```{r phase4_crime}
# === CRIME CONCERNS (prereg 5.6) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the two components of the crime-concerns
# cluster, using compute_composite() as described in 4.4.
# WHY IT MATTERS: this cluster is the FOIL in H2. A foil is the rival
# explanation a prediction has to beat. H2 predicts that punitiveness tracks
# hostile aggression more closely than it tracks worry about crime. Without the
# foil, a correlation between punitiveness and hostile aggression would settle
# less, because ordinary worry about crime is a rival account that predicts a
# correlation of its own.
# THE TWO COMPONENTS. 4.9 combines them into the `crime_concerns` cluster,
# because each is a way of being worried about crime: what a person takes the
# crime rate to be, and how afraid a person is. Both rates items enter as
# scored, neither reversed, so a high score is seeing more crime about. fear_1
# asks how safe the respondent feels walking at night, so feeling safe is LOW
# fear and the item is reversed in, meaning the answer is flipped before
# averaging. Left unreversed it would pull against the other two fear items,
# and the average would run feeling safe together with being afraid.
d$crimerates <- compute_composite(d, paste0("rates_", 1:2), "perceived crime rates")
d$fear       <- compute_composite(d, c("fear_1_R", "fear_2", "fear_3"), "fear of crime")
```

## 4.7 Exclusion, essentialism, choice, society

```{r phase4_exclusion}
# === EXCLUSION, ESSENTIALISM, CHOICE, SOCIETY (prereg 5.9) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the four composites behind H16 (essentialism),
# H17 (crime as a choice) and H19 (rejecting society's responsibility). Each is
# built with compute_composite() as described in 4.4.
# Exclusion serves twice: as the social-exclusion correlate in H1/H13 and as the
# HOSTILE reading of solidarity in E2. Prereg 5.3 is explicit that it is never
# entered twice in the same analysis, and it is not. Entering it twice would put
# one column on both sides under two different names.
d$exclusion     <- compute_composite(d, paste0("exclusion_", 1:3), "social exclusion")
# essential_3 ("crime comes from tough life circumstances") is a situational
# explanation, the opposite of an essentialist one. Essentialism here is the
# belief that people who commit crimes are a different kind of person
# underneath, so essential_3 is reversed in and agreeing with it lowers the
# score.
d$essentialism  <- compute_composite(d, c("essential_1", "essential_2",
                                          "essential_3_R", "essential_4"),
                                     "essentialism")
# Crime as a choice, the H17 measure. Both items enter as scored, so a high
# score is treating crime as a freely chosen act. It is worth testing because
# punishing someone for what they deserve assumes an offender who could have
# done otherwise, and H17 predicts retributivists hold that picture more
# strongly than everyone else does (see 9.7).
d$choice        <- compute_composite(d, paste0("choice_", 1:2), "crime as a choice")
# H19 predicts that retributivists REJECT society's responsibility, so the scale
# is keyed in the rejection direction. All three Society items are worded as
# accepting responsibility, so all three are reversed in -- the name
# society_reject is the reminder of which way it points. Read the scale the
# other way round and H19's predicted direction comes out backwards.
d$society_reject <- compute_composite(d, c("Society_1_R", "Society_2_R", "Society_3_R"),
                                      "reject society's responsibility")
```

## 4.8 Personality, CRT, and the remaining single items

```{r phase4_personality}
# === PERSONALITY, CRT, AND THE SINGLE-ITEM MEASURES (prereg 5.10, 5.12, 5.13) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores the four exploratory (E1) personality scales, the
# cognitive reflection score, the binary shark decision used in H15, and the
# prosecution-defense leaning used in H18. "Binary" means a measure with exactly
# two possible values, here yes or no.
#
# `d` is the working table, one row per participant. Every line below adds one
# more scored column to it, built out of the raw survey answers.

# THE FOUR PERSONALITY SCALES. All four are standard published scales, used with
# the wording and the scoring rules their own authors set out. That is exactly
# why they are used. A score on a borrowed scale can be set beside everyone
# else's published scores on the same scale. A set of questions invented for
# this study would have nothing to be set beside.
#
# A REVERSED item is one worded back to front, so that agreeing with it means
# LESS of the thing the scale measures rather than more. Reversed items are
# flipped before they are averaged in, and the `_R` on the end of a column name
# below is the visible record that the flip has already happened. Which items
# get flipped is not our choice. These reversals are specified by each scale's
# own authors and listed in prereg 5.12: RWA (Bizumic & Duckitt 2018, 5 items),
# the SDO7 short form (Ho et al. 2015, 8 items with 3, 4, 7 and 8 reversed),
# violence proneness (4 items), racial resentment (Kinder & Sanders 1996,
# 4 items with 1 and 4 reversed).
#
# GET A FLIP WRONG AND NOTHING BREAKS. R will average the item the wrong way
# round, print no error and no warning, and hand back a scale score that means
# the opposite of what its name says. That silence is the reason the flips
# follow the published list and nothing else.
d$rwa        <- compute_composite(d, c("rwa_1", "rwa_2", "rwa_3_R", "rwa_4", "rwa_5"), "RWA")
d$sdo        <- compute_composite(d, c("sdo_1", "sdo_2", "sdo_3_R", "sdo_4_R",
                                       "sdo_5", "sdo_6", "sdo_7_R", "sdo_8_R"), "SDO7")
d$vprone     <- compute_composite(d, paste0("vprone_", 1:4), "violence proneness")
d$raceresent <- compute_composite(d, c("Raceresent_1_R", "Raceresent_2",
                                       "Raceresent_3", "Raceresent_4_R"),
                                  "racial resentment")

# CRT is the Cognitive Reflection Test: three short puzzles, each built so that
# one answer leaps to mind and is wrong, and the right answer arrives only if
# you stop and check. The score is the count of correct answers, 0 to 3, so
# higher = more reflective (prereg 5.12). It is here because E1 asks whether
# retributive judgment goes with the quick answer rather than the checked one.
#
# The three standard items and their REFLECTIVE answers are the bat-and-ball
# (5 cents, against the intuitive 10), the widget machines (5 minutes, against
# 100), and the lily pads (47 days, against 24).
#
# These items were answered on numeric sliders, so what is stored IS the number
# the participant gave, and it can be compared with the right answer directly.
# The attention checks are not like that. Their stored values are option codes,
# numbers that stand for answer choices rather than for quantities, so testing
# them this way would compare against the wrong thing entirely.
#
# Each comparison returns a logical, R's TRUE/FALSE value. Summing logicals
# coerces them to numbers, coercion being R's silent conversion of a value from
# one type to another. Every TRUE becomes 1 and every FALSE becomes 0, so the
# sum IS the 0-3 count of correct answers and no separate counting step is
# needed.
d$CRT <- (d$CRT_1 == 5) + (d$CRT_2 == 5) + (d$CRT_3 == 47)

# BOTH SCORINGS ARE CARRIED, BECAUSE ONE ITEM REACHED PARTICIPANTS BROKEN. The
# lily-pad slider was labelled "Minutes" while its answer, 47, is in days. So
# that item went out with the wrong unit printed on it. `CRT` keeps all three
# items and is the registered scoring (prereg 5.12). `CRT_2item` throws the
# mislabelled item away and keeps the other two. Every analysis that uses
# cognitive reflection is run on BOTH scorings. A reader can then see whether
# the wording defect is doing any of the work in a result, instead of being
# asked to take one scoring on faith.
d$CRT_2item <- (d$CRT_1 == 5) + (d$CRT_2 == 5)

cat(sprintf("  %-34s 0-3, mean = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n", "CRT correct (registered)",
            mean(d$CRT, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$CRT, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("  %-34s 0-2, mean = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n", "CRT correct (lily pad dropped)",
            mean(d$CRT_2item, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$CRT_2item, na.rm = TRUE)))

# The share of people who got each item right, printed one item at a time. It
# puts the mislabelled lily-pad item's own pass rate in front of the reader.
# The item can then be judged on how it behaved, rather than on the typo alone.
cat(sprintf("  per-item correct: bat-and-ball %.1f%%, widgets %.1f%%, lily pads %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(d$CRT_1 == 5,  na.rm = TRUE),
            100 * mean(d$CRT_2 == 5,  na.rm = TRUE),
            100 * mean(d$CRT_3 == 47, na.rm = TRUE)))

# The shark decision (prereg 5.10), the yes-or-no outcome in H15. The stored
# values are option codes, numbers standing for answer choices: 1 = "No, do not
# put it to death", 2 = "Yes, put it to death". They are recoded to 0/1 because
# logit_reg() and prop_ci() both expect a 0/1 indicator, a column where 1 means
# the thing happened and 0 means it did not.
#
# logit_reg() runs the logistic regression H15 calls for, which is the kind of
# regression built for a yes-or-no outcome. prop_ci() puts a confidence
# interval, a range of plausible values, around the percentage saying yes.
# Handed the raw 1/2 codes, prop_ci() would count every answer as a yes,
# because it counts any value above 0 as an endorsement.
#
# WHY A SHARK, of all things. A shark can neither be deterred nor reformed, and
# it has no human agency, no capacity to choose. So a vote to put it to death
# cannot be defended as forward-looking: there is no future behaviour to
# discourage and no character to improve. That is what makes the item useful.
d$shark_kill <- as.integer(d$Shark_1 == 2)
cat(sprintf("  %-34s %.1f%% say yes\n", "shark: put it to death",
            100 * mean(d$shark_kill, na.rm = TRUE)))

# Prosecution-defense leaning (H18; prereg 5.13). The two items ask who the
# respondent identifies with in a real trial and which role they would rather
# serve.
#
# The option codes are 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense, 3 = about the same. That
# ordering is nominal, meaning the numbers are name tags for the answers and
# carry no sense of low-to-high. Averaging the codes as they stand would treat
# 3, "about the same", as further toward the defense than 2, the defense answer
# itself. The neutral answer would come out as the most pro-defense one, which
# is nonsense.
#
# Recoding to +1 / -1 / 0 puts the neutral option in the middle where it
# belongs. The mean of the two items then runs from -1 (defense on both) through
# 0 to +1 (prosecution on both), which is a scale a reader can interpret at
# sight.
recode_lean <- function(x) dplyr::case_when(x == 1 ~ 1, x == 2 ~ -1, x == 3 ~ 0,
                                            TRUE ~ NA_real_)
d$leanPros <- rowMeans(cbind(recode_lean(d$leanPros_1), recode_lean(d$leanPros_2)),
                       na.rm = TRUE)
# Someone who answered neither item leaves rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) with nothing
# to average, and it returns NaN for that row, not NA. NaN is "not a number",
# what R hands back from an impossible arithmetic step. NA_real_ is R's marker
# for a number that is simply missing. is.na() reports TRUE for both, but they
# are still two different values. Turn such a column into text or into a factor
# and NaN becomes a category of its own, spelled "NaN", while NA stays missing.
# This line puts the column on one missing marker, the same idiom
# compute_composite() uses on its all-NA rows.
d$leanPros[is.nan(d$leanPros)] <- NA_real_
cat(sprintf("  %-34s mean = %.2f (-1 defense .. +1 prosecution)\n",
            "prosecution leaning", mean(d$leanPros, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

## 4.9 Cluster aggregates for the Steiger comparisons

```{r phase4_clusters}
# === CLUSTER AGGREGATES FOR THE STEIGER COMPARISONS (prereg 5.6, 5.8) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the two clusters H2 pits against each other, and
# names the hostile reading of solidarity used in E2. Also records alpha and
# omega for the two clusters in the reliability table.
#
# A cluster here is a single score made by averaging several separate measures,
# so that a broad idea like "hostility toward offenders" can be one number
# instead of five.
#
# Both clusters are means of Z-SCORED constituents. A z-score restates a value
# as how many standard deviations above or below the sample average it sits, so
# measures on different scales become directly comparable. This is not cosmetic.
# H2 compares two correlations, and if one cluster were dominated by whichever
# component happens to have the largest raw SD -- the standard deviation, the
# usual measure of how spread out a set of values is -- part of what the
# comparison picked up would be scaling rather than content.
#
# Membership follows the plan exactly. Hostile aggression is hatred, revenge,
# degradation, suffering and prison-violence tolerance -- five composites.
# Harsh conditions is deliberately NOT among them: it is an H1 correlate, but
# prereg 5.8 assigns only the first three of the harshness measures to the
# cluster. Adding it would change what H2 tests, which is not a change anyone
# gets to make after the fact.
d$hostile_agg    <- zmean(d$hatred, d$revenge, d$degradation, d$suffering, d$prisonviol)
d$crime_concerns <- zmean(d$crimerates, d$fear)
# E2 reads the solidarity items two ways; the hostile reading IS the exclusion
# composite (prereg 5.3). It is aliased rather than recomputed, aliasing being
# the giving of a second name to the same column. So the two names always hold
# identical values, and the E2 call site reads as the hypothesis does.
d$solidarity_hostile <- d$exclusion   # E2: the hostile reading of solidarity

cat(sprintf("hostile aggression cluster: M = %.2f, SD = %.2f (n = %d)\n",
            mean(d$hostile_agg, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$hostile_agg, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(!is.na(d$hostile_agg))))
cat(sprintf("crime concerns cluster:     M = %.2f, SD = %.2f (n = %d)\n",
            mean(d$crime_concerns, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$crime_concerns, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(!is.na(d$crime_concerns))))

# RELIABILITY OF THE TWO CLUSTERS. Cronbach's alpha asks how consistently a set
# of measures moves together, and McDonald's omega asks the same question
# without assuming that every measure captures the underlying idea equally well.
# The plan asks for both beside every composite, so both are recorded here.
#
# They are computed over the z-scored constituents rather than over raw survey
# items, because these are scale-level aggregates: the "items" whose consistency
# is being estimated are the composites themselves. compute_composite() cannot
# do this job, because its scoring rule is a row-mean of raw item columns, so
# the two rows are assembled here and appended to the table directly.
#
# The k >= 3 rule for omega is the same one compute_composite() applies, where k
# is the number of parts. A single-factor omega is not identified with only two
# parts -- there is not enough information in the data to pin the model down --
# so the two-component crime-concerns cluster gets alpha only.
for (cl in list(list("hostile aggression cluster",
                     c("hatred", "revenge", "degradation", "suffering", "prisonviol")),
                list("crime concerns cluster", c("crimerates", "fear")))) {
  mm <- as.data.frame(scale(d[, cl[[2]]]))
  aa <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::alpha(mm, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_)
  oo <- if (ncol(mm) >= 3) tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::omega(mm, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_) else NA_real_
  # mean and sd are left as NA, R's marker for a missing value, on purpose. Each
  # cluster is a mean of z-scores, so its average is about 0 no matter what the
  # participants said. Printing that number would tell a reader nothing.
  alpha_table <- rbind(alpha_table, data.frame(
    composite = cl[[1]], k = length(cl[[2]]), alpha = aa, omega = oo,
    mean = NA_real_, sd = NA_real_, n = sum(stats::complete.cases(mm)),
    items = paste(cl[[2]], collapse = ", "), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
}
```
## 4.9b The hostile aggression cluster with harsh conditions included

Section 4.9 builds the hostile-aggression cluster with exactly the five
constituents the registration names: hatred, revenge, degradation, infliction of
suffering, and tolerance of prison violence. A constituent is one of the
separate measures that get averaged together to make the cluster score. Harsh
prison conditions sits outside it, because prereg 5.8 puts only three of the
four harshness measures inside the cluster -- degradation, suffering and
prison-violence tolerance -- and both H2 and H13 are tested on the cluster as
registered.

There is a substantive case for a sixth constituent. Harsh conditions is one of
the twelve H1 correlates. It is scored from the same sort of survey items as
degradation and tolerance of prison violence. And it asks about the same thing
the other five ask about: how much unpleasantness a convicted offender should be
made to absorb. If punitiveness is a single coherent outlook rather than a
bundle of loosely related attitudes, harsh conditions ought to sit with the
other five about as closely as those five sit with one another.

This subsection builds that six-constituent version beside the registered one.
It then shows both against three things: punitiveness, the sentence the
participant actually handed down, and the crime-concerns cluster that H2
contrasts the hostile cluster with. The two versions share five of their six
constituents. What follows is therefore a rescoring of one cluster, not a second
and independent measure of it, and how closely the two agree is printed rather
than left to be assumed. It is a deviation from the registration. Nothing
registered is displaced: `hostile_agg` keeps its five constituents and its
value, and it stays the cluster on which H2 and H13 are tested.

```{r phase4_clusters6}
# === HOSTILE AGGRESSION WITH HARSH CONDITIONS (companion to 4.9) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `hostile_agg6`, the hostile-aggression cluster
# with harsh prison conditions as a sixth constituent, records its alpha and
# omega in the reliability table, prints the five- and six-constituent versions
# side by side against punitiveness, the sentence and crime concerns, and
# separates the part of the reliability difference that is about coherence from
# the part that is about length.
# PREREG: a companion to 5.8, reported alongside the registered five-constituent
#         cluster and never in place of it.
# CONSUMES: hatred, revenge, degradation, suffering, prisonviol, harsh (all from
#           4.5), hostile_agg and crime_concerns (4.9), punitiveness (4.2),
#           Sentence1_z (3.2).
#
# WARNING TO ANYONE EDITING THIS DOCUMENT. `hostile_agg` in 4.9 is the
# registered cluster. It is the k in H2's Steiger test (7.2) -- the letter that
# test uses for the hostile cluster -- and it is an outcome row in the master
# contrast set that carries H13 (9.3, 9.4). BOTH were registered on the
# five-constituent definition. Adding "harsh" to the zmean() call in 4.9, or
# pointing either of those call sites at `hostile_agg6`, would silently change a
# pre-registered result: the numbers would still print, and they would no longer
# be the test that was promised. The six-constituent version travels under its
# own name for exactly that reason, and every registered call site keeps
# pointing at `hostile_agg`.

# Same construction rule as 4.9: a mean of Z-SCORED constituents. A z-score
# restates each part as how many standard deviations it sits above or below the
# sample average, so no part can dominate the cluster merely because its raw
# spread happens to be the widest. zmean() standardises each argument across the
# whole sample first and then averages row-wise, and that order of operations is
# what puts the six on an equal footing.
#
# QUIRK, RESTATED HERE BECAUSE IT MATTERS FOR THE n. zmean() averages over
# whatever a participant answered, so a person is scored NA -- R's marker for a
# missing value -- only if they are missing EVERY constituent. That means
# `hostile_agg6` is defined for at least as many people as `hostile_agg`:
# someone who answered the harshness items and none of the other five has a
# five-constituent score of NA and a six-constituent score. The two versions can
# therefore rest on slightly different numbers of people. That is why every n is
# printed below rather than assumed to match.
d$hostile_agg6 <- zmean(d$hatred, d$revenge, d$degradation, d$suffering,
                        d$prisonviol, d$harsh)

cat(sprintf("hostile aggression, 6 parts: M = %.2f, SD = %.2f (n = %d)\n",
            mean(d$hostile_agg6, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$hostile_agg6, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(!is.na(d$hostile_agg6))))
cat(sprintf("hostile aggression, 5 parts: M = %.2f, SD = %.2f (n = %d)\n",
            mean(d$hostile_agg, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$hostile_agg, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(!is.na(d$hostile_agg))))

# RELIABILITY OF THE SIX. Computed exactly the way 4.9 computes it for the two
# registered clusters: over the z-scored constituents rather than over raw
# items, because these are scale-level aggregates and the "items" whose
# consistency is at issue are the composites themselves. compute_composite()
# cannot be used, since its scoring rule is a row-mean of RAW item columns.
#
# Alpha is Cronbach's alpha, which asks how consistently a set of measures moves
# together. Omega is McDonald's omega, which asks the same question without
# assuming that every measure carries the underlying construct equally well.
# Both are reported because prereg 5.1 asks for both. Six constituents sits
# comfortably above the k >= 3 floor for omega. Below that floor a single-factor
# omega is not identified: there is too little information in the data to pin
# the model down. So omega is available here, where it was not for the
# two-component crime-concerns cluster.
#
# check.keys = FALSE, matching 4.9. Every constituent is already keyed so that
# higher means more willing to see the offender treated badly. Letting psych
# decide for itself which components to flip, on the evidence of their
# correlations, would quietly redefine what the cluster measures.
#
# The whole psych::alpha object is kept rather than only $total$raw_alpha,
# because two further quantities from that same call carry the comparison at the
# end of this chunk: $total$average_r, the mean correlation among the
# constituents, and $alpha.drop, which reports the scale recomputed with each
# constituent in turn taken out of it.
hostile6_parts <- c("hatred", "revenge", "degradation", "suffering",
                    "prisonviol", "harsh")
mm6 <- as.data.frame(scale(d[, hostile6_parts]))
aa6_obj <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::alpha(mm6, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE))),
  error = function(e) NULL)
aa6 <- if (is.null(aa6_obj)) NA_real_ else aa6_obj$total$raw_alpha
oo6 <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::omega(mm6, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)

# WHERE THIS CHUNK HAS TO SIT, AND WHY IT CANNOT MOVE. 4.10 takes a COPY of
# alpha_table into `alpha_table_out`, and every export downstream reads that
# copy. A row appended after 4.10 would print on screen here and reach no file
# at all. Between 4.9 and 4.10 is the placement that works, and appending after
# every registered row leaves each of those rows at the position it already had.
#
# WHAT THIS SUBSECTION PLACES IN THE SHIPPED OUTPUTS, none of it in place of
# anything: one row at the foot of the reliability table, which travels to
# output/tables/reliability_alpha_omega.csv and to
# data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv and is counted in the "Composites scored"
# line 10.4 reads off nrow(alpha_table_out); and one column, `hostile_agg6`,
# which travels in d_export to data/cleaned/retribution_scored.csv and .rds and
# so into the column count 10.3 prints.
#
# mean and sd are left NA for the same reason as in 4.9: the cluster is a mean
# of z-scores, so its mean is about 0 no matter what the participants said, and
# reporting that would say nothing about the measure.
#
# The n recorded here counts participants complete on all six constituents,
# matching what 4.9 records for the two registered clusters. It describes the
# sample behind the row. It is NOT the denominator behind alpha, because
# psych::alpha builds its covariance matrix PAIRWISE (its default is
# use = "pairwise"), so each pair of constituents contributes everyone who
# answered both.
alpha_table <- rbind(alpha_table, data.frame(
  composite = "hostile aggression cluster (6 constituents)",
  k = length(hostile6_parts), alpha = aa6, omega = oo6,
  mean = NA_real_, sd = NA_real_,
  n = sum(stats::complete.cases(mm6)),
  items = paste(hostile6_parts, collapse = ", "), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))

# The five-constituent alpha and omega are READ OUT of the row 4.9 wrote, never
# recomputed here. Recomputing would risk this companion table and the published
# reliability table in 4.10 printing two different numbers for the same cluster
# if anything about the scoring ever drifted. The match is on the exact label
# string 4.9 uses, so the six-constituent row just appended -- whose label
# carries a suffix -- cannot be picked up by mistake.
reg5 <- alpha_table[alpha_table$composite == "hostile aggression cluster", ]

# Labels used in both tables below, defined once so the two cannot disagree.
lab5 <- "Hostile aggression, 5 constituents (registered)"
lab6 <- "Hostile aggression, 6 constituents (companion)"

# THE THREE COMPARISONS, RUN FOR EACH VERSION.
#
# Punitiveness here is the 8-item SELF-REPORT scale and deliberately not
# `punitiveness_full`. The full index embeds Sentence1_z, and the sentence is
# itself one of the three outcomes below, so using the full index would put the
# sentence on both sides of a correlation. Part of the result would then be the
# sentence agreeing with itself, which happens for arithmetic reasons whatever
# the participants think. Prereg 5.11 forbids precisely that. None of the eight
# punitiveness items is a constituent of either cluster, so these are
# correlations between measures that share no content.
#
# The sentence enters as Sentence1_z, the first sentence standardised WITHIN
# vignette (3.2). The raw sentence cannot be used across the sample, because the
# three vignettes describe different crimes and carry different sentence ranges.
# A raw correlation would partly be a correlation with which vignette a
# participant happened to be shown, rather than with how harsh that participant
# was.
#
# All six rows are two-sided. For a correlation that means the test allows an
# association away from zero in either direction, positive or negative. This is
# a descriptive comparison of two scorings of one cluster, not a directional
# prediction, so there is no one side to test on.
lab_punit <- "Punitiveness (8 items)"
lab_sent  <- "Sentence 1 (z within vignette)"
lab_crime <- "Crime concerns cluster (z)"
hostile6_rows <- list(
  reg_punit = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg", "punitiveness",
                      label_x = lab5, label_y = lab_punit),
  reg_sent  = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg", "Sentence1_z",
                      label_x = lab5, label_y = lab_sent),
  reg_crime = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
                      label_x = lab5, label_y = lab_crime),
  six_punit = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg6", "punitiveness",
                      label_x = lab6, label_y = lab_punit),
  six_sent  = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg6", "Sentence1_z",
                      label_x = lab6, label_y = lab_sent),
  six_crime = cor_row(d, "hostile_agg6", "crime_concerns",
                      label_x = lab6, label_y = lab_crime))
# unname() before rbind: the list above is named so its values can be looked up
# by name further down, and do.call(rbind, ...) on a NAMED list of one-row
# frames would carry those names through as row names in the printed table.
# Every other do.call(rbind, ...) in this document feeds either an unnamed
# list() or an lapply(), so the result frames all carry the default integer row
# names, and stripping the names here keeps this one looking like the rest.
hostile6_cors <- do.call(rbind, unname(hostile6_rows))
TABLES[["hostile_cluster_six_correlations"]] <- hostile6_cors
show_table(hostile6_cors[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
                             "p_two")],
           paste("4.9b: the two versions of the hostile cluster against",
                 "punitiveness, the sentence, and crime concerns."))

# The short comparison this subsection exists to make: reliability and the three
# correlations, one row per version. The correlations are pulled out of the
# named list above rather than by row number, so inserting or reordering a row
# cannot quietly drop a value into the wrong cell.
#
# n_alpha is the complete-case count each reliability row carries -- the number
# of people with no missing value on any of the parts. It is printed for two
# reasons. The two rows count over different sets of columns, so a participant
# missing only the harshness items counts toward the registered row and not
# toward the companion. And it is a description of the sample beside each alpha,
# not the alpha's own denominator.
#
# If the 4.9 label were ever changed, reg5 would be an empty selection.
# reg5$alpha[1] would then return NA rather than throwing an error. The table
# still prints, and the missing value is visible in it instead of being
# silently wrong.
hostile6_compare <- data.frame(
  cluster          = c(lab5, lab6),
  k                = c(reg5$k[1], length(hostile6_parts)),
  alpha            = c(reg5$alpha[1], aa6),
  omega            = c(reg5$omega[1], oo6),
  n_alpha          = c(reg5$n[1], sum(stats::complete.cases(mm6))),
  r_punitiveness   = c(hostile6_rows$reg_punit$r, hostile6_rows$six_punit$r),
  r_sentence1_z    = c(hostile6_rows$reg_sent$r,  hostile6_rows$six_sent$r),
  r_crime_concerns = c(hostile6_rows$reg_crime$r, hostile6_rows$six_crime$r),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["hostile_cluster_six_reliability"]] <- hostile6_compare
show_table(hostile6_compare,
           paste("4.9b: five- and six-constituent hostile aggression side by",
                 "side. The registered cluster is the first row."))

# HOW TO READ THE n IN THESE TABLES AGAINST H2. The correlations above are
# PAIRWISE: each one is computed on everyone who answered both variables in that
# row. The r_jk that H2 reports in 7.2 is computed on the participants who are
# complete on all three of punitiveness, hostile aggression and crime concerns
# at once, because Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations
# describes a single covariance matrix and needs a single n. The two can differ
# in the last decimal without either being wrong.

# The two versions share five of their six constituents, so they are very nearly
# the same variable. That is printed rather than assumed, because a reader is
# entitled to know how much of the comparison above is a real difference and how
# much of it is arithmetic that was settled before any data arrived.
r_5_6 <- cor_row(d, "hostile_agg", "hostile_agg6")
if (!is.na(r_5_6$r)) {
  cat(sprintf("\nThe two versions correlate r = %.3f (n = %d).\n",
              r_5_6$r, r_5_6$n))
  cat("Five of the six constituents are shared, so a high value here is near\n")
  cat("identity by construction and is not a finding.\n")
}

# WHAT ADDING HARSH CONDITIONS DOES TO THE COHERENCE OF THE CLUSTER.
#
# Cronbach's alpha on its own cannot answer that, and the difference between the
# two alphas MUST NOT be read as though it could. Alpha rises with the NUMBER of
# constituents even when the level of agreement among them does not budge:
# alpha = k * rbar / (1 + (k - 1) * rbar), where k is the number of constituents
# and rbar ("r bar") is the mean correlation among them. A sixth measure of
# almost any kind would push alpha up. The length-free quantity is rbar itself.
# So the informative comparison is between the alpha actually obtained with six
# constituents and the alpha six constituents would have produced had rbar not
# moved at all.
#
# rbar and alpha for the registered five are taken from $alpha.drop, the row for
# harsh, which is the scale recomputed without it. That row is a
# five-constituent quantity from this same call: psych::alpha works from a
# pairwise covariance matrix, and the block of that matrix belonging to the
# five shared constituents does not depend on whether a sixth column sits
# beside them. Taking both figures from one call is what keeps the comparison
# free of the sample and scoring differences that can separate quantities drawn
# from two calls.
#
# The formula above is exact rather than approximate here only because the
# constituents are z-scored, which makes Cronbach's raw alpha and the
# standardized alpha the same number.
if (!is.null(aa6_obj) && "harsh" %in% rownames(aa6_obj$alpha.drop)) {
  rbar5 <- aa6_obj$alpha.drop["harsh", "average_r"]
  rbar6 <- aa6_obj$total$average_r
  a5    <- aa6_obj$alpha.drop["harsh", "raw_alpha"]
  k6    <- length(hostile6_parts)
  a6_at_rbar5 <- k6 * rbar5 / (1 + (k6 - 1) * rbar5)
  cat(sprintf("\nMean correlation among the constituents: %.3f with five,",
              rbar5))
  cat(sprintf(" %.3f with six.\n", rbar6))
  cat(sprintf("Alpha: %.3f with five, %.3f with six. Six constituents at the\n",
              a5, aa6))
  cat(sprintf("five-constituent mean correlation would give %.3f, so it is\n",
              a6_at_rbar5))
  cat("the distance from that figure to the six-constituent alpha, and not\n")
  cat("the distance between the two alphas, that is about coherence.\n")
  # The drop-one figure and the alpha in the table above describe the same five
  # measures only for as long as 4.9's constituent list and hostile6_parts stay
  # in step. They come from two separate psych::alpha calls, so any divergence
  # between them is reported out loud rather than assumed away.
  if (!is.na(reg5$alpha[1]) && abs(reg5$alpha[1] - a5) > .0005) {
    cat(sprintf("The reliability table reports alpha = %.3f for the\n",
                reg5$alpha[1]))
    cat("registered five, so the two calls no longer describe the same\n")
    cat("constituents.\n")
  }
}
```

## 4.10 Reliability table (Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω)

```{r phase4_alpha_table}
# === THE RELIABILITY TABLE (prereg 5.1, 6.1) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: formats the alpha_table accumulated across Phase 4 into
# `alpha_table_out`, exports it as output/tables/reliability_alpha_omega.csv and
# again as data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv in Phase 10.3, and flags any
# composite whose alpha falls below .60.
#
# The plan asks for a reliability coefficient beside every composite, and for
# both Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega. Alpha asks how consistently the
# items in a scale move together; omega asks the same thing without assuming
# every item measures the construct equally well. Reporting them tells a reader
# how much to trust each score before reading any result built on it.
#
# Column order is fixed here rather than left to chance, so the exported table
# comes out the same way every time the document is knitted.
alpha_table_out <- alpha_table[, c("composite", "k", "alpha", "omega",
```
