```{r phase4_alpha_table}
                                   "mean", "sd", "n", "items")]
TABLES[["reliability_alpha_omega"]] <- alpha_table_out
show_table(alpha_table_out[, c("composite", "k", "alpha", "omega", "mean", "sd", "n")],
           "Reliability of every composite: Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega (prereg 5.1). Omega is reported for k >= 3; a single-factor omega is not identified with two items.")

# .60 is a conventional floor for treating a scale as internally consistent
# enough to interpret. It is a REPORTING threshold, not an exclusion rule: no
# composite is dropped for falling below it, and the plan sets no such rule.
# One low value is expected, and it is the point rather than a problem -- H6
# predicts that the two parts of just deserts will NOT form a reliable scale, so
# a low alpha there is the hypothesis coming true, not a fault to be patched.
low_rel <- alpha_table_out[!is.na(alpha_table_out$alpha) &
                             alpha_table_out$alpha < .60, ]
if (nrow(low_rel)) {
  cat("\nComposites with alpha < .60 (interpret with care):\n")
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(low_rel)))
    cat(sprintf("  %-34s alpha = %.3f (k = %d)\n",
                low_rel$composite[i], low_rel$alpha[i], low_rel$k[i]))
} else {
  cat("\nNo composite falls below alpha = .60.\n")
}
```

# PHASE 5: THE RETRIBUTIVIST MEASURES

Who counts as a retributivist? There is no single right answer, so the plan
(prereg 5.3) sets out three measures and treats them as convergent rather than
interchangeable. Convergent means we expect them to point the same way, not
that we expect them to pick out exactly the same people. If we used only one,
and that one happened to be the wrong one, every conclusion would rest on that
single choice and no reader could tell.

  1. **Categorical (primary)** -- ranks *"criminals deserve to be punished"*
     first among the four goals of punishment. This asks what a person puts
     ahead of everything else, not how strongly they agree with anything.
  2. **Continuous (primary)** -- the **relative** retribution subscale:
     retribution minus the mean of deterrence, incapacitation, and
     rehabilitation. It scores everyone on a sliding scale instead of sorting
     them into two boxes. A **median split** (cut the sample in half at its
     middle value) and **tertiles** (cut it into three equal-sized thirds) on
     this subscale give categorical versions of it.
  3. **Behavioral** -- the **sentencing ratio**, `Sentence2 / Sentence1` for
     participants whose first sentence was above zero. This one rests on what
     people did, not on what they said about themselves. A higher ratio (a
     smaller reduction once the forward-looking reasons are removed) is the
     more retributive motive.

## 5.1 Categorical: the goal ranking

```{r phase5_categorical}
# === THE PRIMARY CATEGORICAL DEFINITION (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: creates `retributivist` (0/1) and `grp_rank` (the
# two-level factor used for every primary contrast in Phase 9), and reports the
# distribution of ranks given to retribution. A factor is R's type for a
# grouping variable: a set of named categories held in a declared order.
#
# Prioritization_1 to _4 hold the RANK a participant assigned to each of the
# four goals, not a rating. A low number means high priority, so 1 is first
# place. Prioritization_1 is the rank given to "criminals deserve to be
# punished", so == 1 means retribution was placed first. A retributivist by
# this definition is someone who put desert above deterrence, incapacitation
# and rehabilitation -- prioritizing it, not merely endorsing it.
#
# That distinction carries the whole measure. Rating each goal on its own lets
# a person endorse all four at once, so agreement alone never shows which goal
# they would give up to keep another. A ranking forces exactly that choice, and
# the registered definition is about the choice.
d$retributivist <- as.integer(d$Prioritization_1 == 1)

# The full rank distribution, not just the share at rank 1, so a reader can see
# where retribution sits for the other three quarters of the sample. A person
# who ranks retribution second is very different from one who ranks it last,
# and a lone "this many put it first" figure hides that difference completely.
# useNA = "ifany" adds a row labelled NA if any participant did not supply a
# ranking. NA is R's marker for a missing value. The row keeps missing people
# visible in the table instead of letting them vanish from it.
rank_tab <- as.data.frame(table(Rank_given_to_retribution = d$Prioritization_1,
                                useNA = "ifany"))
rank_tab$Percent <- 100 * rank_tab$Freq / sum(rank_tab$Freq)
show_table(rank_tab, "Rank assigned to retribution ('criminals deserve to be punished')")

cat(sprintf("\nRetributivists (ranked retribution first): %d / %d (%.1f%%)\n",
            sum(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(d$retributivist)),
            100 * mean(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE)))

# === WHICH OF THE FOUR GOALS CAME FIRST ===
# The table above reads down one column: where retribution landed. This one
# reads across all four, and it is the version the write-up quotes, because it
# sets the 39.1% retribution figure beside its competition instead of leaving
# it to stand alone. A percentage with nothing to compare it to can be told as
# either a large story or a small one.
#
# It also double-checks the coding of Prioritization_1 from the other
# direction. The count of participants whose rank-1 goal is retribution must
# equal the retributivist count printed above, and stopifnot() enforces that:
# it halts the whole document the moment the claim is false. That is what we
# want here. A silent mismatch would mean every retributivist comparison in the
# paper was run on the wrong set of people, and nothing on the page would look
# wrong.
#
# Prioritization_1..4 are the ranks given to the four choices in instrument
# order: 1 desert, 2 deterrence, 3 incapacitation, 4 rehabilitation. That order
# is what lets column position stand in for goal name below.
prio_cols   <- paste0("Prioritization_", 1:4)
goal_labels <- c("Criminals deserve to be punished (retribution)",
                 "Punishment deters others (deterrence)",
                 "Locked up, prisoners cannot offend (incapacitation)",
                 "Prisoners get rehabilitated (rehabilitation)")

# A valid ranking is a permutation of 1:4: each of the four numbers used once
# and once only. Every such row must therefore sum to 10, because 1+2+3+4 = 10.
# A row that does not is malformed and would quietly distort every count below.
# na.rm = FALSE is the careful choice: a row with a missing rank comes out NA
# rather than being totalled from whichever ranks happen to be present, which
# would pass as a smaller, innocent-looking number.
prio_sums <- rowSums(d[, prio_cols], na.rm = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("Rankings that are a valid permutation of 1-4 (row sum 10): %d of %d\n",
            sum(prio_sums == 10, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(d)))

# For each participant, which of the four columns holds rank 1. apply() with
# the 1 in the middle runs the function once per row, handing it that row as a
# vector (a simple run of values) called r. A row with any missing rank, or
# with no 1 anywhere in it, returns NA_integer_ rather than a guess. A broken
# ranking is therefore recorded as unknown instead of credited to a goal.
first_choice <- apply(d[, prio_cols], 1, function(r) {
  if (anyNA(r) || !any(r == 1)) return(NA_integer_)
  which(r == 1)[1]
})
ranked_first <- data.frame(
  goal    = goal_labels,
  n       = as.integer(table(factor(first_choice, levels = 1:4))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ranked_first$percent <- 100 * ranked_first$n / sum(ranked_first$n)
# order() on the negated counts sorts them from largest down, so the goal
# chosen first by the most participants becomes the top row of the table.
ranked_first <- ranked_first[order(-ranked_first$n), ]
show_table(ranked_first, "Which goal each participant ranked first")
TABLES[["goal_ranked_first"]] <- ranked_first

# === THE FULL RANK DISTRIBUTION: EVERY GOAL AT EVERY POSITION ===
# Rank 1 alone hides the shape of the ordering. A goal can lead the field and
# still be divisive, collecting many firsts AND many lasts, and a goal almost
# nobody ranks first can still be the consensus second choice. Both of those
# are invisible if we only count first places.
#
# Each row below is one goal and sums to 948; each column is one position and
# also sums to 948. Mean rank is the average position a goal was given, on the
# same 1-to-4 scale, and it summarises a whole row in one number. That lets the
# four goals be ordered overall rather than only by their share of firsts.
rank_matrix <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(prio_cols), function(j) {
  counts <- table(factor(d[[prio_cols[j]]], levels = 1:4))
  data.frame(goal      = goal_labels[j],
             first     = as.integer(counts[1]),
             second    = as.integer(counts[2]),
             third     = as.integer(counts[3]),
             fourth    = as.integer(counts[4]),
             mean_rank = mean(d[[prio_cols[j]]], na.rm = TRUE),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
# Rank 1 is the best position, so the LOWEST mean rank is the most preferred
# goal overall. Ascending order, meaning smallest number first, therefore puts
# the goal participants collectively favour at the top. That is the opposite of
# the usual instinct to sort the big numbers to the top.
rank_matrix <- rank_matrix[order(rank_matrix$mean_rank), ]
show_table(rank_matrix,
           "Full rank distribution: how often each goal was placed 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th")
TABLES[["goal_rank_matrix"]] <- rank_matrix

# The same counts as percentages, which is the form that goes in the paper.
# The denominator is nrow(d), the whole analysed sample. The check below
# confirms that each row of counts already totals nrow(d), so each row of
# percentages comes to 100.
rank_matrix_pct <- rank_matrix
for (nm in c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")) {
  rank_matrix_pct[[nm]] <- 100 * rank_matrix[[nm]] / nrow(d)
}
show_table(rank_matrix_pct, "Full rank distribution (% of the analysed sample)")
TABLES[["goal_rank_matrix_pct"]] <- rank_matrix_pct

# Every goal must be placed exactly once per participant, so both margins --
# the row totals and the column totals -- have to come to the sample size. A
# failure here means the ranking was mis-parsed, and a mis-parsed ranking would
# sort people into the wrong groups in every analysis that follows. Better to
# stop now.
stopifnot(all(rowSums(rank_matrix[, c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")]) == nrow(d)),
          all(colSums(rank_matrix[, c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")]) == nrow(d)))

# The two routes to the same number must agree. One tested Prioritization_1
# == 1 directly; the other scanned the four columns and took the position of
# the 1. Both routes key on column position 1, so neither would notice if the
# instrument's columns arrived in some other order.
#
# What a mismatch here does catch is a damaged ranking. first_choice is NA for
# any row with a missing rank anywhere in it, while the direct test scores a
# row on Prioritization_1 alone, whatever the other three columns hold. So the
# check fails if anybody has been counted a retributivist on a ranking that is
# incomplete elsewhere.
stopifnot(sum(first_choice == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == sum(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE))

# The grouping factor. LEVEL ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, not cosmetic:
# welch_contrast() contrasts level 1 minus level 2 and reports M1/SD1 for level
# 1. Cohen's d is the size of the gap between two groups, measured in standard
# deviations. Putting "Retributivist" first is what makes a positive t and a
# positive d read as "retributivists score higher" throughout Phase 9.
# DO NOT reorder these levels. Doing so would silently flip the sign of every
# contrast in the document while leaving the p-values of the two-sided tests
# untouched, so nothing would look broken and every stated direction would be
# backwards.
d$grp_rank <- factor(ifelse(d$retributivist == 1, "Retributivist", "Other"),
                     levels = c("Retributivist", "Other"))

# Coverage of the written explanation of the ranking -- the pre-registration's
# Q333, exported as Priorit_Explain and aliased to both names in Phase 1.2, so
# code written against either name finds the same column. It is reported here
# only so the reader knows how many substantive texts the language pipeline
# will have to work with. The prompt is soft, meaning a participant could move
# on without answering (prereg 5.15), so a count below the sample size is not a
# sign of a fault. The nchar(trimws(...)) > 0 test requires at least one
# non-space character, because an entry of pure whitespace is not an answer.
if ("Q333" %in% names(d)) {
  n_sub <- sum(!is.na(d$Q333) & nchar(trimws(d$Q333)) > 0)
  cat(sprintf("Ranking explanations written (Q333 / Priorit_Explain): %d of %d (%.1f%%)\n",
              n_sub, nrow(d), 100 * n_sub / nrow(d)))
  cat("(Text scoring is out of scope here — it is the exploratory E3-E7 pipeline.)\n")
}
```

## 5.2 Continuous: the relative retribution subscale

```{r phase5_continuous}
# === THE PRIMARY CONTINUOUS DEFINITION (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: creates `retribution_rel`, the relative retribution
# subscale, and the descriptive table `goal_subscales`. A subscale is the
# average of the survey items belonging to one goal. `retribution_rel` is the
# predictor in every prereg 6.5 continuous rerun. A predictor is the variable
# whose value we use to explain differences in an outcome. It is also the basis
# of the median split and tertiles in 5.3.
#
# WHY RELATIVE RATHER THAN RAW. Endorsement of all four goals is highly
# correlated: an agreeable respondent rates every justification highly. So the
# raw retribution subscale largely measures how much a person endorses
# punishing at all, not whether they favour desert over the alternatives. Used
# raw, it would tell us who is punitive in general and we would report it as
# though it told us who is a retributivist.
#
# Subtracting the mean of the other three isolates PRIORITIZING retribution,
# which is the same idea the categorical ranking captures from the other side.
# Both are reported in Phase 9.9, so a reader can see for themselves whether a
# result depends on which of the two contrasts was used.
#
# na.rm = TRUE inside rowMeans() averages over whichever of the three other
# goals a participant answered, so one missing subscale does not wipe out the
# whole relative score.
d$retribution_rel <- d$retribution -
  rowMeans(cbind(d$deterrence, d$incapacitation, d$rehabilitation), na.rm = TRUE)

# Because it is a difference of 1-7 means, retribution_rel is centred near zero
# and runs roughly -6 to +6: zero means retribution is endorsed exactly as much
# as the average of the other three, and positive means it is preferred. Read
# it as a gap, never as a level. Someone who rates all four goals 7 and someone
# who rates all four goals 2 both score zero here, and that is the intent.
goal_desc <- data.frame(
  measure = c("retribution (7 items)", "deterrence", "incapacitation",
              "rehabilitation", "relative retribution (retribution - mean of other three)"),
  mean = c(mean(d$retribution, na.rm = TRUE), mean(d$deterrence, na.rm = TRUE),
           mean(d$incapacitation, na.rm = TRUE), mean(d$rehabilitation, na.rm = TRUE),
           mean(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE)),
  sd = c(sd(d$retribution, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$deterrence, na.rm = TRUE),
         sd(d$incapacitation, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$rehabilitation, na.rm = TRUE),
         sd(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# The four raw subscales sit next to the relative one on purpose, so a reader
# can see the levels that the relative score nets out. The SD column reports
# the standard deviation, how spread out a measure's scores are. The SD of the
# relative score is the spread the splits in 5.3 have to work with.
TABLES[["goal_subscales"]] <- goal_desc
show_table(goal_desc, "The four goals and the relative retribution subscale")
```

## 5.3 Median split and tertiles on the relative subscale

```{r phase5_splits}
# === CATEGORICAL VERSIONS OF THE CONTINUOUS MEASURE (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: creates two more grouping factors from
# retribution_rel -- `grp_med` (median split: cut the sample in half at its
# middle value) and `grp_tert` (top third versus bottom third) -- so that every
# Phase 9 contrast can be repeated under them.
#
# Prereg 5.3 asks for a median split "with the top and bottom thirds alongside
# it". The pair is informative because the two trade off against each other in
# opposite directions. The median split uses everyone, but it compares people
# who sit right next to each other across an arbitrary cut. The tertile
# contrast throws away the middle third, so it compares genuinely distinct
# groups. It pays for that in n, the number of people left in the comparison,
# and in generalizability, how far the result carries beyond the people it
# compared. A result that appears under one and not the other is telling the
# reader something real about how fragile it is.
#
# These splits exist for readability, not for inference. Dichotomizing a
# continuous predictor, chopping a full range of scores into two boxes, throws
# away variance -- how spread out the scores are. Every difference between two
# people who land in the same box is discarded. That is exactly why prereg 6.5
# requires the continuous rerun in Phase 9.9. WHERE THE TWO DISAGREE, THE
# CONTINUOUS VERSION IS THE ONE TO TRUST.
med_rel <- median(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE)
# Strict ">" so participants sitting exactly at the median fall in the low
# group. The subscale is near-continuous with few exact ties, so the choice
# barely moves the split here. That is NOT true of the sentencing ratio in 5.4,
# where the same decision changes almost everything, so do not carry the
# casualness of this line over to that one.
d$retrib_medsplit <- as.integer(d$retribution_rel > med_rel)
# High level first, again so a positive Cohen's d means "the more retributive
# group scores higher" (see the note on grp_rank in 5.1). Every grouping factor
# in this document follows the same convention, and that consistency is what
# lets a reader interpret a sign the same way on every table.
d$grp_med <- factor(ifelse(d$retrib_medsplit == 1, "High rel. retribution",
                           "Low rel. retribution"),
                    levels = c("High rel. retribution", "Low rel. retribution"))

# Tertile cutpoints: the 33rd and 67th percentiles of the subscale. A
# percentile is the value below which that share of the sample falls, so these
# two numbers are the boundaries that carve the sample into three equal-sized
# thirds.
tert <- quantile(d$retribution_rel, c(1/3, 2/3), na.rm = TRUE)
d$retrib_tertile <- cut(d$retribution_rel, c(-Inf, tert, Inf),
                        labels = c("Bottom third", "Middle third", "Top third"))
# `retrib_tertile` just above is the three-level factor and keeps the "Middle
# third" level. `grp_tert` declares only two levels, "Top third" and "Bottom
# third", and maps everyone in the middle to NA, R's marker for a missing
# value. That is the point: this factor is the TOP-versus-BOTTOM comparison,
# and keeping the middle would make it something else. welch_contrast() deletes
# rows with a missing group before testing, so the middle third simply leaves
# every contrast. Top first, for the sign convention above.
#
# NOTE FOR THE AUTHORS: welch_contrast() calls droplevels(), which discards
# declared levels that nobody is in, and its own comment gives grp_tert as the
# reason, saying grp_tert "retains an unused Middle third level". Built as it
# is here, grp_tert declares two levels and no more, so there is nothing for
# droplevels() to remove. Either that comment is stale or grp_tert was meant to
# be built with all three levels declared. Please settle which.
d$grp_tert <- factor(ifelse(d$retrib_tertile == "Top third", "Top third",
                     ifelse(d$retrib_tertile == "Bottom third", "Bottom third", NA)),
                     levels = c("Top third", "Bottom third"))

cat(sprintf("Median of relative retribution: %.3f\n", med_rel))
cat(sprintf("Median split: %d high / %d low\n",
            sum(d$retrib_medsplit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(d$retrib_medsplit == 0, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Tertile cutpoints: %.3f and %.3f\n", tert[1], tert[2]))
print(table(d$retrib_tertile, useNA = "ifany"))
```

## 5.4 Behavioral: the sentencing ratio

```{r phase5_ratio}
# === THE BEHAVIORAL MEASURE: THE SENTENCING RATIO (prereg 5.3, 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: creates `sentence_ratio`, its regression-adjusted
# robustness twin `sentence_resid`, and the grouping factor `grp_ratio`. It also
# produces the table `sentencing_ratio_by_vignette`.
#
# THE LOGIC. After setting a first sentence, participants read added facts that
# strip away the forward-looking reasons for punishment: the defendant is
# permanently disabled and no longer dangerous, and procedural rules remove any
# prospect of general deterrence. Whatever punishment they still impose cannot
# rest on deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation, because the facts have
# taken those reasons off the table. What is left is a behavioral read on
# desert. The index is the share of the first sentence RETAINED in the second,
# so a higher ratio, meaning a smaller reduction, is the more retributive
# response.
#
# Sentence1 > 0 is required for two reasons. Arithmetically the ratio is
# undefined at zero, and R does not complain about it: Sentence2 / 0 evaluates
# to Inf, which without this guard would run straight into the means below.
# Substantively, a participant who gave no prison time at all has nothing to
# retain, so a retention share would be meaningless for them even if it could
# be computed. Their ratio is NA -- R's marker for a missing value -- and they
# simply do not contribute to the ratio-based analyses.
d$sentence_ratio <- ifelse(!is.na(d$Sentence1) & d$Sentence1 > 0,
                           d$Sentence2 / d$Sentence1, NA_real_)

# THE ROBUSTNESS VERSION named in prereg 5.11: the second sentence regressed on
# the first, keeping the residual. Regressing one on the other means fitting
# the line that best predicts Sentence2 from Sentence1. The residual is what
# that line leaves over for each person: how far above or below it they landed.
# A positive residual means a person kept more of the sentence than the typical
# participant who started where they did.
#
# A ratio and a residual answer the same question under different assumptions.
# The ratio assumes retention is proportional, so halving a long sentence
# counts the same as halving a short one. The residual assumes a linear
# relation -- a straight line -- with an intercept, the height at which that
# line sets off. Reporting both is what shows whether a finding depends on that
# choice rather than on the data. It is used in Phase 9.10 alongside the
# continuous ratio.
d$sentence_resid <- NA_real_
ok_sr <- stats::complete.cases(d$Sentence1, d$Sentence2)
# complete.cases() marks the rows where BOTH sentences are present, since a
# line cannot be fitted through a half-missing pair. The > 10 guard skips the
# fit when 10 or fewer rows are usable, so sentence_resid stays entirely NA.
# Better that than a wildly unstable line passed off as a measurement.
if (sum(ok_sr) > 10) {
  m_sr <- stats::lm(Sentence2 ~ Sentence1, data = d[ok_sr, ])
  # residuals() returns one value per row that entered the fit, in that order,
  # which is shorter than the full data frame. The [ok_sr] index lands each
  # value back on the row it came from, so positions line up with the full
  # frame and nobody gets another participant's residual.
  d$sentence_resid[ok_sr] <- stats::residuals(m_sr)
}

cat(sprintf("Sentence1: M = %.1f (SD %.1f); Sentence2: M = %.1f (SD %.1f) years\n",
            mean(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$Sentence1, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$Sentence2, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Sentencing ratio: median = %.2f, mean = %.2f (n = %d with Sentence1 > 0)\n",
            median(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio))))
cat(sprintf("Did NOT reduce the sentence at all (ratio >= 1): %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(d$sentence_ratio >= 1, na.rm = TRUE)))

# The ratio by vignette. Being a proportion rather than a count of years, it is
# already comparable across the three blocks with no standardization needed.
# That is one of the reasons prereg 5.11 prefers it to the raw drop: the raw
# drop is bigger wherever the sentences are longer. The plan also asks that
# results be confirmed to hold within each vignette, and this table is where a
# reader checks that the pattern is not driven by one crime story.
ratio_by_vig <- as.data.frame(
  d %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(sentence_ratio)) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(Vignette) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(),
                     median_ratio = median(sentence_ratio),
                     mean_ratio = mean(sentence_ratio), .groups = "drop"))
TABLES[["sentencing_ratio_by_vignette"]] <- ratio_by_vig
show_table(ratio_by_vig,
           "Sentencing ratio by vignette (a proportion, so comparable across them)")

# Median split on the ratio; used to repeat every contrast under prereg 5.3.
#
# CAREFUL: the ratio has a large point mass at exactly 1.00. A point mass is a
# pile of participants stacked on one single value. Here they are the ones who
# did not reduce the sentence at all once the forward-looking reasons were
# removed. That is precisely the most retributive response, and 1.00 is ALSO
# the median. So a strict "> median" split strands almost everyone in the low
# group and leaves a high group too small to test. Ties at the median are
# therefore assigned to whichever side keeps the split closer to even, which
# here puts the "no reduction" group on the HIGH (more retributive) side. The
# rule actually used is printed below, so nothing about it is hidden. Remember
# that the split is only ever a readability device: the continuous version in
# Phase 9.10 sidesteps the tie question entirely and is the primary form of
# this robustness check.
med_ratio <- median(d$sentence_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
n_ratio   <- sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio))
n_tied    <- sum(d$sentence_ratio == med_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
# The two candidate high-group sizes: strict ">" excludes the tied mass,
# inclusive ">=" includes it. Computing both means the consequence of the tie
# rule is a number on the page rather than an assumption.
n_hi_gt   <- sum(d$sentence_ratio >  med_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
n_hi_ge   <- sum(d$sentence_ratio >= med_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)

# Pick whichever assignment lands the high group closer to half the sample.
# The criterion is written down and evaluated from the data rather than chosen
# by eye. That matters: choosing by eye after seeing the results is how a split
# gets tuned to produce a finding. Both candidate splits are printed, so the
# reader can see what the other choice would have given.
ties_to_high <- abs(n_hi_ge - n_ratio / 2) <= abs(n_hi_gt - n_ratio / 2)
is_high <- if (ties_to_high) d$sentence_ratio >= med_ratio else
                             d$sentence_ratio >  med_ratio

# High level first, matching the sign convention used by every other grouping,
# so a positive t and a positive d again mean the more retributive group
# scored higher.
# Participants with no ratio (Sentence1 == 0, or a missing sentence) stay NA and
# are dropped from these contrasts by welch_contrast().
d$grp_ratio <- factor(ifelse(is.na(d$sentence_ratio), NA,
                      ifelse(is_high, "High sentencing ratio",
                             "Low sentencing ratio")),
                      levels = c("High sentencing ratio", "Low sentencing ratio"))

cat(sprintf("\nSentencing ratio: %d of %d participants (%.1f%%) sit exactly at the median of %.2f.\n",
            n_tied, n_ratio, 100 * n_tied / n_ratio, med_ratio))
cat(sprintf("Tie rule used: ratio %s median goes to the HIGH group (the more balanced split;\n",
            ifelse(ties_to_high, ">=", ">")))
cat(sprintf("  '>' would have given %d high / %d low, '>=' gives %d / %d).\n",
            n_hi_gt, n_ratio - n_hi_gt, n_hi_ge, n_ratio - n_hi_ge))
cat(sprintf("Sentencing-ratio split: %d high / %d low\n",
            sum(d$grp_ratio == "High sentencing ratio", na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(d$grp_ratio == "Low sentencing ratio", na.rm = TRUE)))
```
## 5.4b The sentencing ratio grouped by what participants did

The two-group split in 5.4 has to settle a question that the ratio itself makes
awkward. Half of the participants who set a first sentence above zero kept that
sentence in full once the forward-looking reasons for punishment were taken
away. Their ratio is exactly 1.00, and 1.00 is also the median. On the
convention set in 5.4, where a higher ratio means a smaller reduction and so the
more retributive response, retaining the whole sentence is the modal answer,
and a high one. Modal means the single most common. It is not the highest
available: a small group raised the second sentence above the first. Any
two-group cut has to send the entire tied block to one side, and whichever side
it goes to decides which way most of the contrasts run.

Grouping by what participants did, rather than by percentile, puts that block in
a group of its own. There are only three things a person could do with the
second sentence -- reduce it, leave it exactly as it was, raise it -- and the
three groups below are those three answers. Nothing here replaces anything. The
registered median split stands as written in 5.4, and Phase 9.10 still runs the
full contrast set under it. The continuous form used there, the ratio entered as
a number rather than as a group, is and remains the primary version of that
robustness check.

The percentile version of the same idea is in 5.4c, kept as a secondary display
only. A percentile cut can only place boundaries between values, and with half
of the sample sitting on one single value, no set of quartile boundaries can
separate that value from its neighbours. That is why the quartiles cannot show
what these three groups show.

```{r phase5_ratio_groups}
# === THE SENTENCING RATIO AS THREE GROUPS (prereg 5.3, 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `grp_ratio_dir`, a three-way grouping on
# sentence_ratio separating the participants who reduced the second sentence,
# those who left it exactly as it was, and those who raised it; prints the group
# sizes; summarises the main outcomes within each group; and crosstabs the three
# groups against the registered median split. A crosstab is a table counting how
# many people fall into each combination of two groupings. Produces the tables
# `sentencing_ratio_direction_cells` and `sentencing_ratio_by_direction`.
# PREREG: an addition to 5.3, reported alongside the registered `grp_ratio` and
#         never in place of it.
# CONSUMES: sentence_ratio and grp_ratio, both built in 5.4, and the outcome
#           composites built in Phase 4.
#
# HAZARD -- DO NOT FEED grp_ratio_dir TO welch_contrast() OR run_contrast_set().
# Both require a factor with exactly TWO levels whose FIRST level is the
# more-retributive side, which is what makes a positive t and a positive Cohen's
# d read the same way everywhere in this document. grp_ratio_dir breaks that on
# both counts: it has three levels, and it runs the other way, from the largest
# reduction up to the increase, so that a table of it reads along the scale
# rather than against it.
#
# The danger is that the mistake is quiet. Passing it to welch_contrast() would
# not stop the document. That function refuses any grouping without exactly two
# populated levels and hands back a row of NAs. The mistake would then arrive
# as a table full of NA, R's marker for a missing value. NA reads as a failed
# measurement, not as a coding error. The grouping that feeds the contrast set
# is still `grp_ratio`, untouched in 5.4.
#
# WHY == 1.00 IS SAFE HERE. Comparing decimal numbers with == is normally
# unsafe. A value that should be 0.3 can be stored a hair away from it, and the
# test then fails for no visible reason. This case is the exception.
# The value that matters is exactly 1.00, and it arises as Sentence2 /
# Sentence1 when the two are the same number. Dividing a number by itself gives
# exactly 1 with no rounding error, so `== 1` catches every participant who
# retained the sentence in full and nobody else. The three comparisons <, ==
# and > therefore partition the participants who have a ratio: nobody is left
# over and nobody is counted twice.
n_rated <- sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio))
n_tie   <- sum(d$sentence_ratio == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_up    <- sum(d$sentence_ratio >  1, na.rm = TRUE)

# The three labels live in one object so the factor levels, the rows of the
# cell-size table and the headings of the crosstab cannot drift apart. Typed out
# three times, they would eventually disagree and a table would be mislabelled
# without anything failing.
#
# The order is substantive rather than conventional: the smallest ratio first,
# so the columns of the summary table run in the same direction as the ratio
# itself. This is deliberately NOT the retributive-first ordering used by
# grp_rank, grp_med, grp_tert and grp_ratio, because those four feed
# welch_contrast() and this one never does.
dir_labels <- c("Reduced the sentence", "No reduction",
                "Increased the sentence")
d$grp_ratio_dir <- factor(
  ifelse(is.na(d$sentence_ratio), NA_character_,
  ifelse(d$sentence_ratio <  1,   dir_labels[1],
  ifelse(d$sentence_ratio == 1,   dir_labels[2], dir_labels[3]))),
  levels = dir_labels)

# table() over a factor returns one count per DECLARED level, in level order,
# including a level with nobody in it. That is what lets the counts below be
# paired with dir_labels by position alone: an empty group still occupies its
# slot, so the labels cannot slide onto the wrong numbers.
dir_n <- as.integer(table(d$grp_ratio_dir))
ratio_dir_cells <- data.frame(
  group = dir_labels,
  # The rule is carried in the table itself so the exported CSV states its own
  # definition and a reader never has to reconstruct the boundaries.
  rule  = c("ratio < 1.00", "ratio = 1.00", "ratio > 1.00"),
  n     = dir_n,
  # Percent of the participants who HAVE a ratio, not of the full 948. A
  # participant whose first sentence was zero has no ratio at all (5.4) and is
  # not part of this grouping. Dividing by 948 would spread these counts over
  # participants the grouping never covered.
  pct_of_rated = round(100 * dir_n / n_rated, 1),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["sentencing_ratio_direction_cells"]] <- ratio_dir_cells
show_table(ratio_dir_cells,
           "5.4b: what participants did with the second sentence, and how many did each.")

cat(sprintf("\nParticipants with a ratio: %d; with none (a first sentence of zero, or a missing sentence): %d\n",
            n_rated, sum(is.na(d$sentence_ratio))))
cat(sprintf("Retained the sentence in full (ratio exactly 1.00): %d (%.1f%% of those with a ratio)\n",
            n_tie, 100 * n_tie / n_rated))

# The group that a percentile split would bury. Guarded on the count, because
# the sentence below is only true of a sample in which somebody raised the
# second sentence. Printing it unconditionally would state a fact about zero
# people as though it described a real group.
if (n_up > 0) {
  cat(sprintf("Raised the second sentence above the first: %d (%.1f%% of those with a ratio).\n",
              n_up, 100 * n_up / n_rated))
  cat("The added facts removed deterrence and incapacitation as reasons\n")
  cat("to punish, and nothing in the vignette calls for an increase, so\n")
  cat("this group is kept on its own rather than folded into a top group.\n")
}

# The outcomes summarised within each group. This list drives BOTH the table
# below and the correlations in 5.4d, so the two displays cannot drift apart.
# Two hand-maintained lists would eventually stop matching, and a reader
# comparing the displays would have no way to know which one was stale.
#
# `punitiveness` here is the 8-item self-report scale. `punitiveness_full` is
# deliberately absent: it embeds Sentence1_z, and the ratio is built from
# Sentence1, so the two share a term. Any association between them would be
# partly the first sentence correlated with itself, which is not a finding
# about punitiveness at all. This is the same reason the sentencing-ratio runs
# in Phase 9.10 set drop_sentence_based = TRUE.
#
# The six measures marked also_run_in_9_10 carry the label text used for them in
# `contrast_spec` (Phase 9.3), which is the join key for the side-by-side table
# in 9.12, so a reader can line these rows up with the ones there. Change a
# label here and the join loses the row. The desert rows are not in that spec
# and take their label from 8.3b instead. The flag is set by hand and mirrors
# the spec: contrast_spec is defined in Phase 9, far below this point, so it
# cannot be consulted from here. Check the flag against it if that spec ever
# gains or loses a row.
#
# The two soft desert tiers come from 4.3b. They are the same purpose items with
# one or two dropped, so they share most of their content with `deserved`. Their
# rows are a robustness display on the desert row, NOT independent readings of
# it, and must never be counted as extra evidence. Both tiers are listed because
# the placement of R3 is an open question for the authors, and reporting both is
# what keeps the answer from depending on it.
ratio_outcome_spec <- data.frame(
  variable = c("punitiveness", "hostile_agg", "revenge",
               "deserved", "deserved_soft", "deserved_soft_strict",
               "proportionality_principle", "rwa", "sdo", "raceresent"),
  label    = c("Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)",
               "Hostile-aggression cluster (z)",
               "Revenge",
               "Desert (purpose items)",
               "Desert, soft core (R1, R3, R4): 3 of Desert's 4 items",
               "Desert, soft core without R3 (R1, R4): 2 of Desert's 4 items",
               "Proportionality principle (single item)",
               "Right-Wing Authoritarianism",
               "Social Dominance Orientation",
               "Racial resentment"),
  also_run_in_9_10 = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE,
                       FALSE, FALSE, FALSE,
                       FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# Keep only the columns present in this run, the same guard Phase 6.2 applies to
# its descriptives list: a measure that is not in the data frame drops out of
# the table instead of stopping the document with an error. The two soft tiers
# are what this guard is for -- without 4.3b the table simply has two fewer
# rows, and everything else still reports.
ratio_outcome_spec <-
  ratio_outcome_spec[ratio_outcome_spec$variable %in% names(d), ]

#' Average one group's scores, giving NA rather than NaN when the whole group
#' is missing
#'
#' Ask R for the mean of a vector (a simple run of values) that holds nothing
#' but NA, R's marker for a missing value, and it returns NaN, short for "not a
#' number", even when told to skip missing values with na.rm = TRUE. NaN sitting
#' in a results table reads like a calculation that went wrong, when all it
#' really means is that this group had nothing to average. NA is the marker that
#' says exactly that, so NA is what this function returns. A group with NO
#' MEMBERS AT ALL never reaches this function: tapply() fills an empty cell from
#' its own `default` argument, which is NA, without ever calling the function.
cell_mean <- function(x) if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

ratio_group_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  seq_len(nrow(ratio_outcome_spec)), function(i) {
  v    <- ratio_outcome_spec$variable[i]
  cell <- tapply(d[[v]], d$grp_ratio_dir, cell_mean)
  out  <- data.frame(measure = ratio_outcome_spec$label[i],
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  # One column per group. Assigning with [[ ]] keeps the group labels exactly as
  # they were written. Building the same columns inside data.frame() instead
  # would mangle them into syntactic column names. Syntactic means spelled the
  # way R's own naming rules demand, with no spaces allowed, so "Reduced the
  # sentence" would come back as "Reduced.the.sentence". Those dots would then
  # show up in the printed table and in the exported CSV.
  for (lv in dir_labels) out[[lv]] <- unname(cell[lv])
  out
}))
TABLES[["sentencing_ratio_by_direction"]] <- ratio_group_means
show_table(ratio_group_means,
           "5.4b: mean of each outcome within each of the three sentencing-ratio groups, with no test attached.")

# READ THESE CELL MEANS ALONGSIDE THE GROUP SIZES ABOVE. Those sizes count the
# people in each group. A measure that some of them skipped contributes fewer
# than that to its own cell, so the number of people behind any one cell can be
# smaller than the number behind the group. Nothing here is tested: these are
# descriptive means only. The two-group means that DO carry a test are in 9.10,
# under the registered median split. These stand beside them, never in place of
# them.
#
# Now the three groups against the registered median split. A median split cuts
# the sample in two at its middle value; a crosstab is a table that counts
# people by two groupings at once. This one shows the picture that the split in
# 5.4 has to compress into two groups. The tie rule in 5.4 works out from the
# data which side the "No reduction" block goes to and prints its choice there;
# this table shows where it landed. useNA = "no" keeps participants who have no
# ratio at all out of the table, so they cannot form a phantom row.
cat("\nThe three groups against the registered median split from 5.4:\n\n")
print(table(Direction = d$grp_ratio_dir, MedianSplit = d$grp_ratio,
            useNA = "no"))
```

## 5.4c What a quartile split does to the same variable

Cutting a continuous measure into equal-sized groups by percentile is the usual
move. A percentile is the value a given share of people fall below, so the
quartiles are the values that would slice the sample into four equal quarters.
On this variable the move does not work. A quantile cut cannot slice through a
pile of people who all gave the identical number, and half of the ratios are the
single value 1.00. Two of the five quartile boundaries therefore come back as
the same number, and fewer than four groups survive. The boundaries that do
survive run into 1.00 rather than fencing it off, which leaves the tied block
sharing a group with the people who did reduce the sentence. What follows is
kept as a secondary check on 5.4b. It is here to show what the percentile form
costs, not as a result to interpret.

```{r phase5_ratio_quartiles}
# === QUARTILES ON THE SENTENCING RATIO, SECONDARY (prereg 5.3, 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: cuts sentence_ratio at its quartile boundaries, prints
# both the boundaries and the group sizes the data actually produced, and
# crosstabs those groups against the three groups from 5.4b (a crosstab counts
# people by two groupings at once). Produces the table
# `sentencing_ratio_quartile_cells`.
# PREREG: an addition to 5.3, secondary to 5.4b and to the registered
#         `grp_ratio`, and never in place of either.
# CONSUMES: sentence_ratio, built in 5.4; grp_ratio_dir, n_tie and n_rated, all
#           built in 5.4b.
#
# THE QUARTILE FACTOR IS NEVER WRITTEN INTO `d`. A factor is R's type for a
# grouping variable, and `d` is the data frame -- the big table with one row per
# participant -- that every analysis in this document draws on. Every knitted
# chunk shares one environment, an environment being the single store where R
# keeps the objects it has made. So `grp_ratio_q` is visible below this point
# like any other object. Keeping it OUT of `d` buys two things. It cannot ride
# along inside `d` into run_contrast_set(), which is handed the NAME of a
# column. And it cannot reach the exported dataset in 10.3. Nothing downstream
# asks for it. Its levels also run from the largest reduction upward, which is
# the opposite of the retributive-first ordering welch_contrast() requires.
#
# KEEP EVERY show_table() CALL AT THE TOP LEVEL OF THE CHUNK. knitr, the engine
# that turns this document into the HTML report, prints a table by taking the
# value of an expression that sits on its own at the outer level of the chunk.
# Move a show_table() call inside an if() block and its value goes to that block
# instead. The table then VANISHES from the knitted report while still being
# written to CSV. That is the hardest kind of loss to notice. Nothing errors,
# the file exists, and only the report is quietly missing a table. That is why
# the conditional work below merely builds objects, and every print happens
# afterwards, outside any if().
#
# ASSUME NOTHING ABOUT THE CUT POINTS. The boundaries and the group sizes the
# data actually produced are printed below, and both must be read before anyone
# interprets these groups. They will NOT be four equal quarters of about 237
# people each.

# The five boundaries of a quartile split: the minimum, the 25th, 50th and 75th
# percentiles, and the maximum. A percentile that falls between two
# participants has to be filled in somehow, and type = 7 is R's default rule for
# doing it. It interpolates, meaning it takes a weighted blend of the two values
# on either side. The rule is named here in full so the cut points cannot move
# if R ever changes that default.
q_probs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1)
q_raw   <- stats::quantile(d$sentence_ratio, probs = q_probs,
                           na.rm = TRUE, type = 7)

# Print the requested boundaries before any cutting happens, so a reader can see
# the repeats with their own eyes rather than taking the count below on trust.
cat("Quartile boundaries requested on the sentencing ratio:\n\n")
print(round(q_raw, 3))

# Drop repeated boundaries. cut() stops with an error if two of its breaks are
# the same number, so the duplicates have to go, and the factor left standing
# then has fewer than four levels. unname() strips the names R hangs on those
# boundaries, "0%", "25%" and so on. Left in place they would travel into the
# factor levels and label each group by the percentile it came from rather than
# by the range of ratios it actually holds.
q_brk <- unique(unname(q_raw))
# Boundaries fence off intervals, and there is always one fewer interval than
# boundary. This is the number of groups the data can actually support. It, and
# not the four the code asked for, is the number to believe.
n_int <- length(q_brk) - 1L

cat(sprintf(
  "\n%d of the %d boundaries are distinct: the ratio supports %d group(s).\n",
  length(q_brk), length(q_probs), n_int))
# If the boundaries did collide, say so in the report itself. Otherwise a reader
# has to notice unaided that a table headed "quartiles" has three rows.
if (n_int < 4) {
  cat("Boundaries collided: a value held by enough participants spans more\n")
  cat("than one quartile, so fewer than four groups form. Which value that\n")
  cat("is, and what it costs, is printed under the table below.\n")
}

if (n_int >= 1) {
  # Each group is labelled by the range of ratios it holds rather than by a bare
  # quartile number. Printing the two ratios that bound a group shows at a
  # glance that these groups are neither equal in width nor, in this data, equal
  # in size. A label reading only "Q1" would hide both facts.
  q_labels <- paste0("Q", seq_len(n_int), " (",
                     sprintf("%.2f", q_brk[-length(q_brk)]), " to ",
                     sprintf("%.2f", q_brk[-1]), ")")
  # Those labels print two decimal places. Two boundaries differing only further
  # out than that would produce two identical labels, and a factor cannot carry
  # two levels with the same name. make.unique() adds a suffix in exactly that
  # case and leaves the labels alone otherwise.
  q_labels <- make.unique(q_labels)
  # right = TRUE is R's default, spelled out here for the record. It means every
  # group is open at the bottom and closed at the top, so a participant sitting
  # exactly ON a cut point falls in the group BELOW it. include.lowest = TRUE
  # closes the bottom end of the first group as well. Without it the
  # participants at the very lowest ratio would fall outside every interval and
  # be dropped to NA rather than counted in Q1. NA is R's marker for a missing
  # value, and table() does not count NAs, so those people would simply go
  # missing from the group sizes below. Neither setting can rescue the tie. With
  # right = TRUE the block sitting at 1.00 joins the people below 1.00, and with
  # right = FALSE it joins the people above.
  grp_ratio_q <- cut(d$sentence_ratio, breaks = q_brk, labels = q_labels,
                     include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE)
} else {
  # This branch is reached only if every participant with a ratio gave the very
  # same value, in which case there is nothing to split. The empty label vector
  # (a simple run of values, here holding none) and the all-NA factor let the
  # table below still build rather than stopping the whole document. It comes
  # out with no rows, which is the honest answer.
  q_labels    <- character(0)
  grp_ratio_q <- factor(rep(NA_character_, nrow(d)))
  cat("Every participant with a ratio gave the same value: no split exists.\n")
}

# The cells the split actually produced. The counts are worked out once and
# reused everywhere below, so the table printed in the report and the CSV
# exported beside it cannot end up disagreeing with each other.
q_n <- as.integer(table(grp_ratio_q))
q_cells <- data.frame(
  group        = q_labels,
  lower_bound  = q_brk[-length(q_brk)],
  upper_bound  = q_brk[-1],
  n            = q_n,
  # Percent of the participants who HAVE a ratio, the same base 5.4b uses. A
  # participant whose first sentence was zero has no ratio at all, so dividing
  # by the full analytic sample here would quietly shrink every percentage.
  pct_of_rated = round(100 * q_n / n_rated, 1),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["sentencing_ratio_quartile_cells"]] <- q_cells
show_table(q_cells,
           "5.4c: the quartile cut points on the sentencing ratio and the group sizes they actually produce.")

# WHERE THE TIED BLOCK LANDED. A boundary is worth reporting only if
# participants can sit on it exactly, and on this variable that means 1.00 and
# nothing else. An interpolated boundary falls between two participants, so
# finding nobody on it is the expected result rather than a finding, and
# boundaries with nobody on them are skipped. The loop is written with lapply()
# rather than as a for loop so the boundary variable stays inside the function
# and does not leak into the rest of the document.
if (n_int >= 2) {
  invisible(lapply(q_brk[-c(1, length(q_brk))], function(cut_pt) {
    n_on <- sum(d$sentence_ratio == cut_pt, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (n_on > 0)
      cat(sprintf("  %d participants sit exactly on the cut point %.2f, and so fall in the group below it.\n",
                  n_on, cut_pt))
  }))
}

# What that costs, counted out rather than left for the reader to work out. The
# interval that closes at 1.00 holds the tied block TOGETHER WITH everyone
# between the boundary below it and 1.00, which is exactly the mixing that the
# three groups in 5.4b avoid. The guard means this prints only when 1.00 really
# is one of the boundaries and is not the lowest one.
idx_one <- which(q_brk == 1)
if (n_tie > 0 && length(idx_one) == 1 && idx_one > 1) {
  lv_at_one <- q_labels[idx_one - 1L]
  n_mixed <- sum(grp_ratio_q == lv_at_one & d$sentence_ratio < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("  The group closing at 1.00 holds those %d together with %d who did reduce the sentence.\n",
              n_tie, n_mixed))
}

# The percentile groups against the three groups from 5.4b. This is the whole
# point of the display: read across a row, and if its count spreads over two
# columns then that single percentile group is holding two different answers
# about what the participant did with the sentence. useNA = "no" keeps
# participants without a ratio from forming a phantom row or column.
if (n_int >= 1) {
  cat("\nQuartile groups against the three groups from 5.4b:\n\n")
  print(table(Quartile = grp_ratio_q, Direction = d$grp_ratio_dir,
              useNA = "no"))
}
```

## 5.4d The sentencing ratio against the desert measures

Here the ratio is used as a number rather than chopped into groups, and set
against the measures of desert. The other outcomes in the 5.4b table are already
run this way in Phase 9.10, where `contrasts_continuous_ratio` regresses each of
them on the ratio. To regress one measure on another is to fit the straight line
that best predicts the first from the second. Both sides are standardized first,
meaning every value is turned into a z-score: how many standard deviations it
sits above or below the average. With a single predictor, that standardized
slope IS the Pearson correlation, computed on the same participants. Printing
those rows again here would show the same coefficient twice with two differently
built intervals beside it, so they are read from 9.10 instead.

```{r phase5_ratio_correlates}
# === THE SENTENCING RATIO AGAINST THE DESERT MEASURES (prereg 5.3, 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: correlates sentence_ratio, used as a number rather than
# as a group, with the measures from the 5.4b list that are not already run
# against it in Phase 9.10. Produces the table `sentencing_ratio_correlates`.
# PREREG: descriptive, reported outside the registered FDR family and alongside
#         the registered ratio analyses rather than in place of any of them.
# CONSUMES: sentence_ratio, built in 5.4, and `ratio_outcome_spec`, built in
#           5.4b.
#
# HOW TO READ THE SIGN. The ratio is the share of the first sentence RETAINED in
# the second one. A HIGHER ratio therefore means a SMALLER reduction once the
# forward-looking reasons for punishment were stripped away, and that is the
# more retributive response. r is the correlation: one number between -1 and +1
# saying how tightly two measures move together. A POSITIVE r here means the
# people who held on to the sentence score HIGHER on that measure. A negative r
# means they score lower.
#
# WHY EVERY ROW IS TWO-SIDED. A two-sided test asks only whether there is any
# association at all, without betting in advance on which way it runs. These are
# descriptive correlations, not the registered directional predictions of H13 to
# H21, so there is no direction to bet on. A null result -- finding nothing --
# is as informative here as a positive one, and a two-sided p keeps every row on
# the same footing. Read the confidence intervals rather than the p-values. Each
# one is the two-sided 95% interval: the range of values for the true
# correlation that these data are consistent with.
#
# NOT AN FDR FAMILY. Run enough tests and a few come out "significant" on luck
# alone. The registered family that guards against that is punitiveness against
# its twelve correlates in H1, and nothing else. Inside that family the false
# discovery rate, meaning the expected share of false positives among the
# correlates declared significant, is held down by the Benjamini-Hochberg
# procedure (BH-FDR). These rows sit OUTSIDE that family. They are not
# corrected, and they are not a confirmatory test.
#
# WHY THE ROWS OVERLAP EACH OTHER. The soft desert tiers are the same purpose
# items with one or two of them dropped, so each shares most of its content with
# `deserved`. Their correlations are near-repeats of the desert row, and they
# are printed to show that the desert result does not depend on which items are
# counted. DO NOT READ THEM AS THREE INDEPENDENT PIECES OF EVIDENCE. Nothing in
# them tests anything the four-item composite does not already test.
#
# WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THIS TABLE. `punitiveness_full`, Sentence1 and
# Sentence1_z are all excluded. Each of them carries the first sentence, and the
# ratio is BUILT from the first sentence. Correlating them would be running part
# of the same number against itself and calling the answer a finding. The six
# measures flagged also_run_in_9_10 are excluded for a different reason: they
# already appear in `contrasts_continuous_ratio`, where the standardized
# slope IS this Pearson r on this n and the two-sided p is the same p. That
# table also carries the registered one-sided p, which is the number the paper
# reports for those six. The ratio against the other retributivism measures --
# the relative subscale, the retribution subscale and the ranking-based
# grouping -- is in 5.5 and is not repeated here.
#
# THE BIND CANNOT COME BACK EMPTY, which is why nothing below is wrapped in a
# guard. Stacking zero rows with rbind() would give back NULL, and picking
# columns out of NULL for the display would fail. That cannot happen here.
# `deserved` and `proportionality_principle` are built in 4.3 no matter what, so
# at least those two rows always survive the name check in 5.4b. The two soft
# tiers join them whenever 4.3b has run. KEEP THE show_table() CALL AT THE TOP
# LEVEL of the chunk. That is what makes the table appear in the knitted
# document at all -- moved inside an if() block it would still export to CSV and
# still be missing from the report.
ratio_correlates <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  which(!ratio_outcome_spec$also_run_in_9_10), function(i)
    cor_row(d, "sentence_ratio", ratio_outcome_spec$variable[i],
            alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = "Sentencing ratio",
            label_y = ratio_outcome_spec$label[i])))
TABLES[["sentencing_ratio_correlates"]] <- ratio_correlates
show_table(ratio_correlates[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
                                "p_two")],
           "5.4d: the sentencing ratio entered continuously against the desert measures, two-sided and uncorrected.")

# The n sits near 947 rather than 948. One participant set a first sentence of
# zero, and nothing can be divided by zero, so that person has no ratio at all
# (5.4). A measure with an incomplete composite trims the n further. A composite
# is a scale score built as the mean of several survey items, and a participant
# who answered too few of them is left with no score on it. Because that trim
# differs from measure to measure, the range is printed rather than a single
# number.
cat(sprintf("\nCorrelations computed on %d to %d participants.\n",
            min(ratio_correlates$n, na.rm = TRUE),
            max(ratio_correlates$n, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Rows with a positive r: %d of %d. Rows with a two-sided p below .05, before any correction: %d.\n",
            sum(ratio_correlates$r > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(ratio_correlates),
            sum(ratio_correlates$p_two < .05, na.rm = TRUE)))

# WHAT SHAPE THESE CORRELATIONS REST ON. The ratio cannot fall below zero but
# has no ceiling above, and in practice it piles up on three answers: below
# 1.00, at exactly 1.00, and above 1.00. A Pearson correlation on a variable
# shaped that way ends up close to a comparison of the three groups in 5.4b.
# One difference matters: a single extreme ratio pulls a correlation around far
# harder than it pulls a group mean. The registered continuous run in 9.10
# stands on exactly this same shape, so this is the footing the document already
# has rather than a new one. Either way the intervals, not the p-values, are
# what carry the inference.
```


## 5.5 Convergence among the retributivist measures

```{r phase5_convergence}
# === CONVERGENCE AMONG THE RETRIBUTIVIST MEASURES (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reports how far the three measures of retributivism
# agree with one another -- pairwise correlations among the continuous ones,
# meaning one correlation for each pair of them, the categorical measure tested
# against each of the others, and the crosstab overlap of the groups they
# define. It produces the table `retributivist_measure_convergence`.
#
# The plan treats the measures as CONVERGENT rather than interchangeable, and
# expects every single one of them to be imperfect on its own. Demand
# characteristics -- participants guessing what a study wants and answering to
# match -- push self-reports toward the forward-looking justifications. People
# punish on desert while describing utilitarian aims, that is, aims about future
# good rather than about what was earned. And introspective access to one's own
# punitive motive is limited: looking inward only tells a person so much about
# why they want to punish (prereg 5.3). MODEST AGREEMENT HERE IS THE EXPECTED
# RESULT, not a failure of the measures. It is also the reason every Phase 9
# contrast is reported under all four groupings instead of under the one that
# happens to read best.
conv <- rbind(
  cor_row(d, "retribution_rel", "sentence_ratio",
          label_x = "Relative retribution", label_y = "Sentencing ratio"),
  cor_row(d, "retribution", "sentence_ratio",
          label_x = "Retribution subscale", label_y = "Sentencing ratio"),
  cor_row(d, "retribution_rel", "retribution",
          label_x = "Relative retribution", label_y = "Retribution subscale"))
TABLES[["retributivist_measure_convergence"]] <- conv
show_table(conv[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")],
           "Pairwise agreement among the continuous retributivist measures")

# The categorical measure -- who ranked retribution first -- against the
# continuous ones. Prereg 5.3 asks only that the measures' agreement be
# reported; it names no direction for these comparisons, so under prereg 6.8
# the two-sided p (p_two) is the one to report. The one-sided "greater" p is
# kept beside it: if the ranking captures what the scales capture, people who
# rank retribution first should score higher on them, not merely differently.
# Each row is a Welch t-test, which compares two group averages without
# assuming the two groups are equally spread out. Each row also carries
# Cohen's d, the gap between the two averages measured in standard deviations.
# Beside d sits its 95% confidence interval, the range of values for the true d
# that these data are consistent with.
conv_cat <- rbind(
  welch_contrast(d, "retribution_rel", "grp_rank", "greater",
                 label = "Relative retribution"),
  welch_contrast(d, "retribution", "grp_rank", "greater",
                 label = "Retribution subscale"),
  welch_contrast(d, "sentence_ratio", "grp_rank", "greater",
                 label = "Sentencing ratio"))
# Export it. The sentencing-ratio row of this table sets a measure of what
# people SAY against a measure of what they DID under a manipulation, so it
# belongs in the replication bundle and has to be citable from a file rather
# than read off the knitted page.
TABLES[["retributivist_measure_contrasts"]] <- conv_cat
show_table(conv_cat[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2", "t", "p_two", "p_dir",
                        "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "Ranking-based retributivists vs others on the other retributivism measures")

# Overlap among the groups the measures define. Each crosstab sorts the same
# people twice, once by each measure, and counts how often the two sorts land in
# the same place. Both factors are ordered retributive-first, so the diagonal --
# the top-left cell and the bottom-right cell -- holds the people the two
# measures classify the SAME way, and sum(diag)/sum is their raw agreement rate.
#
# HOW TO READ THE PERCENTAGE, because the obvious reading is wrong. These come
# out near 56% and 58%, which sounds like solid majority agreement. It is not.
# Every one of these measures cuts the sample near the middle: the ranking
# splits it 371 to 577, the median split 470 to 478, the sentencing ratio 514 to
# 433. Sort the same people twice with cuts like those and roughly HALF will land
# in the same cell by chance alone, having nothing to do with the measures
# agreeing about anything.
#
# So the number that matters is the distance above chance, not the percentage
# itself:
#   ranking x median split          56.4% against 50.1% by chance = 6.3 points
#   ranking x sentencing ratio      58.1% against 49.1% by chance = 9.0 points
#   relative retribution x ratio    52.3% against 50.0% by chance = 2.3 points
# Those distances are what Cohen's kappa expresses, on a scale where 1.00 is
# perfect agreement and 0.00 is two coin flips. On the splits THIS document
# builds, the three kappas are .127, .177 and .046.
#
# WHERE THE KAPPAS ARE COMPUTED: in 9.17, on the groupings THIS document builds,
# exported as P3_grouping_agreement with chance agreement and a 95% interval
# for each kappa. Those are the values to cite, beside the raw percentages
# this section prints. Cohen's kappa is also computed, on a different median
# split (see the hazard below), in
# 03_supplementary_analyses.Rmd, which writes it to
# output/tables/retributivist_group_overlap.csv alongside Jaccard and phi.
# Anyone quoting the percentages above should quote the 9.17 kappa with them.
#
# HAZARD, AND IT IS LIVE. That CSV does NOT report the same numbers as the
# tables printed just above, because 03 does not reuse `grp_med`; it rebuilds
# the median split with its own balanced_split() helper. Six participants sit
# exactly at the median of `retribution_rel`. The strict ">" in 5.3 puts
# all six in the low group, giving 470 high and 478 low. balanced_split() uses
# ">=" instead, because that lands closer to an even cut, giving 476 and 472.
# Those six people are the entire difference, and they move:
#     ranking x relative      56.4% here   vs 56.6% in 03,  kappa .127 vs .134
#     relative x ratio        52.3% here   vs 52.9% in 03,  kappa .046 vs .058
#     ranking x ratio         58.1% in both, kappa .177 in both, since that
#                             split is built the same way in the two documents
# Nothing about the study turns on six people. What does matter is that two
# documents report different values for one named quantity, and a reader moving
# between them will find the mismatch and not know which to believe. Until the
# two are reconciled, the numbers printed HERE are the ones built from the
# grouping factors this document freezes and hands downstream in Phase 10.3.
#
# Read the raw percentage on its own and this section looks like the measures
# broadly agree. They do not, and the third line is the one to keep in view: our
# two continuous measures are very nearly unrelated to each other.
#
# useNA = "no" leaves out anyone missing either measure. Left in, they would form
# a phantom cell that still counts in the denominator and would drag the
# percentage down for no real reason.
overlap <- table(Ranking = d$grp_rank, MedianSplit = d$grp_med, useNA = "no")
cat("\nOverlap: ranking-based group x median split on relative retribution\n\n")
print(overlap)
cat(sprintf("\nAgreement: %.1f%%\n",
            100 * sum(diag(overlap)) / sum(overlap)))

# The same comparison again, this time against the sentencing-ratio median
# split. Two agreement rates are reported rather than one combined figure. A
# measure can line up well with one alternative grouping and poorly with the
# other, and a single averaged number would hide that.
overlap2 <- table(Ranking = d$grp_rank, SentencingRatio = d$grp_ratio, useNA = "no")
cat("\nOverlap: ranking-based group x sentencing-ratio median split\n\n")
print(overlap2)
cat(sprintf("\nAgreement: %.1f%%\n",
            100 * sum(diag(overlap2)) / sum(overlap2)))
```

# PHASE 6: DEMOGRAPHICS AND DESCRIPTIVES

## 6.1 Sample demographics

```{r phase6_demographics}
# === SAMPLE DEMOGRAPHICS (prereg 5.13) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the table `demographics` (exported as
# output/tables/demographics.csv) and prints age, ideology and prosecution
# leaning. This is the "who actually took the survey" section that every reader
# and reviewer looks for first: without it, nobody can judge who the results
# apply to. Descriptive only -- NOTHING HERE FEEDS A HYPOTHESIS TEST. Prereg
# 5.13 names political orientation and party ID as covariates. A covariate is a
# background variable held constant while a relationship is examined. No test in
# this document adds either one as a covariate. Political orientation and
# prosecution leaning enter only the exploratory moderator models of 9.18, each
# as a moderator, together with its product with retributivism.

#' Attach value labels to a numeric option-code column
#'
#' Qualtrics exports each answer as a bare number: gender comes back as 1, 2 or
#' 3. Numbers like that are unreadable in a printed table, so each code is
#' swapped for the wording the participant actually saw on screen.
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x  the numeric codes; labels  the option text IN EXPORT ORDER,
#'            so labels[i] must be the wording of option code i.
#' RETURNS    a factor (R's type for a grouping variable) carrying an explicit
#'            NA level whenever any value is missing.
#' addNA() is what adds that level, turning "gave no answer" into a category in
#' its own right. Non-responders then stay visible as a row of their own rather
#' than being dropped, so every demographic column adds up to the full analytic
#' N.
lab <- function(x, labels) {
  out <- factor(x, levels = seq_along(labels), labels = labels)
  addNA(out, ifany = TRUE)
}
#' One block of the demographics table: counts and percentages for one variable
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  x  a labelled factor; name  the variable name for the first column.
#' RETURNS    a long-format data frame (a table with one row per answer option,
#'            holding variable, level, n, percent).
#' Long format is what makes the blocks stackable. Gender has three options and
#' race has seven, so a wide layout would need a different set of columns for
#' every variable. In long format each block has the same four columns, and
#' rbind() can simply pile one on top of the next.
demo_tab <- function(x, name) {
  tt <- as.data.frame(table(x, useNA = "ifany"))
  names(tt) <- c("level", "n")
  tt$percent <- 100 * tt$n / sum(tt$n)
  tt$variable <- name
  tt[, c("variable", "level", "n", "percent")]
}

# WATCH THE ORDER HERE. Each label set below must follow the option order in the
# Qualtrics instrument exactly, because the code only matches labels to codes by
# position. Put one label out of order and a demographic group is MISLABELLED
# while every n stays exactly the same, so nothing looks broken and the table
# quietly reports the wrong thing. These are the lines to check against the
# codebook printed in Phase 1.2.
demographics <- rbind(
  demo_tab(lab(d$gender, c("Male", "Female", "Other")), "Gender"),
  demo_tab(lab(d$race, c("White, non-Hispanic", "Black / African-American",
                         "Asian", "Hispanic / Latino", "Middle Eastern",
                         "Native American", "Pacific Islander")), "Race/ethnicity"),
  demo_tab(lab(d$education, c("Did not graduate HS", "High school only",
                              "1-2 years post-HS", "3-4 years post-HS",
                              "5-6 years post-HS", "More than 6 years post-HS")),
           "Education"),
  demo_tab(lab(d$PoliticalID, c("Democrat", "Republican", "Independent",
                                "Other", "Not politically identified")),
           "Party identification"))
TABLES[["demographics"]] <- demographics
show_table(demographics, "Sample demographics (analytic sample)", digits = 1)

# Age, political orientation and prosecution leaning are numbers on a scale
# rather than categories, so they are summarised by mean and SD instead of by
# counts. The n printed beside the age line is sum(!is.na(d$age)), the count of
# participants who gave an age. It is printed because a mean means little
# without knowing how many people stand behind it.
cat(sprintf("\nAge: M = %.1f, SD = %.1f, range %g-%g (n = %d)\n",
            mean(d$age, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$age, na.rm = TRUE),
            min(d$age, na.rm = TRUE), max(d$age, na.rm = TRUE),
            sum(!is.na(d$age))))
cat(sprintf("Political orientation (1 strongly liberal - 7 strongly conservative): M = %.2f, SD = %.2f\n",
            mean(d$libcons, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$libcons, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Prosecution leaning (-1 defense .. +1 prosecution): M = %.2f, SD = %.2f\n",
            mean(d$leanPros, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$leanPros, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

## 6.2 Composite descriptives

One table holding the basic summary numbers for every scored variable in the
study. It is the key for reading every result that follows, because a mean means
nothing until you know the scale it sits on.

```{r phase6_descriptives}
# === COMPOSITE DESCRIPTIVES ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reports n, mean, SD, min, max and skew for every scored
# variable in the document, as the table `descriptives` (exported as
# output/tables/descriptives.csv).
#
# The column names, in plain terms: n is how many people have a score, SD is the
# standard deviation (the typical distance of one person from the mean), and min
# and max are the smallest and largest values anyone recorded.
#
# WHY IT MATTERS. This is the reference table for reading everything that
# follows. A mean on its own tells a reader nothing, because "4.2" cannot be
# judged without knowing what scale it sits on. The min and max columns supply
# that at a glance: 1-7 for the attitude composites, roughly -6 to +6 for
# relative retribution, and standardized (centred near zero) for the z-score
# aggregates.
#
# The n column is the early-warning column. Every composite is scored only for
# people who answered at least half of its items, so if a composite failed that
# at-least-half rule for many participants its n drops here. Without this table
# that loss would stay invisible, and a later test would be read as though it
# rested on the whole sample when it did not.
desc_vars <- c("punitiveness", "punitiveness_full", "Sentence1", "Sentence1_z",
               "Sentence2", "sentence_ratio",
               "retribution", "retribution_rel", "deterrence", "incapacitation",
               "rehabilitation", "solidarity_durk",
               "deserved", "proportionality_jd", "just_deserts", "revenge",
               "dueprocess", "uncertain", "kant_core", "kant_nonoverlap",
               "hatred", "anger", "exclusion", "degradation", "suffering",
               "prisonviol", "harsh", "crimerates", "fear",
               "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
               "essentialism", "choice", "society_reject", "leanPros",
               "Shark_2", "Shark_3", "shark_kill",
               "rwa", "sdo", "vprone", "raceresent", "CRT")
# intersect() keeps only the names that really exist as columns of `d`. If a
# composite failed to build earlier, it is quietly dropped from the table rather
# than stopping the whole document with an error.
desc_vars <- intersect(desc_vars, names(d))

# One row per variable. vapply() walks the vector of variable names and computes
# the same summary for each; na.rm = TRUE tells R to ignore NA (its marker for a
# missing value) rather than returning NA for the whole column.
descriptives <- data.frame(
  variable = desc_vars,
  n    = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) sum(!is.na(d[[v]])), integer(1)),
  mean = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) mean(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  sd   = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) sd(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  min  = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) min(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  max  = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) max(d[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  # Skew says how lopsided a distribution is: zero is symmetric, a positive
  # value means a long tail stretching to the right, a negative one a long tail
  # to the left. It is reported because two variables are expected to be badly
  # non-normal -- that is, badly out of the tidy bell-curve shape. The
  # sentencing ratio piles up at 1.00, and the raw sentence stacks at the slider
  # bound of 50. A reader should be able to see that BEFORE reading a t-test run
  # on them. It is descriptive ONLY: no transformation and no exclusion follows
  # from it, and the plan sets no normality gate.
  skew = vapply(desc_vars, function(v) {
    x <- d[[v]][!is.na(d[[v]])]
    # Fewer than 3 values, or no spread at all, leaves skew undefined. Return
    # NA (R's marker for a missing value) rather than invent a number.
    if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0) return(NA_real_)
    # The moment-based coefficient, m3 / s^3: average the cubed distances from
    # the mean, then divide by the SD cubed. Cubing keeps the sign, which is
    # what makes a long right tail come out positive. Computed on the complete
    # cases: `x` holds only the people who have a value for this variable.
    mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3 }, numeric(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# Stored in TABLES under the name "descriptives". That name is also the filename
# the export step in Phase 10 writes it out as.
# show_table() then prints it: it is the shared helper this document uses to
# render a data frame as a formatted table in the knitted report.
TABLES[["descriptives"]] <- descriptives
show_table(descriptives, "Descriptive statistics for every scored variable")
```

## 6.3 Vignette assignment

A check on how the three crime stories were handed out: how many people saw each
one, and whether the share of retributivists -- a measure taken before the
sentencing task -- is the same across the three.

```{r phase6_vignette}
# === RANDOMIZATION CHECK ON THE VIGNETTE ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reports how many participants saw each vignette block
# and tests whether the retributivist share differs across them. Descriptive; no
# hypothesis depends on it.
#
# WHY DO IT. Assignment used an even-weight randomizer (prereg 3.2), meaning the
# survey handed out the three vignettes with equal probability. So in the
# surviving sample the three counts should each land close to a third. The
# retributivist measure was taken BEFORE the sentencing task, which puts it
# causally upstream of the vignette: nothing about which story a person read can
# have changed it, so the retributivist share should not differ by block either.
#
# WHAT WOULD GO WRONG WITHOUT THE CHECK. If the shares DO differ, the likely
# cause is differential attrition -- different kinds of people dropping out of
# different vignettes -- and that would quietly bias every comparison made
# across vignettes later on. Far better to see it here than to be surprised by
# it after the results are written up.
vig_tab <- as.data.frame(table(Vignette = d$Vignette, useNA = "ifany"))
# The share of the sample in each block, which is easier to eyeball against
# "a third each" than the raw counts are.
vig_tab$percent <- 100 * vig_tab$Freq / sum(vig_tab$Freq)
# Turn the stored vignette code (1, 2, 3) into readable text for the printed
# table. as.integer(as.character(...)) is the safe route out of a factor (a
# labelled category variable): a factor stores its levels internally as 1, 2,
# 3..., so as.integer() on its own would hand back that internal position rather
# than the code itself, and the descriptions could end up on the wrong rows.
vig_tab$description <- c("Robbery that turns deadly",
                         "Intimate-partner violence",
                         "Killing inside a criminal operation")[
                           as.integer(as.character(vig_tab$Vignette))]
show_table(vig_tab, "Random vignette assignment", digits = 1)
```
