```{r phase6_vignette}
# A 3 x 2 chi-square: the three vignettes crossed against the two retributivist
# categories. A chi-square test asks whether a table of counts departs from what
# chance alone would produce. Two-sided, meaning no direction is predicted --
# this is a check rather than a prediction, so prereg 6.8 leaves it two-sided.
# suppressWarnings covers the small-expected-count warning, which R raises when
# a cell is too thin for the test's approximation to hold. That does not arise
# at these cell sizes, but it would if the document were rerun on a subset.
chi_v <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table(d$Vignette, d$retributivist)))
cat(sprintf("\nRetributivist share by vignette: chi-square = %.2f, df = %d, p %s\n",
            chi_v$statistic, chi_v$parameter, format_p(chi_v$p.value)))
```

# PHASE 7: H1–H3 -- WHOLE-SAMPLE REPLICATION OF THE DARK SIDE PATTERN

> **Confirmatory.** These are the pre-registered tests -- the ones written down
> before anyone looked at the data -- run on the full dataset (N = 948 after
> exclusions). Collection is complete, so this is the single confirmatory
> reading the pre-registration provides for (Section 4.4). There is no second
> bite at the apple.

## 7.0 Hypothesis test functions (reused for H11)

H11 asks for H1–H10 to be rerun *inside* the retributivist group. So each test
is written once, as a function: a recipe that takes a data frame (a table of
participants, one row per person) and runs on whatever it is handed. Each recipe
is then called twice, on the whole sample here and in Phase 9 on the
retributivist subset. Writing the test once is what guarantees that the two runs
are the same test.

```{r phase7_functions}
# === THE HYPOTHESIS FUNCTIONS run_h1() ... run_h10() ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: defines the correlate list and one function per
# hypothesis H1 to H10. It runs no test itself -- it only writes down how each
# test works. Phase 7 and Phase 8 call these on the whole sample, and Phase 9.1
# calls the SAME functions on `d_retrib`, the retributivists on their own.
#
# WHY FUNCTIONS. H11 is the claim that the H1-H10 relationships also hold inside
# the retributivist group (prereg 6.5). A function is a recipe written once and
# reused, with the data frame it works on left open. That is what makes the
# whole-sample and the within-group runs guaranteed identical in method, so a
# difference between the two tables can only be a difference in the DATA and
# never a difference in the analysis. Write the test out twice by hand instead
# and one copy eventually drifts from the other, at which point nobody can tell
# a real subgroup effect from a typo.
#
# HAZARD: every one of these takes `punit = "punitiveness"` -- the 8-item
# self-report scale -- as its default. `punitiveness_full` has Sentence1_z built
# into it (the sentence, z-scored within vignette), so substituting it here
# would put the sentence on BOTH sides of the analysis wherever the sentence or
# the sentencing ratio is also in play. That is circular, and it would
# manufacture a correlation out of nothing. Prereg 5.11 forbids it. The full
# index appears only where a call site explicitly labels it as a robustness row.

# The 12 pre-registered correlates of punitiveness (prereg 2.1; scored in
# Phase 4 per prereg 5.5 to 5.9). This vector (a simple run of values) is the H1
# family: the group of tests that belong together and are therefore corrected
# together. The correction controls the false discovery rate -- the expected
# share of claimed findings that are false alarms -- across exactly these 12 and
# nothing else. So ADDING OR REMOVING AN ENTRY CHANGES THE BH ADJUSTMENT for
# every other correlate in the table, and can change which correlates come out
# significant.
# This vector is also what H3 factor-analyses and what H13 contrasts between
# groups.
correlate_vars <- c("dueprocess", "uncertain", "hatred", "anger", "exclusion",
                    "degradation", "suffering", "prisonviol", "harsh",
                    "revenge", "crimerates", "fear")
# Display names for the printed tables, keyed BY VARIABLE NAME rather than by
# position. A plain parallel vector of labels would silently mislabel every row
# if anyone reordered correlate_vars; a keyed lookup cannot drift out of order.
correlate_labels <- c(
  dueprocess  = "Due-process permissiveness",
  uncertain   = "Convicting on uncertain evidence",
  hatred      = "Hatred",
  anger       = "Anger",
  exclusion   = "Social exclusion",
  degradation = "Degradation",
  suffering   = "Infliction of suffering",
  prisonviol  = "Tolerance of prison violence",
  harsh       = "Harsh prison conditions",
  revenge     = "Revenge",
  crimerates  = "Perceived crime rates",
  fear        = "Fear of crime")

#' H1 -- punitiveness against each of the 12 correlates, BH-FDR across the set
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on; punit  the punitiveness column, which
#'            defaults to the 8-item self-report scale.
#' RETURNS    a 12-row data frame (a table of results, one row per correlate)
#'            sorted by r from high to low: y (correlate label), n, r, ci_lower,
#'            ci_upper, p_one_sided, p_two, p_BH_one_sided, p_BH_two_sided, sig.
#' USED BY    Phase 7.1 (whole sample, twice -- once with each punitiveness
#'            version) and Phase 9.1 (retributivists only, for H11).
#'
#' WHAT H1 CLAIMS. People who score higher on punitiveness should also score
#' higher on each of the 12 correlates. r is the correlation: a number between
#' -1 and +1 saying how tightly two measures move together, with 0 meaning not
#' at all. ci_lower and ci_upper give the two-sided 95% confidence interval that
#' cor_row() always reports, the range of true values the data still leave
#' plausible.
#'
#' The prediction is that each correlation is POSITIVE, which names a direction,
#' so the one-sided p is the inferential quantity -- the number the decision
#' actually rests on (prereg 6.8) -- and the BH adjustment is applied to it. A
#' one-sided p counts only evidence running in the predicted direction. The
#' unadjusted one-sided p and both two-sided p-values travel alongside it,
#' because prereg 6.1 requires reporting adjusted AND unadjusted values: a
#' reader has to be able to see what the correction did.
#'
#' WHY BH AND ACROSS EXACTLY THESE 12. Run twelve tests at once and the chance
#' that at least one of them clears the significance cutoff on luck alone is far
#' higher than it is for any single test. H1 is a single family of related
#' correlations tested together, and prereg 6.1 controls the false discovery
#' rate within such a set with Benjamini-Hochberg (BH-FDR). BH rather than
#' Bonferroni because the aim is to bound the expected PROPORTION of false
#' claims among the correlates declared significant, not to guard against a
#' single false positive anywhere. With twelve measures that are genuinely
#' intercorrelated, Bonferroni would be needlessly severe and would bury real
#' effects. The family is these twelve and nothing else: the robustness run with
#' the full punitiveness index is adjusted within its own set of twelve, and the
#' exploratory E-hypotheses are not part of it.
run_h1 <- function(data, punit = "punitiveness") {
  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(correlate_vars, function(v)
    cor_row(data, punit, v, alternative = "greater",
            label_x = punit, label_y = unname(correlate_labels[v]))))
  # Adjust within this table only -- p.adjust() is handed exactly these 12 rows
  # and nothing else, which is what keeps the family the pre-registered twelve.
  res$p_BH_one_sided <- p.adjust(res$p_dir, method = "BH")
  res$p_BH_two_sided <- p.adjust(res$p_two, method = "BH")
  # The stars mark the ADJUSTED one-sided p, never the raw one. Star the
  # unadjusted value instead and a reader skimming the table would credit
  # findings that the multiple-testing correction had already thrown out.
  res$sig <- sig_stars(res$p_BH_one_sided)
  # Sort by r, the effect size, most positive first. Note that the sort is
  # SIGNED, not by strength: a correlation of -0.40 sorts LAST, below one of
  # 0.05. That suits H1, which predicts positive correlations, and it makes the
  # table read as a ranking of the correlates rather than as the arbitrary order
  # of correlate_vars.
  res <- res[order(-res$r), ]
  # Rename the directional p column to say plainly what it is here: every row in
  # this table is one-sided, so "p_one_sided" cannot be misread.
  names(res)[names(res) == "p_dir"] <- "p_one_sided"
  # Return only the reporting columns, in the order the printed table uses.
  res[, c("y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_one_sided", "p_two",
          "p_BH_one_sided", "p_BH_two_sided", "sig")]
}

#' H2 -- hostile aggression vs crime concerns as correlates of punitiveness
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data; punit  the punitiveness column.
#' RETURNS    the one-row steiger_overlap() frame.
#' USED BY    Phase 7.2 (whole sample) and Phase 9.1 (retributivists, H11).
#'
#' The question is which of two things punitiveness tracks more closely, so the
#' test compares two correlations rather than testing one. It uses STEIGER'S
#' TEST FOR DEPENDENT OVERLAPPING CORRELATIONS: dependent because both
#' correlations are measured on the same people, overlapping because both
#' include punitiveness. The two r's are therefore not independent: how far
#' apart they can fall by chance depends on how strongly hostile aggression and
#' crime concerns correlate with EACH OTHER. A test that treated them as coming
#' from two separate samples would ignore that and use the wrong yardstick --
#' see the fuller note on steiger_overlap().
#'
#' One-sided "greater": the prediction names hostile aggression as the stronger
#' correlate. That is the substantive claim, that punitiveness is driven by
#' antagonism toward offenders rather than by worry about crime.
run_h2 <- function(data, punit = "punitiveness") {
  steiger_overlap(data, punit, "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "r(punitiveness, hostile aggression) > r(punitiveness, crime concerns)")
}

#' H3 -- do the 12 correlates form one punitiveness dimension?
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    a list: cor_matrix, n_pairs, share_positive, mean_r, eigenvalues,
#'            var_explained_1, n_eigen_gt1, fa (a psych::fa object, or NULL when
#'            the model could not be fitted), n_obs. Phases 7.3 and 9.1 format
#'            the pieces they need.
#' USED BY    Phase 7.3 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' THE QUESTION. H3 says the 12 correlates are 12 windows onto one underlying
#' attitude, not 12 separate opinions. Prereg 6.3 asks for three summaries
#' rather than one test, because "a single dimension runs through them" is a
#' claim about structure and no one p-value expresses it. The three are:
#'   1. The SHARE of the intercorrelations that are positive.
#'   2. The FIRST EIGENVALUE and the scree. An eigenvalue is how much of the
#'      shared variation one underlying dimension accounts for; the scree is the
#'      run of eigenvalues from largest to smallest, and one dimension
#'      dominating shows up as a big first value with a sharp drop after it.
#'   3. A one-factor exploratory factor analysis (EFA): a model that asks how
#'      well a single factor -- one hidden dimension the items are taken to
#'      reflect -- can reproduce the whole pattern of correlations.
#' Read together, a high share positive PLUS a dominant first eigenvalue PLUS
#' uniformly positive loadings is the pattern that supports H3. Any one of the
#' three on its own can mislead, which is why all three are reported.
run_h3 <- function(data) {
  # Keep only the correlates that exist as columns, so a composite that failed
  # to build cannot bring the whole analysis down.
  vars <- intersect(correlate_vars, names(data))
  # "pairwise.complete.obs" computes each cell of the correlation matrix on
  # everyone who answered BOTH of that cell's two variables, instead of throwing
  # a participant out of the entire matrix over one missing composite. That
  # keeps the sample sizes up. The cost is that a matrix stitched together from
  # slightly different subsets is not guaranteed to be positive definite -- the
  # mathematical consistency condition a correlation matrix computed on one
  # single sample will meet, short of exact redundancy among the variables. That
  # is why eigen() below is read descriptively, and why the factor analysis is
  # wrapped in tryCatch, R's catch-the-error-and-keep-going wrapper.
  cm <- suppressWarnings(cor(data[, vars], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
  # A correlation matrix is a square grid, so it lists every pair twice -- once
  # above the diagonal and once below -- and carries 1s down the diagonal where
  # a variable meets itself. upper.tri() takes just the top half: the 66 unique
  # pairs (12*11/2), each counted once. Using the whole matrix instead would
  # double-count every pair and drag the average toward 1.
  off <- cm[upper.tri(cm)]
  # The eigenvalues of the matrix, largest first. The first one is the size of
  # the single strongest dimension running through the 12 correlates.
  ev  <- eigen(cm)$values
  # The factor analysis wants ONE sample size, but the matrix above was built
  # pairwise and so has a different n behind every cell. The listwise n is used
  # instead -- listwise meaning only people with no missing value on ANY of the
  # 12 count -- which is the conservative choice, since it is the smallest of
  # those n's.
  n_obs <- sum(stats::complete.cases(data[, vars]))
  # rotate = "none" because a ONE-factor solution has nothing to rotate.
  # Rotation is the step that redistributes variance -- how spread out the
  # values are -- among SEVERAL factors to make them readable. With a single
  # factor there is nothing to spread around.
  # fm = "minres" is minimum residual. It picks the loadings that leave the
  # smallest residuals: the leftover gaps between the observed correlations and
  # the ones the model implies. It is used here instead of maximum likelihood
  # for two reasons. Maximum likelihood assumes multivariate normality and
  # minres does not, and minres converges on a pairwise matrix that maximum
  # likelihood can reject outright.
  # max(n_obs, 20) is a floor that keeps the call legal on a small subgroup. On
  # failure the result is NULL and the caller prints a message, rather than the
  # whole document stopping.
  fa1 <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::fa(cm, nfactors = 1, n.obs = max(n_obs, 20), rotate = "none",
              fm = "minres"))), error = function(e) NULL)
  # Everything the two call sites might want, handed back in one list so each
  # can format the pieces it needs.
  list(cor_matrix = cm,
       n_pairs = length(off),
       share_positive = mean(off > 0),
       mean_r = mean(off),
       eigenvalues = ev,
       var_explained_1 = ev[1] / sum(ev),
       n_eigen_gt1 = sum(ev > 1),
       fa = fa1,
       n_obs = n_obs)
}

#' H4 -- is strict proportionality endorsed?
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    a list of two data frames: `tests` (two one-sample midpoint tests,
#'            each comparing one mean against the fixed value 4) and `shares`
#'            (three proportions with exact Clopper-Pearson confidence
#'            intervals, the range of true shares the data leave plausible).
#' USED BY    Phase 8.1 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' Two halves to the hypothesis, answering two different questions.
#'
#' The MEAN half asks whether agreement sits at or below 4, the neutral point of
#' the 1-7 scale. It is tested one-sided "less" because that is the direction
#' the hypothesis names. It is run on BOTH the single proportionality item and
#' the three-item just-deserts component, so the result cannot hinge on the
#' wording of any one item.
#'
#' The SHARE half asks how many people endorse punishment beyond the crime,
#' which a mean cannot show. A mean sitting at the midpoint is equally
#' consistent with everybody being indifferent and with a split sample where
#' half agree strongly and half disagree strongly. Report the mean alone and
#' those two very different pictures would be indistinguishable.
run_h4 <- function(data) {
  # The mean half: each measure against the neutral midpoint of 4, one-sided in
  # the "less" direction that H4 names.
  tests <- rbind(
    one_sample_mid(data, "proportionality", mu = 4, alternative = "less",
                   label = "Proportionality item vs midpoint 4"),
    one_sample_mid(data, "proportionality_jd", mu = 4, alternative = "less",
                   label = "Proportionality component (JD) vs midpoint 4"))
  # The share half: three thresholds, all read against the midpoint of 4.
  # WARNING: severity_1 enters RAW here, never severity_1_R. The reversed
  # version exists only for the proportionality component. Swap it in and this
  # block would report the share who want punishment BELOW the crime while the
  # label says the exact opposite -- a published number with its meaning
  # inverted.
  shares <- rbind(
    # The strict reading: strictly above the neutral point.
    prop_ci(as.integer(data$severity_1 > 4),
            "Endorse punishment GREATER than the crime (severity_1 > 4)"),
    # The permissive reading, which also counts people sitting exactly on the
    # neutral point. It is reported beside the strict one so the headline share
    # does not quietly depend on which side of the line the fence-sitters land.
    prop_ci(as.integer(data$severity_1 >= 4),
            "At least neutral on punishment greater than the crime (severity_1 >= 4)"),
    # The mirror image of endorsing strict proportionality: everyone at or below
    # neutral on the proportionality item, i.e. those who do NOT endorse it.
    prop_ci(as.integer(data$proportionality <= 4),
            "Do NOT endorse strict proportionality (proportionality <= 4)"))
  list(tests = tests, shares = shares)
}

#' H5 -- exceeding the crime versus falling short of the harm
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    the one-row paired_test() frame.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.2 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' Both items come from the SAME participant, so the test is paired: it works on
#' each person's own difference between their two answers. That strips out the
#' fact that some people simply agree with everything, which is noise here and
#' not the question.
#'
#' One-sided "greater" because H5 names the direction: support for punishing
#' BEYOND the crime should exceed support for punishing BELOW the harm. If
#' proportionality really were a symmetric constraint -- no more than deserved
#' and no less -- the two would be endorsed equally. The asymmetry is the
#' finding.
#'
#' HAZARD: both items are used RAW here. severity_1_R and severity_2_R exist
#' only for the proportionality component in Phase 4.3. Substituting either one
#' would invert the comparison, reporting the opposite result under the same
#' label.
run_h5 <- function(data) {
  paired_test(data, "severity_1", "severity_2", alternative = "greater",
              label = "severity_1 (punish beyond the crime) vs severity_2 (punish below the harm)")
}

#' H6 -- does just deserts hold together?
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    a list: cor (the one-row cor_row frame), alpha_two_parts,
#'            fit (the lavaan model object, or NULL if it could not be fitted),
#'            fit_measures (named numeric, or NULL), loadings (a data frame, or
#'            NULL).
#' USED BY    Phase 8.3 (whole sample) and Phase 9.1 (retributivists, H11).
#'
#' THE HYPOTHESIS. Just deserts is usually treated as one idea, but it bundles
#' two claims: that punishment is DESERVED (the purpose items, Retribution_1-4)
#' and that it should be PROPORTIONATE (the proportionality item plus the two
#' severity items reverse-keyed). H6 predicts they do not cohere -- that a
#' person can hold one without the other. Prereg 6.4 asks for three pieces of
#' evidence, and they are computed below in that order.
#'
#' HOW TO READ THE OUTPUT -- this is the one place in the document where the
#' "bad" numbers are the predicted ones. A NEAR-ZERO CORRELATION and a LOW ALPHA
#' are H6 coming true. They are NOT a measurement failure and must not be
#' reported as one. The incoherence IS the finding: if desert and
#' proportionality do not travel together, then "just deserts" names two
#' separable commitments, and any single score for it conceals which of the two
#' a given respondent actually holds.
run_h6 <- function(data) {
  # (a) The correlation between the two parts. TWO-SIDED, meaning the test looks
  # for a departure from zero in EITHER direction: H6 predicts the absence of a
  # relationship, and "absent" names no direction, so prereg 6.8 leaves it
  # two-sided.
  r6 <- cor_row(data, "deserved", "proportionality_jd",
                alternative = "two.sided",
                label_x = "Deserved (Retribution_1-4)",
                label_y = "Proportionality component")
  # (b) Cronbach's alpha of the two parts treated as a two-item scale. Alpha is
  # an index of internal consistency: how far a set of items behaves like
  # several readings of one single thing. It reaches 1 at the top, but it has NO
  # floor at 0. Two parts that are unrelated give an alpha of about zero, and
  # two that pull in opposite directions give a negative one. Expect that here
  # rather than treating it as a broken calculation -- H6 predicts a low alpha.
  # Both parts are z-scored first -- put on a common footing, mean 0 and SD 1 --
  # so that alpha is computed over comparable variances, that is, over parts
  # that are equally spread out. The parts are means of 4 and 3 items
  # respectively and need not spread alike; without the rescaling the
  # wider-spread part would dominate the number.
  two_parts <- data.frame(deserved = as.numeric(scale(data$deserved)),
                          proportionality = as.numeric(scale(data$proportionality_jd)))
  a6 <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::alpha(two_parts, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_)

  # (c) A one-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA): a model that states in
  # advance that one hidden factor explains a set of items, then reports how
  # badly that story fits the answers people actually gave. It is run over the
  # seven constituent ITEMS rather than over the two composites. At the item
  # level a single latent "just deserts" factor has to account for all seven at
  # once, so a two-cluster structure shows up either as poor fit or as a
  # collapsed loading. The composite-level correlation in (a) could not tell
  # either of those apart from plain unreliability.
  cfa_items <- c(paste0("Retribution_", 1:4), "proportionality",
                 "severity_1_R", "severity_2_R")
  # Start all three outputs at NULL, so the caller gets a well-formed result
  # even when lavaan is missing or an item is absent.
  fit <- NULL; fitm <- NULL; loadings <- NULL
  if (HAVE("lavaan") && all(cfa_items %in% names(data))) {
    # The model in lavaan's notation: "=~" reads "is measured by", so this line
    # says one factor named JustDeserts is measured by all seven items.
    mod <- paste0("JustDeserts =~ ", paste(cfa_items, collapse = " + "))
    # A CFA needs a unit of measurement for the invisible factor, and there are
    # two ways to supply one. std.lv = TRUE fixes the latent variance -- the
    # spread of the factor itself -- at 1, rather than fixing the first item's
    # loading. Every item's loading is then freely estimated, and all seven are
    # comparable with one another. That matters here because of the
    # |lambda| < .30 rule: lambda is the loading, and a loading weaker than .30
    # counts as weak. The rule has to be able to catch a weak loading on ANY
    # item, the first one included.
    # missing = "fiml" is full-information maximum likelihood: it keeps people
    # who answered some but not all seven items and uses everything they did
    # answer, instead of listwise deletion, which discards a whole person over
    # one unanswered item. That matches the at-least-half rule used to score the
    # composites.
    fit <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(lavaan::cfa(
      mod, data = as.data.frame(data[, cfa_items]), std.lv = TRUE,
      missing = "fiml")), error = function(e) NULL)
    # Fitting is an iterative search, and it does not always reach convergence
    # -- that is, settle on one stable set of estimates and stop moving. A
    # non-converged model is DISCARDED rather than reported: its fit indices
    # would be meaningless numbers, and "the search never settled" is not the
    # same evidence as "the model settled and then fitted badly".
    if (!is.null(fit) && lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged")) {
      # CFI (comparative fit index: how much better this model does than one
      # with no factor at all, higher being better) and RMSEA (root mean square
      # error of approximation: the model's average error per degree of freedom,
      # lower being better) are the two indices the pre-registered rule names.
      # TLI, SRMR (standardized root mean square residual: the typical gap
      # between the observed correlations and the ones the model implies) and
      # the RMSEA confidence interval are reported for context. chisq, df and
      # pvalue are reported too, but read them with care: at N = 948 a
      # chi-square is expected to reject the model regardless, because a large
      # enough sample makes even a trivial misfit detectable.
      fitm <- tryCatch(lavaan::fitMeasures(
        fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea",
               "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr")),
        error = function(e) NULL)
      # The STANDARDIZED solution, which restates every loading on one common
      # scale. Without it each loading would sit in its own item's units, and
      # the |lambda| < .30 threshold would mean something different for every
      # item in the table.
      pe <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit)
      # lavaan returns one row per estimated quantity, of several kinds. The
      # operator "=~" marks the measurement rows -- the loadings, factor on to
      # item -- so this keeps those and drops the variances and intercepts.
      loadings <- pe[pe$op == "=~", c("rhs", "est.std", "se", "z", "pvalue",
                                      "ci.lower", "ci.upper")]
      # Rename to plain reporting names, so the printed table does not make a
      # reader learn lavaan's internal vocabulary.
      names(loadings) <- c("item", "std_loading", "se", "z", "p",
                           "ci_lower", "ci_upper")
    } else fit <- NULL
  }
  list(cor = r6, alpha_two_parts = a6, fit = fit, fit_measures = fitm,
       loadings = loadings)
}

#' Deterrence and incapacitation against parsimony -- do they hold together?
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data        the sample to run on.
#'            goal_var    the goal composite already scored in Phase 4.3:
#'                        "deterrence" or "incapacitation".
#'            goal_items  that composite's purpose items, for example
#'                        paste0("Deterrence_", 1:3).
#'            goal_label  the display name used in the printed tables.
#' RETURNS    a list in the same shape run_h6() returns -- cor, alpha_two_parts,
#'            fit, fit_measures, loadings -- plus `items`, a two-row cor_row
#'            frame setting the goal against each parsimony item on its own,
#'            and `goal_items`, echoed back so 8.3c can tell the goal's
#'            loadings apart from the limit's.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.3c only. Nothing registered calls it.
#'
#' WHY THIS MIRRORS run_h6() STEP FOR STEP. H6 asks whether a goal of
#' punishment travels with the limit its own theory places on punishment:
#' desert with proportionality. Consequentialist theory has a limit of its own.
#' If punishment is justified only by what it prevents, any punishment beyond
#' what prevention requires is suffering that buys nothing, so the limit is
#' PARSIMONY: punish no more than necessary. The same question can therefore be
#' put to deterrence and to incapacitation, and it is put in H6's own three
#' steps so the answers can be laid beside H6's: (a) the correlation between
#' the goal and the limit, (b) the alpha of the two treated as one scale,
#' (c) a one-factor CFA over the items. DANGER: a change made to run_h6() must
#' be made here too, or the side-by-side comparison in 8.3c stops being like
#' for like and nothing will say so.
#'
#' THE PARSIMONY ITEMS ARE USED RAW. THIS IS THE HAZARD IN THIS FUNCTION.
#' parsimony_1 ("Criminal punishments should be as light as possible") and
#' parsimony_2 ("The state should not punish more than is absolutely
#' necessary") enter punitiveness reverse-coded, as parsimony_1_R and
#' parsimony_2_R, because agreeing with them is the LESS punitive answer. Here
#' the question is whether people ACCEPT the limit, so agreeing must score
#' high, and the raw columns are the right ones. Substituting either _R column
#' would flip the sign of every number below and report the opposite finding
#' under the same label.
#'
#' THE PARSIMONY SCORE IS BUILT HERE, NOT WITH compute_composite(). That helper
#' appends every scale it scores to alpha_table, which becomes the published
#' Phase 4.10 reliability table, so calling it this late would quietly add a
#' row to a registered output. Its scoring rule is copied instead: the mean of
#' the two items for anyone who answered at least one of them (half of two,
#' rounded up, is one). The score exists only inside this function. `d` is not
#' changed.
run_goal_parsimony <- function(data, goal_var, goal_items, goal_label) {
  pars_items <- c("parsimony_1", "parsimony_2")
  # A private copy, so the parsimony score added below cannot leak into `d`.
  # (Named `dat` rather than `local`, which is the name of a base R function.)
  dat <- as.data.frame(data)
  n_answered <- rowSums(!is.na(dat[, pars_items]))
  dat$parsimony_pair <- rowMeans(dat[, pars_items], na.rm = TRUE)
  # The at-least-half rule, enforced after the mean exactly as
  # compute_composite() enforces it, then NaN (nobody answered either item)
  # turned into a real missing value.
  dat$parsimony_pair[n_answered < 1] <- NA_real_
  dat$parsimony_pair[is.nan(dat$parsimony_pair)] <- NA_real_

  # (a) The goal against the limit. TWO-SIDED, as H6 is. Consequentialist
  # theory implies a positive relationship, but nothing about these pairs was
  # registered, so no direction is claimed in advance.
  r_gp <- cor_row(dat, goal_var, "parsimony_pair", alternative = "two.sided",
                  label_x = goal_label,
                  label_y = "Parsimony (parsimony_1 and _2, raw)")

  # The same goal against each parsimony item separately. The two items do not
  # say the same thing. parsimony_2 states the principle: no more than
  # necessary. parsimony_1 asks for punishment as light as possible, which goes
  # beyond the principle and reads partly as a lean toward leniency. 8.3b found
  # desert tracking a lean far more closely than it tracks a principle, so the
  # items are shown apart in case the same split is at work here. ORDER
  # MATTERS: parsimony_2 is row 1 and 8.3c reads it by position.
  r_items <- do.call(rbind, list(
    cor_row(dat, goal_var, "parsimony_2", alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = goal_label,
            label_y = "  parsimony_2 alone (the principle: no more than necessary)"),
    cor_row(dat, goal_var, "parsimony_1", alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = goal_label,
            label_y = "  parsimony_1 alone (as light as possible)")))

  # (b) Alpha of the two parts treated as a two-item scale. Both parts are
  # z-scored first, for the reason given in run_h6(): the goal is a mean of two
  # or three items and parsimony a mean of two, and without the rescaling the
  # more spread-out part would dominate the number. Alpha has no floor at zero.
  # Two parts that pull in opposite directions give a negative alpha, and that
  # is a result, not a broken calculation.
  two_parts <- data.frame(goal = as.numeric(scale(dat[[goal_var]])),
                          parsimony = as.numeric(scale(dat$parsimony_pair)))
  a_gp <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::alpha(two_parts, check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
    error = function(e) NA_real_)

  # (c) The one-factor CFA over the constituent items: the goal's purpose items
  # plus the two raw parsimony items. The settings are run_h6()'s, for the
  # reasons given there: std.lv = TRUE so every loading is freely estimated and
  # the |lambda| < .30 rule can catch any item, including the first;
  # missing = "fiml" so partial responders are kept.
  # A SMALL-MODEL CAUTION. Incapacitation has only two items, so its model has
  # four indicators and 2 degrees of freedom: 10 pieces of observed information
  # (four variances and six covariances) against 8 estimated numbers (four
  # loadings and four residual variances). An RMSEA computed on 2 degrees of
  # freedom swings widely, so for that pair the loadings carry more weight than
  # the fit indices. Deterrence, with three items, has 5 degrees of freedom.
  cfa_items <- c(goal_items, pars_items)
  fit <- NULL; fitm <- NULL; loadings <- NULL
  if (HAVE("lavaan") && all(cfa_items %in% names(dat))) {
    # "=~" reads "is measured by": one factor measured by every item listed.
    factor_name <- paste0(gsub("[^A-Za-z]", "", goal_label), "Parsimony")
    mod <- paste0(factor_name, " =~ ", paste(cfa_items, collapse = " + "))
    fit <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(lavaan::cfa(
      mod, data = dat[, cfa_items], std.lv = TRUE, missing = "fiml")),
      error = function(e) NULL)
    # A model that never converged is discarded, not reported, as in run_h6():
    # "the search never settled" is not the same evidence as "it fitted badly".
    if (!is.null(fit) && lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged")) {
      fitm <- tryCatch(lavaan::fitMeasures(
        fit, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea",
               "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper", "srmr")),
        error = function(e) NULL)
      pe <- lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit)
      loadings <- pe[pe$op == "=~", c("rhs", "est.std", "se", "z", "pvalue",
                                      "ci.lower", "ci.upper")]
      names(loadings) <- c("item", "std_loading", "se", "z", "p",
                           "ci_lower", "ci_upper")
    } else fit <- NULL
  }
  list(cor = r_gp, items = r_items, alpha_two_parts = a_gp, fit = fit,
       fit_measures = fitm, loadings = loadings, goal_items = goal_items)
}

#' H7 -- the Kantian limits against revenge and against just deserts
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    a 12-row data frame: six limit measures against revenge, then the
#'            same six against just deserts. p_dir is renamed p_directional
#'            because the two blocks use different alternatives.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.4 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' The two sides carry different predictions, so they get different tests. The
#' REVENGE side has a direction -- willingness to set the limits aside should go
#' WITH revenge -- so it is one-sided "greater". The JUST DESERTS side predicts
#' NO relationship at all, and "none" points nowhere, so that side is two-sided
#' (prereg 6.8). Together the two sides make the substantive point: setting the
#' Kantian limits aside is a vengeful posture, not a desert-based one.
#'
#' Six measures rather than one, and both limit aggregates, so a reader can see
#' whether the pattern rests on the components the two aggregates share.
#' kant_nonoverlap drops hatred, which is itself a hostile-aggression
#' constituent, and so is the stricter of the two: it cannot be dismissed as
#' correlating with revenge merely because a piece of hostility is already baked
#' into it (prereg 5.5).
run_h7 <- function(data) {
  # The six limit measures: the two aggregates first, then the four component
  # composites they are built from. The components are listed alongside the
  # aggregates so a reader can see whether a result holds across the whole
  # limit construct or rests on just one of its parts.
  limit_vars <- c("kant_core", "kant_nonoverlap", "dueprocess", "uncertain",
                  "hatred", "anger")
  # Display names, matched to limit_vars BY POSITION, so the two vectors must
  # stay in the same order. Reorder one without the other and every row of the
  # printed table gets the wrong name.
  limit_labs <- c("Kantian limits (core: process, evidence, dispassion)",
                  "Kantian limits (non-overlapping: process, evidence, anger)",
                  "Due-process permissiveness", "Convicting on uncertain evidence",
                  "Hatred (dispassion, reversed)", "Anger (dispassion, reversed)")
  # Side one: each of the six limit measures against revenge, one-sided
  # "greater", because that is the direction H7 predicts.
  rev_side <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(limit_vars), function(i)
    cor_row(data, limit_vars[i], "revenge", alternative = "greater",
            label_x = limit_labs[i], label_y = "Revenge")))
  # Side two: the same six against just deserts, two-sided, because the
  # prediction there is of no relationship in either direction.
  jd_side <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(limit_vars), function(i)
    cor_row(data, limit_vars[i], "just_deserts", alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = limit_labs[i], label_y = "Just deserts")))
  out <- rbind(rev_side, jd_side)
  # Renamed because half these rows carry a one-sided p and half a two-sided
  # one, so a column simply labelled p_dir would invite reading the whole column
  # the same way. The `alternative` column travels with the frame and says which
  # is which, row by row.
  names(out)[names(out) == "p_dir"] <- "p_directional"
  out
}

#' H8 -- the Kantian limits against punitiveness
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data; punit  the punitiveness column (self-report by default).
#' RETURNS    a 6-row data frame (a table with named columns), one row per limit
#'            measure, with p_dir renamed p_one_sided.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.5 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' All six rows are one-sided "greater". One-sided means the test looks for a
#' difference in ONE named direction only, and here that direction is up. The
#' six limit measures are keyed as willingness to SET THE LIMITS ASIDE, so a
#' high score marks a respondent who is less restrained. The prediction follows
#' from that keying: the less restrained a respondent is, the more punitive.
#' That is a directional claim (prereg 6.8), and a directional claim gets a
#' one-sided test, because a two-sided test spends half its sensitivity watching
#' for a result nobody predicted.
#'
#' Same six measures as H7, in the same order, so the two tables line up row for
#' row and a reader can read straight across from one to the other.
run_h8 <- function(data, punit = "punitiveness") {
  limit_vars <- c("kant_core", "kant_nonoverlap", "dueprocess", "uncertain",
                  "hatred", "anger")
  limit_labs <- c("Kantian limits (core)", "Kantian limits (non-overlapping)",
                  "Due-process permissiveness", "Convicting on uncertain evidence",
                  "Hatred", "Anger")
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(limit_vars), function(i)
    cor_row(data, limit_vars[i], punit, alternative = "greater",
            label_x = limit_labs[i], label_y = "Punitiveness (self-report)")))
  names(out)[names(out) == "p_dir"] <- "p_one_sided"
  out
}

#' H9 -- self-reported support for just deserts versus revenge
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data  the sample to run on.
#' RETURNS    a 2-row data frame (a table with named columns) of paired_test()
#'            results.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.6 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' Paired means each participant's two scores are compared against each other,
#' and the test works on the gap between them. That is the right test here
#' because both scores come from the SAME person. A participant who agrees
#' readily with everything scores high on both, and that shared tendency drops
#' out of the gap instead of adding noise. Treat the two scores as though they
#' came from two separate groups of people and the shared tendency stays in, so
#' the test has to work through noise the design had already removed.
#'
#' One-sided "greater" means the test looks in one named direction only. The
#' prediction is that people endorse desert more readily than revenge, which is
#' the socially respectable ordering and the one the just-deserts tradition
#' assumes.
#'
#' Two rows on purpose. The first uses the combined just_deserts score; the
#' second uses `deserved` alone. If H6 shows the two parts do not cohere -- that
#' is, they do not behave like two readings of one idea -- then the combined
#' score is an average of two separable things. The second row is the version of
#' H9 that does not lean on that averaging. Read them together.
run_h9 <- function(data) {
  rbind(
    paired_test(data, "just_deserts", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
                label = "Just deserts vs revenge"),
    paired_test(data, "deserved", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
                label = "Deserved (purpose items) vs revenge"))
}

#' H10 -- revenge versus just deserts as correlates of punitiveness
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data; punit  the punitiveness column (self-report by default).
#' RETURNS    the one-row steiger_overlap() frame.
#' USED BY    Phase 8.7 and Phase 9.1.
#'
#' Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations again, for the same
#' reason as H2. Two correlations are compared. Both are measured on the same
#' people, and both contain punitiveness, which is what "overlapping" means.
#' Their sampling distributions are therefore dependent. A sampling distribution
#' is the range of values one r would take if the whole study were run again and
#' again, and here the two ranges are tied to each other: the strength of
#' r(revenge, just deserts), the correlation between the two rivals themselves,
#' determines how far apart the two can drift by chance. A test that assumed
#' independence has no way to use that number, so it would measure the gap
#' against the wrong yardstick.
#'
#' This is the hinge of the construct-validity block, the part of the document
#' asking whether these measures capture what they claim to. Paired with H9 it
#' makes a pointed contrast: people SAY they support desert more than revenge
#' (H9), and yet punitiveness tracks revenge more closely than it tracks desert
#' (H10). The two together are the case that reported justification and
#' operative motive come apart: the reason a person gives for punishing is not
#' the motive actually moving them. One-sided "greater", meaning the test looks
#' in one direction only, since the prediction names revenge as the stronger
#' correlate.
run_h10 <- function(data, punit = "punitiveness") {
  steiger_overlap(data, punit, "revenge", "just_deserts",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "r(punitiveness, revenge) > r(punitiveness, just deserts)")
}

cat("Hypothesis functions defined: run_h1() ... run_h10().\n")
cat("Each takes a data frame, so Phase 9 can rerun them inside the\n")
cat("retributivist group for H11.\n")
```

## 7.1 H1 -- punitiveness and the 12 correlates (BH-FDR)

**H1.** Punitiveness correlates positively with each of the 12 correlates. The
prediction names a direction, so each test is one-sided: it looks for a positive
correlation and nothing else.

Running 12 tests at once creates a problem. Each test carries its own chance of
a false alarm, and those chances accumulate across the set. The fix used here is
**BH-FDR**, the Benjamini-Hochberg control of the false discovery rate, which
holds down the expected share of false claims among the results declared
significant. It works on the family as a whole: the 12 p-values are sorted, and
each is adjusted by an amount that depends on where it falls in that order. The
adjustment never moves a p-value down, and the largest p-value in the family
comes through unchanged. **Both adjusted and unadjusted p-values are reported**
(prereg 6.1), so a reader can see exactly what the correction did.

The **self-report** punitiveness scale is used here, not the version that folds
in the sentence a participant handed down. That matters. If the sentence sat
inside punitiveness and inside a correlate at the same time, the same numbers
would appear on both sides of one correlation. The measure would then be partly
correlated with itself.

```{r phase7_h1}
# === H1: PUNITIVENESS AND ITS 12 CORRELATES (prereg 2.1, 6.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the H1 family on the whole sample and produces two
# tables -- `H1_correlations` (the confirmatory test, meaning the registered one
# that counts, run on the self-report punitiveness scale) and
# `H1_correlations_full_index` (the robustness rerun, meaning the same test done
# a second way to see whether the answer holds up).
#
# `h1_full` is also reused in Phase 9.1. There it is merged against the run on
# retributivists only, so the two sets of correlations sit side by side and a
# reader can see whether the pattern holds inside that group. Do not rename
# `h1_full` here without fixing Phase 9.1 as well.
h1_full <- run_h1(d)
TABLES[["H1_correlations"]] <- h1_full
show_table(h1_full,
           "H1: punitiveness (self-report) with each pre-registered correlate. p_one_sided is the directional test; p_BH_one_sided is BH-FDR adjusted across the 12.")

cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d correlations are positive; %d significant at BH-adjusted p < .05.\n",
            sum(h1_full$r > 0, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(h1_full),
            sum(h1_full$p_BH_one_sided < .05, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Correlations range from r = %.3f (%s) to r = %.3f (%s).\n",
            min(h1_full$r, na.rm = TRUE), h1_full$y[which.min(h1_full$r)],
            max(h1_full$r, na.rm = TRUE), h1_full$y[which.max(h1_full$r)]))

# ROBUSTNESS ONLY -- THIS IS NOT THE REGISTERED TEST OF H1. The same twelve
# correlations are run a second time, against the full punitiveness index. That
# index adds the sentence a participant handed down, after that sentence has
# been z-scored within each vignette.
#
# A z-score restates a value as how far above or below its own group's average
# it sits, counted in standard deviations, which is that group's own measure of
# typical spread. Because the unit is the group's own spread, z-scores from
# different groups can be put side by side. That is the whole reason for doing
# it WITHIN vignette: the three crime stories drew different sentence lengths,
# and z-scoring inside each one strips that difference out before the sentences
# are pooled.
#
# The rerun is legitimate HERE because none of the twelve correlates is built
# from the sentence, so the sentence cannot turn up on both sides of any one
# correlation. It would NOT be legitimate anywhere the sentencing ratio or H14
# is involved, because those are built from the sentence themselves, and the
# index would then be correlated partly with itself.
#
# BH-FDR is applied again inside these twelve, on its own. It leaves the
# adjusted p-values in the table above untouched: that family is the registered
# twelve and nothing else.
h1_full_index <- run_h1(d, punit = "punitiveness_full")
TABLES[["H1_correlations_full_index"]] <- h1_full_index
show_table(h1_full_index,
           "H1 robustness: the same correlations using the full punitiveness index (self-report + within-vignette sentence)")

# === COMPANION: SEVERITY AND THE PROPORTIONALITY PRINCIPLE ===
# WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE TABLE AND NOT TWO MORE ROWS ABOVE. The registered H1
# family is twelve correlates, and BH-FDR is applied across exactly those
# twelve. The size of the BH adjustment depends on how many tests are in the
# family, so adding a thirteenth row would move every adjusted p-value in the
# registered test. The two measures introduced in Phase 4.3 are therefore
# reported BESIDE the family rather than inside it, with no correction applied
# and none implied.
#
# They are here because the two behave in opposite ways, and that contrast is
# the point. `severity_index` is the direction-of-departure measure: how far a
# person wants punishment to run BEYOND the crime. `proportionality_principle`
# is the principle itself: punishment should FIT the crime, no more and no less.
# The direction of departure tracks punitiveness closely, while the principle is
# flat against it. Section 8.3b puts the same pair against desert.
h1_companion <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "severity_index", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "punitiveness", label_y = "Severity index (punish beyond the crime)"),
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "severity_1", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "punitiveness", label_y = "  severity_1 alone"),
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "severity_2_R", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "punitiveness", label_y = "  severity_2 reversed alone"),
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "proportionality_principle",
          label_x = "punitiveness", label_y = "Proportionality principle (two-sided)")
))
TABLES[["H1_companion_severity"]] <- h1_companion
show_table(h1_companion,
           "Beside H1, not within it: severity and the proportionality principle against punitiveness. Outside the registered FDR family; a deviation from prereg 5.4.")

cat(sprintf("\nSeverity index would rank %d of %d against the registered correlates (r = %.3f).\n",
            sum(h1_full$r > h1_companion$r[1], na.rm = TRUE) + 1,
            nrow(h1_full) + 1, h1_companion$r[1]))
cat(sprintf("The proportionality principle is flat against punitiveness (r = %+.3f), which is itself the result:\n",
            h1_companion$r[4]))
cat("endorsing proportionality as a principle predicts nothing about how punitive a participant is.\n")
```

```{r phase7_h1_figure, fig.height=6}
# === FIGURE: H1 FOREST PLOT ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: draws the twelve correlations as a forest plot -- one
# dot per correlate with a horizontal line running through it -- and writes
# output/figures/H1_correlate_forest.png, appending the path to FIGURES for the
# Phase 10.2 manifest, which is the list of every figure the document produced.
#
# The dot is the correlation. The line is its 95% confidence interval: the range
# of true values the data leave standing, wide when the estimate is loose and
# short when it is tight.
#
# A forest plot rather than a bar chart because the interval is the whole point.
# With N = 948 almost everything comes out "significant", so a chart built
# around significance would tell a reader nothing they could not guess in
# advance. What they need to see is how precisely each r is pinned down and how
# far it sits from zero. The dashed line at zero is the reference.
#
# CAREFUL: DO NOT JUDGE SIGNIFICANCE BY EYE FROM THIS PLOT. The interval drawn
# here is the two-sided, unadjusted 95% CI that cor.test() returns, while the
# significance reported in the H1 table is one-sided and BH-adjusted. Those are
# not the same test, so whether a line clears the dashed zero need not match
# what the table says about that correlate. The table is where significance is
# read; the plot is where precision and rank are read.
h1_plot <- h1_full
# Reorder the factor by r, so the plot reads as a ranking from bottom to top. A
# factor is R's type for a grouping variable, and it carries its categories in a
# fixed order. On a discrete y axis -- ggplot's own term for an axis of named
# categories rather than numbers -- ggplot draws the FIRST level at the BOTTOM.
# So ordering the levels from the smallest r upward puts the largest correlation
# at the top. Leave this out and the correlates appear in whatever order they
# happen to be listed in, which reads as no order at all.
h1_plot$label <- factor(h1_plot$y, levels = h1_plot$y[order(h1_plot$r)])
p_h1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(h1_plot, ggplot2::aes(x = r, y = label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  ggplot2::geom_linerange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper),
                          colour = "grey30") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c3e50") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "H1: punitiveness and its correlates",
    subtitle = sprintf("Pearson r with 95%% CI (confirmatory, N = %d)", nrow(d)),
    x = "Correlation with punitiveness (self-report)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
print(p_h1)

# Saved at 300 dpi (dots per inch), the resolution journals ask for; save a
# figure at screen resolution instead and it prints blurred. Every figure in
# this document follows the same four steps: build the plot, print it into the
# knitted report, ggsave it into OUT_FIGURES, then append the path to FIGURES so
# Phase 10.2 can list it. Skip that last step and the file is written but never
# listed, so nobody reading the report knows it exists.
fig_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "H1_correlate_forest.png")
ggplot2::ggsave(fig_path, p_h1, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
FIGURES <- c(FIGURES, fig_path)
```

## 7.2 H2 -- hostile aggression versus crime concerns (Steiger)

**H2.** The hostile-aggression cluster (hatred, revenge, degradation, suffering,
prison violence) correlates more strongly with punitiveness than the
crime-concerns cluster (perceived crime rates, fear) does. Put plainly: what
drives punitiveness is antagonism toward offenders, not worry about crime.

Two correlations are being compared, and they are **dependent** (measured on the
same people) and **overlapping** (both of them contain punitiveness). That
combination rules out the ordinary way of comparing two correlations, which
assumes each of them came from its own separate sample of people. These two did
not. How far apart they can drift by chance depends on how strongly the two
clusters correlate with each other, and a separate-samples comparison has no way
to take that into account. The test used instead is **Steiger's (1980) test for
dependent overlapping correlations**, run through
`cocor::cocor.dep.groups.overlap`. It is one-sided because the prediction names
which of the two correlations should be the larger.

```{r phase7_h2}
# === H2: HOSTILE AGGRESSION VERSUS CRIME CONCERNS (prereg 2.1, 6.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs Steiger's test for dependent overlapping
# correlations on the whole sample, produces the table `H2_steiger`, and prints
# the cocor package's own full output beneath it.
#
# HOW TO READ IT. Three correlations go in, and their column names are terse:
#   r_jk -- punitiveness with hostile aggression, the predicted-stronger one
#   r_jh -- punitiveness with crime concerns, the rival it is measured against
#   r_kh -- the two clusters with each other. This is what makes the first two
#           depend on one another, and it is why Steiger's test is needed here
#           instead of an ordinary comparison of two correlations.
# The quantity of interest is `diff` = r_jk - r_jh, the gap between the two,
# reported with its zou2007 confidence interval: the range of true gaps the data
# leave standing. An interval that EXCLUDES zero is the substantive result,
# namely that punitiveness is better explained by antagonism toward offenders
# than by fear of crime. An interval straddling zero would mean the data do not
# separate the two rivals.
h2_full <- run_h2(d)
TABLES[["H2_steiger"]] <- h2_full
show_table(h2_full, "H2: Steiger's test for two dependent overlapping correlations")

cat(sprintf("\nr(punitiveness, hostile aggression) = %.3f\n", h2_full$r_jk))
cat(sprintf("r(punitiveness, crime concerns)     = %.3f\n", h2_full$r_jh))
cat(sprintf("r(hostile aggression, crime concerns) = %.3f\n", h2_full$r_kh))
cat(sprintf("Difference = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]; z = %.3f, p %s (one-sided)\n",
            h2_full$diff, h2_full$diff_lower, h2_full$diff_upper,
            h2_full$z, format_p(h2_full$p)))

# cocor's own printout, reproduced verbatim -- word for word, with nothing
# summarised away -- so a reader can see the test as the package itself states
# it: the null hypothesis, the alternative, and the exact statistic, not only
# the summarised row above. A reviewer checking this analysis against the
# package docs reads this block. It recomputes the same complete-case n that
# steiger_overlap() used, meaning the count of people who answered ALL THREE
# measures, so the two cannot disagree.
if (HAVE("cocor")) {
  ok2 <- stats::complete.cases(d$punitiveness, d$hostile_agg, d$crime_concerns)
  print(cocor::cocor.dep.groups.overlap(
    r.jk = h2_full$r_jk, r.jh = h2_full$r_jh, r.kh = h2_full$r_kh,
    n = sum(ok2), alternative = "greater", test = "steiger1980"))
}
```

## 7.2b H2 with the six-constituent cluster

H2 asks whether punitiveness tracks hostility toward offenders more closely than
it tracks worry about crime. Section 7.2 answers it with the registered
five-constituent cluster, using Steiger's test for dependent overlapping
correlations. That test asks whether one correlation is reliably larger than a
second when both are measured on the same people and both share a variable.
That answer stands. This subsection puts the same question a second time to the
six-constituent companion built in 4.9b, which brings harsh prison conditions
inside the cluster.

This is a rescoring check, not an independent test of H2. The two clusters share
five of their six constituents and correlate very nearly perfectly, which 4.9b
prints. So the companion row has to land close to the registered row before any
data are consulted. A matching answer here is arithmetic before it is evidence,
and reading it as confirmation would be a mistake. What the row can show is the
narrow thing it is run for: whether the H2 result depends on harsh conditions
having been scored outside the cluster rather than inside it.

Neither row is corrected for multiplicity, the extra risk of false alarms that
comes with running more than one test. The second row is not a second test in
any case. It shares punitiveness, it shares the crime-concerns foil, and it
shares five of its six constituents with the first. So it adds a description of
the registered result, not another chance of producing one.

```{r phase7_h2b}
# === H2 REPEATED WITH THE SIX-CONSTITUENT CLUSTER (companion to 7.2) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the H2 Steiger comparison twice, once with the
# registered five-constituent hostile-aggression cluster and once with
# `hostile_agg6`, which adds harsh prison conditions as a sixth constituent, and
# prints the two side by side as `H2b_hostile_cluster_five_vs_six`.
# PREREG: a companion to 6.3. H2 AS TESTED AND REPORTED IS THE FIVE-CONSTITUENT
#         VERSION IN 7.2. This chunk reproduces that result unchanged and sets a
#         companion beside it; the companion is NOT the test of H2.
# CONSUMES: run_h2() and steiger_overlap() (0.3 and 7.0), punitiveness (4.2),
#           hostile_agg and crime_concerns (4.9), hostile_agg6 (4.9b).
#
# The five-constituent row is produced by calling run_h2() itself, not by
# writing out a fresh steiger_overlap() call with the same arguments. That is
# deliberate. run_h2() is the registered function, and nothing between 7.2 and
# here changes `d`, the data frame that holds one row per participant. So this
# row IS the row 7.2 prints and cannot quietly drift away from it. A hand-copied
# call would drift. Someone later edits run_h2(); 7.2 changes and the copy does
# not; the document then reports two different numbers for one test.
h2b_five <- run_h2(d)

# The companion is identical in every respect except which cluster goes in. It
# keeps the same shared variable (punitiveness), the same foil (crime concerns),
# and the same one-sided "greater" direction. The foil is the rival the hostile
# cluster is measured against, and the direction carries the substantive claim
# that punitiveness is driven by antagonism toward offenders rather than by fear
# of crime. Keeping the foil and the direction fixed is the whole point. Change
# either one and the two rows stop answering the same question, so setting them
# side by side would tell a reader nothing.
h2b_six <- steiger_overlap(
  d, "punitiveness", "hostile_agg6", "crime_concerns",
  alternative = "greater",
  label = paste("r(punitiveness, hostile aggression, 6 constituents)",
                "> r(punitiveness, crime concerns)"))

h2b <- rbind(h2b_five, h2b_six)
# A plain-language key saying which row is which, carried as a column of the
# table rather than left to the row order. Left to row order, a reader who
# sorted the table, or who quoted a single row on its own, could easily take the
# companion for the registered test.
h2b$cluster <- c("5 constituents (registered, prereg 5.8)",
                 "6 constituents (companion, adds harsh conditions)")
h2b <- h2b[, c("cluster", "comparison", "r_jk", "r_jh", "r_kh", "n", "z", "p",
               "diff", "diff_lower", "diff_upper", "alternative")]
TABLES[["H2b_hostile_cluster_five_vs_six"]] <- h2b
# The long `comparison` string is dropped from the PRINTED version only, because
# it is wide enough to push the numbers off the edge of the page. The exported
# CSV still carries it, so the archived file records which comparison each row
# came from even though the printed table does not.
show_table(h2b[, c("cluster", "r_jk", "r_jh", "r_kh", "n", "z", "p", "diff",
                   "diff_lower", "diff_upper")],
           paste("7.2b: H2 with the registered cluster and with the",
                 "six-constituent companion. The registered test is the",
                 "first row."))

# HOW TO READ IT, the same way 7.2 reads. r_jk is punitiveness with the hostile
# cluster, r_jh is punitiveness with crime concerns, and r_kh is the two
# clusters with each other, which is the quantity that makes the first two
# depend on one another. The number of interest is diff = r_jk - r_jh, the gap
# between the two, with its confidence interval, the range of true gaps the data
# leave standing. An interval that excludes zero is the substantive result.
cat("\nRegistered, 5 constituents (this is H2):\n")
cat(sprintf("  r(punit, hostile) = %.3f; r(punit, crime) = %.3f\n",
            h2b_five$r_jk, h2b_five$r_jh))
cat(sprintf("  difference = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]; z = %.3f, p %s\n",
            h2b_five$diff, h2b_five$diff_lower, h2b_five$diff_upper,
            h2b_five$z, format_p(h2b_five$p)))
cat("Companion, 6 constituents:\n")
cat(sprintf("  r(punit, hostile) = %.3f; r(punit, crime) = %.3f\n",
            h2b_six$r_jk, h2b_six$r_jh))
cat(sprintf("  difference = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]; z = %.3f, p %s\n",
            h2b_six$diff, h2b_six$diff_lower, h2b_six$diff_upper,
            h2b_six$z, format_p(h2b_six$p)))

# DO NOT READ ANYTHING INTO A SMALL WOBBLE IN r_jh. The crime-concerns
# correlation uses the SAME variable in both rows, and yet its value can move by
# a hair between them. Steiger's test needs complete cases across all three
# columns at once, meaning people who answered every one of the three measures.
# Swapping in a cluster with slightly different missingness -- a different
# pattern of who left items unanswered -- changes which participants qualify, so
# the two rows rest on slightly different sets of people. A small difference in
# r_jh is that, and nothing more. Both n's are printed below so the shift is
# visible instead of mysterious.
if (!is.na(h2b_five$r_jk) && !is.na(h2b_six$r_jk) &&
    !is.na(h2b_five$r_jh) && !is.na(h2b_six$r_jh)) {
  cat(sprintf("\nHarsh conditions moves the hostile correlation by %+.3f and\n",
              h2b_six$r_jk - h2b_five$r_jk))
  cat(sprintf("the crime-concerns correlation by %+.3f, on n = %d and %d.\n",
              h2b_six$r_jh - h2b_five$r_jh, h2b_five$n, h2b_six$n))
}
cat("The pre-registered test of H2 is the five-constituent row, and that is\n")
cat("the row reported as H2 wherever H2 is reported.\n")
```


## 7.3 H3 -- do the correlates form one dimension?

**H3.** The correlates should be mostly positively intercorrelated, that is,
they should mostly rise and fall together. That is what one would expect if a
single punitiveness outlook runs through all twelve of them.

No single p-value can express a claim of that shape, so prereg 6.3 asks for
three summaries, read together.

The first is the share of the intercorrelations that come out positive. The
second is the first **eigenvalue**. Every component of the correlation matrix
has an eigenvalue attached to it. That number says how much of the total
variance -- the total amount the 12 measures vary -- the component carries, and
the first eigenvalue is the largest of the twelve. The third is the **scree**,
the plot of all the eigenvalues in order, taken from an **exploratory factor
analysis (EFA)**. An EFA is a model that hunts for the hidden dimension, or
dimensions, running behind a set of measures without being told in advance what
they are.

```{r phase7_h3}
# === H3: DO THE CORRELATES FORM ONE DIMENSION? (prereg 2.1, 6.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the three H3 summaries on the whole sample and
# produces the tables `H3_eigenvalues` and `H3_efa_loadings`. No one of the
# three settles the question alone, which is why prereg 6.3 asks for all three.
#
# HOW TO READ THE THREE PIECES TOGETHER.
#   share positive  -- of the 66 unique pairs of correlates, how many run the
#                      same way, meaning both rise together. A high share is the
#                      minimum one dimension requires: a negative pair is a
#                      correlate pulling against the rest.
#   first eigenvalue -- how much of the total variance, the total amount the 12
#                      measures vary, the leading component carries. A component
#                      is one common thread running through the 12 correlates,
#                      and the leading one is the thread they share most. With
#                      12 standardized variables an eigenvalue of 1 is the
#                      average share, so a first eigenvalue well above 1 plus a
#                      large first-to-second ratio is the pattern of one
#                      dominant factor.
#   one-factor EFA  -- an exploratory factor analysis fitted with a single
#                      hidden dimension. Its loadings say how strongly each
#                      correlate leans on that dimension, and loadings that are
#                      positive across the board mean every correlate is pulling
#                      on the same latent punitiveness outlook. Latent means the
#                      outlook is never measured directly; it is inferred from
#                      the way the twelve correlates move together.
# CAREFUL: the count of eigenvalues > 1 is printed but is NOT used to decide
# anything. That rule of thumb, the Kaiser criterion, overextracts -- it keeps
# more dimensions than the data support. Prereg 6.3 asks for the SHAPE of the
# scree, not for a count of values clearing a line.
h3_full <- run_h3(d)

cat(sprintf("Intercorrelations among the %d correlates: %d unique pairs\n",
            length(correlate_vars), h3_full$n_pairs))
cat(sprintf("  share positive: %.1f%%\n", 100 * h3_full$share_positive))
cat(sprintf("  mean intercorrelation: r = %.3f\n", h3_full$mean_r))
cat(sprintf("  first eigenvalue: %.2f of %d (%.1f%% of the variance)\n",
            h3_full$eigenvalues[1], length(h3_full$eigenvalues),
            100 * h3_full$var_explained_1))
cat(sprintf("  eigenvalues > 1: %d\n", h3_full$n_eigen_gt1))
cat(sprintf("  ratio of first to second eigenvalue: %.2f\n",
            h3_full$eigenvalues[1] / h3_full$eigenvalues[2]))

h3_eigen <- data.frame(component = seq_along(h3_full$eigenvalues),
                       eigenvalue = h3_full$eigenvalues,
                       proportion = h3_full$eigenvalues / sum(h3_full$eigenvalues))
TABLES[["H3_eigenvalues"]] <- h3_eigen
show_table(h3_eigen, "H3: eigenvalues of the correlate correlation matrix")

if (!is.null(h3_full$fa)) {
  # Column 1 of $loadings is the single factor, the one hidden dimension the
  # model was told to look for. Each value in that column is how strongly one
  # correlate leans on the dimension. Sorted from largest value downward, so the
  # table shows at a glance which correlates define the dimension and which sit
  # at its edge. WATCH FOR A NEGATIVE LOADING: it would be evidence AGAINST H3,
  # because it would mean one correlate runs against the common outlook.
  fa_load <- data.frame(correlate = rownames(h3_full$fa$loadings),
                        loading = as.numeric(h3_full$fa$loadings[, 1]),
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  fa_load <- fa_load[order(-fa_load$loading), ]
  TABLES[["H3_efa_loadings"]] <- fa_load
  print(show_table(fa_load, "H3: one-factor EFA loadings (minres)"))
  # Vaccounted row 2 is the proportion of the total variance -- the total amount
  # the correlates vary -- that the single factor accounts for. EXPECT IT TO
  # COME OUT LOWER than the raw first-eigenvalue share printed above, and do not
  # read the gap as a contradiction. A factor model excludes item-specific
  # variance, the part of each correlate that is peculiar to that one measure,
  # while an eigenvalue from a principal component analysis (PCA) counts that
  # part in.
  cat(sprintf("\nOne-factor EFA: %.1f%% of the variance explained.\n",
              100 * h3_full$fa$Vaccounted[2, 1]))
} else {
  cat("\nEFA could not be fitted on this sample.\n")
}
```

```{r phase7_h3_scree, fig.height=5}
# === FIGURE: H3 SCREE PLOT ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: plots the 12 eigenvalues in order, largest first, and
# writes output/figures/H3_scree.png. A scree plot takes its name from the slope
# of loose rubble at the foot of a cliff, which is what the flat tail of the
# plot is meant to look like. Prereg 6.3 names the scree specifically.
#
# The reference line at 1 is the eigenvalue a component would have if it carried
# no more than its fair share: with 12 standardized variables the total variance
# is 12, so spread evenly each component gets 1.
#
# READ THE SHAPE, NOT THE COUNT. What supports H3 is a large first value and
# then a sharp drop to a flat tail. How many values happen to clear the line is
# not the test, and treating it as one is the Kaiser-criterion mistake warned
# about in the chunk above.
scree_df <- h3_eigen
p_scree <- ggplot2::ggplot(scree_df, ggplot2::aes(x = component, y = eigenvalue)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#2c3e50") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#2c3e50") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = scree_df$component) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "H3: scree plot of the 12 punitiveness correlates",
                subtitle = sprintf("N = %d — a dominant first component supports one punitiveness dimension",
                                   h3_full$n_obs),
                x = "Component", y = "Eigenvalue") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
print(p_scree)
fig_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "H3_scree.png")
ggplot2::ggsave(fig_path, p_scree, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
FIGURES <- c(FIGURES, fig_path)
```

```{r phase7_h3_heatmap, fig.height=8}
# === FIGURE + TABLE: THE CORRELATE INTERCORRELATION MATRIX ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: draws the 12 x 12 matrix of every correlate against
# every other one as a heatmap -- a grid in which each cell is shaded by how big
# the correlation sitting in it is -- writing
# output/figures/H3_correlate_heatmap.png, and stores the rounded matrix as the
# table `H3_correlate_matrix`.
#
# This is the raw material behind H3's summary statistics. The share positive
# and the eigenvalues are both computed FROM this matrix, so the heatmap is
# where a reader checks those summary statistics by eye. One dark negative cell
# in a field of positive ones is obvious here and invisible in a summary number.
cm <- h3_full$cor_matrix
# Swap the short variable names for readable display labels on both margins,
# rows and columns alike. The heatmap has to be readable by someone who has
# never seen `prisonviol` before and should not have to look it up.
dimnames(cm) <- list(unname(correlate_labels[rownames(cm)]),
                     unname(correlate_labels[colnames(cm)]))
# type = "upper" prints only the top half of the grid, so each pair shows up
# once instead of twice. That matches the 66 unique pairs H3 counts, and stops a
# reader counting the same correlation twice by eye.
#
# THE PLOT IS DRAWN TWICE ON PURPOSE, AND THE TWO CALLS MUST STAY IDENTICAL.
# corrplot draws straight onto whatever graphics device is currently open,
# instead of returning an object, so it cannot be printed once and then saved
# the way a ggplot can. The first call renders into the knitted report, the
# second into the PNG file. Edit one and not the other, and the figure in the
# report quietly stops matching the figure in output/figures.
if (HAVE("corrplot")) {
  corrplot::corrplot(cm, method = "color", type = "upper", addCoef.col = "black",
                     number.cex = 0.65, tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
                     tl.cex = 0.8, mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
                     title = "Intercorrelations among the punitiveness correlates")
  fig_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "H3_correlate_heatmap.png")
  grDevices::png(fig_path, width = 2200, height = 2000, res = 220)
  corrplot::corrplot(cm, method = "color", type = "upper", addCoef.col = "black",
                     number.cex = 0.65, tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45,
                     tl.cex = 0.8, mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
                     title = "Intercorrelations among the punitiveness correlates")
  invisible(grDevices::dev.off())
  FIGURES <- c(FIGURES, fig_path)
}
TABLES[["H3_correlate_matrix"]] <- data.frame(correlate = rownames(cm),
                                              round(cm, 3), check.names = FALSE)
```

## 7.4 Punitiveness scored by its five parts

The registered punitiveness scale is the mean of eight items (prereg 5.2). The
eight come from five parts: support for more punishment (two items), rejection
of parsimony (two), three-strikes laws (two), life without parole (one) and the
death penalty (one). The sentence is a sixth part, and it enters only the full
index. Averaging items rather than parts has a consequence that is easy to miss:
each two-item part carries a quarter of the scale and each one-item part an
eighth, so life without parole and the death penalty count for half as much as
three-strikes does. In the full index the imbalance runs the other way, because
that index averages two things, the eight-item scale and the sentence, so the
sentence alone carries half of it.

This subsection scores punitiveness one vote per part: the mean of the five part
scores, and, with the sentence, the mean of six standardized parts. It reports
how reliable each version is, how closely each agrees with the registered
version, and whether H1, H2 and H10 change when punitiveness is scored this way.

This is a robustness check and is not in the registration. The registered
eight-item scale remains the one every hypothesis is tested on, nothing here
replaces it, and no multiplicity correction is applied or implied.

```{r phase7_punit_parts}
# === 7.4 PUNITIVENESS SCORED BY ITS FIVE PARTS (a robustness check) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: scores punitiveness one vote per PART instead of one
# vote per ITEM, with and without the sentence; reports the nominal weight each
# part carries under each scoring, the reliability of each version, its
# agreement with the registered version, and H1, H2 and H10 rerun on the
# part-weighted scale. Produces `punit5_weights`,
# `punit5_reliability_agreement`, `punit5_H1_compare` and
# `punit5_H2_H10_compare`.
# PREREG: not registered. Prereg 5.2 scores the eight items, and that scale
#         stays the one every hypothesis is tested on.
# CONSUMES: punit_items (4.2), punitiveness, punitiveness_full, Sentence1_z,
#           hostile_agg, crime_concerns, revenge, just_deserts; run_h1(),
#           run_h10(), steiger_overlap(), cor_row().
#
# NOTHING HERE TOUCHES `d`. The part scores live in p5_d, a private copy, and
# they are never scored with compute_composite(), which would append them to
# the published Phase 4.10 reliability table.
# NAMING: every object this chunk leaves behind starts with p5_, so no later
# chunk can pick one up by accident.

# --- The at-least-half rule, as every composite applies it ------------------
# The mean of the columns for anyone who answered at least half of them (half
# rounds up), NaN turned into a real missing value. This is compute_composite()'s
# scoring rule without its side effect on alpha_table.
p5_mean_half <- function(df) {
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  m <- rowMeans(df, na.rm = TRUE)
  m[rowSums(!is.na(df)) < ceiling(ncol(df) / 2)] <- NA_real_
  m[is.nan(m)] <- NA_real_
  as.numeric(m)
}
# Cronbach's alpha with the same settings used everywhere else in this document
# (check.keys = FALSE, so no item is silently flipped).
p5_alpha <- function(df) tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::alpha(as.data.frame(df), check.keys = FALSE,
               warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)

# --- The five parts ---------------------------------------------------------
# Each part uses exactly the columns punit_items uses, already reverse-coded,
# so high means more punitive on every part. DANGER: the parsimony part must be
# built from parsimony_1_R and parsimony_2_R. 8.3c uses the RAW parsimony
# columns on purpose, because there the question is whether people accept the
# limit; using those here would turn one part of five upside down.
# The guard below stops the knit if punit_items is ever edited, so the two
# scorings can never quietly describe different scales.
stopifnot(setequal(punit_items,
                   c("punishmore_1_R", "punishmore_2", "parsimony_1_R",
                     "parsimony_2_R", "threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2",
                     "LWOP", "deathpenalty")))
p5_parts <- data.frame(
  punish_more        = p5_mean_half(d[, c("punishmore_1_R", "punishmore_2")]),
  parsimony_rejected = p5_mean_half(d[, c("parsimony_1_R", "parsimony_2_R")]),
  three_strikes      = p5_mean_half(d[, c("threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2")]),
  life_without_parole = as.numeric(d$LWOP),
  death_penalty      = as.numeric(d$deathpenalty))

p5_d <- d
# FIVE PARTS, NO SENTENCE. A plain mean, not zmean(), because all five parts
# sit on the same 1-7 metric -- the same reason the registered scale is a plain
# mean of its items. The at-least-half rule asks for three of the five parts.
p5_d$punit_parts5 <- p5_mean_half(p5_parts)
# SIX PARTS, WITH THE SENTENCE. The sentence is a within-vignette z-score and
# the parts are 1-7 means, so every part is standardized before averaging, as
# the registered full index is. The difference is weighting only: the sentence
# is one part of six here, where in the registered index it is one of two.
p5_d$punit_parts6 <- zmean(p5_parts$punish_more, p5_parts$parsimony_rejected,
                           p5_parts$three_strikes, p5_parts$life_without_parole,
                           p5_parts$death_penalty, d$Sentence1_z)
# FIVE PARTS, EACH STANDARDIZED, NO SENTENCE. The same five parts as
# punit_parts5, but each is standardized across the sample before the five are
# averaged, as the six-part score does. The plain mean above lets a part with a
# wider spread count for more (the parts' SDs run from about 1.4 to 2.1); this
# version gives each part exactly a fifth. Nothing in 7.4 uses it and no 7.4
```
