```{r phase7_punit_parts}
# table reports it. It is built
# here, beside punit_parts6, so that the two part scores the paper uses have one
# source: 7.5 and 7.6 (the comparisons with Study 1) and 9.19 (the paper's
# scorings) read both from p5_d. NOT REGISTERED; see 9.19.
p5_d$punit_parts5z <- zmean(p5_parts$punish_more, p5_parts$parsimony_rejected,
                            p5_parts$three_strikes, p5_parts$life_without_parole,
                            p5_parts$death_penalty)
# GUARD: both part scores exist for every participant (every part was
# required), so no later analysis silently drops a row; and the standardized
# five-part score still describes the registered scale's content (it agrees
# with the eight-item scale to about .99; a slip that turned a part upside down
# would pull this far lower).
stopifnot(!anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts6), !anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts5z),
          round(stats::cor(p5_d$punit_parts5z, d$punitiveness), 2) == 0.99)

# --- How much each part counts under each scoring ---------------------------
# NOMINAL shares: each part's share of the average, before any difference in
# how spread out the parts are. The registered full index is two standardized
# halves, so its attitude half is split by item (1/16 per item) and the
# sentence takes the other half.
p5_weights <- data.frame(
  part = c("Punish more (2 items)", "Parsimony rejected (2 items)",
           "Three strikes (2 items)", "Life without parole (1 item)",
           "Death penalty (1 item)", "Sentence (within-vignette z)"),
  registered_8_items    = c(2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0) / 8,
  five_parts            = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0) / 5,
  registered_full_index = c(c(2, 2, 2, 1, 1) / 16, 1 / 2),
  six_parts             = rep(1, 6) / 6,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["punit5_weights"]] <- p5_weights
show_table(p5_weights, "7.4: nominal share of each part under each scoring")

# --- Reliability of each version, and agreement with the registered one ----
# The nine-part alpha is recomputed here with exactly the construction Phase 4.2
# uses for the full index (the eight items z-scored, plus Sentence1_z), so the
# two rows with a sentence are computed on the same footing.
p5_agree5 <- cor_row(p5_d, "punitiveness", "punit_parts5",
                     label_x = "Registered: 8 items", label_y = "Five parts")
p5_agree6 <- cor_row(p5_d, "punitiveness_full", "punit_parts6",
                     label_x = "Registered full index", label_y = "Six parts")
p5_rel <- data.frame(
  scoring = c("Registered: 8 items", "Five parts (one vote per part)",
              "Registered full index: 8 items z-scored + sentence",
              "Six parts: five parts z-scored + sentence"),
  k = c(8, 5, 9, 6),
  alpha = c(p5_alpha(d[, punit_items]),
            p5_alpha(p5_parts),
            p5_alpha(data.frame(scale(d[, punit_items]), s = d$Sentence1_z)),
            p5_alpha(data.frame(scale(p5_parts), s = d$Sentence1_z))),
  r_with_registered = c(NA, p5_agree5$r, NA, p5_agree6$r),
  ci_lower = c(NA, p5_agree5$ci_lower, NA, p5_agree6$ci_lower),
  ci_upper = c(NA, p5_agree5$ci_upper, NA, p5_agree6$ci_upper),
  n = c(sum(!is.na(d$punitiveness)), p5_agree5$n,
        sum(!is.na(d$punitiveness_full)), p5_agree6$n),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["punit5_reliability_agreement"]] <- p5_rel
show_table(p5_rel, paste(
  "7.4: reliability of each scoring, and its correlation with the registered",
  "version it replaces (five parts against the 8-item scale; six parts against",
  "the full index)"))

# --- H1 on the part-weighted scale ------------------------------------------
# run_h1() is the registered function, called twice on the same private copy:
# once on the registered scale, once on the five parts. Nothing about the 12
# correlates or the BH correction changes; only the punitiveness column does.
p5_h1_reg   <- run_h1(p5_d, punit = "punitiveness")
p5_h1_parts <- run_h1(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts5")
p5_h1 <- merge(p5_h1_reg[, c("y", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "sig")],
               p5_h1_parts[, c("y", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "sig")],
               by = "y", suffixes = c("_registered", "_parts5"))
p5_h1$diff <- p5_h1$r_parts5 - p5_h1$r_registered
p5_h1 <- p5_h1[order(-p5_h1$r_registered), ]
rownames(p5_h1) <- NULL
TABLES[["punit5_H1_compare"]] <- p5_h1
show_table(p5_h1, paste(
  "7.4: H1's twelve correlations with the registered scale and with the five",
  "parts. sig marks the BH-adjusted one-sided p within each column's own run."))
p5_big <- which.max(abs(p5_h1$diff))
cat(sprintf(paste(
  "\nAcross the twelve correlates the largest change in r is %+.3f (%s).",
  "\nRank order of the twelve, registered against five parts: Spearman = %.3f.",
  "\nBH significance marks: %s.\n"),
  p5_h1$diff[p5_big], p5_h1$y[p5_big],
  stats::cor(p5_h1$r_registered, p5_h1$r_parts5, method = "spearman"),
  ifelse(identical(p5_h1$sig_registered, p5_h1$sig_parts5),
         "identical in every row", "differ in at least one row -- read the table")))

# --- H2 and H10 on the part-weighted scale ----------------------------------
# Same functions, same one-sided direction as registered. H2's cluster columns
# (hostile_agg, crime_concerns) are the registered ones; only punitiveness
# changes between the paired rows.
p5_steiger <- rbind(
  steiger_overlap(p5_d, "punitiveness", "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "H2 hostile aggression vs crime concerns: registered 8 items"),
  steiger_overlap(p5_d, "punit_parts5", "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "H2 hostile aggression vs crime concerns: five parts"),
  run_h10(p5_d, punit = "punitiveness"),
  run_h10(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts5"))
p5_steiger$comparison[3:4] <- c("H10 revenge vs just deserts: registered 8 items",
                                "H10 revenge vs just deserts: five parts")
TABLES[["punit5_H2_H10_compare"]] <- p5_steiger
show_table(p5_steiger, "7.4: H2 and H10 with the registered scale and with the five parts (Steiger, one-sided)")
```

## 7.5 Three quantities the Dark Side comparison needs

The Dark Side study reports eighteen correlates of punitiveness; this study
registered twelve. Setting the two side by side in one table needs three
quantities that the registered analyses above do not produce, and this section
produces them. None is registered, none enters the H1 family, and none of the
false-discovery-rate corrections above is recomputed to include them.

The first is punitiveness against the four personality and ideology measures.
Right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, racial resentment and
violence proneness are correlates of punitiveness in the Dark Side study. Here
they were registered differently: prereg 2.4's E1 predicts that retributivists
score higher on them, which is a comparison between two groups of people, not a
correlation. Section 9.15 runs E1 as registered. The correlations below are what
the Dark Side table needs and are reported only as that.

The second is the sentence against hostile aggression and against crime
concerns. H2 asks whether punitiveness travels with hostility more closely than
with crime concern, and answers it with the punitiveness scale. The same
question can be asked of the sentence itself, which is the one thing
participants did rather than reported. The Dark Side study found its weakest
version of the hostility result on that measure, so this is the row a reader
comparing the two studies will look for.

The third is revenge scored the way the Dark Side study scored it. That study
used three items; this one added a fourth, "Rather than showing criminals so much
tolerance, we should be punishing them more severely." Section 8.7b takes the
scale apart item by item. What is needed here is narrower: the three original
items against punitiveness scored as the paper scores it in both studies. One
caution belongs with that row. The third item
is not word for word across the two studies: the offender in the Dark Side
version raped the daughter, and in this version sexually assaulted her. The
scales are matched in content, not in wording, and a table setting them side by
side should say so.

**Which punitiveness score the comparisons use.** The paper scores punitiveness
the same way in both studies: its six components (support for more punishment,
rejection of parsimony, three-strikes laws, life without parole, the death
penalty, and the first sentence standardized within vignette) are each
standardized and then averaged, so each carries a sixth of the weight. That is
7.4's six-part score. The co-authors settled this on 27 September 2026, after
the registered analyses were run; it is not registered. Every row of 7.5 and 7.6
that sets this study beside Study 1 carries the six-part score, so the two
studies are compared on one scoring. Study 1's published measure, the full index
(the eight-item scale and the sentence, each standardized and averaged, so that
the sentence carries half the weight), is not used here. Where the sentence is on
the other side of a row, the score is the five attitude components, each
standardized and averaged, without the sentence. The rows on the registered
eight-item scale are kept as they were.

Study 1's own numbers are not recomputed here. This document has this study's
data and not that one's, so the rows below are one column of a two-column table,
and the other column comes from that study's own output (04_two_study_figures.Rmd
computes Study 1 on the same six-part score).

```{r phase7_darkside_compare}
# === 7.5 THE THREE QUANTITIES THE DARK SIDE COMPARISON TABLE NEEDS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: computes three things the registered analyses do not
# produce, each needed to set this study beside the Dark Side study in one
# table. (A) punitiveness against the four personality and ideology measures,
# under both scorings of punitiveness. (B) the within-vignette sentence against
# hostile aggression and against crime concerns, with the Steiger comparison
# between those two, which is H2 asked of the sentence instead of the scale.
# (C) revenge scored with the three Dark Side items, against both scorings of
# punitiveness. Produces `DS_personality_correlates`,
# `DS_sentence_correlates`, `DS_sentence_steiger` and `DS_revenge_darkside`.
# PREREG: NOT REGISTERED, none of it. The registered H1 family is the twelve
#         correlates in 7.1 and the Benjamini-Hochberg correction there is
#         applied across exactly those twelve. Nothing here is added to that
#         family, and no correction above is recomputed. The four personality
#         measures are registered in this study as E1 GROUP CONTRASTS
#         (prereg 2.4), which 9.15 runs; a correlation is a different test of a
#         different thing and must not be reported as E1.
# CONSUMES: punitiveness (4.2), revenge and just_deserts (4.3), rwa, sdo,
#           raceresent, vprone (4.8), hostile_agg and crime_concerns (4.9),
#           hostile_agg6 (4.9b), Sentence1_z (3.2), revenge_1 to revenge_3;
#           p5_d$punit_parts6 and p5_d$punit_parts5z (7.4); cor_row(),
#           steiger_overlap().
#
# NOTHING HERE TOUCHES `d`, alpha_table, OR ANY REGISTERED OBJECT. The new
# variables this chunk builds live in ds_d, a private copy of `d`.
# NAMING: every object starts with ds_ ("Dark Side").
# WHICH PUNITIVENESS: two scorings, on purpose, and each row says which.
#   - The paper's score in both studies (NOT REGISTERED; settled by the
#     co-authors on 27 Sep 2026): the six components, each standardized, then
#     averaged (7.4's punit_parts6), carried here as ds_d$punit_six. Every row
#     that sets the two studies side by side uses it, so they are compared on
#     one scoring; the full index (`punitiveness_full`, Study 1's published
#     measure) is not used in 7.5 or 7.6. 04_two_study_figures.Rmd scores
#     Study 1 the same way.
#   - Where the sentence is on the other side of a row (7.5B's reference row),
#     the six-part score would put the sentence on both sides, so the row uses
#     the five attitude components, each standardized, then averaged (7.4's
#     punit_parts5z), carried as ds_d$punit_five.
#   - The registered eight-item self-report scale (`punitiveness`), kept in
#     every row that used it, for the registered side of the comparison.

ds_d <- d
# The paper's two punitiveness scores, carried across from 7.4's copy.
# GUARD: 7.4's copy holds the same participants in the same order, so the
# columns can be carried across row for row; and neither score is missing for
# anyone.
stopifnot(identical(p5_d$ResponseId, d$ResponseId),
          !anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts6), !anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts5z))
ds_d$punit_six  <- p5_d$punit_parts6
ds_d$punit_five <- p5_d$punit_parts5z
# The labels every DS_ export uses for the three scorings, set once so that a
# row can never carry one score under another's name.
DS_LAB_SIX   <- "Punitiveness (six components)"
DS_LAB_FIVE  <- "Punitiveness (five attitude components)"
DS_LAB_EIGHT <- "Punitiveness (8 items)"

# --- A. Punitiveness against the four personality and ideology measures -----
# Two-sided, because these rows are descriptive companions to another study's
# table rather than tests of a directional prediction made here.
ds_personality_spec <- list(
  c("rwa",        "Right-Wing Authoritarianism"),
  c("sdo",        "Social Dominance Orientation"),
  c("raceresent", "Racial resentment"),
  c("vprone",     "Violence proneness"))
# The second row of each pair is the paper's six-part score (see WHICH
# PUNITIVENESS above).
ds_personality <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ds_personality_spec, function(v) rbind(
  cor_row(ds_d, "punitiveness", v[1],
          label_x = DS_LAB_EIGHT, label_y = v[2]),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_six", v[1],
          label_x = DS_LAB_SIX, label_y = v[2]))))
TABLES[["DS_personality_correlates"]] <- ds_personality
show_table(ds_personality, paste(
  "7.5A: punitiveness against the four personality and ideology measures.",
  "Not registered; outside the H1 family; no correction. E1 tests these as",
  "group contrasts, in 9.15."))

# --- B. The sentence against hostile aggression and crime concerns ----------
# One-sided "greater" to match the direction H2 registers for the scale: more
# hostility goes with a longer sentence. The punitiveness rows are reprinted
# alongside so the sentence version can be read against the registered one.
ds_sentence <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cor_row(ds_d, "Sentence1_z", "hostile_agg", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "Sentence (z within vignette)",
          label_y = "Hostile aggression (registered five parts)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "Sentence1_z", "hostile_agg6", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "Sentence (z within vignette)",
          label_y = "Hostile aggression (six parts, + harsh conditions)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "Sentence1_z", "crime_concerns", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "Sentence (z within vignette)",
          label_y = "Crime concerns"),
  # The reference row relates punitiveness to the sentence itself, so the
  # sentence is on the other side and the paper's sentence-free score is used:
  # the five attitude components, each standardized (it agrees with the
  # eight-item scale to about .99, 7.4).
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_five", "Sentence1_z", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_FIVE,
          label_y = "Sentence (z within vignette), for reference")))
TABLES[["DS_sentence_correlates"]] <- ds_sentence
show_table(ds_sentence,
           "7.5B: the sentence against hostility and against crime concern. Not registered.")

# The Steiger comparison, run through the same function as H2 in 7.2, so the
# two are computed the same way and can be set beside each other. The three
# variables enter as (common, first competitor, second competitor), exactly as
# in 7.2, and the test uses one set of complete cases across all three.
ds_sentence_steiger <- rbind(
  steiger_overlap(ds_d, "Sentence1_z", "hostile_agg", "crime_concerns",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "Sentence: hostile aggression (five parts) vs crime concerns"),
  steiger_overlap(ds_d, "Sentence1_z", "hostile_agg6", "crime_concerns",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "Sentence: hostile aggression (six parts) vs crime concerns"))
TABLES[["DS_sentence_steiger"]] <- ds_sentence_steiger
show_table(ds_sentence_steiger, paste(
  "7.5B: H2 asked of the sentence rather than the punitiveness scale",
  "(Steiger, one-sided). Not registered."))

# --- C. Revenge scored with the three Dark Side items -----------------------
# The scoring rule is compute_composite()'s: the mean of the items, with a row
# left missing unless at least half the items were answered. It is restated
# here rather than borrowed, because compute_composite() also appends a row to
# alpha_table, and this scale is not one of the study's composites.
ds_mean_half <- function(df) {
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  m <- rowMeans(df, na.rm = TRUE)
  m[rowSums(!is.na(df)) < ceiling(ncol(df) / 2)] <- NA_real_
  m[is.nan(m)] <- NA_real_
  as.numeric(m)
}
ds_rev3_items <- c("revenge_1", "revenge_2", "revenge_3")
ds_d$revenge_ds3 <- ds_mean_half(d[, ds_rev3_items, drop = FALSE])
# GUARD: the same rule applied to all four items must reproduce the registered
# revenge composite. If it does not, the rule above has drifted from the one
# Phase 4 used, and the three-item row would not be comparable to anything.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ds_mean_half(d[, paste0("revenge_", 1:4)]), d$revenge)))
# check.keys = FALSE so psych::alpha reports the scale as scored rather than
# silently flipping an item, which would describe a scale nobody used.
ds_alpha <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::alpha(as.data.frame(d[, ds_rev3_items]), check.keys = FALSE,
               warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)

# Rows 1, 3 and 5 are the paper's six-part score, rows 2 and 4 the registered
# eight-item scale. Row 5's just deserts is the registered
# composite (desert, items 1-4, averaged with the proportionality component),
# labelled as such.
ds_revenge <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_six", "revenge_ds3", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_SIX,
          label_y = "Revenge, Dark Side scoring (revenge_1 to _3)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punitiveness", "revenge_ds3", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_EIGHT,
          label_y = "Revenge, Dark Side scoring (revenge_1 to _3)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_six", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_SIX,
          label_y = "Revenge, registered scoring (revenge_1 to _4)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punitiveness", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_EIGHT,
          label_y = "Revenge, registered scoring (revenge_1 to _4)"),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_six", "just_deserts", alternative = "greater",
          label_x = DS_LAB_SIX,
          label_y = "Just deserts (registered), for reference")))
TABLES[["DS_revenge_darkside"]] <- ds_revenge
show_table(ds_revenge, paste(
  "7.5C: revenge scored with the three Dark Side items and with the registered",
  "four, against the paper's six-part score and the eight-item scale. Not registered."))
cat(sprintf(paste("\nRevenge on the three Dark Side items: alpha = %.3f (k = 3),",
                  "M = %.3f.\nThe registered four-item scale: M = %.3f.\n"),
            ds_alpha, mean(ds_d$revenge_ds3, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean(d$revenge, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat("The third item differs in wording across the two studies (raped / sexually\n")
cat("assaulted), so the scales are matched in content, not word for word.\n")

# --- C2. The two clusters rebuilt exactly as the Dark Side study built them -
# Study 1 aggregated RAW ITEMS, not composites, and used plain rowMeans with no
# minimum-answered rule. Both choices are reproduced here so that the matched
# rows below differ from that study in nothing but the sample. The item lists
# are that study's own: six hostility constructs (and note it did NOT include
# hatred), and its three-item revenge scoring rather than the registered four.
s1_mean <- function(df) {
  m <- rowMeans(as.data.frame(df), na.rm = TRUE)
  m[is.nan(m)] <- NA_real_
  as.numeric(m)
}
s1_hostile_items <- c(paste0("exclusion_", 1:3),
                      "degrad_1_R", "degrad_2", "degrad_3",
                      "suffer_1", "suffer_2",
                      "prisonvi_1_R", "prisonvi_2_R",
                      "harsh_1", "harsh_2_R", "harsh_3",
                      "revenge_1", "revenge_2", "revenge_3")
s1_crime_items   <- c("rates_1", "rates_2", "fear_1_R", "fear_2", "fear_3")
# GUARD: every item must be present under the name Study 1 used. A silent
# rename between the two instruments would otherwise drop an item from the
# mean and quietly change the cluster.
stopifnot(all(c(s1_hostile_items, s1_crime_items) %in% names(d)))
ds_d$hostile_s1 <- s1_mean(d[, s1_hostile_items])
ds_d$crime_s1   <- s1_mean(d[, s1_crime_items])

# --- D. H2 on the punitiveness measure the two studies share ----------------
# WHY THIS EXISTS. 7.2 runs H2 on the registered eight-item scale, which is what
# every preregistered test in this document uses. The paper compares the two
# studies on a punitiveness measure that INCLUDES the sentence, the six-part
# score, computed the same way in both (see WHICH PUNITIVENESS above).
# Setting the two studies side by side on H2 therefore needs this study's
# version computed on that score, or the two numbers are about different
# outcomes. run_h2() already takes the punitiveness column as an argument, so
# each row below is the registered test with one substitution and nothing else
# changed.
ds_h2 <- rbind(
  cbind(scoring = "Registered: punitiveness, 8 self-report items",
        run_h2(ds_d, punit = "punitiveness")),
  cbind(scoring = "Matched to Study 1: six components",
        run_h2(ds_d, punit = "punit_six")))
# The third row goes one step further. The Dark Side cluster was built from six
# constructs and did NOT include hatred, while it DID include social exclusion
# and harsh prison conditions, which the registered cluster here leaves out.
# Rebuilding this study's cluster from that study's own six constituents is the
# only row on which the two studies run the same test on the same measure. One
# difference survives even here and must travel with this row wherever it is
# reported: that study averaged its 16 items directly, while zmean() averages
# the five or six composites, so the aggregation still differs.
# BOTH RIVALS ARE REBUILT, not just the hostile one. Study 1 averaged the raw
# ITEMS of its six hostility constructs (16 items) and the raw items of its
# crime concerns constructs (5 items). Averaging items is not the same
# estimator as averaging composites: an item mean lets a three-item construct
# weigh more than a two-item one, while zmean() gives every construct equal
# weight. Rebuilding only one side would leave the two studies' H2 rows
# differing on the other. 7.6 builds these two clusters and reports their
# reliabilities; this row is the H2 test run on them.
ds_h2 <- rbind(ds_h2, cbind(
  scoring = "Matched to Study 1: six components, Study 1's items and aggregation",
  steiger_overlap(ds_d, "punit_six", "hostile_s1", "crime_s1",
                  alternative = "greater",
                  label = "r(punitiveness, hostile aggression) > r(punitiveness, crime concerns)")))
# GUARD: row 1 is the registered test and must reproduce 7.2 exactly. If it does
# not, run_h2() is being handed something other than the registered inputs and
# none of the rows below it could be read against the registered result.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ds_h2$diff[1], h2_full$diff)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(ds_h2$z[1], h2_full$z)))
TABLES[["DS_H2_matched"]] <- ds_h2
show_table(ds_h2[, c("scoring", "r_jk", "r_jh", "r_kh", "n", "diff",
                     "diff_lower", "diff_upper", "z", "p")], paste(
  "7.5D: H2 on the registered scale and on the measure and cluster the Dark",
  "Side study used. One-sided, as registered. Rows 2 and 3 are not registered."))

# --- E. H2 with both correlations corrected for unreliability --------------
# WHY. The two rivals in H2 are not measured equally well: the hostile
# aggression cluster is built from five composites and the crime concerns
# cluster from two. A correlation is held down by the unreliability of both
# variables, so the less reliable rival is held down further, which widens the
# gap between them on its own. Correcting both for attenuation asks whether the
# gap survives when that is taken out. The classic correction divides each
# correlation by the square root of the product of the two reliabilities.
# 9.13 sets out this document's standing policy of NOT correcting, and that
# policy still governs every registered result. This is one companion table,
# outside it, reported because the comparison it qualifies is the study's
# central one.
ds_alpha_of <- function(nm) {
  i <- match(nm, alpha_table$composite)
  stopifnot(!is.na(i))
  alpha_table$alpha[i]
}
ds_a_punit  <- ds_alpha_of("punitiveness (self-report, 8)")
ds_a_host   <- ds_alpha_of("hostile aggression cluster")
ds_a_crime  <- ds_alpha_of("crime concerns cluster")
# Row 2 of ds_h2 is the six-part score, so its reliability is the alpha of
# the six parts exactly as that score is built: the five components and the
# within-vignette sentence z-score, EACH standardized across the sample.
# (7.4's p5_rel row enters the sentence z-score without that second
# standardization, where its SD is .999 rather than 1; the difference is in the
# fourth decimal, but the alpha reported for a score should be the alpha of the
# parts that score averages.) It is not in alpha_table, which holds the
# registered composites only.
# GUARD: the six parts, standardized, average exactly to the six-part score, so
# this alpha describes the score in row 2 and no other.
ds_six_parts <- data.frame(scale(p5_parts), s = as.numeric(scale(d$Sentence1_z)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(rowMeans(ds_six_parts), p5_d$punit_parts6)))
ds_a_six    <- p5_alpha(ds_six_parts)
ds_disatt <- function(r, a1, a2) r / sqrt(a1 * a2)
ds_att <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(i) {
  ap <- c(ds_a_punit, ds_a_six)[i]
  data.frame(
    scoring = ds_h2$scoring[i],
    alpha_punitiveness = ap, alpha_hostile = ds_a_host, alpha_crime = ds_a_crime,
    r_hostile_observed = ds_h2$r_jk[i], r_crime_observed = ds_h2$r_jh[i],
    gap_observed = ds_h2$diff[i],
    r_hostile_corrected = ds_disatt(ds_h2$r_jk[i], ap, ds_a_host),
    r_crime_corrected   = ds_disatt(ds_h2$r_jh[i], ap, ds_a_crime),
    gap_corrected = ds_disatt(ds_h2$r_jk[i], ap, ds_a_host) -
                    ds_disatt(ds_h2$r_jh[i], ap, ds_a_crime),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
TABLES[["DS_H2_attenuation"]] <- ds_att
show_table(ds_att, paste(
  "7.5E: H2 before and after correcting both correlations for unreliability.",
  "Not registered; descriptive only."))
# NO TEST IS REPORTED ON THE CORRECTED VALUES, deliberately. A Steiger z or a
# confidence interval computed on disattenuated correlations treats estimated
# reliabilities as if they were known exactly, which they are not, and the
# resulting p-value would be far too small. The corrected numbers are read as an
# upper bound on what the gap could be if both measures were perfect, nothing
# more.
cat(sprintf(paste("\nThe gap between the two rivals, before and after correcting",
                  "for unreliability:\n  registered 8-item scale: %.3f -> %.3f",
                  "\n  six components:          %.3f -> %.3f\n"),
            ds_att$gap_observed[1], ds_att$gap_corrected[1],
            ds_att$gap_observed[2], ds_att$gap_corrected[2]))
cat(sprintf(paste("A corrected correlation near 1 is a sign of how unstable this",
                  "correction becomes\nwhen one reliability is modest: the crime",
                  "concerns cluster has just two parts\n(alpha = %.3f).\n"),
            ds_a_crime))
```


## 7.6 The Dark Side analyses, repeated here

Section 7.5 supplies the quantities the cross-study table needs. This section
goes further and repeats the analyses the Dark Side study ran, on this sample,
scored the way that study scored them. Four of them travel with the paper: the
ordering of the four attitude clusters, the sensitivity ladder that answers the
objection that hostility and punitiveness are the same thing, the comparison run
on each part of punitiveness separately, and the stability of the correlations
across the three vignettes.

None of it is registered. It is reported beside the registered tests, never in
place of them, and no correction above is recomputed to include it. Punitiveness
is the six-part score here, as in 7.5, the paper's scoring in both studies. Two
of the
four clusters can be matched exactly, because every item is common to both
studies. The personality cluster cannot: that study's version pooled thirty
items including trait vengefulness and blood sports viewership, neither of which
was fielded here, so the version below is built from the four measures the two
studies share and is not the same aggregate.

```{r phase7_darkside_repeat}
# === 7.6 THE DARK SIDE ANALYSES REPEATED ON THIS SAMPLE ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: rebuilds the Dark Side study's four attitude clusters
# from raw items, correlates each with punitiveness under two scorings (the
# paper's six-part score and the registered eight-item scale), runs
# that study's three-level sensitivity ladder, repeats H2 on each part of
# punitiveness separately, and reports how far the H1 correlations move across
# the three vignettes. Produces `DS_clusters_reliability`,
# `DS_cluster_correlations`, `DS_tautology_ladder`, `DS_H2_by_part` and
# `DS_vignette_stability`.
# PREREG: NOT REGISTERED, none of it. These are the companion study's analyses,
#         run here so the two can be read side by side.
# CONSUMES: the raw attitude items, punitiveness (4.2), the composites of 4.5
#           and 4.7, ds_d with its punit_six column and the DS_LAB_ labels
#           (7.5), s1_mean(), s1_hostile_items and s1_crime_items (7.5C2),
#           cor_row(), steiger_overlap(), run_h1(), correlate_vars and
#           correlate_labels (7.0).
# NOTHING HERE TOUCHES `d`. Everything lives on ds_d, the private copy 7.5
# opened, and on s1_ objects created here.

# --- A. The four clusters, built from raw items as Study 1 built them ------
ds_d$emotions_s1 <- s1_mean(d[, c("hate_1", "hate_2_R", "hate_3",
                                  "anger_1", "anger_2")])
# The personality cluster is NOT a match; see the section text. It is built here
# from the four shared measures so that the row is not simply missing.
s1_personality_items <- c("rwa_1", "rwa_2", "rwa_3_R", "rwa_4", "rwa_5",
                          "sdo_1", "sdo_2", "sdo_3_R", "sdo_4_R", "sdo_5",
                          "sdo_6", "sdo_7_R", "sdo_8_R",
                          paste0("vprone_", 1:4),
                          "Raceresent_1_R", "Raceresent_2", "Raceresent_3",
                          "Raceresent_4_R")
stopifnot(all(s1_personality_items %in% names(d)))
ds_d$personality_s1 <- s1_mean(d[, s1_personality_items])

s1_alpha <- function(items) tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
  psych::alpha(as.data.frame(d[, items]), check.keys = FALSE,
               warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)), error = function(e) NA_real_)
s1_cluster_spec <- list(
  "Hostile aggression (Study 1 items, 16)" = s1_hostile_items,
  "Emotions (Study 1 items, 5)"            = c("hate_1", "hate_2_R", "hate_3",
                                               "anger_1", "anger_2"),
  "Personality and ideology (4 shared measures, 21 items)" = s1_personality_items,
  "Crime concerns (Study 1 items, 5)"      = s1_crime_items)
ds_clusters_rel <- data.frame(
  cluster = names(s1_cluster_spec),
  k = vapply(s1_cluster_spec, length, integer(1)),
  alpha = vapply(s1_cluster_spec, s1_alpha, numeric(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
TABLES[["DS_clusters_reliability"]] <- ds_clusters_rel
show_table(ds_clusters_rel, paste(
  "7.6A: the Dark Side study's clusters rebuilt from raw items on this sample.",
  "Not registered."))

# --- B. Each cluster against punitiveness, both scorings -------------------
# Study 1 read the ORDER of these four correlations as its macro-level result.
# Reporting the same four here is what lets the two orderings be set side by
# side. cor_row() carries the 95% interval, so the overlap between neighbouring
# clusters is visible rather than implied.
s1_cluster_cols <- c("hostile_s1", "emotions_s1", "personality_s1", "crime_s1")
s1_cluster_names <- c("Hostile aggression", "Emotions",
                      "Personality and ideology", "Crime concerns")
# The first row of each pair is the six-part score, the second the registered
# eight-item scale.
ds_cluster_cor <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(s1_cluster_cols), function(i) rbind(
  cor_row(ds_d, "punit_six", s1_cluster_cols[i],
          label_x = DS_LAB_SIX,
          label_y = s1_cluster_names[i]),
  cor_row(ds_d, "punitiveness", s1_cluster_cols[i],
          label_x = DS_LAB_EIGHT,
          label_y = s1_cluster_names[i]))))
TABLES[["DS_cluster_correlations"]] <- ds_cluster_cor
show_table(ds_cluster_cor, paste(
  "7.6B: the four clusters against punitiveness, with 95% intervals.",
  "Study 1 reports the same four on its own sample. Not registered."))

# --- C. The three-level sensitivity ladder --------------------------------
# THE OBJECTION THIS ANSWERS. Some hostility constructs are close in content to
# punitiveness itself, so a critic can say the H2 advantage is two names for one
# thing. Study 1 answered it by rerunning the comparison on progressively
# narrower versions of the cluster: all six constructs, then four with the two
# most punitiveness-like dropped, then the two whose content is furthest from
# the punitiveness items. The same ladder is built here, on this study's
# composites, with Study 1's own rungs. Punitiveness is the six-part score, as
# in Study 1's column of the comparison. NOTE the mixed metric this inherits
# from
# that study: the top rung is the raw item mean built above, while the two
# narrower rungs average composites, which is how that study built them.
ds_d$hostile_cons <- s1_mean(ds_d[, c("exclusion", "degradation",
                                      "prisonviol", "revenge_ds3")])
ds_d$hostile_strict <- s1_mean(ds_d[, c("exclusion", "revenge_ds3")])
ds_ladder <- do.call(rbind, list(
  cbind(rung = "All six constructs (Study 1's original)",
        steiger_overlap(ds_d, "punit_six", "hostile_s1", "crime_s1",
                        alternative = "greater", label = "hostility vs crime concern")),
  cbind(rung = "Four constructs (suffering and harsh conditions dropped)",
        steiger_overlap(ds_d, "punit_six", "hostile_cons", "crime_s1",
                        alternative = "greater", label = "hostility vs crime concern")),
  cbind(rung = "Two constructs (exclusion and revenge only)",
        steiger_overlap(ds_d, "punit_six", "hostile_strict", "crime_s1",
                        alternative = "greater", label = "hostility vs crime concern"))))
# GUARD: the top rung is the same test as 7.5D's third row (the same score, the
# same two rebuilt clusters), so the two exports cannot disagree.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(ds_ladder$diff[1], ds_h2$diff[3])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(ds_ladder$z[1], ds_h2$z[3])))
TABLES[["DS_tautology_ladder"]] <- ds_ladder
show_table(ds_ladder[, c("rung", "r_jk", "r_jh", "n", "diff", "diff_lower",
                         "diff_upper", "z", "p")], paste(
  "7.6C: the hostility advantage at three levels of stringency, as in Study 1.",
  "Not registered."))
cat(sprintf(paste("\nThe advantage at each rung: %.3f, %.3f, %.3f.",
                  "Every interval excludes zero: %s.\n"),
            ds_ladder$diff[1], ds_ladder$diff[2], ds_ladder$diff[3],
            ifelse(all(ds_ladder$diff_lower > 0), "yes", "NO -- read the table")))

# --- D. The comparison run on each part of punitiveness --------------------
# Study 1 ran H2 once per punitiveness measure and found the advantage on five
# of six, the exception being the sentencing decision. The same six outcomes are
# rebuilt here. The five attitude parts use the same item pairs 7.4 uses; the
# sixth is the within-vignette standardized sentence.
ds_d$part_punish_more   <- s1_mean(d[, c("punishmore_1_R", "punishmore_2")])
ds_d$part_parsimony     <- s1_mean(d[, c("parsimony_1_R", "parsimony_2_R")])
ds_d$part_three_strikes <- s1_mean(d[, c("threestrikes_1", "threestrikes_2")])
ds_d$part_lwop          <- as.numeric(d$LWOP)
ds_d$part_death_penalty <- as.numeric(d$deathpenalty)
ds_parts <- c(part_punish_more = "Punish more",
              part_parsimony = "Parsimony rejected",
              part_three_strikes = "Three strikes",
              part_lwop = "Life without parole",
              part_death_penalty = "Death penalty",
              Sentence1_z = "The sentencing decision")
ds_by_part <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ds_parts), function(v)
  cbind(outcome = unname(ds_parts[v]),
        steiger_overlap(ds_d, v, "hostile_s1", "crime_s1",
                        alternative = "greater",
                        label = "hostility vs crime concern"))))
TABLES[["DS_H2_by_part"]] <- ds_by_part
show_table(ds_by_part[, c("outcome", "r_jk", "r_jh", "n", "diff", "diff_lower",
                          "diff_upper", "z", "p")], paste(
  "7.6D: the hostility advantage on each part of punitiveness separately,",
  "as in Study 1. Not registered; no correction across the six."))
cat(sprintf(paste("\nThe advantage holds on %d of the %d parts by the interval.",
                  "In Study 1 the sentencing\ndecision was the one exception.\n"),
            sum(ds_by_part$diff_lower > 0, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(ds_by_part)))

# --- E. Do the correlations hold inside each vignette? --------------------
# Study 1 reports that no correlate reverses direction across its three
# vignettes and that the spread across them is small. run_h1() already takes the
# sample as an argument, so the registered family is simply rerun three times.
# The BH column each run produces is ignored here: what is being read is the
# spread of r, not significance in a subsample.
# PUNITIVENESS is the six-part score, the score Study 1's side of this
# comparison uses. It is passed explicitly, because run_h1()'s default is the
# registered eight-item scale.
# The six-part score is standardized across the whole sample (the sentence
# part within vignette, as always), and each vignette's run takes that score
# as it stands for its own participants.
ds_by_vig <- lapply(sort(unique(d$Vignette)), function(v)
  run_h1(ds_d[ds_d$Vignette == v, , drop = FALSE], punit = "punit_six"))
ds_vig <- data.frame(outcome = ds_by_vig[[1]]$y, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for (i in seq_along(ds_by_vig)) {
  ds_vig[[paste0("r_vignette_", i)]] <-
    ds_by_vig[[i]]$r[match(ds_vig$outcome, ds_by_vig[[i]]$y)]
}
# Both summaries come from the SAME matrix of the three vignette columns,
# captured before either is appended: computing r_max from ds_vig[, -1] after
# r_min had been added would hand the second call a column it should not see.
ds_vig_mat <- as.matrix(ds_vig[, paste0("r_vignette_", seq_along(ds_by_vig))])
ds_vig$r_min <- apply(ds_vig_mat, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)
ds_vig$r_max <- apply(ds_vig_mat, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE)
ds_vig$range <- ds_vig$r_max - ds_vig$r_min
ds_vig$all_positive <- ds_vig$r_min > 0
TABLES[["DS_vignette_stability"]] <- ds_vig
show_table(ds_vig, paste(
  "7.6E: each registered correlate rerun inside each vignette. Not registered;",
  "read for stability, not for significance."))
cat(sprintf(paste("\nAcross the three vignettes the median spread of r is %.3f,",
                  "and %d of %d correlates\nstay positive in every vignette.\n"),
            median(ds_vig$range, na.rm = TRUE), sum(ds_vig$all_positive, na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(ds_vig)))
```

# PHASE 8: H4–H10 -- CONSTRUCT VALIDITY OF RETRIBUTION

## 8.1 H4 -- is strict proportionality endorsed?

**H4.** Two claims in one hypothesis. First, agreement with the proportionality
item sits **at or below** the scale midpoint, the neutral point in the middle.
The agree-disagree items run 1-7, so that midpoint is 4, and "at or below 4" is
what "not consistently endorsed" looks like as a number. The test is
directional, one-sided `less`, because the hypothesis names that direction in
advance. Second, a sizeable share of people endorse punishment beyond the
seriousness of the crime. That is the share scoring above the midpoint on
`severity_1`, reported with an exact confidence interval (CI), the range of true
shares the data are consistent with.

```{r phase8_h4}
# === H4: IS STRICT PROPORTIONALITY ENDORSED? (prereg 2.2, 6.4) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs run_h4() on the whole sample and produces the
# tables `H4_midpoint_tests` and `H4_shares`.
#
# WHY THE MIDPOINT IS 4. The agree-disagree items run 1-7, and 4 is the neutral
# anchor in the middle, neither agreeing nor disagreeing (prereg 5.1). So "sits
# at or below 4" is the operational form of "not consistently endorsed" -- the
# form the claim takes once a test has to be run on it. The test is one-sided
# "less" because the hypothesis names that direction before the data were seen.
# A two-sided test would answer a different question -- does agreement differ
# from neutral in either direction -- and would not be the test that was
# registered.
#
# WHY TWO TABLES AND NOT ONE. They answer different questions and both are
# needed. The mean says where the sample sits on average. The shares say how the
# sample is distributed, that is, how people are spread across the scale. A mean
# sitting right at 4 could be a room in which everyone is indifferent. It could
# equally be a split population, a room divided between people who agree
# strongly and people who disagree strongly, with almost nobody in between.
# Those are opposite findings, and only the shares can tell them apart.
h4_full <- run_h4(d)
TABLES[["H4_midpoint_tests"]] <- h4_full$tests
TABLES[["H4_shares"]] <- h4_full$shares

# The midpoint tests first. Here d is the one-sample Cohen's d: how far the mean
# sits from 4, counted in standard deviations. A standard deviation is the usual
# size of one person's gap from the mean. Counting in that unit means d does not
# depend on this scale happening to run 1-7. Each d carries a 95% confidence
# interval (CI), the range of true values the data are consistent with. Note
# which interval is which: d_lower and d_upper bracket the effect size, while
# ci_lower and ci_upper bracket the mean itself.
show_table(h4_full$tests[, c("measure", "n", "mean", "sd", "t", "df",
                             "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper",
                             "ci_lower", "ci_upper")],
           "H4: one-sample tests against the scale midpoint of 4 (one-sided, 'less'). d is the one-sample Cohen's d with its 95% CI; ci_lower/upper are for the mean.")
# Then the shares, which are the second half of the hypothesis. Each share
# carries an exact Clopper-Pearson confidence interval. "Exact" means it is
# built from the binomial distribution, the exact arithmetic of yes/no counts.
# The usual alternative is a normal approximation, which can hand back an
# interval running past 0% or past 100% when a share sits near either end.
show_table(h4_full$shares,
           "H4: share endorsing punishment beyond proportionality (exact Clopper-Pearson CIs)")

# The two headline numbers written out as sentences, so the results narrative
# can be quoted straight from here instead of somebody reading a figure off a
# table and retyping it.
cat(sprintf("\nProportionality item: M = %.2f (SD %.2f) against a midpoint of 4.\n",
            mean(d$proportionality, na.rm = TRUE), sd(d$proportionality, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Share endorsing punishment GREATER than the crime: %.1f%% [%.1f%%, %.1f%%]\n",
            100 * h4_full$shares$prop[1], 100 * h4_full$shares$ci_lower[1],
            100 * h4_full$shares$ci_upper[1]))
```

## 8.2 H5 -- punishment beyond proportionality versus below it

**H5.** Agreement that punishment should *exceed* the seriousness of the crime
(`severity_1`) is higher than agreement that it should *fall short* of the harm
(`severity_2`). The test is paired, meaning the two answers being compared come
from the same person, and one-sided, because the hypothesis names the direction
in advance. Both items are used **raw** here. `severity_1_R` is the
reverse-scored copy of the first item and it exists only for the just-deserts
component; putting it in here would make this a different comparison
altogether, and the table would print all the same.

```{r phase8_h5}
# === H5: BEYOND THE CRIME VERSUS BELOW THE HARM (prereg 2.2, 6.4) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the paired test on the whole sample and produces
# the table `H5_paired`.
#
# WHY THE TEST IS PAIRED. The same person answered both items, so these are not
# two separate groups of people. A paired test compares each person against
# themselves and then averages those within-person gaps. That takes the
# differences BETWEEN people out of the comparison, which is what lets a modest
# gap show up against the noise.
#
# WHAT THE NUMBER MEANS. Strict proportionality is a two-sided constraint, one
# that cuts both ways -- punishment should be neither more nor less than the
# crime deserves. If people held it symmetrically, that is, evenly in both
# directions, agreement with "punish beyond the crime" and agreement with
# "punish below the harm" would come out about equal. A positive mean_diff
# says they do not: the constraint is far more readily relaxed upward than
# downward, which is the asymmetry that makes proportionality a weak brake in
# practice.
h5_full <- run_h5(d)
TABLES[["H5_paired"]] <- h5_full
show_table(h5_full[, c("comparison", "n", "M1", "M2", "mean_diff", "t", "df",
                       "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper",
                       "ci_lower", "ci_upper")],
           "H5: paired comparison of severity_1 (exceed the crime) and severity_2 (fall short of the harm)")

# The same comparison in sentences. Read the confidence interval before the
# p-value. The p says only how easily a gap this big could turn up by chance.
# The interval says how big the gap plausibly is, which is the question anyone
# writing about punishment policy actually has. Cohen's d then puts that same
# gap into standard deviations, so it can be set beside effects measured on
# other scales.
cat(sprintf("\nseverity_1 (exceed) M = %.2f vs severity_2 (fall short) M = %.2f\n",
            h5_full$M1, h5_full$M2))
cat(sprintf("Paired difference = %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]; t(%.0f) = %.2f, p %s (one-sided)\n",
            h5_full$mean_diff, h5_full$ci_lower, h5_full$ci_upper,
            h5_full$df, h5_full$t, format_p(h5_full$p_dir)))
cat(sprintf("Paired Cohen's d = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            h5_full$d, h5_full$d_lower, h5_full$d_upper))
```

## 8.3 H6 -- does just deserts hold together?

**H6.** "Just deserts" is spoken of as one idea, but it bundles two claims: that
punishment is *deserved* (`Retribution_1` to `_4`) and that it should be
*proportionate* (`proportionality`, `severity_1_R`, `severity_2_R`). H6 predicts
that the two parts correlate weakly and do not form a reliable scale, which
would mean that a single just-deserts score hides which of the two claims a
person actually holds. Tested three ways (prereg 6.4). First, the correlation
between the two parts. Second, the Cronbach's alpha of the two together: alpha
asks how consistently a set of measures behaves as readings of one thing. Third,
a one-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), a model that asks whether one
hidden attitude can account for the answers to all of the items at once. In that
model **poor fit or a near-zero loading counts as failure to cohere**.

```{r phase8_h6}
# === H6: DOES JUST DESERTS HOLD TOGETHER? (prereg 2.2, 6.4) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs run_h6() on the whole sample, prints the three
# pieces of evidence in order, applies the pre-registered verdict rule, and
# produces the tables `H6_cfa_fit`, `H6_cfa_loadings` and `H6_summary`.
#
# READ THE OUTPUT IN REVERSE OF THE USUAL WAY. A near-zero correlation between
# the parts and a low Cronbach's alpha are the PREDICTED results here. Alpha
# asks how consistently a set of items behaves as one scale, and normally a low
# value means the measure is broken and needs fixing. Not here. The hypothesis
# is that "just deserts" does not name one thing, so incoherence is the finding,
# not a measurement problem to be fixed. The consequence is substantive: if
# desert and proportionality come apart, then endorsing just deserts tells you
# nothing about whether a person also accepts the limit that proportionality is
# supposed to impose.
h6_full <- run_h6(d)

# (a) THE CORRELATION BETWEEN THE TWO PARTS. A correlation runs from -1 through
# 0 to +1 and says how strongly two measures move together. Near zero means
# knowing where a person stands on desert tells you nothing about where they
# stand on proportionality. The 95% confidence interval matters more than the p
# here. With a prediction of a near-zero relationship, the evidence is a narrow
# interval sitting close to zero. A non-significant p on its own would not show
# the relationship is absent. Data too thin to settle the question return a
# non-significant p as well, and the two look identical.
cat("--- (a) correlation between the two parts ---\n")
cat(sprintf("r(deserved, proportionality) = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], p %s (n = %d)\n",
            h6_full$cor$r, h6_full$cor$ci_lower, h6_full$cor$ci_upper,
            format_p(h6_full$cor$p_two), h6_full$cor$n))

# (b) THE TWO PARTS TREATED AS A TWO-ITEM SCALE. run_h6() z-scores both parts
# before computing alpha, so that alpha is computed over comparable variances.
# A z-score rescales a measure to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1;
# variance is how spread out a set of values is. The rescaling is needed because
# one part is an average of 4 items and the other an average of 3, and two such
# averages need not spread alike.
cat("\n--- (b) reliability of the two parts together ---\n")
cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha of the two standardized parts = %.3f\n",
            h6_full$alpha_two_parts))
cat("(A low alpha means the two parts do NOT form one reliable scale.)\n")

# (c) THE ONE-FACTOR CFA, run over the 7 individual items rather than over the 2
# composites. A confirmatory factor analysis asks whether one hidden attitude
# can explain the answers to every item at once. That hidden attitude is called
# the factor, or the latent variable: latent because no question asks about it
# directly, so it is only ever inferred from the items. At the item level a
# two-cluster structure has nowhere to hide: it shows up either as bad overall
# fit or as one item whose link to the factor collapses.
#
# THE GUARD. If lavaan is missing, or the model failed to converge, run_h6()
# hands back NULL for the fit measures and the else branch at the bottom says so
# in plain words. A model that never converged is not the same evidence as a
# model that fitted badly, and printing its numbers as though they meant
# something would be a false result rather than a missing one.
cat("\n--- (c) one-factor CFA over the 7 constituent items ---\n")
if (!is.null(h6_full$fit_measures)) {
  fm <- h6_full$fit_measures
  # The fit measures arrive as a named vector (a simple run of values, each with
  # a name attached). Turning it into a two-column data frame -- a table with
  # one row per index -- is what lets it print and export like every other table
  # in this document.
  cfa_fit_tab <- data.frame(index = names(fm), value = as.numeric(fm),
                            stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  TABLES[["H6_cfa_fit"]] <- cfa_fit_tab
  # print() is REQUIRED on both of these calls because they sit inside an if()
  # block. knitr, the engine that turns this document into the HTML report,
  # places a table in the report by taking the value of an expression that sits
  # on its own at the OUTER level of a chunk. Drop the print() and these two
  # tables vanish from the report while still being written to CSV: nothing
  # errors, the files exist, and only the report is missing its evidence.
  print(show_table(cfa_fit_tab, "H6: fit of the one-factor just-deserts CFA"))
  TABLES[["H6_cfa_loadings"]] <- h6_full$loadings
  print(show_table(h6_full$loadings,
             "H6: standardized loadings (a near-zero loading counts as failure to cohere)"))

  # THE PRE-REGISTERED FAILURE RULE (prereg 6.4): "poor fit OR a near-zero
  # loading counts as failure to cohere". Two independent routes to the same
  # verdict, because they catch different structures.
  #
  # POOR FIT -- CFI < .90 or RMSEA > .08, the conventional cutoffs (Hu & Bentler
  # and the wider literature). CFI, the comparative fit index, scores the model
  # against a baseline of completely uncorrelated items, one in which no item is
  # related to any other. Below .90 means the one-factor model explains little
  # more than "these items are related at all". RMSEA, the root mean square
  # error of approximation, is misfit per degree of freedom. Above .08 means
  # substantial residual covariance is left over: shared movement among the
  # items that the single factor cannot account for. That is the signature of
  # two clusters where one factor was posited.
  # `||` is R's "or", so either condition alone is enough to fail the model.
  # The chi-square is deliberately NOT part of the rule: at N = 948 it will
  # reject almost any model, which is why it is printed but not used.
  poor_fit <- (!is.na(fm[["cfi"]]) && fm[["cfi"]] < .90) ||
              (!is.na(fm[["rmsea"]]) && fm[["rmsea"]] > .08)
  # NEAR-ZERO LOADING -- |lambda| < .30 on the STANDARDIZED solution. A loading
  # (lambda) is the strength of the link between one item and the factor.
  # Standardizing puts every item on the same footing, so lambda reads as the
  # item-factor correlation, the correlation between that item and the factor.
  # Below .30 the factor accounts for under 9% of that item's variance, that is,
  # under 9% of how much its answers vary from person to person. It explains
  # almost nothing about how people answered. This is the second route because a
  # model can fit acceptably overall while one part of the construct simply
  # detaches: the average misfit stays small, but that item is not measuring the
  # latent variable. The line collects the NAMES of any such items. abs() is
  # there because a negative loading of the same magnitude -- the same size,
  # ignoring the sign -- is just as much a failure to cohere in the intended
  # direction.
  weak <- h6_full$loadings$item[abs(h6_full$loadings$std_loading) < .30]
  # The fit indices in one line. TLI and SRMR are printed for context rather
  # than used by the rule. SRMR is the standardized root mean square residual.
  # A residual is the gap between what was observed and what the model predicts,
  # so SRMR is the typical size of what this model gets wrong.
  cat(sprintf("\nCFI = %.3f, TLI = %.3f, RMSEA = %.3f [%.3f, %.3f], SRMR = %.3f\n",
              fm[["cfi"]], fm[["tli"]], fm[["rmsea"]],
              fm[["rmsea.ci.lower"]], fm[["rmsea.ci.upper"]], fm[["srmr"]]))
  cat(sprintf("Poor fit by the pre-registered rule (CFI < .90 or RMSEA > .08): %s\n",
              ifelse(poor_fit, "YES", "no")))
  cat(sprintf("Items with a near-zero standardized loading (|lambda| < .30): %s\n",
              ifelse(length(weak), paste(weak, collapse = ", "), "none")))
  # The verdict line does not say WHICH of the two routes fired; the two lines
  # printed just above it do. Either route on its own is failure to cohere,
  # exactly as registered. The wording was fixed before the data were seen, so
  # no reader has to take the writer's word for how the rule was applied.
  cat(sprintf("\nH6 verdict: just deserts %s cohere by the pre-registered criteria.\n",
              ifelse(poor_fit || length(weak) > 0, "does NOT", "DOES")))
} else {
  cat("CFA not available (lavaan missing or the model did not converge).\n")
}

# A compact summary of parts (a) and (b) for the results narrative. The CFA is
# left out because it has no single scalar to report -- no one number that
# stands for the whole model. Its evidence is the fit table and the loadings
# table above. The alpha row carries NA, R's marker for a missing value, in the
# interval and p columns, because Cronbach's alpha here comes with neither.
TABLES[["H6_summary"]] <- data.frame(
  test = c("r(deserved, proportionality)", "alpha of the two parts"),
  value = c(h6_full$cor$r, h6_full$alpha_two_parts),
  ci_lower = c(h6_full$cor$ci_lower, NA), ci_upper = c(h6_full$cor$ci_upper, NA),
  p = c(h6_full$cor$p_two, NA), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

## 8.3b Desert against the principle and against the direction of departure

H6 asks whether the two halves of just deserts hold together as one scale. This
subsection puts a sharper question to the same items: **what does desert
actually track?** A defensible retributivism makes two commitments, and they can
be tested one at a time.

  - Desert should go **with** proportionality. Punishment is owed because of
    what was done, and owed in the amount the offense warrants, so believing
    punishment is deserved should carry with it believing that it should fit the
    crime.
  - Desert should be **unrelated** to severity. Wanting punishment to run beyond
    the offense is not a desert claim at all; it is a separate appetite, and a
    retributivism doing its own work should have nothing to say about it.

Both are tested against `deserved`, the four purpose items, and never against
`just_deserts`. That restriction is the point. `just_deserts` is built from the
proportionality item, so correlating the two would be correlating that item with
itself. The chunk prints that contaminated figure too, labelled as such, because
it is the number a reader will otherwise work out for themselves and misread.

This subsection deviates from the registration, which specifies the three-item
component only. Nothing registered is displaced. H6 above stands exactly as
written and this sits beside it.

```{r phase8_h6b}
# === DESERT AGAINST PROPORTIONALITY AND AGAINST SEVERITY ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: tests the two commitments above; writes the table
# `H6b_desert_principle_vs_severity`.
# PREREG: a deviation from 5.4, reported alongside the registered H6 and never
#         in place of it.
# CONSUMES: deserved, proportionality_principle, severity_index, severity_1,
#           severity_2_R, punitiveness, just_deserts.
#
# Every row is two-sided, meaning the test counts a departure in either
# direction. The first prediction names a direction; the second is a null
# prediction, a prediction of no relationship at all. A null prediction has no
# side to be one-sided about. Keeping every row on the same footing is what lets
# the reader compare them down the page. What they weigh is the confidence
# intervals, the range of true values each correlation is consistent with,
# rather than the p-values.
h6b <- do.call(rbind, list(
  # The commitment that should hold.
  cor_row(d, "deserved", "proportionality_principle",
          label_x = "Desert (purpose items)",
          label_y = "Proportionality principle -- expected POSITIVE"),
  # The commitment that should be absent.
  cor_row(d, "deserved", "severity_index",
          label_x = "Desert (purpose items)",
          label_y = "Severity index -- expected ZERO"),
  # severity_index is formative, meaning its two items are two separate ways of
  # departing upward rather than two readings of one attitude, so each item is
  # shown on its own line as well. Were the pair one scale these rows would be
  # redundant. They are not, which is the same reason the index carries no
  # Cronbach's alpha.
  cor_row(d, "deserved", "severity_1",
          label_x = "Desert (purpose items)",
          label_y = "  severity_1 alone (punish MORE than the crime)"),
  cor_row(d, "deserved", "severity_2_R",
          label_x = "Desert (purpose items)",
          label_y = "  severity_2 reversed alone (reject punishing LESS)"),
  # Punitiveness against both. This is the pair of rows that earns severity a
  # place beside the H1 family and leaves the principle out of it.
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "severity_index",
          label_x = "Punitiveness (8 items)", label_y = "Severity index"),
  cor_row(d, "punitiveness", "proportionality_principle",
          label_x = "Punitiveness (8 items)", label_y = "Proportionality principle"),
  # Printed only to be disarmed. This is a part-whole correlation, meaning one
  # side of it is contained in the other: just_deserts is built partly from the
  # proportionality item. A part-whole coefficient comes out high whatever the
  # participants think, so it is not evidence that two measures converge.
  cor_row(d, "just_deserts", "proportionality_principle",
          label_x = "CONTAMINATED, do not interpret",
          label_y = "just_deserts x proportionality (part-whole)")
))
TABLES[["H6b_desert_principle_vs_severity"]] <- h6b
show_table(h6b, "8.3b: what desert tracks. Tested on the purpose items, not on the just-deserts composite.")

# The comparison this subsection exists to make. Both correlations share
# `deserved` and are measured on the same participants, so the ratio below is
# descriptive only; the two intervals in the table carry the inference. Treat
# the ratio as a way of stating the contrast in one sentence, never as a test.
r_prop <- h6b$r[1]
r_sev  <- h6b$r[2]
cat(sprintf("\nDesert x proportionality principle : r = %+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]\n",
            r_prop, h6b$ci_lower[1], h6b$ci_upper[1]))
cat(sprintf("Desert x severity index           : r = %+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]\n",
            r_sev,  h6b$ci_lower[2], h6b$ci_upper[2]))
# The guard is arithmetic, not statistical. The two is.na() checks skip the line
# if either correlation could not be computed at all. The .01 floor skips it
# when the correlation with the principle sits that close to zero: dividing by
# a number that small would make the ratio enormous and meaningless.
if (!is.na(r_prop) && !is.na(r_sev) && abs(r_prop) > .01) {
  cat(sprintf("Desert tracks the direction of departure %.1f times as strongly as the principle.\n",
              r_sev / r_prop))
}
cat("A retributivism that bounded punishment would show the reverse ordering.\n")
```

**An objection to the desert scoring, and the answer to it.** Prereg 5.4 scores
desert as `Retribution_1` to `_4`, and one of those four, `Retribution_2`, says
justice *requires* that crimes be punished. That is positive retributivism, the
claim that punishment is not merely permitted but owed, and a large part of the
contemporary literature rejects it while holding on to the rest of the theory. A
reader can therefore ask whether the table above says something about
retribution or something about a demanding version of it that few of its
defenders accept.

The tiers scored in 4.3b put that question to the data. `deserved_soft`
(`Retribution_1`, `_3`, `_4`) is the registered composite with the obligation
item taken out; `retribution_hard` (`_2`, `_5`) and `retribution_rationale`
(`_6`, `_7`) carry the rest of the seven-item scale. Each tier goes against the
same two criteria used above, with the registered composite in the same table,
so the two scorings can be read against each other row by row.

**This is a robustness check, and the useful outcome is the one that changes
nothing.** `deserved_soft` shares three of its four items with `deserved`, so
the two are very nearly one variable, and the soft core cannot supply an
independent test of anything. The first rows of the tier table report how
nearly. They are part-whole correlations, a composite against a set that
contains it, inflated by construction in exactly the way the contaminated row
above is, and they are printed to be disarmed rather than read. What they buy
is the reading of every row beneath them. If the part of retributivism nobody
disputes behaves as the registered composite behaves, the objection has nothing
left to work on.

**Where `Retribution_3` belongs is an open question.** The item says justice is
restored when criminals are punished. That is not a claim about what punishment
is permitted; it says punishment ACHIEVES something, which is close to the
positive-retributive position the split exists to hold apart. So both readings
are reported rather than one: `deserved_soft` keeps the item, as 4.3b scores
it, and `deserved_soft_strict` (`Retribution_1` and `_4` alone) drops it. The
two sit together in the table so that nothing below rests on the choice between
them.

The tiers are a deviation from prereg 5.3 and 5.4, which score the seven
retribution items as one scale and the first four as desert. They fall outside
every registered family; no multiplicity correction is applied to them and none
is implied.

```{r phase8_h6b_tiers}
# === 8.3b THE SAME TWO CRITERIA, TIER BY TIER (prereg 5.4, a deviation) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: runs the two criteria used above against each of the
# three retribution tiers and against a two-item variant of the soft core, with
# the registered `deserved` in the same table as the yardstick, then tests the
# ordering of the two criteria formally. Writes `H6b_desert_tiers` and
# `H6b_desert_tiers_steiger`.
# PREREG: outside every registered family and outside every FDR family. No
#         multiplicity correction is applied here and none is implied. (A
#         multiplicity correction raises the evidence each test needs when many
#         are read together. The correction the registered families use is FDR,
#         the false discovery rate, which bounds the EXPECTED share of false
#         claims among the results called significant.)
# CONSUMES: deserved_soft, retribution_hard, retribution_rationale (4.3b);
#           deserved, proportionality_principle, severity_index (4.3);
#           Retribution_1 and Retribution_4 as raw items.
#
# WHY THESE ROWS ARE A SECOND TABLE RATHER THAN MORE ROWS ABOVE. Phase 10.1
# takes each export filename from the name its table carries in TABLES, so the
# rows above are written as output/tables/H6b_desert_principle_vs_severity.csv.
# Folding the tiers into that entry, or renaming it to cover both, would stop
# that file being written under the name any manuscript citing it expects. The
# two tables are therefore kept apart, and the registered composite appears in
# both so that each table can be read on its own.
#
# EVERY ROW IS TWO-SIDED. The tier split names no direction in advance, and
# prereg 6.8 reserves the one-sided test for predictions made before the data
# were seen. cor_row()'s `alternative` argument therefore stays at its default.

# THE SOFT CORE WITHOUT Retribution_3. Retribution_1 (society has a moral right
# to punish) and Retribution_4 (punishment is justified because criminals
# deserve it). R3 says justice is RESTORED when criminals are punished, which
# asserts that punishment achieves something rather than that it is permitted,
# so whether it belongs in a permissibility tier is a question about the item
# and not about these data. Both answers are reported.
#
# rowMeans() rather than compute_composite(), and the reliability table is the
# reason. compute_composite() appends a row to `alpha_table` with <<-, R's way
# of writing to a table that lives outside the function, and 4.10 has already
# COPIED that table into TABLES by value. A row appended at this point in the
# document would therefore print here and be missing from
# output/tables/reliability_alpha_omega.csv and from
# data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv. The page and the exported files would
# disagree, and nothing would flag it. At two items the two routes are
# arithmetically the same in any case: compute_composite() keeps a participant
# who answered at least half the items, which for two items is at least one, and
# that is exactly what rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) already does. The alpha is printed
# below instead of being appended where it cannot reach the export.
d$deserved_soft_strict <- rowMeans(
  cbind(d$Retribution_1, d$Retribution_4), na.rm = TRUE)
# For a participant who answered neither item there is nothing left to average.
# rowMeans() returns NaN there, R's "not a number", rather than NA, R's marker
# for a missing value. Convert it, the same two-line pattern 4.3 uses for
# `just_deserts`. Left alone the value prints and exports as NaN, which reads as
# a calculation that went wrong rather than as an ordinary missing answer.
d$deserved_soft_strict[is.nan(d$deserved_soft_strict)] <- NA_real_

# Cronbach's alpha for that pair, which asks how consistently two items behave
# as readings of one thing. check.keys = FALSE for the reason
# compute_composite() gives: with the default, psych::alpha silently flips a
# negatively-loading item and reports the reliability of a scale that is not the
# one being scored. tryCatch runs the calculation and catches any error instead
# of letting it stop the knit, and the dash that a failure prints is visible on
# the page rather than silent.
h6b_alpha_strict <- tryCatch(
  suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::alpha(
    as.data.frame(d[, c("Retribution_1", "Retribution_4")]),
    check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)),
  error = function(e) NA_real_)
cat(sprintf("\n  %-40s k=2  alpha=%s  n=%d\n", "soft core without R3 (R1, R4)",
            ifelse(is.na(h6b_alpha_strict), "  -  ",
                   sprintf("%.3f", h6b_alpha_strict)),
            sum(!is.na(d$deserved_soft_strict))))

# NAMED VECTORS, so a display label can never drift out of order relative to the
# variable it names. A named vector is a simple run of values with a name
# attached to each one, so here the variable name and the label a reader sees
# travel together as one thing. This is the arrangement 7.0 uses for the H1
# correlate labels, and it is here for the same reason. Two parallel plain
# vectors are one careless insertion away from mislabelling a whole table. A
# mislabelled table is wrong in a way that still looks perfectly sensible.
#
# The registered composite is listed last and marked REGISTERED. It is in the
# table so the tiers can be read against the preregistered scoring on the same
# page, in the same sample, on the same criteria. It is NOT recomputed: these
# rows read the column 4.3 built, exactly as 4.3 left it.
h6b_tier_labels <- c(
  deserved_soft         = "Soft core R1, R3, R4",
  deserved_soft_strict  = "Soft core without R3 (R1, R4)",
  retribution_hard      = "Obligation R2, R5",
  retribution_rationale = "Rationales R6, R7",
  deserved              = "REGISTERED deserved R1-R4 (prereg 5.4)")

# THE TWO CRITERIA, labelled exactly as 7.1 labels them. One criterion under two
# names in one document is one criterion that a later join, pivot or group_by
# splits into two without saying so, and the H1 companion table in 7.1 already
# prints the severity index under this wording.
h6b_crit_labels <- c(
  proportionality_principle = "Proportionality principle",
  severity_index            = "Severity index (punish beyond the crime)")

# Short handles for the two criterion labels, used by the lookup below and in
# the printed lines, so the strings are written once and then matched against
# themselves rather than retyped. A retyped label that differs by one character
# matches nothing and quietly produces NA.
h6b_y_princ <- unname(h6b_crit_labels["proportionality_principle"])
h6b_y_sev   <- unname(h6b_crit_labels["severity_index"])

# THE PART-WHOLE ROWS, PRINTED TO BE DISARMED. `deserved_soft` is the registered
# `deserved` with one of its four items removed and `deserved_soft_strict` is
# the same composite with two removed, so each of these correlates a composite
# with a set that contains it. Such a coefficient reports what share of the
# parent composite the tier makes up; it comes out high whatever the
# participants think, and it is not evidence that two measures converge. It is
# printed because a reader deciding how much weight the tier rows can carry will
# otherwise work it out for themselves, and because the size of it is the whole
# reason the tier rows are a robustness check rather than a second finding.
h6b_overlap_y <- "REGISTERED deserved R1-R4 (PART-WHOLE, not a finding)"
h6b_overlap <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  c("deserved_soft", "deserved_soft_strict"),
  function(tier_var) cor_row(d, tier_var, "deserved",
                             label_x = unname(h6b_tier_labels[tier_var]),
                             label_y = h6b_overlap_y)))

# Every tier crossed with both criteria: the outer lapply walks the tiers, the
# inner one walks the criteria, and the two rbinds stack the one-row data frames
# that cor_row() returns into a single table. Writing the rows out by hand would
# invite the two mistakes this avoids, a pair left out and a label pasted onto
# the wrong row. Row order follows the order of the two label vectors, so the
# table is rearranged by rearranging them and nowhere else.
#
# The two REGISTERED rows reproduce rows 1 and 2 of the table above exactly.
# Both calls read the same two columns through cor_row(), which deletes pairwise
# -- it keeps everyone who answered both of the two variables in that row -- so
# the r, the interval and the p are the same numbers. The labels differ only
# because the table above marks its two predictions in the label and this one
# does not.
h6b_crit_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(h6b_tier_labels),
  function(tier_var) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(h6b_crit_labels),
    function(crit_var) cor_row(d, tier_var, crit_var,
                               label_x = unname(h6b_tier_labels[tier_var]),
                               label_y = unname(h6b_crit_labels[crit_var]))))))

# The part-whole rows go on top, so that a reader meets the caveat before the
# rows it applies to rather than after them.
h6b_tiers <- rbind(h6b_overlap, h6b_crit_rows)
TABLES[["H6b_desert_tiers"]] <- h6b_tiers

# The columns worth printing from a cor_row() frame: the two labels, the number
# of participants who answered both, the correlation with its 95% interval, and
# the two-sided p. The directional p and the `alternative` column are left out
# of the printout because every row here is two-sided, so they would only repeat
# p_two and the word "two.sided" down the page. Both stay in the exported CSV,
# since TABLES holds the whole frame.
h6b_tier_cols <- c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")
show_table(h6b_tiers[, h6b_tier_cols], paste(
  "8.3b: each tier of the retribution scale against the two criteria used",
  "above, with the registered desert composite beneath them; the two opening",
  "rows are part-whole overlaps and are not findings."))

# A lookup by variable name rather than by row number. Row numbers keep working
# and quietly point at the wrong row if a tier or a criterion is ever added to
# the vectors above; matching on the same label strings that built the table
# cannot do that. [1] because a lookup that matched nothing must give one NA
# rather than an empty vector, which would silently shorten a printed line
# instead of showing a gap where the number should be.
h6b_pick <- function(tier_var, y_label, field = "r") {
  hit <- h6b_tiers$x == unname(h6b_tier_labels[tier_var]) &
         h6b_tiers$y == y_label
  h6b_tiers[[field]][hit][1]
}

# The three desert scorings side by side, one line each, so the answer to the
# objection can be read in one glance instead of hunted for in the table above.
cat("\n=== WHAT THE TIER SPLIT CHANGES ===\n")
cat(sprintf("  %-40s %10s %10s\n", "", "principle", "severity"))
for (tier_var in c("deserved", "deserved_soft", "deserved_soft_strict")) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-40s %+10.3f %+10.3f\n", unname(h6b_tier_labels[tier_var]),
              h6b_pick(tier_var, h6b_y_princ),
              h6b_pick(tier_var, h6b_y_sev)))
}
# The overlaps are reprinted directly beneath, and labelled again, because these
# two numbers are the ones a reader is likeliest to lift out of the table and
# quote as though they showed agreement between two measures.
cat("\n  Overlap with the registered composite (part-whole, not a finding):\n")
for (tier_var in c("deserved_soft", "deserved_soft_strict")) {
  cat(sprintf("  %-40s %+10.3f\n", unname(h6b_tier_labels[tier_var]),
              h6b_pick(tier_var, h6b_overlap_y)))
}

# THE VERDICT IS GUARDED ON THE NUMBERS, because which sentence is true of this
# table depends on how the table comes out. Fixing the wording in advance and
# letting the data pick which sentence prints is what stops a summary line
# describing a result the table does not show. The two thresholds decide wording
# and NOTHING ELSE: no test branches on them, and neither is a criterion of
# significance. .90 is an overlap high enough that two composites are the same
# measure under two names, and .05 is a gap in r too small for two coefficients
# in this range to be telling different stories.
h6b_overlap_soft <- h6b_pick("deserved_soft", h6b_overlap_y)
h6b_gap_soft <- abs(h6b_pick("deserved_soft", h6b_y_princ) -
                    h6b_pick("deserved", h6b_y_princ))
if (!is.na(h6b_overlap_soft) && !is.na(h6b_gap_soft) &&
    h6b_overlap_soft > .90 && h6b_gap_soft < .05) {
  cat("\nDropping the obligation item leaves the registered answer where it\n")
  cat("was. The soft core is the registered composite less one item, so this\n")
  cat("is the objection to that scoring being answered rather than a second\n")
  cat("finding on top of it.\n")
} else if (!is.na(h6b_gap_soft) && h6b_gap_soft >= .05) {
  cat("\nThe scoring matters here: the soft core and the registered\n")
  cat("composite give different answers on the principle, so both are\n")
  cat("reported and neither stands in for the other.\n")
} else {
  cat("\nRead the rows above directly. The overlap and the gap between\n")
  cat("the two scorings fall outside the range these lines describe.\n")
}

# The same guard for the placement of R3, on the same .05 wording threshold. If
# the two soft cores agree, where R3 sits does not move what this table shows.
# If they disagree, nothing below may lean on either soft core alone. Either
# way the question about the item itself stays open.
h6b_gap_r3 <- abs(h6b_pick("deserved_soft", h6b_y_princ) -
                  h6b_pick("deserved_soft_strict", h6b_y_princ))
if (!is.na(h6b_gap_r3) && h6b_gap_r3 < .05) {
  cat("Where Retribution_3 sits does not move the answer: the two soft cores\n")
  cat("stand or fall together on the principle.\n")
} else {
  cat("Where Retribution_3 sits moves the correlation with the principle, so\n")
  cat("the two soft cores are read as two measures rather than one.\n")
}

# A FORMAL TEST OF THE ORDERING. Each pair of correlations shares its desert
# variable and comes from the same participants, so the two are dependent (same
# people) and overlapping (they share a variable). That is precisely the case
# steiger_overlap() handles. Comparing the two by eye, or by asking whether the
# two confidence intervals touch, would be wrong. How far apart two such
# correlations can drift by chance alone depends on how strongly the two
# criteria relate to EACH OTHER, and only this test takes that into account.
#
# TWO-SIDED, unlike the H2 and H10 calls, whose direction was registered. The
# tier split registered no direction, and prereg 6.8 reserves the one-sided test
```
