```{r phase9_h12}
# The threshold is > 4, the neutral anchor of the 1-7 scale, so the cutoff sits
# at the midpoint. Putting it at the neutral point forces "endorse" to mean
# agreeing. A lower threshold would let people who merely failed to disagree be
# counted as endorsing hatred, or degradation, or tolerance of prison violence.
h12_spec <- data.frame(
  var = c("dueprocess", "uncertain", "hatred", "degradation", "suffering",
          "prisonviol", "harsh", "Shark_3"),
  label = c("Restricting due-process rights", "Convicting on substandard evidence",
            "Hatred toward offenders", "Degradation of prisoners",
            "Infliction of suffering", "Tolerance of prison violence",
            "Harsh prison conditions", "A painful death for the shark"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Shark_3 (how painful the death should be) is on the same 1-7 metric as the
# composites -- the same measurement scale -- so it takes the same > 4 threshold
# as the rest of the list. Using one threshold for every row is what keeps the
# shares comparable down the column; a different threshold on one row would make
# that row's percentage mean something else while still looking like the others.
h12_shares <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h12_spec)), function(i) {
  v <- h12_spec$var[i]
  prop_ci(as.integer(d_retrib[[v]] > 4), h12_spec$label[i])
}))
# The shark DECISION is not among the attitudes H12 lists, which name only the
# shark's pain. Prereg 5.10 says only that H12 and H15 together use the three
# shark items, and the decision is H15's outcome; it is reported beside the H12
# list as an addition. It is a yes-or-no answer, already stored as 0 or 1, so it is
# appended separately rather than thresholded. A yes/no item has no midpoint to
# be above, and prop_ci() takes the 0/1 indicator (a column that is 0 for no and
# 1 for yes) exactly as it stands. Running it through the > 4 threshold would
# test 1 against 4 and count nobody at all.
h12_shares <- rbind(h12_shares,
                    prop_ci(d_retrib$shark_kill, "Putting the shark to death (yes)"))

# The correlation half of H12. cor_row() is called once per attitude and always
# on d_retrib, so every correlation here is computed among retributivists only,
# never on the whole sample. H12 says only that each attitude "correlates with
# punitiveness" and names no direction, so under prereg 6.8 the registered
# test is TWO-sided: p_two_sided in the table below. alternative = "greater"
# only adds the one-sided p beside it, kept for reference. The shark
# decision is appended afterwards because it is not one of the rows in h12_spec.
h12_cors <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h12_spec)), function(i)
  cor_row(d_retrib, "punitiveness", h12_spec$var[i], alternative = "greater",
          label_x = "Punitiveness (self-report)", label_y = h12_spec$label[i])))
h12_cors <- rbind(h12_cors,
                  cor_row(d_retrib, "punitiveness", "shark_kill",
                          alternative = "greater",
                          label_x = "Punitiveness (self-report)",
                          label_y = "Putting the shark to death (yes)"))

# Join the share half to the correlation half on the display LABEL. The label is
# the only key the two halves share, and each stores it under a different name:
# prop_ci() keeps it in a column called `measure`, cor_row() keeps it in `y`,
# which is why the join names both. all.x = TRUE keeps every attitude that has a
# share even when its correlation could not be computed. Such a row then shows
# NA (R's marker for a missing value) in the r columns rather than disappearing
# from the table. A silently shorter table is the failure this guards against.
h12 <- merge(h12_shares, h12_cors[, c("y", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
                                      "p_dir", "p_two")],
             by.x = "measure", by.y = "y", all.x = TRUE,
             suffixes = c("_prop", "_r"))
# Rename the merged columns to the names the report uses. This assignment works
# by POSITION, so the list below has to match the column order coming out of
# merge() above. Change the merge and this line has to change with it, or the
# table will print correct numbers under the wrong headings.
names(h12) <- c("attitude", "n", "k_endorsing", "share", "share_ci_lower",
                "share_ci_upper", "r_with_punitiveness", "r_ci_lower",
                "r_ci_upper", "p_one_sided", "p_two_sided")
# Sort the table by share. order() puts the smallest value first, so the minus
# sign in front of h12$share reverses it and the most widely endorsed attitude
# lands at the top. The ranking is the point of this table: a reader should be
# able to see at a glance which of these attitudes are the common ones.
h12 <- h12[order(-h12$share), ]
# Park the finished table in TABLES, the register that Phase 10 writes out to
# CSV, and print it here in the report.
TABLES[["H12_retributivist_endorsement"]] <- h12
show_table(h12,
           "H12: share of retributivists endorsing each attitude (above the midpoint), with exact CIs, and its correlation with punitiveness inside the group")

# Two summary lines beneath the table, so the headline numbers are readable
# without scanning every row. which.min() and which.max() return the position of
# the smallest and largest share, which is how the matching attitude name is
# picked out; the shares are multiplied by 100 to print as percentages.
#
# THE n ON THIS LINE. It is nrow(d_retrib), every retributivist, and it does
# govern every row of the table: each attitude here, the shark pain item
# included, was answered by all of them. prop_ci() drops non-responders before
# counting, so a row's own n would fall below this one if an item ever went
# unanswered; none does in these data.
cat(sprintf("\nAmong retributivists (n = %d), endorsement ranges from %.1f%% (%s) to %.1f%% (%s).\n",
            nrow(d_retrib), 100 * min(h12$share), h12$attitude[which.min(h12$share)],
            100 * max(h12$share), h12$attitude[which.max(h12$share)]))
# na.rm = TRUE means an attitude whose correlation could not be computed counts
# as not significant instead of turning the whole count into NA. It is still
# included in the denominator, which is nrow(h12), so the count is honest about
# how many attitudes were on the list.
cat(sprintf("%d of %d attitudes correlate with punitiveness at two-sided p < .05.\n",
            sum(h12$p_two_sided < .05, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(h12)))
```

## 9.3 The master contrast set

Every group comparison in this phase (H13, H14, H15's pain rating, H16–H21, and
the exploratory E1 personality measures) is written down once, in a single
table. That one table is then reused for every run. It is run once under each
way of dividing people into a more-retributive group and a comparison group.
It is run again in 9.9 as a continuous regression, which uses the whole
retribution scale rather than dividing anyone into groups. Writing the set down
once is what guarantees that all of those runs test exactly the same things.

```{r phase9_spec}
# === THE MASTER CONTRAST SPECIFICATION ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: three things. It declares `contrast_spec`, the single
# table that lists every group contrast in Phase 9. A contrast is one comparison
# of the more-retributive group against the comparison group on one outcome.
# Which people fall in those two groups depends on the grouping, and four
# groupings are used: under the tertile grouping in 9.11, for instance, the
# middle third is in neither group. It defines run_contrast_set(), the function
# that walks down that table and runs each comparison. Then it runs the whole
# set under the primary grouping, the one taken from the goal ranking, producing
# `contrasts_rank`, which is exported under the name `contrasts_ranking`.
#
# WHY ONE SPEC. Prereg 5.3 requires that every contrast be reported under EACH
# definition of retributivism "rather than only the one that gives the strongest
# result", and prereg 6.5 requires the whole set again with retributivism
# entered continuously, as a full scale rather than a two-group split. Listing
# the outcomes, their predicted directions and their hypothesis labels in one
# place means all six runs -- four groupings plus two continuous predictors --
# test exactly the same things. Edit one row here and every table and the
# summary figure change together. That is the point. It makes it impossible for
# one run to quietly test a different set of outcomes than another.
#
# THE COLUMNS:
#   outcome         the name of the column in `d` that gets compared.
#   label           the display name printed in tables. It doubles as the key
#                   that joins the runs together in the side-by-side table in
#                   9.12, and as the factor level (a factor is R's type for a
#                   fixed set of named categories) that fixes the row order in
#                   the summary figure.
#   hypothesis      which hypothesis the row belongs to. Sections 9.4 to 9.8,
#                   9.15 and 9.17 use it to pull out their own rows from the
#                   finished result set rather than recomputing anything.
#   alternative     the direction of the one-sided test. "greater" for every
#                   hypothesis that predicts retributivists score higher;
#                   "less" for cognitive reflection, the one measure predicted
#                   to run the other way (prereg 6.8: only directional
#                   predictions are one-sided, and each is one-sided in ITS OWN
#                   direction, never in one blanket direction for the table).
#   sentence_based  TRUE if the outcome is built from the sentence. See the
#                   note on run_contrast_set() below -- this flag is what keeps
#                   the sentence off both sides of the ratio-based analyses.
#   feature         which of the six features of retributive theory the row
#                   speaks to, or NA (R's marker for a missing value) for a row
#                   that speaks to none of them. The six codes are:
#                     F1  dignity of the person punished
#                     F2  proportionality
#                     F3  leniency relative to consequentialist punishment
#                     F4  hard treatment as a necessary feature, not a goal
#                     F5  certainty of guilt
#                     F6  transcending revenge and the negative emotions
#                   Each claim is stated in full, in the manuscript's own
#                   wording, in `feature_defs` in 9.16. Deciding which measure
#                   belongs to which feature is an analytic judgement of ours
#                   rather than part of that wording, so 9.16 writes the mapping
#                   down and checks it.
#
# THE feature COLUMN IS A LABEL AND NOTHING ELSE. No test reads it.
# run_contrast_set(), run_continuous_set(), the four grouping runs, the
# side-by-side grid in 9.12 and the forest plot (the figure that draws each
# effect as a dot with its interval as a line through it) all ignore it
# entirely. Exactly one place reads it: 9.16, which reprints rows that were
# already computed, grouped by feature. Every number in Phase 9 is therefore
# what it would be with the column left blank. The column organises the
# reporting; it never touches a result.
#
# No row carries F2, and that is deliberate. Proportionality is not tested
# anywhere in this document as a difference between two groups. It is a
# one-sample question in 8.1, a paired question in 8.2 and a correlational one
# in 8.3b. So section 9.16 prints the F2 heading with that pointer beneath it
# instead of leaving a silent gap. A reader who found no F2 row and no
# explanation would reasonably conclude the feature had been forgotten.
#
# WARNING, AND IT IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Adding, removing or reordering a ROW of
# this table changes, all at once and with no error message,
# `contrasts_ranking`, `contrasts_median_split`, `contrasts_tertiles`,
# `contrasts_sentencing_ratio`, `contrasts_continuous`, the side-by-side grid in
# 9.12 and the forest plot beneath it. Those carry out prereg 5.3 and 6.5; their
# rows were fixed before anyone saw the data, except the two-item cognitive-
# reflection row, an unregistered rescoring. The counts 9.17 builds from these
# rows (P3_scorecard, P3_rows_across_groupings) change with them too; those
# counts, and the deterrence- or incapacitation-first run among them, are not
# registered. The rows below are frozen. DO NOT add, drop or reorder them.
# Editing the feature column of an existing row is safe, because nothing
# computes from it. Touching the rows themselves is not.
contrast_spec <- tibble::tribble(
  ~outcome,            ~label,                                   ~hypothesis, ~alternative, ~sentence_based, ~feature,
  "hostile_agg",       "Hostile-aggression cluster (z)",         "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "hatred",            "Hatred",                                 "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F6",
  "revenge",           "Revenge",                                "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F6",
  "degradation",       "Degradation",                            "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F1",
  "suffering",         "Infliction of suffering",                "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F4",
  "prisonviol",        "Tolerance of prison violence",           "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F4",
  "anger",             "Anger",                                  "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F6",
  "exclusion",         "Social exclusion",                       "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F1",
  "harsh",             "Harsh prison conditions",                "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F3",
  "crimerates",        "Perceived crime rates",                  "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "fear",              "Fear of crime",                          "H13",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  # H14 uses the WITHIN-VIGNETTE z-score, as prereg 6.5 requires, not raw years.
  # A z-score says how far above or below the average a value sits, counted in
  # standard deviations. The three vignettes differ in severity, so raw years
  # are not comparable across them; rescaling inside each vignette makes them
  # comparable. The row is flagged sentence_based, which removes it from the
  # sentencing-ratio grouping entirely. That ratio is built from this very
  # sentence. Using it here would be circular: one sentence would sort people
  # into groups and serve as the outcome compared between them.
  "Sentence1_z",       "Sentence 1 (z within vignette)",         "H14",       "greater",    TRUE,            "F3",
  # Only the PAIN RATING is here. The yes/no shark decision is binary, so it
  # gets a logistic regression in 9.6 instead, as prereg 6.5 specifies. A
  # logistic regression is a model built for yes/no outcomes, and it reports how
  # the odds of a yes change. A Welch t-test, which is what every row of this
  # table gets, compares two group averages and would be the wrong model for a
  # 0/1 answer.
  "Shark_3",           "Shark: how painful the death should be", "H15",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "essentialism",      "Essentialism about criminals",           "H16",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "choice",            "Crime is a choice",                      "H17",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "leanPros",          "Leaning toward the prosecution",         "H18",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "society_reject",    "Rejecting society's responsibility",     "H19",       "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "dueprocess",        "Due-process permissiveness",             "H20",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F5",
  "uncertain",         "Convicting on uncertain evidence",       "H20",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F5",
  # H21 runs on BOTH versions of punitiveness. The 8-item self-report scale is
  # the primary test. The full index is the same scale with the sentence added
  # in, so it is flagged sentence_based and drops out under the
  # sentencing-ratio grouping. Without that flag the sentence would sit on both
  # sides of the comparison at once.
  "punitiveness",      "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)",    "H21",       "greater",    FALSE,           "F3",
  "punitiveness_full", "Punitiveness (full index, + sentence)",  "H21",       "greater",    TRUE,            "F3",
  # E1 is EXPLORATORY (prereg 6.6). These rows are reported with the same
  # methods and the same effect sizes as the confirmatory rows, so they read the
  # same way on the page, but they were not pre-registered predictions. They are
  # not folded into the confirmatory family that gets the multiplicity
  # correction, and they must NOT be written up as pre-registered tests.
  "rwa",               "Right-Wing Authoritarianism",            "E1",        "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "sdo",               "Social Dominance Orientation",           "E1",        "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "vprone",            "Violence proneness",                     "E1",        "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  "raceresent",        "Racial resentment",                      "E1",        "greater",    FALSE,           NA,
  # The one "less" row in the whole table. The CRT (Cognitive Reflection Test)
  # is scored as the NUMBER CORRECT, so a higher score means more reflective
  # thinking, and the expectation is that retributivists score LOWER. The
  # prediction is recorded here, in the alternative column, rather than by
  # flipping the scoring. That keeps the CRT on its natural, published metric,
  # so these numbers can still be compared with other studies' numbers.
  "CRT",               "Cognitive reflection (0-3)",             "E1",        "less",       FALSE,           NA,
  # The same contrast on the two-item scoring. The lily-pad item's slider
  # carried a mislabelled unit, so that item is suspect. Both scorings are run
  # through every grouping: the registered 0-3 score, and the 0-2 score that
  # drops the faulty item. Two rows rather than a footnote, because a reader
  # should be able to SEE how much the defect moved the answer instead of being
  # told that it was small.
  "CRT_2item",         "Cognitive reflection (0-2, lily pad dropped)", "E1",   "less",       FALSE,          NA
)

#' Run the whole contrast set under one two-level grouping
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   data                 the data frame (a data frame is a table of rows and
#'                        columns, one row per participant here).
#'   group_col            the NAME of a two-level factor column: "grp_rank",
#'                        "grp_med", "grp_tert" or "grp_ratio". A factor is R's
#'                        type for a fixed set of named categories. The FIRST
#'                        level of that column must be the more-retributive
#'                        group. That ordering is what makes a positive result
#'                        mean "retributivists higher" everywhere.
#'   spec                 the contrast specification; contrast_spec by default.
#'   drop_sentence_based  see below.
#' RETURNS  one row per outcome: the columns welch_contrast() returns, plus
#'          `hypothesis` and `grouping`. Those two extra columns are what let
#'          several runs be stacked into one frame and still be told apart.
#' USED BY  Phases 9.3 (ranking), 9.10 (sentencing ratio) and 9.11 (median split
#'          and tertiles); the four results are combined in 9.12.
#'
#' drop_sentence_based = TRUE removes every outcome flagged sentence_based in
#' the spec, and is REQUIRED whenever the GROUPING is itself built from the
#' sentence -- which means the sentencing ratio, and only it. Two things go
#' wrong otherwise. First, H14 cannot be defined at all without circularity,
#' because the ratio is Sentence2/Sentence1 and H14's outcome is Sentence1, so
#' the same sentence would be splitting people into groups and being compared
#' between them. Second, the full punitiveness index contains Sentence1_z, so
#' contrasting it by a sentence-derived grouping would put the sentence on both
#' sides of the analysis, which prereg 5.11 forbids. Turning this flag off for
#' the ratio run would produce two impressive results that are entirely
#' circular and tell us nothing.
run_contrast_set <- function(data, group_col, spec = contrast_spec,
                             drop_sentence_based = FALSE) {
  # Either the whole spec, or the spec with the sentence-based rows taken out.
  # `!spec$sentence_based` keeps the rows whose flag is FALSE.
  sp <- if (drop_sentence_based) spec[!spec$sentence_based, ] else spec
  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sp)), function(i) {
    # One row of the spec becomes one Welch t-test: a comparison of two group
    # averages that does not assume the two groups are equally spread out. The
    # direction comes from that row's own entry, so each outcome is tested
    # one-sided in the direction predicted FOR IT, never in one blanket
    # direction imposed on the whole table.
    row <- welch_contrast(data, sp$outcome[i], group_col,
                          alternative = sp$alternative[i], label = sp$label[i])
    # Tag each result with its hypothesis and with the grouping that produced
    # it. Without those tags the runs would be indistinguishable once stacked
    # together in 9.12, and no section could pull out only its own rows.
    row$hypothesis <- sp$hypothesis[i]
    row$grouping   <- group_col
    row
  }))
  # Return the columns in a fixed order, so every call to this function hands
  # back a frame with the same columns in the same places. That is what lets the
  # four grouping runs be stacked on top of each other later without conflict.
  res[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "variable", "grouping", "n1", "n2",
          "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2", "t", "df", "p_dir", "p_two",
          "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "alternative")]
}

# The PRIMARY run: the categorical grouping from the goal ranking (prereg 5.3),
# where retributivists are the people who ranked retribution first. Categorical
# means the two groups are named categories rather than positions on a scale.
# Sections 9.4 to 9.8 and 9.15 take their rows out of this one object rather
# than running anything again, so every contrast in the report comes from a
# single pass. Recomputing per section would invite the same comparison
# appearing twice with two slightly different numbers.
contrasts_rank <- run_contrast_set(d, "grp_rank")
TABLES[["contrasts_ranking"]] <- contrasts_rank
# A count, plus a one-line key for reading the table. The key matters because
# the column names alone do not say which group is which: subscript 1 is the
# first level of the grouping factor, which is always the retributive side.
cat(sprintf("Contrast set run under the primary (ranking) grouping: %d outcomes.\n",
            nrow(contrasts_rank)))
cat("M1/SD1 = retributivists; M2/SD2 = everyone else. Positive d = retributivists higher.\n")
```

## 9.4 H13 -- hostile aggression and the wider correlate set

**H13.** Retributivists score higher than non-retributivists on the
hostile-aggression measures and on the wider set of punitiveness correlates,
the things that move together with punitiveness. Each row is a Welch t-test, a
comparison of two group averages that does not assume the groups are equally
spread out. Each is reported with Cohen's d and a 95% confidence interval.
Cohen's d is the gap between the two averages counted in standard deviations,
which is what lets measures on different scales be compared. The tests are
one-sided, because the prediction names a direction.

```{r phase9_h13}
# === H13: HOSTILE AGGRESSION AND THE WIDER CORRELATE SET ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: pulls the eleven H13 rows out of `contrasts_rank` and
# prints them. Nothing is recomputed here -- these contrasts were all run in
# 9.3, and taking them from one place is what stops a single test producing two
# different printed numbers.
#
# Row 1 is the hostile-aggression CLUSTER: five composites averaged together
# after each has been turned into a z-score, a score expressed as how many
# standard deviations it sits above or below the average. Z-scoring first is
# what makes it legitimate to average measures that use different scales. The
# rows beneath it are those five parts plus the remaining correlates. The
# cluster row is the hypothesis. The part rows are printed so a reader can see
# whether the effect is spread across all five or is carried by just one.
#
# No multiplicity correction is applied to this set. Multiplicity correction
# adjusts p-values when many tests are run together, because running enough
# tests will throw up a "significant" result by luck alone. Prereg 6.1 names the
# H1 correlate family as the set that gets BH-FDR control. BH-FDR is the
# Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure, which holds down the share
# of significant findings that are flukes. Prereg 6.5 then specifies Welch
# t-tests with Cohen's d for these group contrasts, without adding them to that
# family. Each row therefore carries its own effect size and its own interval.
# Across eleven related outcomes those intervals are what to read, rather than
# counting up which rows happened to land under p < .05.
h13 <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis == "H13", ]
show_table(h13[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2", "t", "df",
                   "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H13: retributivists versus everyone else on hostile aggression and the correlates (Welch t, Cohen's d with 95% CI)")

# Two summary lines under the table: how many outcomes point the predicted way
# (d > 0 means retributivists scored higher), how many clear one-sided p < .05,
# and which effect is the largest with its interval. na.rm = TRUE stops a row
# whose test could not be computed from turning the whole count into NA, so a
# single failed row does not blank out the summary.
cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d outcomes favour retributivists (d > 0); %d reach one-sided p < .05.\n",
            sum(h13$d > 0, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(h13),
            sum(h13$p_dir < .05, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Largest effect: %s, d = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\n",
            h13$outcome[which.max(h13$d)], max(h13$d, na.rm = TRUE),
            h13$d_lower[which.max(h13$d)], h13$d_upper[which.max(h13$d)]))
```

## 9.5 H14 -- sentence length

**H14.** Retributivists give longer prison sentences in the vignette. The
outcome is the standardized sentence (`Sentence1_z`), as the plan requires:
each person's sentence expressed as how far above or below the average it sits
for the vignette that person read. This contrast is **never** run under the
sentencing-ratio grouping, which is built from the same sentence. One sentence
cannot both sort people into groups and be the thing compared between them.

```{r phase9_h14}
# === H14: SENTENCE LENGTH ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: prints the standardized-sentence contrast that was
# already computed in `contrasts_rank`, then adds two supplementary runs. The
# first is raw years, for both sentences. The second repeats the comparison
# separately inside each vignette, again in raw years, and is stored as the
# table `H14_by_vignette`.
#
# HAZARD: this contrast is run under the ranking grouping ONLY. It must never be
# run under grp_ratio. The sentencing ratio is Sentence2/Sentence1 and this
# hypothesis is about Sentence1, so the grouping and the outcome would be built
# out of the same numbers -- the sentence_based flag in contrast_spec is what
# enforces that in 9.10. Note too that the outcome here is Sentence1_z and the
# predictor -- the variable used to explain it -- is retributivist status, so
# `punitiveness_full`, which has Sentence1_z built into it, has no business
# anywhere near this test.
h14 <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis == "H14", ]
show_table(h14[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2", "t", "df",
                   "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H14: standardized sentence by retributivist status")

# Raw years reported alongside the standardized test, so the difference can be
# read in the units participants actually used. A gap stated in years means
# something to a reader in a way that a gap stated in standard deviations does
# not. But this is REPORTING, not the test. Pooling raw years across three
# vignettes of differing severity is exactly what the within-vignette
# standardization in Phase 3.2 exists to prevent, so these two lines must not be
# quoted as the result. The per-vignette table below is the honest version of
# the same comparison.
h14_raw <- welch_contrast(d, "Sentence1", "grp_rank", "greater",
                          label = "Sentence 1 (raw years)")
h14_s2  <- welch_contrast(d, "Sentence2", "grp_rank", "greater",
                          label = "Sentence 2 (raw years)")
show_table(rbind(h14_raw, h14_s2)[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2", "t",
                                      "df", "p_dir", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H14 in raw years, reported alongside the standardized test")

# The same contrast run separately inside each vignette. Prereg 5.11 asks that
# results be confirmed to hold within vignette, and this is where that is done.
# Inside a single vignette every participant read identical facts, so raw years
# ARE comparable there and no standardization is needed. Splitting the sample by
# vignette leaves three smaller tests with wider intervals. Read them for
# whether the direction is consistent across the three, not for whether each one
# reaches significance. Each has only part of the sample behind it, so expecting
# all three to reach significance would be a mistake about statistical power --
# the chance a test detects a real effect at a given sample size -- and not a
# finding about retributivists.
h14_by_vig <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(d$Vignette)), function(v) {
  # `d$Vignette == v` on its own returns NA for anyone whose vignette is
  # missing, and subsetting on NA keeps those cases as all-NA rows rather than
  # dropping them. The !is.na() guard removes them at the source.
  # welch_contrast() deletes cases with a missing group or outcome anyway, so
  # this keeps the subset clean rather than changing any printed number.
  row <- welch_contrast(d[!is.na(d$Vignette) & d$Vignette == v, ],
                        "Sentence1", "grp_rank", "greater",
                        label = paste("Vignette", v, "(raw years)"))
  row
}))
# Park the per-vignette table in TABLES, the register that Phase 10 writes out
# to CSV, then print the columns worth reading: the two group averages, the
# test, and the effect size with its interval.
TABLES[["H14_by_vignette"]] <- h14_by_vig
show_table(h14_by_vig[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2", "t", "p_dir",
                          "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H14 within each vignette (the plan asks that results hold within vignette)")
```

## 9.6 H15 -- the shark

**H15.** Retributivists are more willing to put the shark to death, and endorse
a more painful death. Two outcomes of different kinds, so two different models.
The yes/no decision gets a **logistic regression**, a model built for yes/no
outcomes that reports how the odds of a yes change. The pain rating, which runs
1-7, gets a **t-test** comparing the two group averages.

```{r phase9_h15}
# === H15: THE SHARK ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: tests the two shark outcomes with the two different
# models prereg 6.5 specifies. The yes/no decision gets a logistic regression, a
# model for yes/no outcomes reported as an odds ratio. The 1-7 pain rating gets
# a Welch t-test, a comparison of two group averages that does not assume equal
# spread. It then adds a descriptive comparison of how confident people were in
# their decision. Produces the table `H15_logistic`.
#
# WHY THE SHARK MATTERS. A shark cannot be deterred and cannot be rehabilitated,
# so punishing it can accomplish nothing in the future. Lacking human agency, it
# cannot be a moral agent that deserves anything either. A willingness to put it
# to death, and to make that death painful, therefore cannot rest on any
# forward-looking rationale, and it defies the Kantian premise that desert
# presupposes agency (prereg 5.10). Nothing else in the survey reads punitive
# impulse this cleanly with the justifications stripped away.

# A 0/1 numeric copy of the grouping, because logit_reg() needs a numeric
# predictor rather than a factor. It is built from grp_rank instead of from the
# `retributivist` column so that it is guaranteed to code the two groups the
# same way round as every contrast in this phase: 1 = retributivist. That is
# what makes a positive b (the coefficient, on the log-odds scale) and an odds
# ratio above 1 both read as "retributivists are more likely to say yes". Coded
# the other way round, the sign of b and the direction of the odds ratio would
# both silently invert.
d$retrib_num <- as.integer(d$grp_rank == "Retributivist")

# One-sided "greater", matching H15's directional prediction: the hypothesis
# says retributivists are MORE willing, so the test is run against that specific
# direction rather than against "different in some way".
h15_logit <- logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "retrib_num", alternative = "greater",
                       label = "Put the shark to death (yes/no)")
# Park the one-row result in TABLES, the register that Phase 10 writes out to
# CSV, and print it here in the report.
TABLES[["H15_logistic"]] <- h15_logit
show_table(h15_logit, "H15: logistic regression of the shark decision on retributivist status")

# The plain counts behind the model: how many people in each group said yes and
# how many said no. A reader should be able to see the four raw numbers the odds
# ratio was computed from, not just the odds ratio itself.
shark_tab <- table(Group = d$grp_rank, Kill = ifelse(d$shark_kill == 1, "Yes", "No"))
cat("\nShark decision by group:\n\n")
print(shark_tab)
# The same finding stated twice over: as two percentages, and as an odds ratio
# with its 95% interval. d_retrib and d_other are the two group subsets, so the
# percentages describe the same people the model was fitted on.
cat(sprintf("\nRetributivists saying yes: %.1f%%; everyone else: %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(d_retrib$shark_kill, na.rm = TRUE),
            100 * mean(d_other$shark_kill, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Odds ratio = %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f], z = %.2f, p %s (one-sided)\n",
            h15_logit$OR, h15_logit$OR_lower, h15_logit$OR_upper,
            h15_logit$z, format_p(h15_logit$p_dir)))

# The pain rating, taken from the contrast set already run in 9.3. Shark_3 is a
# 1-7 item rather than a yes/no one, so it takes the Welch t-test that
# prereg 6.5 pairs with the logistic model above. The pain question is put to
# EVERY participant, whatever they decided: it opens "Assuming that the
# authorities decided to put the shark to death". So n1 and n2 on this row are
# the two whole groups, and the row is a test on everybody. Read it with the
# item's floor in mind: most participants choose the lowest point.
h15_pain <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis == "H15", ]
show_table(h15_pain[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2", "t",
                        "df", "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H15: how painful the shark's death should be (Welch t, one-sided)")

# Confidence in the shark decision. This one is TWO-SIDED, meaning it looks for
# a difference in either direction, because no hypothesis says which way it
# should go: retributivists could be more certain because the position is
# considered, or less certain because it is impulsive. Prereg 6.8 leaves
# undirected predictions two-sided, and picking a direction after seeing the
# data is precisely the move a pre-registration exists to rule out. This line is
# descriptive and is NOT part of H15's test.
h15_conf <- welch_contrast(d, "Shark_2", "grp_rank", "two.sided",
                           label = "Confidence in the shark decision")
show_table(h15_conf[, c("outcome", "M1", "M2", "t", "p_two", "d",
                        "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H15 (descriptive): confidence in the shark decision")
```

## 9.7 H16–H19 -- essentialism, choice, prosecution leaning, society

**H16** essentialism, the idea that crime expresses what an offender is; **H17**
crime as a choice; **H18** siding with the prosecution; **H19** rejecting
society's responsibility. All four are Welch t-tests, reported with Cohen's d
and its confidence interval, one-sided.

```{r phase9_h16_h19}
# === H16-H19: ESSENTIALISM, CHOICE, PROSECUTION LEANING, SOCIETY ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: pulls the four rows for these hypotheses out of
# `contrasts_rank`, prints them as a table and then again as one compact line
# per hypothesis, and adds an item-level crosstab for H18 (a crosstab is a
# simple count of who gave which answer, broken down by group).
#
# These four are one coherent picture rather than four unrelated tests. Crime as
# an expression of an offender's nature (H16), as a freely chosen act (H17),
# with the state as the party to side with (H18), and society owing nothing
# (H19). Taken together they describe the moral picture that desert-based
# punishment requires in order to hold up: an agent who could have done
# otherwise, and no shared responsibility to complicate the account. All four
# are one-sided "greater", since each predicts retributivists score higher.
h16_19 <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis %in% c("H16", "H17", "H18", "H19"), ]
show_table(h16_19[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2",
                      "SD2", "t", "df", "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower",
                      "d_upper")],
           "H16-H19: retributivists versus everyone else")

# One line per hypothesis beneath the table. The widths inside sprintf() pad the
# text so the effect sizes and intervals line up in a column, which is what lets
# four hypotheses be compared at a glance instead of read one at a time.
for (i in seq_len(nrow(h16_19))) {
  cat(sprintf("%s  %-38s d = %5.2f [%5.2f, %5.2f], p %s\n",
              h16_19$hypothesis[i], h16_19$outcome[i], h16_19$d[i],
              h16_19$d_lower[i], h16_19$d_upper[i], format_p(h16_19$p_dir[i])))
}

# H18 is also reported item by item. The leanPros composite recodes three
# nominal options to +1 / -1 / 0 and averages them. Nominal means the three
# answers -- prosecutor, defense, about the same -- are named categories with no
# natural order. That recoding is a defensible summary, but it is not a
# measurement on an interval scale, where the step from 1 to 2 would have to
# mean the same as the step from 2 to 3. So the crosstabs below print the raw
# counts sitting behind the composite. They let a reader see whether a
# difference in means comes from more prosecution answers or merely from fewer
# "about the same" ones, which the mean alone cannot distinguish.
cat("\nH18 detail — identification in a real trial (leanPros_1):\n\n")
print(table(Group = d$grp_rank,
            Identifies_with = factor(d$leanPros_1, levels = 1:3,
                                     labels = c("Prosecutor", "Defense", "About the same"))))
# The second item, printed the same way. Naming levels = 1:3 explicitly, with
# matching labels, keeps an option that nobody chose in the table as a zero.
# Left to itself, an unused category would vanish from the crosstab. The two
# tables would then no longer have the same three columns, and a reader could
# not lay them side by side.
cat("\nH18 detail — which role would you rather serve (leanPros_2):\n\n")
print(table(Group = d$grp_rank,
            Would_serve_as = factor(d$leanPros_2, levels = 1:3,
                                    labels = c("Prosecutor", "Defense", "About the same"))))
```

## 9.8 H20 and H21 -- the limits, and punitiveness

**H20.** Retributivists are more willing to set aside the limits on due process
and reliable evidence. **H21.** Retributivists score higher on punitiveness.

These two hypotheses ask what retributive commitment costs. H20 is about the
protections a defendant is owed: a fair procedure, and evidence strong enough to
convict on. H21 is about how much punishment a person wants in general. Both are
tested the same way as the hypotheses above, with a one-sided Welch t-test (a
t-test that does not assume the two groups have equal variance, that is, the
same spread of scores) and Cohen's d (the gap between the two groups, measured
in standard deviations) with a 95% confidence interval (the range of values the
data leave plausible).

```{r phase9_h20_h21}
# === H20 AND H21: THE LIMITS, AND PUNITIVENESS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: pulls the H20 and H21 rows out of `contrasts_rank`, the
# results already computed in 9.3, and adds the two limit COMPOSITES (a
# composite is one score built by combining several related measures) as an
# extra contrast.
#
# The H20 and H21 rows are not recomputed. Slicing one stored set of results,
# rather than running those tests a second time, is what guarantees the numbers
# reported here are the same numbers as in the full table in 9.3.
#
# WHY H20 IS THE SHARPEST CLAIM IN THE BLOCK. Due process and reliable evidence
# are the two limits a defensible retributivism is supposed to insist on most:
# punish only the guilty, and only after a fair procedure. So if retributivists
# turn out to be MORE willing to set those limits aside, then retributive
# commitment is not tracking the theory that bears its name. Both limit measures
# are scored so that a high score means more willing to set the limit aside,
# which is why the one-sided test asks for "greater".
h20_21 <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis %in% c("H20", "H21"), ]
show_table(h20_21[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2",
                      "SD2", "t", "df", "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower",
                      "d_upper")],
           "H20 (due process, uncertain evidence) and H21 (punitiveness)")

# The two combined limit measures. They are run here instead of being added to
# contrast_spec, because the spec's H20 rows are the two individual limits that
# prereg 6.5 names, and those rows are frozen.
#
# Read the two lines against each other. `kant_core` combines due process,
# reliable evidence, hatred and anger. `kant_nonoverlap` drops hatred, which
# also belongs to the hostile-aggression cluster -- the z-score aggregate of
# five composites that carries H13. One shared component sitting on both sides
# of an analysis can carry a result on its own, so a result that survives the
# second line is not being carried by that shared component (prereg 5.5).
h20_extra <- rbind(
  welch_contrast(d, "kant_core", "grp_rank", "greater",
                 label = "Kantian limits (core composite)"),
  welch_contrast(d, "kant_nonoverlap", "grp_rank", "greater",
                 label = "Kantian limits (non-overlapping composite)"))
show_table(h20_extra[, c("outcome", "M1", "M2", "t", "df", "p_dir", "d",
                         "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "H20 with the limit composites")

# The H21 result as a sentence, so the headline number does not have to be
# hunted down in the table above. The rows are picked by matching the outcome
# label text exactly. CAREFUL: if that label were ever changed in contrast_spec,
# the match would find nothing and this line would print nothing at all rather
# than raising an error.
cat(sprintf("\nH21: punitiveness M = %.2f (retributivists) vs %.2f (others), d = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], p %s\n",
            h20_21$M1[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"],
            h20_21$M2[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"],
            h20_21$d[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"],
            h20_21$d_lower[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"],
            h20_21$d_upper[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"],
            format_p(h20_21$p_dir[h20_21$outcome == "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"])))
```

## 9.9 Every contrast rerun with retributivism entered continuously (prereg 6.5)

Everything above sorts people into two groups, retributivists and everyone else.
The plan requires that no result depend on where that line was drawn, so every
group contrast is run a second time as a **regression on the retribution
subscale**. Instead of two groups, each person keeps their own score, and the
question becomes whether the outcome rises as that score rises.

Two predictors are used. The first is the **relative** retribution subscale, the
primary continuous measure (prereg 5.3): it measures how far above the other
three goals of punishment a person places retribution. The second is the raw
retribution subscale, which measures endorsement of retribution on its own. Both
the outcome and the predictor are turned into z-scores (rescaled so the average
is 0 and one unit is one standard deviation), so `beta`, the standardized slope,
means the same thing for every outcome no matter what units it was measured in.
Each beta comes with a 95% confidence interval.

```{r phase9_continuous}
# === EVERY CONTRAST RERUN CONTINUOUSLY (prereg 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: defines run_continuous_set(), the regression twin of
# run_contrast_set(), and runs the whole contrast set against two continuous
# predictors. Produces `contrasts_continuous` and `H15_logistic_continuous`.
#
# The plan requires this rerun "so the result does not depend on the split".
# Dichotomizing a continuous predictor, meaning cutting the score in two at a
# single point, discards variance: variance is how spread out the scores are,
# and the spread inside each half is thrown away, so everyone above the cut is
# treated as identical. Depending on where the cut lands, that can manufacture
# an effect that is not there or hide one that is. The regressions below use
# everyone's actual score, so where the split-based tables and these disagree,
# THESE are the numbers to trust.

#' Run the whole contrast set as regressions on one continuous predictor
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  data; predictor  the name of a column holding one continuous
#'            measure of retributivism; spec  the table of outcomes to run;
#'            drop_sentence_based -- the same flag, for the same reason, as in
#'            run_contrast_set().
#' RETURNS    one row per outcome, carrying beta (the standardized slope), its
#'            95% confidence interval, t, both p-values, and r2 (the share of
#'            the outcome's variance -- how spread out its values are -- that
#'            the predictor accounts for).
#' USED BY    Phases 9.9 (relative and raw retribution) and 9.10 (sentencing
#'            ratio, and the residualized sentence -- the second sentence with
#'            the part predictable from the first taken out).
#'
#' It mirrors run_contrast_set() deliberately: same spec, same hypothesis
#' labels, same per-row `alternative` (the spec column holding each outcome's
#' predicted direction). ONLY THE MODEL CHANGES. That is what lets a reader lay
#' the split-based table beside this one and read row against row. If the two
#' functions ever drifted apart, matching rows would quietly stop testing the
#' same thing.
run_continuous_set <- function(data, predictor, spec = contrast_spec,
                               drop_sentence_based = FALSE) {
  # Optionally drop every outcome built from the sentence. See the HAZARD
  # note in 9.10 for when that is required, and what goes wrong without it.
  sp <- if (drop_sentence_based) spec[!spec$sentence_based, ] else spec
  res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(sp)), function(i) {
    # One regression per row of the spec. The direction comes from the spec row,
    # so each outcome is tested one-sided in ITS OWN predicted direction rather
    # than in a single direction applied to all of them.
    row <- cont_reg(data, sp$outcome[i], predictor,
                    alternative = sp$alternative[i], label = sp$label[i])
    # Tag the row with its hypothesis number, so stacked results can still be
    # sliced by hypothesis further down.
    row$hypothesis <- sp$hypothesis[i]
    row
  }))
  # A fixed column order, so every continuous table in the document prints its
  # columns in the same places.
  res[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "predictor", "n", "beta", "ci_lower",
          "ci_upper", "t", "p_dir", "p_two", "r2", "alternative")]
}

# The PRIMARY continuous predictor (prereg 5.3): retribution scored relative to
# the other three goals. Rating retribution 6 on the 1-7 scale means little if a
# person rates all four goals 6. Subtracting the mean of the other three leaves
# how far a person puts desert AHEAD of the rest, rather than simply how much
# punishment they endorse in general, and that is what the hypotheses are about.
cont_rel <- run_continuous_set(d, "retribution_rel")
# The raw subscale, reported alongside so a reader can see whether a result
# depends on the relative construction. The raw version carries general
# endorsement of punishment with it, so where the two diverge, the relative
# one is the measure the plan designates.
cont_raw <- run_continuous_set(d, "retribution")
# Both runs are stacked into one exported table. The `predictor` column is what
# tells the two halves apart afterwards.
continuous_all <- rbind(cont_rel, cont_raw)
TABLES[["contrasts_continuous"]] <- continuous_all

# Printed as two tables rather than one stack, so each has one predictor and
# a caption that says which one it is.
show_table(cont_rel,
           "Prereg 6.5: every contrast rerun on the RELATIVE retribution subscale (primary continuous measure)")
show_table(cont_raw,
           "Prereg 6.5: the same set on the raw retribution subscale")

# A one-line count of how the whole set came out. CAREFUL: "predicted sign" has
# to respect each row's own direction. Cognitive reflection (CRT) is the one
# measure predicted to run the OTHER way, so its predicted beta is NEGATIVE
# while every other row's is positive. The ifelse() therefore reads each row's
# stored `alternative` instead of blindly counting positive betas. Counting
# positives blindly would miscount the CRT row.
cat(sprintf("\nRelative subscale: %d of %d outcomes show the predicted sign; %d reach directional p < .05.\n",
            sum(ifelse(cont_rel$alternative == "less", cont_rel$beta < 0,
                       cont_rel$beta > 0), na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(cont_rel), sum(cont_rel$p_dir < .05, na.rm = TRUE)))

# The shark DECISION is a yes-or-no answer, so it cannot join the linear set
# above: a straight line fitted to a 0/1 outcome predicts probabilities below 0
# and above 1. It gets the same continuous rerun in logistic regression form, a
# model built for yes-or-no outcomes. Logistic regression reports an odds ratio
# (OR): the factor by which the odds of a "yes" multiply for each one-unit step
# up the predictor. All three continuous measures of retributivism are used.
shark_cont <- rbind(
  logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "retribution_rel", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Shark put to death ~ relative retribution"),
  logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "retribution", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Shark put to death ~ retribution subscale"),
  logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "sentence_ratio", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Shark put to death ~ sentencing ratio"))
TABLES[["H15_logistic_continuous"]] <- shark_cont
show_table(shark_cont[, c("outcome", "predictor", "n", "b", "OR", "OR_lower",
                          "OR_upper", "z", "p_dir", "p_two")],
           "H15 with retributivism entered continuously (logistic regression)")
```

## 9.10 Every contrast repeated under the sentencing-ratio grouping (prereg 5.3)

The sentencing ratio is the one measure of retributivism built from what people
did rather than from what they said about themselves. After setting a first
sentence, participants read added facts that strip away the forward-looking
reasons for punishing: the defendant is permanently disabled and no longer
dangerous, and procedural rules remove any prospect of general deterrence. The
ratio is the share of the first sentence kept in the second. Keeping more of it,
with those reasons gone, is the more retributive response. That may make the
ratio the sharpest of the retributivism measures.

It is used as a grouping variable for **every outcome except the sentence-based
ones**. H14 is excluded because the ratio is built from the very sentence H14
tests, so grouping by the ratio would mean using the sentence to explain itself.
The full punitiveness index is excluded for the same reason: it has the sentence
inside it, and the sentence must not sit on both sides of one analysis. The
self-report punitiveness scale, which contains no sentence, is used throughout.

One thing to keep in mind about the split rule set in Phase 5.4. A large group
kept the whole first sentence, giving a ratio of exactly 1.00, and 1.00 is also
the median. Everyone tied at the median has to go to one side, and here they
go to the high side. So "high ratio" means **did not reduce the sentence** once
the forward-looking reasons were removed. The continuous version below never has
to answer that question at all, and it is the form of this robustness check to
read as primary.

```{r phase9_ratio_grouping}
# === THE SENTENCING-RATIO RERUNS (prereg 5.3, 5.11) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: repeats the contrast set under the median split on the
# ratio (a median split cuts the sample in two at the middle value), then twice
# more with the ratio and its residualized twin entered continuously, and reruns
# H15 against the ratio. Produces `contrasts_sentencing_ratio`,
# `contrasts_continuous_ratio` and `contrasts_continuous_sentence_resid`.
#
# HAZARD -- drop_sentence_based = TRUE ON EVERY CALL HERE, AND IT IS NOT
# OPTIONAL. All four runs are driven by the sentence, so every outcome built
# from the sentence has to be thrown out first. H14's outcome IS Sentence1, and
# `punitiveness_full` has Sentence1_z inside it. Leave the flag off and those
# outcomes get predicted by something computed from themselves. That returns
# large, impressive numbers that mean absolutely nothing. This is the ONE
# grouping in the document that sets the flag, and it is set on all four calls.
contrasts_ratio <- run_contrast_set(d, "grp_ratio", drop_sentence_based = TRUE)
TABLES[["contrasts_sentencing_ratio"]] <- contrasts_ratio
show_table(contrasts_ratio[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2",
                               "t", "df", "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower",
                               "d_upper")],
           "Prereg 5.3: every contrast repeated under a median split on the sentencing ratio (M1 = high ratio = more retributive). Sentence-based outcomes are excluded.")

# The continuous version, and the one to read as primary for this measure. It
# never has to decide which side the people tied at exactly 1.00 belong on,
# which is what makes the median split awkward (see Phase 5.4's split rule),
# and it uses everyone's whole ratio rather than a high-or-low label.
cont_ratio <- run_continuous_set(d, "sentence_ratio", drop_sentence_based = TRUE)
TABLES[["contrasts_continuous_ratio"]] <- cont_ratio
show_table(cont_ratio,
           "The same set with the sentencing ratio entered continuously")

# The robustness twin named in prereg 5.11: the second sentence residualized on
# the first, built in Phase 5.4. A residual is what is left of the second
# sentence once the part predictable from the first is subtracted off. A
# positive residual means the person kept more than others who started from the
# same first sentence. The ratio and the residual make different assumptions
# about how retention scales with the first sentence. The ratio assumes
# retention is proportional; the residual assumes a straight line with an
# intercept. The two tables agreeing is what shows the finding does not turn on
# that choice.
cont_resid <- run_continuous_set(d, "sentence_resid", drop_sentence_based = TRUE)
TABLES[["contrasts_continuous_sentence_resid"]] <- cont_resid
show_table(cont_resid,
           "Robustness: the same set using the second sentence residualized on the first")

# H15 once more, predicted by the ratio itself rather than by group membership.
# The shark answer is yes-or-no, so it needs logistic regression here too, and
# the OR (odds ratio) reported below is per one-unit step up the ratio.
h15_ratio <- logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "sentence_ratio", alternative = "greater",
                       label = "Shark put to death ~ sentencing ratio")
cat(sprintf("\nH15 under the sentencing ratio: OR = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], p %s\n",
            h15_ratio$OR, h15_ratio$OR_lower, h15_ratio$OR_upper,
            format_p(h15_ratio$p_dir)))
```

## 9.11 The median-split and tertile groupings

Two more ways of drawing the line between more and less retributive. A **median
split** cuts the sample in half at the middle score, so everyone is used, but
the two people either side of the cut are nearly identical. A **tertile** split
takes the top third against the bottom third and discards the middle third, so
fewer people are used, but the two groups really are far apart. Neither is
better than the other, and running both shows whether a result depends on where
the line was drawn.

```{r phase9_split_groupings}
# === THE MEDIAN-SPLIT AND TERTILE GROUPINGS (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: repeats the full contrast set under the two categorical
# versions of the relative retribution subscale: the median split (a cut at the
# middle score) and the tertiles (top third against bottom third). Produces
# `contrasts_median_split` and `contrasts_tertiles`.
#
# drop_sentence_based is deliberately NOT set here, and that is safe. Both of
# these groupings are built from the goal-endorsement items, not from the
# sentence, so H14 and the full punitiveness index can be contrasted under them
# without circularity -- that is, without the outcome being used to build the
# thing that is supposed to predict it. The sentencing-ratio runs above are the
# case where that danger is real; these are not.
#
# The tertile run compares the top and bottom thirds and throws the middle away,
# so its n's are smaller but its two groups sit further apart on the scale.
# Expect larger d's there than in the median split for that reason alone. Read
# the two as bracketing the same effect, NOT as two independent pieces of
# evidence: they are the same people, cut two ways.
contrasts_med  <- run_contrast_set(d, "grp_med")
contrasts_tert <- run_contrast_set(d, "grp_tert")
TABLES[["contrasts_median_split"]] <- contrasts_med
TABLES[["contrasts_tertiles"]] <- contrasts_tert

# Fewer columns here than in the ranking table in 9.8: `SD1`, `SD2` and `p_two`
# are left out. What prints is each group's n and mean, the test itself, the
# directional p, and Cohen's d with its interval, which is what a reader
# compares from one grouping to the next.
show_table(contrasts_med[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2",
                             "t", "df", "p_dir", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "Median split on the relative retribution subscale (M1 = high)")
show_table(contrasts_tert[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2",
                              "t", "df", "p_dir", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "Top versus bottom third of the relative retribution subscale (M1 = top third)")
```

## 9.12 All four measures side by side

The plan asks that every contrast be reported under **each** measure of
retributivism, not only under the one that gives the strongest result. That is
what the grid below does. One row per outcome, one column per definition of
retributivism, so a result that shows up under one definition and disappears
under the other three has nowhere to hide.

```{r phase9_all_measures}
# === ALL FOUR MEASURES SIDE BY SIDE (prereg 5.3) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: stacks the four contrast runs, pivots the effect sizes
# into one grid of outcomes by measures, and summarises how far the four
# definitions agree. Produces `contrasts_all_measures`, `contrasts_side_by_side`
# and `contrast_measure_agreement`.
#
# This is where the plan's commitment is honoured: report every contrast under
# EACH measure "rather than only the one that gives the strongest result". The
# grid makes selective reporting visibly impossible. An outcome that works under
# one definition but not the others shows it in its own row, for anyone to see.

#' Tag a contrast set with the name of the measure that produced it, so the four
#' stacked runs can still be told apart after rbind() has joined them into one
#' data frame (a table of rows and columns). Without the tag the four sets of
#' rows would be indistinguishable and the grid below could not be built.
lbl <- function(x, nm) { x$measure <- nm; x }
# The names are numbered "1." to "4." on purpose. These labels become the column
# headings of the grid below, and the numbers hold them in a stable, meaningful
# reading order: the primary categorical measure first, then the two splits on
# the subscale, then the behavioral measure.
all_contrasts <- rbind(
  lbl(contrasts_rank,  "1. Ranking (categorical, primary)"),
  lbl(contrasts_med,   "2. Median split on relative retribution"),
  lbl(contrasts_tert,  "3. Tertiles on relative retribution"),
  lbl(contrasts_ratio, "4. Sentencing ratio (behavioral)"))
TABLES[["contrasts_all_measures"]] <- all_contrasts

# One cell per outcome x measure: Cohen's d (the gap between the two groups
# measured in standard deviations) with stars marking its DIRECTIONAL p-value.
# Cohen's d is the right thing to tabulate across measures because it is
# scale-free: it does not depend on the units the outcome was measured in. The
# four groupings produce very different group sizes, so raw differences between
# means, and p-values, would not be comparable across the columns.
d_wide <- all_contrasts[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "measure", "d", "p_dir")]
d_wide$d_p <- sprintf("%.2f%s", d_wide$d, sig_stars(d_wide$p_dir))
# A cell that is not a number means the test was NEVER RUN, not that it ran and
# came out null. This line catches rows that are present but whose d came back
# NA -- R's marker for a missing value -- which happens when welch_contrast()
# refused a contrast. The sentence-based outcomes are the other case: under the
# sentencing-ratio measure those rows are absent altogether (see the HAZARD note
# in 9.10), so pivot_wider() below has nothing to put in that cell and leaves NA
# there.
#
# NOTE -- INTENT AND BEHAVIOUR DISAGREE HERE, and the authors should settle it.
# The caption below promises "-" for a cell "not run under that measure", but
# only the refused-contrast case gets a "-". The sentence-based cells under the
# sentencing ratio are the ones the caption most obviously describes, and they
# print as NA. Either the caption or the filling of those cells needs to change.
d_wide$d_p[is.na(d_wide$d)] <- "-"
# pivot_wider turns the stacked list of results into the grid: one row per
# outcome, one column per measure, the d-with-stars string in each cell.
side_by_side <- tidyr::pivot_wider(
  d_wide[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "measure", "d_p")],
  names_from = measure, values_from = d_p)
TABLES[["contrasts_side_by_side"]] <- as.data.frame(side_by_side)
show_table(as.data.frame(side_by_side),
           "Cohen's d under each definition of retributivism (stars use the directional p; '-' = not run under that measure)")

# A scorecard, one row per measure. CAREFUL: n_outcomes is not the same on every
# row: the sentencing-ratio run excludes the two sentence-based outcomes.
# Every count beside it must therefore be read against its own n_outcomes, and
# never compared as a raw total.
agreement <- data.frame(
  measure = unique(all_contrasts$measure),
  n_outcomes = as.integer(table(all_contrasts$measure)[unique(all_contrasts$measure)]),
  # Again the sign check reads each row's own predicted direction, so the
  # cognitive reflection (CRT) row counts as predicted when its d is NEGATIVE.
  # Counting positive d's for every row would mark that row wrong every time.
  n_predicted_sign = vapply(unique(all_contrasts$measure), function(m) {
    s <- all_contrasts[all_contrasts$measure == m, ]
    sum(ifelse(s$alternative == "less", s$d < 0, s$d > 0), na.rm = TRUE)
  }, integer(1)),
  # How many rows under this measure reach a directional p below .05. A small p
  # means the result is hard to put down to chance, and says nothing about how
  # large the effect is; that is what the median |d| column beside it reports.
  n_directional_p05 = vapply(unique(all_contrasts$measure), function(m) {
    sum(all_contrasts$p_dir[all_contrasts$measure == m] < .05, na.rm = TRUE)
  }, integer(1)),
  # The MEDIAN of |d| rather than the mean, so one unusually large effect cannot
  # make a whole measure look uniformly sharp. |d| is the absolute value of d,
  # its size with the sign dropped, which is what abs() computes here. The
  # absolute value is needed because the CRT row is predicted negative, and a
  # signed average would cancel it against the positive rows.
  median_abs_d = vapply(unique(all_contrasts$measure), function(m) {
    median(abs(all_contrasts$d[all_contrasts$measure == m]), na.rm = TRUE)
  }, numeric(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["contrast_measure_agreement"]] <- agreement
show_table(agreement, "How the four definitions of retributivism compare across the contrast set")
```

```{r phase9_figure, fig.height=8}
# === FIGURE: THE PHASE 9 CONTRASTS UNDER ALL FOUR DEFINITIONS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: draws every confirmatory contrast as a dodged forest
# plot, one colour per definition of retributivism, and writes
# output/figures/retributivist_contrasts.png. A forest plot shows one point per
# result with a horizontal line through it for its confidence interval.
# "Dodged" means the four measures are nudged apart within a row so that they
# do not overprint each other.
#
# This is the picture version of the side-by-side table: four points and four
# intervals per outcome, so agreement or disagreement among the measures can be
# read at a glance. Where an outcome shows three points instead of four, the
# missing one is the sentencing-ratio measure, which does not run the
# sentence-based rows.
# E1 is excluded from the figure -- it is exploratory (prereg 6.6) and does not
# belong in a plot of the confirmatory contrasts, though it is still tabulated
# in 9.15.
plot_df <- all_contrasts[!is.na(all_contrasts$d) &
                           all_contrasts$hypothesis %in%
                           c("H13", "H14", "H15", "H16", "H17", "H18", "H19",
                             "H20", "H21"), ]
# The y axis order comes from making `outcome` a factor (a variable with a fixed
# set of levels in a fixed order) using the spec's order, not the effect sizes.
# Sorting by effect size would scatter the hypotheses through each other; this
# way outcomes stay grouped by hypothesis and the panel reads in H13-to-H21
# order. rev() is needed because ggplot draws the FIRST level at the BOTTOM.
plot_df$outcome <- factor(plot_df$outcome,
                          levels = rev(unique(contrast_spec$label)))
p_contrast <- ggplot2::ggplot(
  plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = d, y = outcome, colour = measure)) +
  # The dashed vertical line marks d = 0, meaning no difference between the two
  # groups. An interval that crosses it is consistent with no effect at all.
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  # position_dodge is what separates the four measures within one row. The width
  # MUST be the SAME here and on the points layer below. If the two widths ever
  # differ, an interval drifts off its own point and sits under a neighbour's,
  # which a reader would take as a result.
  ggplot2::geom_linerange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = d_lower, xmax = d_upper),
                          position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .6),
                          alpha = .6) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .6), size = 2) +
  # Dark2 is a QUALITATIVE ColorBrewer palette: unrelated hues meant to be told
  # apart from one another, not shades of one colour meant to be read as a
  # ranking. The four measures are not ranked, so a graded colour ramp would
  # imply an order that is not there.
  ggplot2::scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  # The N in the subtitle is read from the analysis frame rather than typed in,
  # so it can never disagree with the data the figure was actually drawn from.
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Retributivist contrasts under four definitions of retributivism",
                subtitle = sprintf("Cohen's d with 95%% CI (confirmatory, N = %d)", nrow(d)),
                x = "Cohen's d (positive = more retributive group scores higher)",
                y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p_contrast)
# ggsave() writes the PNG at a stated width, height and dpi (dots per inch, the
# resolution of the saved image), so the file on disk does not depend on the
# size of the plotting window at knit time. The path is then appended to
# FIGURES, the character vector (a simple ordered run of text values) that
# collects every figure written. Phase 10.2 only lists that vector back, so a
# figure left out of it lands on disk but is never reported.
fig_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "retributivist_contrasts.png")
ggplot2::ggsave(fig_path, p_contrast, width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300)
FIGURES <- c(FIGURES, fig_path)
```

## 9.12b Retributivists against the deterrence- and incapacitation-first

The ranking contrasts in 9.3 set the 371 participants who ranked desert first
against everyone else, and everyone else includes the 124 who ranked
rehabilitation first. Of the four goals, rehabilitation is the only one that
aims at the offender's own good, so those participants may well be the least
punitive in the sample. If they are, part of what separates retributivists from
"everyone else" could be a difference from rehabilitationists in particular,
not from people who value punishment for other reasons.

This subsection asks the sharper question. It sets the retributivists against
the participants who ranked deterrence or incapacitation first: people who also
value punishment, but for the crime it prevents. Where retributivists still
differ from them, the difference cannot be put down to the rehabilitation-first
participants alone. The contrast set is the one frozen in 9.3, unchanged: every
row keeps its registered outcome and predicted direction, and only the
comparison group is narrower.

Four limits. The groups are still defined by a
self-reported ranking. Deterrence-first and incapacitation-first participants
are pooled into one comparison group; the table of group means below shows each
separately. The registered and the new comparison share all 371 retributivists
and 453 of the 577 comparison participants, so they are not independent tests,
and the change in d between them is described, not tested. And the comparison
is not in the registration: it sits beside the registered contrasts, never in
place of them, outside every registered family, with no multiplicity
correction applied or implied.

```{r phase9_vs_deter_incap}
# === 9.12b RETRIBUTIVISTS AGAINST THE DETERRENCE- AND INCAPACITATION-FIRST ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds a second grouping from the goal ranking that sets
# the participants who ranked desert first against those who ranked deterrence
# or incapacitation first, leaving the rehabilitation-first participants out.
# Reruns the full contrast set and the H15 logistic regression under it, sets
# every effect beside its registered counterpart from 9.3, and prints each
# outcome's mean for all four first-choice groups. Produces
# `contrasts_vs_deter_incap`, `contrasts_vs_deter_incap_compare`,
# `contrasts_vs_deter_incap_summary`, `first_choice_group_means` and
# `H15_logistic_vs_deter_incap`.
# PREREG: not registered. Prereg 5.3 defines the ranking contrast as desert-first
#         against everyone else, and 9.3 runs exactly that. This sits beside it
#         and never replaces it; outside every registered family; no
#         multiplicity correction applied or implied.
# CONSUMES: prio_cols and goal_labels (5.1), retributivist (5.1),
#           contrast_spec, run_contrast_set() and contrasts_rank (9.3),
#           h15_logit (9.6), logit_reg(), shark_kill.
#
# NOTHING HERE TOUCHES `d` OR contrast_spec. The new grouping lives in cq_d, a
# private copy of `d`. contrast_spec is used exactly as frozen in 9.3 (same
# rows, same order, same predicted directions), so every row below is the
# registered test with a narrower comparison group and nothing else changed.
# DANGER: do not add grp_vs_deter_incap to `d`. `d` is what Phase 10 exports as
# retribution_scored.csv, and a new column there would change a registered
# output file for the sake of a check that is not registered.
# NAMING: every object this chunk leaves behind starts with cq_ ("comparison
# group"), so no later chunk can pick one up by accident.

# --- Which goal each participant ranked first ------------------------------
# Recomputed with the same rule as 5.1 rather than borrowed from its
# `first_choice` vector, because that vector lines up with `d` only by row
# position, and this chunk should not depend on nothing having reordered `d`
# since 5.1. A row with a missing rank, or no rank of 1, is NA: unknown, never
# credited to a goal.
cq_first <- apply(d[, prio_cols], 1, function(r) {
  if (anyNA(r) || !any(r == 1)) return(NA_integer_)
  which(r == 1)[1]
})
# The four goals are found by NAME in goal_labels, so a change to the WORDING of
# a label cannot quietly point this code at the wrong goal: stopifnot() halts the
# knit if a name matches no label or more than one. What the lookup does NOT
# protect against is a change to the label ORDER. cq_first is a position within
# prio_cols, cq_idx() returns a position within goal_labels, and the two are
# compared as one index, which holds only because 5.1 writes the two vectors in
# the same order (it says so at 5.1's own comment on column position standing in
# for goal name). The guard below would catch a reorder that moved retribution,
# because d$retributivist is tied to Prioritization_1 directly; a reorder that
# swapped only deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation would pass silently.
cq_idx <- function(pattern) {
  i <- grep(pattern, goal_labels, ignore.case = TRUE)
  stopifnot(length(i) == 1)
  i
}
cq_ret <- cq_idx("retribution")
cq_det <- cq_idx("deterrence")
cq_inc <- cq_idx("incapacitation")
cq_reh <- cq_idx("rehabilitation")
# GUARD: the desert-first group here must be exactly the registered
# retributivists, person for person. If it were not, this comparison and the
# registered one would be about two different sets of people and could not be
# read side by side.
stopifnot(identical(which(cq_first == cq_ret), which(d$retributivist == 1)))

cq_d <- d
# The FIRST level is the retributive side, as run_contrast_set() requires, so a
# positive d means retributivists score higher, exactly as everywhere else in
# Phase 9. The rehabilitation-first participants get NA, and welch_contrast()
# drops NA-group rows contrast by contrast, as it already does for the middle
# third under the tertile grouping.
cq_d$grp_vs_deter_incap <- factor(
  ifelse(cq_first == cq_ret, "Retributivist",
         ifelse(cq_first %in% c(cq_det, cq_inc),
                "Deterrence or incapacitation first", NA_character_)),
  levels = c("Retributivist", "Deterrence or incapacitation first"))
# The same people coded 1/0 for the logistic regression, NA for the excluded.
cq_d$retrib_vs_deter_incap <- as.integer(cq_d$grp_vs_deter_incap == "Retributivist")

# Who is in this comparison, by the goal they ranked first.
cq_role <- rep("left out", length(goal_labels))
cq_role[cq_ret] <- "retributivists"
cq_role[c(cq_det, cq_inc)] <- "comparison group"
cq_counts <- data.frame(
  first_ranked = goal_labels,
  n = as.integer(table(factor(cq_first, levels = seq_along(goal_labels)))),
  role_here = cq_role, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
show_table(cq_counts, "9.12b: who is in this comparison, by the goal ranked first")

# --- The contrast set against the narrower comparison group ----------------
# drop_sentence_based stays FALSE, as in 9.3 and 9.11. This grouping is built
# from the goal ranking, not from the sentence, so H14 and the full punitiveness
# index can be contrasted under it without circularity.
cq_contrasts <- run_contrast_set(cq_d, "grp_vs_deter_incap")
TABLES[["contrasts_vs_deter_incap"]] <- cq_contrasts
show_table(cq_contrasts[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "M2",
                            "t", "df", "p_dir", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           paste("9.12b: the contrast set, retributivists (M1) against the",
                 "deterrence- or incapacitation-first (M2). One-sided in each",
                 "row's registered direction; not corrected."))

# --- Every effect beside its registered counterpart -------------------------
# Joined on the row label, which contrast_spec keeps unique, and then put back
# into the spec's own order so the table reads H13 to E1 as 9.3 does.
cq_cmp <- merge(
  contrasts_rank[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "alternative", "n1", "n2",
                     "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "p_dir")],
  cq_contrasts[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "p_dir")],
  by = "outcome", suffixes = c("_vs_all_others", "_vs_deter_incap"))
cq_cmp <- cq_cmp[match(contrast_spec$label, cq_cmp$outcome), ]
rownames(cq_cmp) <- NULL
# The change in d, new minus registered. Descriptive only: the two runs share
# most of their participants, so this difference is not a test of anything.
cq_cmp$d_change <- cq_cmp$d_vs_deter_incap - cq_cmp$d_vs_all_others
# The same change read in each row's PREDICTED direction: positive means the
# effect moved further toward the prediction. It differs from d_change only on
# the two cognitive-reflection rows, which predict retributivists LOWER, so
# there a falling d is a gain. Used for the printed summary below, so the rows
# predicted "less" are not averaged in with the wrong sign.
cq_cmp$d_change_toward_prediction <- ifelse(cq_cmp$alternative == "less",
                                            -cq_cmp$d_change, cq_cmp$d_change)
# Whether each interval clears zero on the predicted side. Read off the
# interval, not the p value, and in each row's own direction, so the cognitive
# reflection rows (predicted LOWER for retributivists) count when d is negative.
cq_clears <- function(lo, hi, alt) ifelse(alt == "less", hi < 0, lo > 0)
cq_cmp$clears_vs_all_others <- cq_clears(cq_cmp$d_lower_vs_all_others,
                                         cq_cmp$d_upper_vs_all_others,
                                         cq_cmp$alternative)
cq_cmp$clears_vs_deter_incap <- cq_clears(cq_cmp$d_lower_vs_deter_incap,
                                          cq_cmp$d_upper_vs_deter_incap,
                                          cq_cmp$alternative)
TABLES[["contrasts_vs_deter_incap_compare"]] <- cq_cmp
show_table(cq_cmp[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n2_vs_all_others",
                      "d_vs_all_others", "n2_vs_deter_incap",
                      "d_vs_deter_incap", "d_lower_vs_deter_incap",
                      "d_upper_vs_deter_incap", "d_change",
```
