```{r phase9_vs_deter_incap}
                      "clears_vs_deter_incap")],
           paste("9.12b: Cohen's d against everyone else (registered, 9.3) and",
                 "against the deterrence- or incapacitation-first. n2 is the",
                 "size of the comparison group in each."))

# --- The same comparison in summary -----------------------------------------
# The sign check reads each row's own predicted direction, exactly as the
# scorecard in 9.12 does, and the median of |d| keeps one large effect from
# making a whole column look sharp.
cq_pred_sign <- function(dd, alt) sum(ifelse(alt == "less", dd < 0, dd > 0), na.rm = TRUE)
cq_summary <- data.frame(
  comparison = c("Retributivists vs everyone else (registered, 9.3)",
                 "Retributivists vs deterrence- or incapacitation-first"),
  n_outcomes = c(sum(!is.na(cq_cmp$d_vs_all_others)),
                 sum(!is.na(cq_cmp$d_vs_deter_incap))),
  n_predicted_sign = c(cq_pred_sign(cq_cmp$d_vs_all_others, cq_cmp$alternative),
                       cq_pred_sign(cq_cmp$d_vs_deter_incap, cq_cmp$alternative)),
  n_interval_clears_zero = c(sum(cq_cmp$clears_vs_all_others, na.rm = TRUE),
                             sum(cq_cmp$clears_vs_deter_incap, na.rm = TRUE)),
  median_abs_d = c(median(abs(cq_cmp$d_vs_all_others), na.rm = TRUE),
                   median(abs(cq_cmp$d_vs_deter_incap), na.rm = TRUE)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
TABLES[["contrasts_vs_deter_incap_summary"]] <- cq_summary
show_table(cq_summary, "9.12b: the registered and the narrower comparison in summary")

# The outcomes whose interval cleared zero against everyone else but no longer
# does against the deterrence- or incapacitation-first, named, so no reader has
# to find them in the table. Guarded, so no sentence can print over a table that
# does not support it.
cq_lost <- cq_cmp$outcome[cq_cmp$clears_vs_all_others %in% TRUE &
                            !(cq_cmp$clears_vs_deter_incap %in% TRUE)]
cq_gained <- cq_cmp$outcome[!(cq_cmp$clears_vs_all_others %in% TRUE) &
                              cq_cmp$clears_vs_deter_incap %in% TRUE]
cat(sprintf(paste("\nMedian change in d, narrower minus registered, read in",
                  "each row's predicted direction: %+.3f.\n"),
            median(cq_cmp$d_change_toward_prediction, na.rm = TRUE)))
# Any outcome whose effect GREW when the rehabilitation-first were left out,
# named: on such a row those participants were not at the low end, so leaving
# them out pulled the comparison group's mean down rather than up.
# The parentheses matter: %in% binds tighter than >, and %in% TRUE turns an NA
# comparison into FALSE, so a row with no estimate is never listed.
cq_grew <- cq_cmp$outcome[(cq_cmp$d_change_toward_prediction > 0) %in% TRUE]
if (length(cq_grew)) {
  cat("Effect grew in the predicted direction with the rehabilitation-first left out:\n")
  cat(paste0("  - ", cq_grew, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
}
if (length(cq_lost)) {
  cat("Interval cleared zero against everyone else but not against the\n")
  cat("deterrence- or incapacitation-first:\n")
  cat(paste0("  - ", cq_lost, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
} else {
  cat("Every outcome whose interval cleared zero against everyone else still\n")
  cat("clears it against the deterrence- or incapacitation-first.\n")
}
if (length(cq_gained)) {
  cat("Interval clears zero only against the narrower comparison group:\n")
  cat(paste0("  - ", cq_gained, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
}

# --- H15's yes/no decision, the one outcome outside the contrast set -------
# The shark decision is binary, so it gets logistic regression here as it does
# in 9.6, with the same one-sided direction. The registered row is reprinted
# from 9.6 beside the new one rather than recomputed.
cq_h15 <- logit_reg(cq_d, "shark_kill", "retrib_vs_deter_incap",
                    alternative = "greater",
                    label = "Shark to death (yes/no): vs deterrence- or incapacitation-first")
TABLES[["H15_logistic_vs_deter_incap"]] <- cq_h15
show_table(rbind(h15_logit, cq_h15),
           "9.12b: H15's shark decision against everyone else (registered, 9.6) and against the deterrence- or incapacitation-first")

# --- Where each first-choice group sits -------------------------------------
# Descriptive only, no test: each outcome's mean for all four first-choice
# groups, so a reader can see where the rehabilitation-first participants sit
# relative to the deterrence- and incapacitation-first. Leaving them out changes
# the comparison group's mean, its SD (which is in d's denominator, since d uses
# the unpooled SD) and its size (which sets each interval's width). In these data
# the shift in the mean does almost all the work. Computed on `d`, the full
# sample, since every participant has a first choice.
cq_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(contrast_spec)), function(i) {
  y <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(d[[contrast_spec$outcome[i]]]))
  m <- tapply(y, factor(cq_first, levels = seq_along(goal_labels)), mean,
              na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(hypothesis = contrast_spec$hypothesis[i],
             outcome = contrast_spec$label[i],
             desert_first = unname(m[cq_ret]),
             deterrence_first = unname(m[cq_det]),
             incapacitation_first = unname(m[cq_inc]),
             rehabilitation_first = unname(m[cq_reh]),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
TABLES[["first_choice_group_means"]] <- cq_means
show_table(cq_means, "9.12b: mean of each outcome by the goal ranked first (descriptive)")

# How often the rehabilitation-first group sits at the least-retributive end:
# the LOWEST of the four means on a row predicted "greater", the HIGHEST on the
# rows predicted "less". Counted in each row's own direction for the same reason
# as the sign check above.
cq_rehab_extreme <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(cq_means)), function(i) {
  v <- unlist(cq_means[i, c("desert_first", "deterrence_first",
                            "incapacitation_first", "rehabilitation_first")])
  if (anyNA(v)) return(NA)
  if (contrast_spec$alternative[i] == "less") which.max(v) == 4 else which.min(v) == 4
}, logical(1))
cat(sprintf(paste("\nThe rehabilitation-first group has the least-retributive",
                  "mean on %d of %d outcomes.\n"),
            sum(cq_rehab_extreme, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(cq_rehab_extreme))))
cq_not_extreme <- cq_means$outcome[cq_rehab_extreme %in% FALSE]
if (length(cq_not_extreme)) {
  cat("Outcomes on which it does not:\n")
  cat(paste0("  - ", cq_not_extreme, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
}
```


## 9.13 The contrast set run on each slice of the retribution scale

The survey asked seven questions about retribution. Those seven items fall into
three tiers, three groups that make different kinds of claim: the **soft core**
(R1, R3, R4), the **obligation** items (R2, R5) and the two **rationales** (R6,
R7). A slice, in this section, is any one of the six scorings of these items
entered as a predictor below: the three tiers, the soft core with R3 removed,
and the two registered composites.

Which tier R3 belongs to is genuinely unsettled. *"Justice is restored when
criminals are punished"* is not a claim that punishing is permitted. It says
punishment **achieves** something, and that is the positive-retributive
position, the very thing the soft tier is meant to hold apart from. So the soft
core is scored twice, once with R3 and once without, and every table below
carries both versions. That way no conclusion rests on where R3 is filed.

This section runs the whole contrast set once on each slice, once on the
registered four-item `deserved` composite and once on the registered seven-item
subscale. It prints the runs as one grid: one row per outcome, one column per
slice. A reader can then read along a single row and see whether a conclusion
depends on which part of the scale is used to define retributivism.

What this is, and what it is not. Nothing here displaces the registered runs in
9.9. **One** column, the seven-item subscale, is the registered raw run from 9.9
recomputed by the same function from the same predictor, and the chunk checks
that it comes back identical. The `deserved` column feeds a registered
*composite*, a score made by averaging several items, into the continuous
machinery, which 9.9 does not do. That column is therefore an additional display
and not a registered test. The slices are also not independent measures of
anything. The soft core is three of the four items of `deserved`, so its column
is close to a copy of the `deserved` column rather than a second opinion about
it. This section earns its place by putting a printed number on **whether** the
conclusions turn on which slice of the scale is used. It is a robustness
demonstration, and a result that survives it is the registered result surviving
an objection, not a new finding.

```{r phase9_tier_predictors}
# === THE SLICES OF THE RETRIBUTION SCALE (prereg 5.3, 5.4, 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the continuous predictors used in the grid below,
# then prints how far they overlap in ITEMS and how far they overlap in
# VARIANCE. A continuous predictor is a score that runs along a scale, rather
# than a label that sorts people into groups. Overlapping in ITEMS means two
# slices are built from some of the same questions. Variance is how spread out a
# set of scores is, so overlapping in VARIANCE means two slices spread people
# out in much the same way even where the questions differ. Produces
# `tier_item_sets`, `tier_slice_labels` and `tier_predictor_correlations`.
#
# WHY BOTH KINDS OF OVERLAP MATTER. Two slices that share items MUST correlate,
# because part of each score is literally the same numbers. Reading that as
# agreement between two measures would be circular. Printing the shared-item
# count next to the correlation is what keeps a reader from making that mistake.
#
# THE SLICES, and what each one asserts:
#   deserved_soft          R1, R3, R4. Society has a moral right to punish;
#                          justice is restored when criminals are punished;
#                          punishment is justified because criminals deserve
#                          it. The weaker claim: punishing the guilty is
#                          warranted.
#   deserved_soft_strict   R1, R4. The same tier with R3 removed. R3 says
#                          punishment RESTORES justice, which is an achievement
#                          claim rather than a permission, so it arguably sits
#                          with the obligation tier instead. Both versions are
#                          carried rather than a choice being made silently.
#   retribution_hard       R2, R5. Justice REQUIRES that crimes be punished;
#                          the state has a DUTY to punish. The stronger claim:
#                          failing to punish is itself a wrong. This tier is
#                          the closer of the two to what the philosophical
#                          literature calls positive retributivism, with the
#                          soft tier nearer the negative, permission-only
#                          version.
#   retribution_rationale  R6, R7. Punishment lets criminals repay their debt
#                          to society, and it negates the unfair advantage they
#                          gained over law-abiding citizens. These two give a
#                          REASON why desert holds rather than asserting that
#                          it does, which is why they are the two items a
#                          philosopher is most likely to say do not belong with
#                          the rest.
#   deserved               REGISTERED (prereg 5.4): R1-R4, the purpose items,
#                          scored in Phase 4.3 and used here exactly as scored.
#   retribution            REGISTERED (prereg 5.3): all seven items, scored in
#                          Phase 4.1 and used here exactly as scored.

# The list of items behind every slice, written down in one place. The two
# registered entries RESTATE definitions already made in Phase 4.1 and
# Phase 4.3. They are bookkeeping for the overlap table below and are NEVER used
# to rebuild those composites, which are read out of `d` exactly as Phase 4
# scored them. Writing the item sets down once also means the overlap counts
# below are computed rather than typed, so they cannot drift out of step with
# the scoring.
tier_item_sets <- list(
  deserved_soft         = paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 3, 4)),
  deserved_soft_strict  = paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 4)),
  retribution_hard      = paste0("Retribution_", c(2, 5)),
  retribution_rationale = paste0("Retribution_", c(6, 7)),
  deserved              = paste0("Retribution_", 1:4),
  retribution           = paste0("Retribution_", 1:7))

# The four slices this section is willing to score for itself. `deserved` and
# `retribution` are deliberately absent. Rebuilding either would put a second,
# differently-labelled copy of a registered composite into the reliability
# table, and that copy could drift away from the registered column without
# anyone noticing. The registered composites are used exactly as Phase 4 left
# them.
tier_new_slices <- c("deserved_soft", "deserved_soft_strict",
                     "retribution_hard", "retribution_rationale")
# compute_composite() uses the label as the row key of the reliability table, so
# these labels have to stay unique across the whole document. Reusing a label
# would file two different composites under one name and make the reliability
# table unreadable.
tier_alpha_labels <- c(
  deserved_soft         = "retribution: soft core (R1,R3,R4)",
  deserved_soft_strict  = "retribution: soft core strict (R1,R4)",
  retribution_hard      = "retribution: obligation (R2,R5)",
  retribution_rationale = "retribution: rationales (R6,R7)")

# A guard, not a rebuild. `!nm %in% names(d)` asks whether the slice is already
# a column of `d`. It is, in a normal top-to-bottom knit, because Phase 4 scored
# all four. The loop then does nothing. The guard exists only so this section
# still works when someone runs the chunks out of order in an interactive
# session and Phase 4 has not been executed yet. Going through
# compute_composite() rather than taking a mean by hand keeps the
# at-least-half-the-items scoring rule (prereg 5.1) identical either way. Under
# that rule a person who answered fewer than half the items of a slice gets NA,
# R's marker for a missing value, rather than a score. Half is rounded up, so
# the threshold is 2 of 3 for the soft core and 1 of 2 for the three two-item
# slices, where one answered item is therefore enough to be scored.
#
# WHERE THE RELIABILITY OF A SLICE ENDS UP. Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's
# omega are two numbers saying how consistently a set of questions behaves as
# one scale. compute_composite() appends them to the live `alpha_table` with
# <<-, which writes to a variable outside the function. But Phase 4.10 takes a
# COPY of that table into `alpha_table_out`, and it is the COPY that Phase 10.1
# exports as reliability_alpha_omega.csv and that Phase 10.3 writes to
# data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv. So a row appended after 4.10 reaches
# NEITHER file. It survives only as a line printed to the console during the
# knit, which no reader of the replication package will ever see. Whatever these
# guards append is therefore collected again at the end of 9.14 and registered
# as a table of its own, so the alphas are in the replication package no matter
# where the slices happened to be scored.
for (nm in tier_new_slices) {
  if (!nm %in% names(d)) {
    d[[nm]] <- compute_composite(d, tier_item_sets[[nm]],
                                 tier_alpha_labels[[nm]])
  }
}

# One named vector (a simple run of values, each with a name attached) drives
# everything below. The NAMES are columns in `d`; the VALUES are the labels
# printed in the tables. Numbering the labels "1." to "6." fixes the column
# order of the grid, because the pivot below lays columns out in order of first
# appearance. Without the numbers an alphabetical ordering would scatter the two
# REGISTERED measures into the middle of the grid, where a reader would have to
# hunt for the columns that actually matter.
tier_slice_labels <- c(
  deserved_soft         = "1. Soft core R1,R3,R4",
  deserved_soft_strict  = "2. Soft core strict R1,R4",
  retribution_hard      = "3. Obligation R2,R5",
  retribution_rationale = "4. Rationales R6,R7",
  deserved              = "5. REGISTERED deserved R1-R4",
  retribution           = "6. REGISTERED retribution, 7 items")
# Every count printed in this section is read off this vector rather than typed
# in by hand. If a slice is ever added or reordered, no sentence is left behind
# saying "five" when there are now six.
n_slices <- length(tier_slice_labels)

# HOW CLOSELY THE SLICES TRACK EACH OTHER. This correlation matrix, a square
# table holding the correlation of every slice with every other slice, is the
# reason the grid below is expected to be dull reading. The seven-item scale has
# a Cronbach's alpha of about .90, meaning the seven questions already behave as
# one tight set, so any slice of it carries much of the same information as any
# other slice.
#   use = "pairwise.complete.obs" is pairwise deletion: for each PAIR of slices,
# R uses everyone who has a score on both, so a participant who skipped one item
# still contributes to every pair they did answer. That is exactly the rule
# cor_row() applies to a pair, so a number here matches the corresponding
# cor_row() line elsewhere in the document. It is NOT the rule steiger_overlap()
# uses. Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations, which compares
# two correlations that share a variable, needs complete cases across all THREE
# of its columns, meaning it keeps only people with no missing value on any of
# them. So a correlation that also appears in a Steiger table can differ there
# in the last decimal. That is a difference in who was included, not a mistake.
#   as.data.frame() converts `d` from a tibble (the tidyverse's table type) into
# an ordinary data frame (a table with named columns), because cor() expects an
# ordinary frame.
tier_cor <- stats::cor(as.data.frame(d[, names(tier_slice_labels)]),
                       use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# PART-WHOLE, NAMED CELL BY CELL RATHER THAN COLUMN BY COLUMN. A part-whole
# correlation is one where a measure is correlated with something it is itself
# part of, so the two are guaranteed to agree and the number says nothing about
# whether two separate things go together. A blanket warning that "the
# registered columns are part-whole" would be false and would throw away the
# cells that do carry information. `deserved` is R1-R4: it contains both soft
# versions whole, it shares R2 with the obligation tier's two items, and it
# shares NO item with the rationale tier. That last pair is therefore a clean
# correlation between two disjoint halves of the same block, and it is the most
# informative line in the table. Disjoint means the two slices share no item at
# all, and it is what the "disjoint: clean" cell in the relation column marks.
# The seven-item scale contains every slice, so its column is part-whole
# throughout. Each pair is labelled below with the number of items it shares,
# and the table is sorted so the uncontaminated pairs come first. Without those
# labels a reader would take a high correlation between a part and the whole it
# sits in as strong evidence of agreement, when it is mostly arithmetic.
#
# lower.tri() picks the cells below the diagonal of the correlation matrix, so
# each pair of slices is listed once. Without it every pair would appear twice,
# once as A-with-B and once as B-with-A, and the diagonal of each slice with
# itself would be counted as a pair as well.
tier_pairs <- which(lower.tri(tier_cor), arr.ind = TRUE)
# One row per pair: which two slices, how many items each has, how many items
# they share, what that overlap amounts to, how many people are in the pair, and
# the correlation itself.
tier_overlap <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(tier_pairs)), function(i) {
  a <- rownames(tier_cor)[tier_pairs[i, "row"]]
  b <- colnames(tier_cor)[tier_pairs[i, "col"]]
  ia <- tier_item_sets[[a]]
  ib <- tier_item_sets[[b]]
  # intersect() gives the items the two slices have in common; length() counts
  # them. Zero means the pair is built from entirely separate questions.
  shared <- length(intersect(ia, ib))
  # Full containment is shared == the size of the SMALLER set: every item of one
  # slice is inside the other. Anything between that and zero is partial.
  relation <- if (shared == 0) {
    "disjoint: clean"
  } else if (shared == min(length(ia), length(ib))) {
    "part-whole: one contains the other"
  } else {
    "partial overlap"
  }
  data.frame(slice_x = tier_slice_labels[[a]], slice_y = tier_slice_labels[[b]],
             k_x = length(ia), k_y = length(ib), items_shared = shared,
             relation = relation,
             n = sum(stats::complete.cases(d[[a]], d[[b]])),
             r = tier_cor[a, b], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
# Sorted by items_shared, smallest first, so the pairs that share no item sit at
# the top of the printed table where they will actually be read. Those are the
# only correlations here that mean what a correlation usually means.
tier_overlap <- tier_overlap[order(tier_overlap$items_shared), ]
TABLES[["tier_predictor_correlations"]] <- tier_overlap
show_table(tier_overlap,
           "How the slices overlap in items and how they correlate, sorted so the pairs sharing no item, the only uncontaminated correlations here, come first")

# The same facts stated in a sentence, so a reader who skims the table still
# leaves knowing how many of these correlations are clean and how many are
# part-whole. The counts are computed from the table, never typed.
cat(sprintf("\n%d of the %d slice pairs share no item and are clean correlations; %d are part-whole and describe overlap rather than convergence.\n",
            sum(tier_overlap$items_shared == 0), nrow(tier_overlap),
            sum(tier_overlap$relation == "part-whole: one contains the other")))
cat(sprintf("The %d slices intercorrelate between r = %.2f and r = %.2f (median %.2f).\n",
            n_slices, min(tier_overlap$r, na.rm = TRUE),
            max(tier_overlap$r, na.rm = TRUE),
            median(tier_overlap$r, na.rm = TRUE)))

# THE ONE NUMBER THAT DECIDES HOW TO READ THIS WHOLE SECTION: the soft core
# against the registered `deserved` composite. If they are nearly the same
# number for every person, the section is a robustness demonstration and nothing
# more. If they come apart, the columns carry separate information. Rather than
# assert one reading in advance, the code reads the correlation off the data and
# then prints the sentence that fits it, so BOTH readings are written down here
# and the data picks which one is printed.
r_soft_deserved <- tier_cor["deserved_soft", "deserved"]
# How many items the two share, printed beside the correlation so the reader can
# see immediately that this is a part-whole pair and not two separate measures.
n_shared_soft <- length(intersect(tier_item_sets$deserved_soft,
                                  tier_item_sets$deserved))
# Guarded against NA (R's marker for a missing value), which is what the
# correlation would be if either composite failed to score. Comparing NA to .95
# would give NA and stop the knit with an error instead of a printed line.
if (!is.na(r_soft_deserved)) {
  cat(sprintf("Soft core and registered `deserved`: r = %.3f; the soft core is %d of the %d items of `deserved`.\n",
              r_soft_deserved, n_shared_soft, length(tier_item_sets$deserved)))
  # .95 is where the code switches verdicts: at or above it the two columns are
  # called the same measure under two names, below it two measures that mostly
  # agree. The soft core is three of the four items of `deserved`, so at that
  # height the columns order people almost identically and their agreement is
  # mostly arithmetic rather than a finding.
  if (r_soft_deserved >= .95) {
    cat("The soft-core column is a near-copy of the registered one, so this\n")
    cat("section is a robustness demonstration rather than an independent test\n")
    cat("of the same claim.\n")
  } else {
    cat("The two are far enough apart to carry separate information, so the\n")
    cat("columns below are worth reading against each other rather than as a\n")
    cat("robustness check.\n")
  }
}
```

```{r phase9_tier_continuous}
# === EVERY CONTRAST RERUN ON EACH SLICE (prereg 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: calls run_continuous_set() once per predictor named in
# tier_slice_labels, stacks the runs into one table, checks the registered
# column against 9.9, and pivots the standardized slopes into one
# outcome-by-slice grid. A standardized slope, written beta, says how many
# standard deviations the outcome moves per one standard deviation of the
# predictor. Pivoting means turning a long stack of rows into a wide grid, one
# row per outcome and one column per slice. Produces
# `contrasts_tiers_continuous` and `contrasts_tiers_side_by_side`.
#
# Same function, same spec, same per-row direction as 9.9. Only the predictor
# changes, which is what makes the columns comparable row against row. Change
# anything else at the same time and a difference between two columns could no
# longer be pinned on the item set.
#
# WHY EVERY COLUMN HERE IS A RAW SUBSCALE MEAN. The registered PRIMARY
# continuous measure is the RELATIVE subscale (prereg 5.3, built in Phase 5.2):
# retribution minus the mean of the other three goals. Subtracting the other
# goals isolates PRIORITIZING desert from simply endorsing punishment in
# general, which an agreeable respondent does across the board. This grid
# deliberately holds the construction fixed at raw and varies only the item set,
# because "does the answer depend on which items?" is the question the section
# asks. Its registered comparator is therefore the raw run from 9.9 rather than
# the relative one. The relative counterpart of every slice is built and run in
# the `phase9_tier_relative` chunk below, so the measure the plan designates is
# not missing from this section. It is kept in a separate table so that "which
# items" and "which construction" are never varied inside the same grid, where a
# reader could not tell which of the two moved a number.
#
# drop_sentence_based is deliberately NOT set here, for the same reason as in
# the median-split and tertile runs in 9.11: every predictor comes from the
# goal-endorsement items and none is built from the sentence, so H14 and the
# full punitiveness index can be regressed on them without the sentence
# appearing on both sides of the same equation. Setting the flag here would
# silently drop two outcomes from the grid for no reason at all.
#
# NO MULTIPLICITY CORRECTION HERE, AND NONE ANYWHERE IN PHASE 9. A multiplicity
# correction raises the bar for significance when many tests are run at once,
# because with enough tests some will look impressive by chance. FDR control is
# false discovery rate control, done in 7.1 with the Benjamini-Hochberg
# procedure (BH-FDR). Prereg 6.1 names the H1 correlate family as the set
# requiring it. Prereg 6.5 specifies the group contrasts and their continuous
# reruns WITHOUT adding them to that family, and prereg 6.5 is what governs this
# grid. The note in 9.4 records this for the contrast set, and the registered
# continuous runs in 9.9 are uncorrected on the same grounds. This grid inherits
# that and adds no correction of its own. The reason is NOT that the correction
# happens somewhere else in Phase 9 -- it happens NOWHERE in Phase 9. It is that
# the predictors are slices of ONE scale and intercorrelate highly (see the
# table above), so these are several views of one test rather than several
# independent tests. The quantity worth reading is the agreement across the
# columns, which the next chunk counts. Reading the grid for whichever column
# carries the most stars is exactly the reading it exists to prevent.
tier_runs <- lapply(names(tier_slice_labels), function(p) {
  # lbl() is the tagging helper defined in 9.12. It writes the display label
  # into a column called `measure`, which does two jobs: the six runs can still
  # be told apart once rbind() has stacked them into one table, and the pivot
  # below has a column to spread the grid on. Without the tag the stacked
  # rows would be an anonymous pile with no record of which slice made them.
  lbl(run_continuous_set(d, p), tier_slice_labels[[p]])
})
# rbind() stacks the six runs into one long table: one row per slice per
# outcome, which is the shape the pivot below needs.
tiers_continuous <- do.call(rbind, tier_runs)
TABLES[["contrasts_tiers_continuous"]] <- tiers_continuous

# THE REPRODUCTION CHECK. The seven-item column runs the registered predictor
# through the same function that produced `cont_raw` in 9.9, so it MUST come
# back identical. Rather than assert that in prose, the code checks it and says
# so out loud. If the check ever fails, something upstream has changed and every
# number below is suspect.
#   all.equal() returns TRUE, or else a piece of text describing the
# differences. It never returns FALSE. So `if (all.equal(...))` would be handed
# a sentence and error out, which is why it is wrapped in isTRUE(): isTRUE()
# gives TRUE only for an actual TRUE and FALSE for anything else, including that
# text. check.attributes = FALSE tells all.equal() to ignore the row names,
# which differ only because rbind() renumbered them, and which have nothing to
# do with whether the numbers match.
tier_reg_raw <- tiers_continuous[
  tiers_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["retribution"]],
  names(cont_raw)]
if (isTRUE(all.equal(tier_reg_raw, cont_raw, check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  cat(sprintf("Column '%s' reproduces the registered raw run in 9.9 exactly.\n",
              tier_slice_labels[["retribution"]]))
} else {
  cat("CHECK FAILED: the registered column does not reproduce the raw run in 9.9. The spec or the scored predictor has changed; resolve this before reporting anything below.\n")
}
# The `deserved` column gets no such check and CANNOT have one. 9.9 runs the
# relative and the raw subscales and never puts the four-item composite through
# the continuous machinery at all, so that column has no registered twin to be
# compared against. This is the concrete reason the `deserved` column is an
# additional display rather than a registered test.

# One cell per outcome x slice: the standardized slope with stars on its
# DIRECTIONAL p. The directional p is the p-value for a prediction that names
# which way the effect should go, and it is the inferential p for these
# predictions (prereg 6.8). Both sides of every regression are z-scored, which
# means each variable is rescaled to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
# That is what makes beta the right thing to tabulate across the columns: it
# puts a beta from the two-item rationale tier and a beta from the seven-item
# scale on one common metric. Unstandardized slopes would not be comparable
# across the columns, because the slices spread people out by different amounts.
tier_wide <- tiers_continuous[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "measure",
                                  "beta", "p_dir")]
# Each cell is printed as the beta to two decimal places with any significance
# stars glued straight on, so one short string carries both the size of the
# effect and whether it cleared the threshold.
tier_wide$beta_p <- sprintf("%.2f%s", tier_wide$beta,
                            sig_stars(tier_wide$p_dir))
# "-" marks a cell the model could not fit, rather than one that came out null.
# A fit fails when there are too few complete cases, meaning too few people with
# no missing value on the variables involved, or when there is no variance,
# meaning everyone gave the same answer. A printed NA would leave a reader
# guessing which of the two it was. "-" says plainly that there was never a
# number to report.
tier_wide$beta_p[is.na(tier_wide$beta)] <- "-"
# pivot_wider() turns the long stack into the grid: one row per outcome, one
# column per slice, taking the column names from `measure` and the cell contents
# from `beta_p`. This is the shape that lets a reader scan one row across.
tier_grid <- tidyr::pivot_wider(
  tier_wide[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "measure", "beta_p")],
  names_from = measure, values_from = beta_p)
TABLES[["contrasts_tiers_side_by_side"]] <- as.data.frame(tier_grid)
show_table(as.data.frame(tier_grid),
           "Standardized slope of each outcome on each slice of the retribution scale; stars use the directional p, and the REGISTERED columns are the Phase 4 composites")

# ATTENUATION, WHICH HAS TO BE READ INTO THE COLUMNS. Attenuation is the
# shrinking of a measured relationship caused by noise in the measure itself. A
# slice built from two items is measured less reliably than the seven-item
# scale, because fewer questions means more of each person's score is random
# wobble. A less reliable predictor produces a SMALLER standardized slope even
# when the underlying relationship is exactly the same. So smaller betas in the
# short columns are expected on measurement grounds alone, and reading them as
# "the rationale items matter less" would be a mistake.
#   No correction for attenuation is applied. Correcting would put a
# disattenuated coefficient -- one adjusted upward for unreliability -- next to
# the registered uncorrected one in the same table, and a table mixing the two
# is the harder thing to read correctly. The short columns are worked out from
# the item sets rather than named by hand, so the printed sentence cannot go
# stale if a slice is ever added or reordered.
#
# vapply() counts the items in each slice and returns a vector (a simple run of
# values) of counts, one per slice, in the order the labels set.
tier_k <- vapply(tier_item_sets[names(tier_slice_labels)], length, integer(1))
cat(sprintf("\nShortest columns (%d items each): %s.\n", min(tier_k),
            paste(tier_slice_labels[tier_k == min(tier_k)], collapse = "; ")))
cat("Expect smaller slopes there from lower reliability alone, not from\n")
cat("any real difference between the slices.\n")
```

```{r phase9_tier_agreement}
# === DO THE SLICES AGREE? (prereg 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: boils the grid above down to one row per outcome -- how
# many slices give the predicted sign, how many reach directional p < .05, and
# how far the slopes spread from smallest to largest. It then reruns the shark
# decision, which is binary, that is, yes-or-no, on each slice in logistic form.
# Logistic regression is the form of regression used when the outcome is a
# yes-or-no choice rather than a number. Produces `contrasts_tiers_agreement`
# and `H15_logistic_tiers`.
#
# WHY THIS IS WORTH RUNNING WHEN THE ANSWER IS PREDICTABLE. The seven items have
# a Cronbach's alpha of about .90, a measure of how consistently a set of
# questions behaves as one scale. The slices intercorrelate highly, so the
# columns are expected to agree. The value of the table is not discovery. It is
# that the paper can then SAY they agree, with a printed number, to a reader who
# objects that positive retributivism (the duty to punish) has been lumped in
# with negative retributivism (the mere permission to punish), or that the two
# rationale items are not desert claims at all, or that R3 has been filed on the
# wrong side. The answer to those objections is this table, not an assurance.
# Without it, the only reply available would be "trust us", which is exactly the
# reply a reviewer will not accept.
tier_agreement <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(tiers_continuous$outcome),
                                        function(o) {
  # All six slices for this one outcome, which is the set the row summarises.
  s <- tiers_continuous[tiers_continuous$outcome == o, ]
  # HAZARD. Given a vector (a simple run of values) that is all NA, R's marker
  # for a missing value, min(na.rm = TRUE) returns Inf and max(na.rm = TRUE)
  # returns -Inf, and each only mutters a warning about it. Warnings are
  # switched off across this whole document, so that mutter would never be seen.
  # An outcome that could not be fitted at all would then print infinities in
  # beta_min, beta_max and beta_range as though they were real slopes. So the
  # all-NA case is caught by hand and turned into NA.
  b_min <- if (all(is.na(s$beta))) NA_real_ else min(s$beta, na.rm = TRUE)
  b_max <- if (all(is.na(s$beta))) NA_real_ else max(s$beta, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    hypothesis = s$hypothesis[1],
    outcome    = o,
    n_slices   = nrow(s),
    # n_fitted, how many of those slices actually produced a slope, is carried
    # right beside n_slices so that "same in every fitted slice" can never
    # quietly mean "in the two of six that could be fitted". Where the two
    # counts differ, the verdict is about the fitted subset ONLY, and a reader
    # sees that at a glance instead of trusting a confident-looking verdict.
    n_fitted   = sum(!is.na(s$beta)),
    # The sign test respects each row's OWN predicted direction, stored in
    # `alternative`. The two cognitive reflection rows predict a NEGATIVE slope,
    # so blindly counting positive slopes would score those rows as failures
    # when in fact they behaved exactly as predicted.
    n_predicted_sign = sum(ifelse(s$alternative == "less", s$beta < 0,
                                  s$beta > 0), na.rm = TRUE),
    # How many slices clear the .05 threshold on the directional p. This is the
    # raw material for the verdict column further down, which is decided by
    # comparing this count against n_fitted.
    n_p05      = sum(s$p_dir < .05, na.rm = TRUE),
    # The smallest and largest slope across the slices, and the distance between
    # them. A wide spread is the signal that the answer moves with the item set.
    beta_min   = b_min,
    beta_max   = b_max,
    beta_range = b_max - b_min,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
# "Same in every fitted slice" means the .05 verdict is unanimous in EITHER
# direction: every fitted slice significant, or none of them at all. Anything in
# between earns "differs across slices", and those are the rows where the
# conclusion really does depend on which part of the scale was used. Those are
# the rows a reader should be sent to first.
#   The comparison is against n_fitted, not n_slices, so unanimity is judged
# among the slices that actually produced a slope. That is exactly what the
# verdict text claims, and n_fitted sits in the table beside it, so a row where
# only half the slices fitted can never be read as a unanimous verdict over all
# six. "not estimable" is the separate label for a row where nothing fitted at
# all, which must never be confused with a row where nothing was significant.
tier_agreement$verdict <- ifelse(
  tier_agreement$n_fitted == 0, "not estimable",
  ifelse(tier_agreement$n_p05 == 0 |
           tier_agreement$n_p05 == tier_agreement$n_fitted,
         "same in every fitted slice", "differs across slices"))
TABLES[["contrasts_tiers_agreement"]] <- tier_agreement
show_table(tier_agreement,
           "How far the slices of the retribution scale agree, outcome by outcome")

cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d outcomes give the same verdict at p < .05 across every fitted slice (of %d slices).\n",
            sum(tier_agreement$verdict == "same in every fitted slice"),
            nrow(tier_agreement), n_slices))
# The single widest disagreement, named out loud so the write-up can quote the
# WORST case rather than the average one. Reporting only an average would let a
# single badly-behaved outcome hide inside it. Guarded with any(!is.na(...)),
# because which.max() on a column that is all NA (R's marker for a missing
# value) returns an empty index. tier_worst would then be a frame with no rows,
# sprintf() on zero-length arguments returns character(0), and cat() would print
# nothing at all. The guard states that skip outright rather than leaving it to
# fall out of the way R handles empty vectors.
if (any(!is.na(tier_agreement$beta_range))) {
  tier_worst <- tier_agreement[which.max(tier_agreement$beta_range), ]
  cat(sprintf("Widest spread: %s, beta from %.2f to %.2f (a spread of %.2f).\n",
              tier_worst$outcome, tier_worst$beta_min, tier_worst$beta_max,
              tier_worst$beta_range))
}

# The rationale tier against the registered seven-item scale, head to head. This
# is the specific comparison a philosopher will ask for. R6 and R7 are the items
# most easily argued not to be desert claims at all, so how much moves when the
# analysis leans on those two alone is worth its own printed line.
#   CAREFUL: the seven-item scale CONTAINS the rationale tier, so this is a
# part-whole comparison, a piece of a scale against the scale it sits inside. It
# is NOT a comparison between two independent measurements, and agreement here
# is partly guaranteed by the shared items.
#   Merge on the outcome LABEL, never on row position. Both frames come out of
# the same spec in the same order today, so a positional join would look fine
# right now. The moment a row is added to the spec the two frames would fall out
# of step and the join would silently pair the wrong outcomes together, and the
# printed comparison would be nonsense with no error to warn anyone.
tier_rat <- tiers_continuous[
  tiers_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["retribution_rationale"]], ]
tier_reg <- tiers_continuous[
  tiers_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["retribution"]], ]
tier_rat_cmp <- merge(tier_rat[, c("outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
                      tier_reg[, c("outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
                      by = "outcome", suffixes = c("_rationale", "_registered"))
# Two numbers, because either alone can mislead. The verdict count says how
# often the two columns land on the same side of .05. The mean absolute
# difference in beta is the average size of the gap between the two slopes,
# taken without regard to which one is larger, so opposite gaps cannot cancel
# out to a comfortable-looking zero.
cat(sprintf("Rationale tier versus the registered seven-item scale that contains it: same .05 verdict on %d of %d outcomes; mean absolute difference in beta = %.3f.\n",
            sum((tier_rat_cmp$p_dir_rationale < .05) ==
                  (tier_rat_cmp$p_dir_registered < .05), na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(tier_rat_cmp),
            mean(abs(tier_rat_cmp$beta_rationale -
                       tier_rat_cmp$beta_registered), na.rm = TRUE)))

# The same head-to-head for R3, the item whose placement is unsettled: the soft
# core WITH R3 against the soft core WITHOUT it. If these two columns agree,
# then where R3 is filed does not matter to anything reported here, and the
# argument about it can be set aside. That is the whole reason both versions are
# carried through the document instead of one being picked quietly.
#   Merged on the outcome LABEL again, for the same reason as above: a
# positional join would pair the wrong outcomes without complaining.
tier_soft_full <- tiers_continuous[
  tiers_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["deserved_soft"]], ]
tier_soft_strict <- tiers_continuous[
  tiers_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["deserved_soft_strict"]], ]
tier_r3_cmp <- merge(tier_soft_full[, c("outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
                     tier_soft_strict[, c("outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
                     by = "outcome", suffixes = c("_withR3", "_withoutR3"))
cat(sprintf("Soft core with R3 versus without it: same .05 verdict on %d of %d outcomes; mean absolute difference in beta = %.3f.\n",
            sum((tier_r3_cmp$p_dir_withR3 < .05) ==
                  (tier_r3_cmp$p_dir_withoutR3 < .05), na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(tier_r3_cmp),
            mean(abs(tier_r3_cmp$beta_withR3 -
                       tier_r3_cmp$beta_withoutR3), na.rm = TRUE)))

# The shark DECISION is yes-or-no, so it cannot join the linear grid above: the
# regressions there predict a number, and this outcome is a choice. It gets the
# same slice-by-slice rerun in logistic regression form, the regression used
# when the outcome is yes-or-no, exactly as 9.9 does for the registered
# continuous measures. Leaving it out would mean the H15 result had been checked
# against only one slice of the scale while every other outcome was checked
# against six.
#   NOTE: the outcome label is identical in every row of the output, because it
# IS the same outcome six times over. The `predictor` column and the `measure`
# label added by lbl() are what tell the six runs apart, so do not read the
# repeated label as a duplication error.
tier_shark <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tier_slice_labels), function(p) {
  lbl(logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", p, alternative = "greater",
                label = "Shark put to death"), tier_slice_labels[[p]])
}))
TABLES[["H15_logistic_tiers"]] <- tier_shark
# OR is the odds ratio: how much the odds of putting the shark to death multiply
# for each one-unit rise in the predictor. An odds ratio of 1.00 is no change in
# the odds at all. OR_lower and OR_upper are the ends of the TWO-SIDED 95% Wald
# interval that logit_reg() builds as exp(b +/- 1.96 * se). CAREFUL: the
# inferential p for H15 is the DIRECTIONAL p_dir (prereg 6.8), printed in the
# same table. A two-sided interval and a one-sided p answer different questions.
# An interval that includes 1.00 can therefore sit beside a p_dir below .05, so
# read the verdict off p_dir rather than off the interval.
show_table(tier_shark[, c("measure", "predictor", "n", "b", "OR", "OR_lower",
                          "OR_upper", "z", "p_dir", "p_two")],
           "H15 with each slice of the retribution scale entered continuously (logistic regression)")
```

```{r phase9_tier_relative}
# === THE SLICES ON THE PRIMARY, RELATIVE CONSTRUCTION (prereg 5.3, 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds the relative counterpart of every slice, reruns
# the whole contrast set on each, and reports a per-slice scorecard together
# with a count of how many cells change their .05 verdict between the raw grid
# above and the relative one. "Construction" here means how a score is built --
# raw subscale mean, or that mean with the other three goals subtracted off.
# Produces `contrasts_tiers_continuous_relative` and `tier_relative_scorecard`.
#
# WHY. The registered primary continuous measure is relative, not raw (prereg
# 5.3, Phase 5.2). Endorsement of all four goals is highly correlated, because
# an agreeable respondent rates every justification highly, so a raw subscale
# largely measures general endorsement of punishment rather than a preference
# for desert in particular. The grid above holds the construction fixed so that
# only the item set varies, which is what makes it answer the tier question.
# This chunk puts every slice on the construction the plan designates, so the
# section does not rest on the raw metric alone and a reader looking for the
# primary measure can find every slice on it.
#
# HAZARD -- `retribution_rel` IS NOT REBUILT. It is the registered primary
# measure (prereg 5.3) and the basis of `grp_med` and `grp_tert` in Phase 5.3.
# The loop writes a relative column for each slice and SKIPS any name that
# already exists in `d`. That skip is the whole safeguard: it keeps the
# registered column exactly as Phase 5.2 scored it. The seven-item slice REUSES
# `retribution_rel` instead of recomputing it, and the reproduction check below
# is what proves it did. Rebuild it and the registered median split and tertiles
# could shift underneath every result that depends on them.
#
# The construction mirrors Phase 5.2 term for term: the slice mean minus the
# mean of the deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation subscales.
# rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) tells R to ignore NA (its marker for a missing value),
# so a participant who skipped one of the three other goals is averaged over the
# ones they did answer rather than dropped altogether. A participant missing all
# three gets NaN here, R's "not a number", exactly as they do in Phase 5.2. That
# behaviour is left IDENTICAL rather than quietly improved, so the relative
# slices and the registered relative subscale treat the same person the same
# way. An improvement here would make the two disagree for a reason that had
# nothing to do with retribution.
other_goal_mean <- rowMeans(cbind(d$deterrence, d$incapacitation,
                                  d$rehabilitation), na.rm = TRUE)
# tier_rel_cols records, for each slice, the name of its relative column, so the
# runs below look a name up rather than rebuilding one. The seven-item slice is
# deliberately pointed at `retribution_rel`, the name Phase 5.2 already used,
# which is what lets the skip inside the loop below find an existing column and
# leave it untouched. Every other slice gets a new name ending in `_rel`.
tier_rel_cols <- character(0)
for (p in names(tier_slice_labels)) {
  nm <- if (p == "retribution") "retribution_rel" else paste0(p, "_rel")
  if (!nm %in% names(d)) d[[nm]] <- d[[p]] - other_goal_mean
  tier_rel_cols[p] <- nm
}

# The same six runs as the grid above, on the relative columns this time. Same
# function, same spec, same per-row direction, so the two sets of runs can be
# compared cell for cell further down.
tier_rel_runs <- lapply(names(tier_slice_labels), function(p) {
  lbl(run_continuous_set(d, tier_rel_cols[[p]]), tier_slice_labels[[p]])
})
tiers_rel_continuous <- do.call(rbind, tier_rel_runs)
TABLES[["contrasts_tiers_continuous_relative"]] <- tiers_rel_continuous

# THE SECOND REPRODUCTION CHECK. The seven-item slice on the relative
# construction IS `retribution_rel`, the registered PRIMARY predictor, so this
# run has to come back identical to `cont_rel` from 9.9. This is the check that
# proves the HAZARD above was respected and the registered column was reused
# rather than rebuilt. If it fails, `retribution_rel` has been overwritten
# somewhere and nothing below can be trusted.
tier_reg_rel <- tiers_rel_continuous[
  tiers_rel_continuous$measure == tier_slice_labels[["retribution"]],
  names(cont_rel)]
if (isTRUE(all.equal(tier_reg_rel, cont_rel, check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  cat(sprintf("Column '%s' on the relative construction reproduces the registered PRIMARY run in 9.9 exactly.\n",
              tier_slice_labels[["retribution"]]))
} else {
  cat("CHECK FAILED: the relative registered column does not reproduce the primary run in 9.9. Resolve this before reporting anything below.\n")
}

# A scorecard rather than a second full grid: one row per slice per
# construction, in the same shape as the per-measure table in 9.12. Printing a
# second full grid would double the length of the section for very little gain.
# The row-level slopes for the relative runs are NOT printed, but they are
# exported in full as contrasts_tiers_continuous_relative.csv, so nothing is
# hidden by the summary and anyone can check it against the source.
score_slices <- function(res, construction) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(res$measure), function(m) {
    # All the outcome rows belonging to one slice. Every number in the scorecard
    # row is computed from this subset alone, so one slice's record can never be
    # blended with another's.
    s <- res[res$measure == m, ]
    data.frame(
      slice        = m,
      construction = construction,
      n_outcomes   = nrow(s),
      # The sign count reads each row's own predicted direction, held in
      # `alternative`, so the two cognitive reflection rows count as predicted
      # when their beta is NEGATIVE. Counting positive slopes across the board
      # would mark those two rows down for behaving as the plan said they would.
      n_predicted_sign = sum(ifelse(s$alternative == "less", s$beta < 0,
                                    s$beta > 0), na.rm = TRUE),
      # How many of this slice's outcomes clear .05 on the directional p. This
      # is the column a reader compares down, slice against slice, to see
      # whether any one slice is carrying the section's conclusions on its own.
      n_p05        = sum(s$p_dir < .05, na.rm = TRUE),
      # Median rather than mean, so one unusually large slope cannot make a
      # slice look uniformly sharp. abs() strips the sign because the CRT rows
      # are predicted negative, and a signed average would let them cancel
      # against the positive rows and understate the whole slice.
      median_abs_beta = median(abs(s$beta), na.rm = TRUE),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}
# Both constructions in one table, stacked, so a reader can read a slice's raw
# row directly against its relative row instead of flipping between two tables.
tier_scorecard <- rbind(
  score_slices(tiers_continuous, "raw subscale mean"),
  score_slices(tiers_rel_continuous, "relative (primary)"))
TABLES[["tier_relative_scorecard"]] <- tier_scorecard
show_table(tier_scorecard,
           "Each slice of the retribution scale on the raw and on the registered relative construction (prereg 5.3)")

# HOW MUCH WORK THE CONSTRUCTION IS DOING. Every cell of the raw grid is lined
# up against the matching cell of the relative grid, so the effect of switching
# construction can be counted rather than guessed at. Joined on slice AND
# outcome, never on row position, for the same reason as every other join in
# this section: a positional join would pair the wrong cells the moment either
# table changed length, and would do it silently.
tier_both <- merge(
  tiers_continuous[, c("measure", "outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
  tiers_rel_continuous[, c("measure", "outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
  by = c("measure", "outcome"), suffixes = c("_raw", "_rel"))
# A "flip" is a cell that is significant at .05 under one construction and not
# under the other. != on the two TRUE/FALSE tests counts exactly those cells.
n_construction_flips <- sum((tier_both$p_dir_raw < .05) !=
                              (tier_both$p_dir_rel < .05), na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d slice-by-outcome cells change their .05 verdict between the raw and the relative construction; mean absolute change in beta = %.3f.\n",
            n_construction_flips, nrow(tier_both),
            mean(abs(tier_both$beta_rel - tier_both$beta_raw), na.rm = TRUE)))
# WHICH QUESTION IS WHICH. DO NOT read the count above as the tier question. It
# reports what happens when the SAME items are put on a DIFFERENT construction.
# That count can be large while the slices themselves agree perfectly, because
# subtracting the other three goals strips general endorsement of punishment out
# of every column at once. The tier question -- does the answer depend on which
# items? -- is answered by the agreement table in the previous chunk, which
# holds the construction fixed and varies only the item set. Where the two
# constructions disagree, the relative one is the form the plan designates
# (prereg 5.3) and is the one to report.
if (n_construction_flips > 0) {
  cat("These two columns answer different questions; where they disagree,\n")
  cat("the relative row is the registered primary form (prereg 5.3).\n")
}
```

## 9.14 Relative retribution with the two rationale items dropped

The registered relative subscale (prereg 5.3) is built in two steps. Take a
person's average across all **seven** retribution items. Then subtract their
average across the other three goals of punishment. What is left is how far that
person leans toward desert relative to those other three goals.

The last two items give a rationale for desert rather than asserting desert, so
the same measure is built again over **R1 to R5** alone and the two are reported
side by side. R1 to R5 is not one of the slices in 9.13. It is the whole scale
with the rationale tier removed, which is why it gets its own section.

The registered `retribution_rel` is unchanged and remains the primary continuous
measure. The two versions share five of their seven items and subtract the same
three-goal average. The correlation between them is therefore part-whole: a
smaller measure correlated with the larger one it sits inside. A part-whole
correlation is high by construction, so it is reported to size the overlap and
not to establish that either version is valid.

```{r phase9_rel_norat}
# === RELATIVE RETRIBUTION WITHOUT THE TWO RATIONALE ITEMS (prereg 5.3, 6.5) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `retribution_rel_norat`, runs the whole contrast
# set on it, prints it against the registered run from 9.9, and collects the
# reliability rows for every composite this restructure scored after Phase 4.10.
# Produces `contrasts_continuous_rel_norat`, `rel_norat_comparison`,
# `H15_logistic_rel_norat` and `reliability_retribution_slices`.
#
# WHY WE DO THIS. A reader can object that R6 and R7 are not desert claims at
# all. Every result built on `retribution_rel` -- the continuous reruns in 9.9,
# and the median-split and tertile groupings taken from it -- depends on having
# included those two items. The only way to answer the objection is to rebuild
# the measure without them and show every number over again. If the two columns
# move together, the objection costs nothing. If they do not, that is a fact
# about the measure and it belongs on the page.
#
# THE CONSTRUCTION mirrors Phase 5.2 one term at a time:
#   registered:  mean(R1..R7) - mean(deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation)
#   here:        mean(R1..R5) - the same three-goal mean
# Only the first term changes, so any difference between the two columns below
# is the contribution of R6 and R7 and of nothing else.
#
# HAZARD -- `retribution_rel` IS NOT TOUCHED. It is the registered primary
# continuous measure (prereg 5.3). Phase 5.3 builds two groupings out of it. The
# median split cuts the sample in two at the middle score. The tertiles cut it
# into three equal-sized bands. It is also the predictor in the 9.9 reruns.
# Rebuilding it over five items instead of seven would silently change
# `grp_med`, `grp_tert` and every table that uses them, and nothing on the page
# would say so. The five-item version is a separate column with a separate name,
# and that is the only safe way to have both.
#
# Score the five-item composite, but only if it is not already in `d`. The guard
# is not about the numbers. compute_composite() is deterministic -- the same
# data in gives the same column out -- so a second run would rebuild an
# identical column. The guard is about the side effect. Every call to
# compute_composite() also appends a row to `alpha_table`, so an unguarded
# re-run would append a SECOND row for this composite. That duplicate would then
# print twice in the reliability table at the foot of this chunk.
if (!"retribution_norat" %in% names(d)) {
  d$retribution_norat <- compute_composite(
    d, paste0("Retribution_", 1:5), "retribution (5 items, rationales dropped)")
}
# `other_goal_mean` is each person's average across the deterrence,
# incapacitation and rehabilitation subscales. It is the term the relative
# construction subtracts. It is built in the relative-slices chunk above. It is
# recomputed here only if that chunk has not run, so this section still works on
# its own, and the version above is never overwritten.
if (!exists("other_goal_mean")) {
  other_goal_mean <- rowMeans(cbind(d$deterrence, d$incapacitation,
                                    d$rehabilitation), na.rm = TRUE)
}
# The subtraction itself, again guarded, so the column is built once and a
# re-run of the chunk leaves the existing one alone.
if (!"retribution_rel_norat" %in% names(d)) {
  d$retribution_rel_norat <- d$retribution_norat - other_goal_mean
}
# Like the registered version this is one 1-7 mean minus another 1-7 mean, so it
# is centred near zero. Positive means retribution is endorsed more than the
# average of the other three goals. Negative means less. Zero means no
# preference either way. Reading it as a 1-7 score would be wrong.
cat(sprintf("Relative retribution, registered (7 items): M = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n",
            mean(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$retribution_rel, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Relative retribution, rationales dropped (R1-R5): M = %.2f (SD %.2f)\n",
            mean(d$retribution_rel_norat, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd(d$retribution_rel_norat, na.rm = TRUE)))

# How far the two versions are the same variable at all. The test is two-sided,
# meaning it allows the relationship to run in either direction, because this is
# a description of the overlap and not a directional prediction. The two share
# five of seven items and the identical subtracted term, so this correlation is
# part-whole. Part-whole means a measure correlated with the larger measure that
# contains it, and it will be very high. It sizes the overlap. It is NOT
# evidence of validity, that is, of either version really measuring the thing it
# claims to measure. The 95% confidence interval printed with it is the range of
# true correlations this sample cannot rule out.
norat_r <- cor_row(d, "retribution_rel", "retribution_rel_norat",
                   alternative = "two.sided",
                   label_x = "relative retribution (registered, 7 items)",
                   label_y = "relative retribution (R1-R5)")
cat(sprintf("The two versions correlate r = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], n = %d (part-whole: five of seven items are shared).\n",
            norat_r$r, norat_r$ci_lower, norat_r$ci_upper, norat_r$n))

# The whole contrast set on the five-item relative measure. Same function, same
# spec and the same one-sided direction on each row as the registered run in
# 9.9. That is what lets the two tables be read row against row: any difference
# between them is the item set, and never a difference in how the test was set
# up.
cont_norat <- run_continuous_set(d, "retribution_rel_norat")
TABLES[["contrasts_continuous_rel_norat"]] <- cont_norat
show_table(cont_norat,
           "Every contrast on relative retribution with the two rationale items dropped (R1-R5)")

# Side by side with the registered run. `cont_rel` is the object built in 9.9,
# and it is REUSED here rather than recomputed, so the left-hand column of this
# comparison is literally the registered numbers. It therefore cannot differ
# from what 9.9 printed, which is what leaves the item set as the only thing
# separating the two columns. `hypothesis` is carried across from it so the
# exported CSV can be grouped by hypothesis like every other Phase 9 table.
norat_compare <- merge(
  cont_rel[, c("hypothesis", "outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
  cont_norat[, c("outcome", "beta", "p_dir")],
  by = "outcome", suffixes = c("_registered", "_norationale"))
# The column a reader should look at: five-item slope minus seven-item slope,
# outcome by outcome. It is the entire effect of dropping R6 and R7, expressed
# as a number.
norat_compare$beta_diff <-
  norat_compare$beta_norationale - norat_compare$beta_registered
# merge() sorts by the join key, the column the two tables were matched on,
# which leaves the outcomes in alphabetical order. Restore the spec order so
# this table reads H13 through E1 like every other table in Phase 9. A reader
# can then follow the same row down two pages instead of hunting for it.
norat_compare <- norat_compare[
  order(match(norat_compare$outcome, contrast_spec$label)),
  c("hypothesis", "outcome", "beta_registered", "p_dir_registered",
    "beta_norationale", "p_dir_norationale", "beta_diff")]
TABLES[["rel_norat_comparison"]] <- norat_compare
show_table(norat_compare,
           "Relative retribution as registered (7 items) versus with the rationale items dropped (R1-R5)")

# The whole comparison in one sentence: how often the p < .05 verdict survives
# dropping the two items, and how far the slopes move on average and at their
# worst. A large mean shift, or several flipped verdicts, would mean the two
# versions are not interchangeable and the choice of item set has to be argued
# rather than assumed.
cat(sprintf("\nThe .05 verdict is unchanged on %d of %d outcomes; mean absolute change in beta = %.3f, largest = %.3f.\n",
            sum((norat_compare$p_dir_registered < .05) ==
                  (norat_compare$p_dir_norationale < .05), na.rm = TRUE),
            nrow(norat_compare),
            mean(abs(norat_compare$beta_diff), na.rm = TRUE),
            max(abs(norat_compare$beta_diff), na.rm = TRUE)))

# The binary shark decision again, since it sits outside the linear set. A
# yes/no outcome needs logistic regression, a model built for two-valued
# outcomes. It reports an odds ratio (OR): how much the odds of the "yes"
# answer multiply for a one-point rise in the predictor. The registered
# relative row is taken from `shark_cont`, the object built in 9.9, rather than
# recomputed, so the comparison row is literally the registered one.
norat_shark <- logit_reg(d, "shark_kill", "retribution_rel_norat",
                         alternative = "greater",
                         label = "Shark put to death ~ relative retribution (R1-R5)")
# One table, two rows: the registered seven-item predictor on top and the
# five-item one beneath it, so the odds ratios can be compared at a glance.
h15_norat <- rbind(shark_cont[shark_cont$predictor == "retribution_rel", ],
                   norat_shark)
TABLES[["H15_logistic_rel_norat"]] <- h15_norat
show_table(h15_norat[, c("outcome", "predictor", "n", "b", "OR", "OR_lower",
                         "OR_upper", "z", "p_dir", "p_two")],
           "H15 on relative retribution as registered (7 items) and with the two rationale items dropped (R1-R5)")
cat(sprintf("H15 on relative retribution with the rationales dropped: OR = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], p %s\n",
            norat_shark$OR, norat_shark$OR_lower, norat_shark$OR_upper,
            format_p(norat_shark$p_dir)))

# === THE RELIABILITY ROWS FOR EVERYTHING SCORED IN 9.13 AND 9.14 ===
# Reliability here means Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega: two numbers,
# each topping out at 1, that ask whether the items of a composite agree with
# one another well enough for their average to count as one score. Every
# composite in this document is reported with one, and the composites built in
# 9.13 and 9.14 must not become the exception.
#
# THE TRAP. Phase 4.10 copies the live `alpha_table` into `alpha_table_out`, and
# it is that COPY which Phase 10.1 exports as reliability_alpha_omega.csv and
# which Phase 10.3 writes to data/cleaned/reliability_table.csv. A row appended
# to `alpha_table` after 4.10 reaches NEITHER file. The rows appended by the
# slice guards in 9.13 and by the five-item composite above are therefore
# collected here into a table of their own. The registered reliability table is
# not touched, not renamed and not reopened: this is a second, additional export
# that sits beside it.
#
# The set difference -- the composites in one table that are absent from the
# other -- is taken on the composite NAME. So a slice that was scored earlier in
# Phase 4, in which case its alpha is already in the registered table, is
# correctly left out of this one, and nothing is reported twice.
#
# Both tables have to exist before any of this can run, so the whole block is
# guarded rather than assumed.
if (exists("alpha_table") && exists("alpha_table_out")) {
  late_alpha <- alpha_table[
    !alpha_table$composite %in% alpha_table_out$composite,
    c("composite", "k", "alpha", "omega", "mean", "sd", "n", "items")]
  # Nothing to print if every composite here was already scored in Phase 4; the
  # else branch at the foot says so out loud rather than leaving a silent gap.
  if (nrow(late_alpha)) {
    TABLES[["reliability_retribution_slices"]] <- late_alpha
    # print() is required here. show_table() builds a table object and returns
    # it without printing anything. Inside braces, only the block's final value
    # is auto-printed, and this call is not it. A bare show_table() here would
    # build the table and throw it away, and the section would knit with the
    # table missing.
    print(show_table(late_alpha[, c("composite", "k", "alpha", "omega", "n")],
               "Reliability of the composites scored in 9.13 and 9.14; omega is reported for k >= 3, since a single-factor omega is not identified with two items"))
    # The alpha < .60 flag in Phase 4.10 reads `alpha_table_out`, so it cannot
    # see these rows at all. The same reporting threshold is applied here, on
    # the same terms: it flags a composite for careful reading and drops
    # nothing. Alpha climbs with the number of items. A two-item slice of a
    # longer scale is therefore expected to sit lower than the scale it came
    # from. A value near the floor here is a measurement fact to state, not a
    # failure.
    late_low <- late_alpha[!is.na(late_alpha$alpha) & late_alpha$alpha < .60, ]
    if (nrow(late_low)) {
      cat("\nSlices with alpha < .60 (interpret with care):\n")
      for (i in seq_len(nrow(late_low)))
        cat(sprintf("  %-42s alpha = %.3f (k = %d)\n",
                    late_low$composite[i], late_low$alpha[i], late_low$k[i]))
    } else {
      cat("\nNo composite scored in 9.13 or 9.14 falls below alpha = .60.\n")
    }
  } else {
    cat("\nEvery composite here was scored before Phase 4.10 and appears\n")
    cat("in the registered reliability table.\n")
  }
}
```

## 9.15 Exploratory: E1 personality and E2 solidarity

Reported for completeness. These are exploratory and are **not** corrected as a
confirmatory family (prereg 6.6). A confirmatory family is a group of tests
written down before the data arrived, whose p-values are then adjusted together.
E1 and E2 sit outside that group. No p-value below is a pre-registered test.

```{r phase9_exploratory}
# === E1 AND E2: EXPLORATORY (prereg 6.6) ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: slices the E1 personality rows out of `contrasts_rank`
# and runs the E2 solidarity comparison. Produces `E1_personality` and
# `E2_solidarity_steiger`.
#
# NOT CONFIRMATORY. Prereg 6.6 states that these are exploratory and "are not
# corrected as a confirmatory family". A confirmatory family is a set of tests
# named in advance whose p-values are adjusted together, because running many
# tests makes at least one lucky result likely. E1 and E2 are outside any such
# family. They are reported with the same effect sizes and intervals as
# everything else so they can be read on the same terms, but no p-value here is
# a pre-registered test and none should be reported as one.
# (The separate exploratory language family, E3 to E7, is one family with BH-FDR
# applied within it. BH-FDR is the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate
# correction: it raises the p-values within a family so that only a set share of
# the results called significant are expected to be flukes. That family lives in
# the companion NLP document.)
#
# The E1 rows are TAKEN from `contrasts_rank`, the full set of contrasts already
# run under the primary ranking grouping in 9.3, rather than run a second time.
# Every reported contrast in Phase 9 therefore comes from a single pass. There
# is no second copy of the E1 rows for a later edit to put out of step with the
# registered one. The rows here are Right-Wing Authoritarianism, Social
# Dominance Orientation, violence proneness, racial resentment, and cognitive
# reflection on both its 0-3 and its 0-2 scoring.
e1 <- contrasts_rank[contrasts_rank$hypothesis == "E1", ]
TABLES[["E1_personality"]] <- e1
show_table(e1[, c("outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2", "t", "df",
                  "p_dir", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "E1: personality and cognitive reflection by retributivist status")

# E2 asks which reading of Durkheim's solidarity thesis punitiveness actually
# follows: the HOSTILE one (punishment as expelling the offender -- the
# exclusion items) or the DURKHEIMIAN one (punishment as binding the law-abiding
# together and restating shared norms). Steiger again, meaning Steiger's test
# for dependent overlapping correlations. The two correlations being compared
# both contain punitiveness and come from the same people. They are therefore
# not independent of one another, and that is the case Steiger's test is built
# for. Comparing them as though they came from separate samples would treat
# shared information as new information and overstate the evidence. One-sided
# "greater", predicting the hostile reading is the stronger correlate.
e2 <- steiger_overlap(d, "punitiveness", "solidarity_hostile", "solidarity_durk",
                      alternative = "greater",
                      label = "r(punitiveness, hostile solidarity) > r(punitiveness, Durkheimian solidarity)")
TABLES[["E2_solidarity_steiger"]] <- e2
show_table(e2, "E2: hostile versus Durkheimian solidarity (Steiger, one-sided)")
# The two competing correlations first, then the gap between them with its 95%
# confidence interval -- the range of true gaps this sample cannot rule out. For
# this hypothesis the gap in r IS the effect size, which is why the interval
# carries more of the reading than the z and p beside it.
cat(sprintf("\nr(punitiveness, exclusion) = %.3f; r(punitiveness, Durkheimian solidarity) = %.3f\n",
            e2$r_jk, e2$r_jh))
cat(sprintf("Difference = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]; z = %.3f, p %s\n",
            e2$diff, e2$diff_lower, e2$diff_upper, e2$z, format_p(e2$p)))
```

```{r phase9_distributions, fig.height=5}
# === FIGURE: DISTRIBUTIONS OF THE TWO CONTINUOUS MEASURES ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: draws histograms of relative retribution and the
# sentencing ratio and writes output/figures/retributivism_distributions.png. A
# histogram sorts the scores into equal-width bins and draws one bar per bin, so
# the height of a bar is how many people landed in that range.
#
# WHY IT IS HERE. This is the visual justification for the split rule set in
# Phase 5.4. The relative subscale is roughly continuous and symmetric, so a
# median split on it -- cutting the sample in two at the middle score -- is
# unremarkable. The sentencing ratio is not: it has a large spike at exactly
# 1.00 -- the participants who did not reduce the sentence at all once the
# forward-looking reasons were removed, which is both the most retributive
# response and the median. That means the middle score is a stack of tied
# people, and the rule for which side the ties go to decides the split. Seeing
# that spike is what makes the tie rule, and the preference for the continuous
# version, legible. Without the picture, the tie rule reads as fussiness.
#
# One long column of values plus a second column naming which measure each value
# came from. That is the shape ggplot2 needs to draw one panel per measure. The
# rep() counts must match the stacks above them exactly, which is why the
# sentencing ratio contributes sum(!is.na(...)) values and rows, and the
# relative subscale contributes its full length. Mismatched counts would label
# one measure's values with the other measure's name.
hist_df <- data.frame(
  value = c(d$retribution_rel, d$sentence_ratio[!is.na(d$sentence_ratio)]),
  measure = c(rep("Relative retribution (retribution - mean of other goals)",
                  length(d$retribution_rel)),
              rep("Sentencing ratio (Sentence2 / Sentence1)",
                  sum(!is.na(d$sentence_ratio)))))
# NA is R's marker for a missing value, and a missing value has no bar to draw.
# Those rows are filtered out before plotting, rather than left for ggplot2 to
# complain about.
p_dist <- ggplot2::ggplot(hist_df[!is.na(hist_df$value), ],
                          ggplot2::aes(x = value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2c3e50", colour = "white") +
  # facet_wrap draws one small panel per measure. scales = "free" on both axes:
  # the two measures live on entirely different ranges, and a shared scale would
  # flatten one of them into a single bar.
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Distributions of the two continuous retributivism measures",
                subtitle = sprintf("N = %d", nrow(d)), x = NULL, y = "Count") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
print(p_dist)
# Save the identical figure to disk at 300 dots per inch. The manuscript then
# prints the same picture the report shows, rather than a screenshot of it. The
# path goes into FIGURES so Phase 10 can list every figure this document wrote.
fig_path <- file.path(OUT_FIGURES, "retributivism_distributions.png")
ggplot2::ggsave(fig_path, p_dist, width = 10, height = 5, dpi = 300)
FIGURES <- c(FIGURES, fig_path)
```

## 9.16 The six features of retributive theory, results regrouped

Nothing in this section is a new result. Every mean, effect size and interval
below was computed in 9.3 and has already been reported in 9.4 to 9.8. The same
rows are printed a second time, sorted under the six features of retributive
theory. Each heading carries a plain statement of what the theory claims and of
what a higher score on that feature's measures means.

Grouping measures under features is an interpretive layer and is not
pre-registered. The contrasts it indexes are registered under prereg 5.3, and
none of them is displaced, recomputed or reworded here. Read this section as a
table of contents for results already reported, never as a fresh set of tests.

```{r phase9_features, results='asis'}
# === THE SIX FEATURES, RESULTS REGROUPED ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: takes the contrast results computed in 9.3 and prints
# them again under six headings, one per feature of retributive theory.
# Produces the table `features_F1_to_F6`.
# PREREG: not part of the pre-registration. Nothing is registered at the level
#         of a feature and nothing is tested at that level here. The contrasts
#         reprinted below are the registered ones from prereg 5.3, reported in
#         full in 9.4 to 9.8; this section reorders them and nothing else.
# CONSUMES: contrasts_rank and contrast_spec (9.3); alpha_table_out (4.10) and
#           h6b (8.3b), both read only to quote numbers computed there.
#
# NO REPORTED NUMBER IS COMPUTED HERE. Every group mean, standard deviation,
# Cohen's d and confidence interval below was produced by run_contrast_set() in
# 9.3 and is reprinted without alteration. Cohen's d is the gap between two
# group means expressed in standard deviations, so it does not depend on the
# units of the measure. The confidence interval beside it is the range of true
# values this sample cannot rule out. The chunk performs exactly one
# computation, the verification re-run at the foot of it, and that re-run
# reports nothing but a single line saying whether the reprint is faithful. A
# reader must not take this section for a second set of analyses: it is the
# same analyses, in a different order on the page. Counting a result here and
# again in 9.4 to 9.8 would double-count the same evidence.
#
# WHAT THIS SECTION IS. An index. The document runs in dependency order --
# items before composites, composites before groupings, groupings before
# contrasts. The six features cut across that order, each drawing on contrasts
# registered under three or four different hypotheses. A reader who wants to
# know what the data say about one feature would otherwise have to gather its
# rows out of every section that reports those hypotheses. This chunk collects
# the rows belonging to each feature under one heading and states, in words,
# which way the registered one-sided test points.
#
# WHY results='asis'. This chunk writes its own headings and tables straight
# into the document rather than printing them inside the usual grey output box,
# which is what that chunk option does. Two practical consequences. Every cat()
```
