```{r phase9_features, results='asis'}
# below has to end in a blank line, because the text it emits is read as
# document text and two paragraphs run together without one. And every table
# has to be print()ed explicitly, because the tables are produced inside a for
# loop, where R does not auto-print: a bare show_table() call there would build
# a table and throw it away.

# A hard stop rather than a quietly empty section: if the spec has no feature
# column there is nothing to group by, and an empty section that looks fine on
# the page is worse than a failure that does not. A silent gap gets published;
# an error gets fixed.
if (!"feature" %in% names(contrast_spec)) {
  stop("contrast_spec has no `feature` column, so 9.16 cannot group anything. ",
       "See the column list in 9.3.")
}

# The table below defines the six features. Each column has a job.
#
# `claim` states each feature as the manuscript states it, and `higher_means`
# says what a higher score on that feature's measures amounts to. Neither is a
# finding: the first is the position being tested, the second is what the
# direction of the registered one-sided test comes to once it is put in words.
#
# `expected_outcomes` is not part of the manuscript's framing. It is the
# analytic decision about which measured variable speaks to which claim. That
# decision is made here and recorded here, so that a reader can argue with it.
# It is also checked against the spec at the foot of this chunk. That check is
# what makes a measure named for a feature but never tested under it get
# reported rather than go quietly absent. A name may be added to it before the
# measure exists: the coverage check reports such a name as NOT FOUND rather
# than letting the section imply the measure was computed.
#
# `caution` prints under the table, before the count, wherever the rows under a
# feature are not as independent of one another as a count of rows implies.
# Counting overlapping rows as separate findings would inflate the evidence.
# `alpha_watch` names a composite as the reliability table in 4.10 labels it,
# and triggers a reliability note when that composite's alpha is low.
# `where_else` is used only when the contrast set carries no row for a feature.
# F2 is that case: proportionality is measured in this study, but not as a
# difference between two groups, so its heading carries a pointer and no table.
#
# Adding a seventh feature is one row here plus that code in the feature column
# of the spec in 9.3, and nothing else in this document changes.
feature_defs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~feature, ~feature_name, ~claim, ~higher_means, ~expected_outcomes,
  ~caution, ~alpha_watch, ~where_else,

  "F1", "DIGNITY",
  paste("Retribution is a moral, deontological theory grounded in respect for",
        "the DIGNITY of the person being punished."),
  paste("If that holds, retributivists should be no more willing than anyone",
        "else to degrade or cast out the person they punish. A higher score on",
        "the rows below means MORE endorsement of degrading treatment and MORE",
        "willingness to exclude the offender from society, so a row on which",
        "the retributivists score higher counts AGAINST the claim, not for",
        "it."),
  "degradation, exclusion",
  NA,
  "degradation",
  NA,

  "F2", "PROPORTIONALITY",
  "Central to retribution is the principle of PROPORTIONALITY.",
  paste("If that holds, punishment should fit the offense, neither exceeding",
        "it nor falling short of it. Proportionality is measured in this study",
        "but never as a difference between two groups, so no contrast row and",
        "no count of measures appears under this heading."),
  "proportionality_principle",
  NA,
  NA,
  paste("8.1 (is strict proportionality endorsed at all), 8.2 (punishment",
        "beyond the offense against punishment below it) and 8.3b (what",
        "desert actually tracks). Those are one-sample, paired and",
        "correlational tests, none of which is a difference between two",
        "groups, so none belongs in the contrast set this section regroups.",
        "In 8.3b the row that carries the evidence is `deserved`,",
        "the four purpose items, against `proportionality_principle`, read",
        "against `deserved` versus `severity_index` beneath it. The row a",
        "reader is likeliest to mistake for the evidence is `just_deserts`",
        "against `proportionality_principle`, and it is PART-WHOLE:",
        "`just_deserts` is built from the proportionality item, so that row",
        "correlates the item with itself. 8.3b prints it labelled CONTAMINATED",
        "for exactly that reason and it is not evidence of anything."),

  "F3", "LENIENCY",
  paste("Proportionality exists to harness the state's propensity to",
        "over-punish, so retributive punishment should be MORE LENIENT than",
        "consequentialist punishment."),
  paste("If that holds, retributivists should be no more punitive than anyone",
        "else, and by the letter of the claim less punitive. A higher score on",
        "the rows below means a LONGER sentence, HARSHER prison conditions and",
        "a MORE punitive scale score, so a row on which the retributivists",
        "score higher counts AGAINST the claim, not for it."),
  "punitiveness, punitiveness_full, Sentence1_z, harsh",
  paste("Four rows, three distinct constructs. `punitiveness_full` is",
        "zmean(`punitiveness`, `Sentence1_z`), built in 4.2 out of the items",
        "of two of the other three rows, so it is not independent evidence of",
        "anything those two do not already show, and the four rows must not be",
        "counted as four separate findings. 9.8 treats the self-report scale",
        "as the primary test of H21; this heading keeps that order."),
  NA,
  NA,

  "F4", "HARD TREATMENT",
  paste("HARD TREATMENT is required by retribution, but as a necessary feature",
        "rather than a goal to be pursued."),
  paste("If that holds, retributivists should accept the hardship that",
        "deserved punishment involves without seeking more of it. A higher",
        "score on the rows below means MORE endorsement of inflicting",
        "suffering and MORE tolerance of violence in prison, which is hard",
        "treatment pursued rather than accepted, so a row on which the",
        "retributivists score higher counts AGAINST the claim, not for it."),
  "suffering, prisonviol",
  NA,
  NA,
  NA,

  "F5", "CERTAINTY OF GUILT",
  paste("With its focus on just desert, retribution is deeply committed to the",
        "CERTAINTY OF GUILT."),
  paste("If that holds, retributivists should be the last to relax the",
        "safeguards that establish guilt. A higher score on the rows below",
        "means MORE willingness to set due process aside and MORE willingness",
        "to convict on evidence short of certainty, so a row on which the",
        "retributivists score higher counts AGAINST the claim, not for it."),
  "dueprocess, uncertain",
  NA,
  "due process (permissive)",
  NA,

  "F6", "TRANSCENDING REVENGE",
  "Retribution TRANSCENDS negative emotions and the desire for REVENGE.",
  paste("If that holds, retributivists should be no more vengeful or hostile",
        "toward the offender than anyone else. A higher score on the rows",
        "below means MORE desire for revenge, MORE hatred and MORE anger, so a",
        "row on which the retributivists score higher counts AGAINST the",
        "claim, not for it."),
  "revenge, hatred, anger",
  NA,
  NA,
  NA
)

# A feature code used in the spec but absent from the table above would be
# invisible on the page and present in the export. The loop below iterates
# `feature_defs`, so such a row would never print under any heading. But
# `features_tab` and output/tables/features_F1_to_F6.csv would still carry it.
# The knitted document and the CSV would then disagree, which is the one thing
# this section must not do. Stop instead of printing a partial index.
undefined_codes <- setdiff(
  unique(contrast_spec$feature[!is.na(contrast_spec$feature)]),
  feature_defs$feature)
if (length(undefined_codes) > 0) {
  stop("contrast_spec uses feature code(s) that feature_defs does not define: ",
       paste(undefined_codes, collapse = ", "),
       ". Add a row to feature_defs in 9.16, or clear the code in 9.3.")
}

#' Look up the Cronbach's alpha of one composite. Cronbach's alpha measures
#' internal consistency: how far a set of items behaves like repeated
#' measurements of one single thing. This function READS that number out of the
#' reliability table built in 4.10 instead of working it out again. That way the
#' figure quoted below and the figure in the published reliability table can
#' never drift apart from each other.
#'
#' ARGUMENTS
#'   label  the composite's name, spelled exactly as the reliability table
#'          spells it. The lookup is an exact text match, so a near miss finds
#'          nothing.
#' RETURNS  one number, or NA (R's marker for a missing value) when the table is
#'          absent or does not carry that label.
#' USED BY  the reliability note printed under a feature's table, further down
#'          in this chunk, and nowhere else.
#'
#' WHY IT RETURNS NA INSTEAD OF STOPPING. The reliability note is an extra, not
#' a result. A missing figure should quietly skip the note, not bring the whole
#' document down.
#'
#' NOTE ON THE SOURCE. `alpha_table_out` is the copy 4.10 froze for export, so a
#' composite built AFTER 4.10 is not in it. That is why this returns NA rather
#' than failing, and why the note that uses it is guarded rather than assumed.
alpha_of <- function(label) {
  # No such object at all, or an object that is not a data frame (a rectangular
  # table of rows and columns): give up quietly and let the caller skip its
  # note. Reaching into a non-table would error out instead.
  if (!exists("alpha_table_out") || !is.data.frame(alpha_table_out))
    return(NA_real_)
  hit <- which(alpha_table_out$composite == label)
  # A LENGTH test, not a "did we find anything" test, and it refuses two
  # different problems at once. Zero matches means the label is not in the
  # table. Two or more means the table holds duplicate rows for one composite,
  # so there is no way to tell which alpha was meant. Quoting the wrong
  # composite's alpha is worse than quoting none, so both cases return NA.
  if (length(hit) != 1) return(NA_real_)
  alpha_table_out$alpha[hit]
}

# === HOW THE RESULTS ARE MATCHED TO THE SPEC ===
# Every result row has to be told which of the six features it belongs to, and
# that tag lives in the spec, not in the results. So the two tables have to be
# lined up against each other row by row.
#
# WARNING: THE TWO TABLES USE THE WORD "outcome" FOR TWO DIFFERENT THINGS.
# Joining them on the column that looks obvious returns nothing at all.
#   contrast_spec$outcome   is the COLUMN NAME in `d`  ("degradation")
#   contrast_spec$label     is the DISPLAY NAME        ("Degradation")
#   contrasts_rank$outcome  is the DISPLAY NAME, because welch_contrast() puts
#                           the label it was handed into a column called
#                           `outcome`
#   contrasts_rank$variable is the COLUMN NAME
# So the match below runs contrasts_rank$variable against contrast_spec$outcome
# -- column name against column name. Matching outcome to outcome would find no
# rows at all, and this section would then print six empty headings and never
# complain about it.
#
# match() returns, for each result row, the POSITION of its row in the spec, or
# NA (R's marker for a missing value) when the spec has no such row.
spec_pos <- match(contrasts_rank$variable, contrast_spec$outcome)

# Copy two things from the spec onto each result row: the feature tag (F1 to F6,
# or NA for a row that speaks to none of the six claims) and the position that
# row holds in the spec.
#
# The position is carried across so that the sort below can name spec order
# outright as its second key, rather than leaning on the order the rows happen
# to arrive in. That holds the outcomes inside each feature in the order the
# spec sets them out, rather than alphabetically or by effect size. A table
# sorted by effect size quietly invites a reader to treat the biggest number as
# the headline finding, which is exactly the reading this section is built to
# prevent.
feat_rows <- contrasts_rank
feat_rows$feature    <- contrast_spec$feature[spec_pos]
feat_rows$spec_order <- spec_pos
# The feature's full name ("DIGNITY", not just the code "F1"), so the exported
# CSV can be read on its own without this document open beside it. A row with no
# feature keeps NA here, which is the honest answer. A row that HAS a feature is
# guaranteed to find a name, because the stop() above already refused to run at
# all if the spec used a feature code that `feature_defs` does not define.
feat_rows$feature_name <-
  feature_defs$feature_name[match(feat_rows$feature, feature_defs$feature)]

# Keep only the rows that carry a feature, then sort them: first by feature, and
# within a feature by the spec's own order.
#
# The sort key is match() against feature_defs$feature, NOT a plain alphabetical
# sort of the codes. That gives the features in the order the manuscript sets
# them out, F1 through F6, and they would still come out in that order if a code
# were ever renamed to something that happens to sort differently. Sorting on
# the text of the code would silently reorder this whole section the day someone
# renames one.
features_tab <- feat_rows[!is.na(feat_rows$feature), ]
features_tab <- features_tab[order(match(features_tab$feature,
                                         feature_defs$feature),
                                   features_tab$spec_order), ]
# Name the columns of the EXPORTED table, in the order they should sit in it.
# This drops `spec_order`, which existed only to drive the sort above, and puts
# the feature code and its full name first. Naming the list here, rather than
# exporting whatever columns happen to be attached, is what keeps the CSV
# written in 10.1 carrying the same columns in the same order from one run to
# the next. The tables PRINTED on the page are a narrower set in a different
# order again; `show_cols`, a few lines down, is what sets those.
features_tab <- features_tab[, c("feature", "feature_name", "hypothesis",
                                 "outcome", "variable", "grouping",
                                 "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2",
                                 "t", "df", "p_dir", "p_two",
                                 "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "alternative")]
# Store this under its OWN entry in TABLES, with a name that says what it is:
# the same contrasts as before, indexed by feature. Every other entry of TABLES
# is left exactly as it stands.
#
# DO NOT REUSE OR RENAME AN ENTRY HERE. Phase 10.1 turns each name in TABLES
# into a filename, so this one becomes output/tables/features_F1_to_F6.csv.
# Renaming an entry silently stops writing the file the manuscript points at,
# and the manuscript then cites a stale copy that nothing regenerates. An index
# belongs BESIDE the result tables, never in place of one.
TABLES[["features_F1_to_F6"]] <- features_tab

# The key for reading everything below, stated once at the top so that no reader
# has to work it out from column headers. Group 1 is always the retributivists
# and group 2 is always everyone else. So a positive Cohen's d always means the
# retributivists scored higher. Cohen's d is the gap between the two group
# means, measured in standard deviations.
cat("All results below come from the primary (ranking) grouping run in 9.3:",
    "**M1/SD1 are the retributivists, M2/SD2 everyone else, and a positive d",
    "means the retributivists score higher.** The same contrasts under the",
    "other three definitions of retributivism are in the grid in 9.12.\n\n")

# The columns printed under each heading, in the order they appear: which
# hypothesis the row was registered under, what was compared, how many people
# were in each group, the two group means each with its SD, then Cohen's d with
# the two ends of its 95% confidence interval, and last `p_dir`.
#
# Three of those need a word. SD is the standard deviation, the typical distance
# of one person from the mean. The 95% confidence interval is the range of true
# effect sizes the data leave standing, at 95% confidence. `p_dir` is the
# p-value for the one-sided direction the row was registered to run in. A small
# p-value means the result is hard to put down to chance. It says nothing at all
# about how large the difference is.
#
# t and df are left out HERE for one reason only: to keep these tables narrow
# enough to read on a page. Nothing is being hidden. Both appear in the
# registered tables in 9.4 to 9.8 and in the exported CSV.
show_cols <- c("hypothesis", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2",
               "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "p_dir")

# One pass per feature, in the order feature_defs lists them. The loop walks
# feature_defs rather than the results, and that is deliberate: it guarantees
# all six headings print, including F2, which has no contrast rows at all.
for (i in seq_len(nrow(feature_defs))) {
  # The one feature being written up on this pass, and the result rows tagged
  # with it. `rows` comes back empty for a feature with no two-group contrast,
  # which the branch further down handles rather than crashing on.
  fd   <- feature_defs[i, ]
  rows <- features_tab[features_tab$feature == fd$feature, ]

  # A level-3 heading ("###"), not just bold text, and the difference matters. A
  # real heading gets its own entry in the floating table of contents of the
  # knitted report and its own anchor, so each feature can be linked to and
  # cited on its own. The two "\n" at the end are required by results='asis':
  # without a blank line after it, the heading and the next paragraph run
  # together into one line.
  cat(sprintf("### %s %s\n\n", fd$feature, fd$feature_name))

  # THE CLAIM IS ATTRIBUTED, NOT ASSERTED, and the words "What retributive
  # theory claims" are doing real work. Printed bare, the sentence reads as this
  # document's own position. The count further down then attaches itself to that
  # position and flips meaning: "3 of 3 in the direction tested", sitting under
  # an unattributed "retribution transcends revenge", reads as three results
  # SUPPORTING transcendence. It means the opposite -- three results showing the
  # retributivists MORE vengeful than everyone else.
  cat(sprintf("**What retributive theory claims.** *%s*\n\n", fd$claim))

  # WHAT A HIGHER SCORE MEANS, IN WORDS, BEFORE ANY TABLE OR COUNT. Every row
  # under every feature here is registered as a one-sided test in the "greater"
  # direction, which means the test asks only whether the retributivists score
  # higher. But for all six features, scoring higher is what runs AGAINST the
  # claim. So the statistics and the English pull in opposite directions, and a
  # reader who does not have this sentence in hand reads every count below
  # exactly backwards. That is why it prints before the numbers, never after.
  cat(sprintf("**What a higher score means.** %s\n\n", fd$higher_means))

  if (nrow(rows) == 0) {
    # A feature with no two-group contrast anywhere in the set. This is F2,
    # proportionality, which is tested one-sample, paired and correlationally
    # instead. The heading STILL prints, with a pointer to where the evidence
    # actually is. A feature the paper discusses must not vanish from the index
    # just because its evidence takes a different statistical form: a silent gap
    # reads as "nothing to say here", which is false.
    cat("No row of the contrast set carries this feature, so there is no table",
        "here.\n\n")
    if (!is.na(fd$where_else)) {
      cat(sprintf("Where the evidence is instead: %s\n\n", fd$where_else))
    }

    # The two numbers a reader who follows the F2 pointer is going to want,
    # quoted from `h6b` exactly as 8.3b computed them and NOT recomputed here.
    # Quoting rather than recomputing means the two sections can never print
    # different values for the same correlation.
    #
    # The rows are found by the display labels 8.3b gives them, so this block is
    # tied to F2 and to that one section. If those labels ever change, the
    # reader loses these two figures and nothing else, because the pointer above
    # already names the rows in plain words.
    #
    # Both figures come from cor_row(), which uses pairwise deletion: for each
    # correlation it keeps only the people who answered BOTH measures. So the
    # two sit on the same footing as each other and as everything else in 8.3b,
    # and can be compared.
    if (fd$feature == "F2" && exists("h6b") && is.data.frame(h6b)) {
      i_prop <- which(h6b$x == "Desert (purpose items)" &
                        grepl("Proportionality principle", h6b$y, fixed = TRUE))
      i_sev  <- which(h6b$x == "Desert (purpose items)" &
                        grepl("Severity index", h6b$y, fixed = TRUE))
      i_con  <- which(grepl("part-whole", h6b$y, fixed = TRUE))
      # Both rows must be found exactly once each before either is quoted. If a
      # label has drifted, the sentence simply does not print, which is better
      # than printing a number pulled from whichever row happened to match.
      if (length(i_prop) == 1 && length(i_sev) == 1) {
        cat(sprintf(paste("From 8.3b: desert against the proportionality",
                          "principle, r = %+.3f; desert against the severity",
                          "index, r = %+.3f.\n\n"),
                    h6b$r[i_prop], h6b$r[i_sev]))
      }
      if (length(i_con) == 1) {
        # The part-whole correlation is the largest of the three, and that is
        # precisely why 8.3b prints it disarmed. Part-whole means the two sides
        # of the correlation share an item: `just_deserts` is built FROM the
        # proportionality item, so this row correlates that item partly with
        # itself and is guaranteed to look strong. IT IS NOT EVIDENCE OF
        # ANYTHING.
        #
        # Whether it really is the largest is CHECKED against the numbers rather
        # than asserted, so the sentence cannot outlive the ordering it
        # describes. Note that the comparison is on abs(), the size of each
        # correlation ignoring its sign, because a strongly negative value is
        # just as large as a strongly positive one. If the ordering ever
        # changes, the shorter wording prints instead of a claim that has
        # quietly become false.
        bigger <- length(i_prop) == 1 && length(i_sev) == 1 &&
          abs(h6b$r[i_con]) > max(abs(h6b$r[i_prop]), abs(h6b$r[i_sev]))
        cat(sprintf(paste("The part-whole row in that same table, printed",
                          "there to be disarmed rather than used, is",
                          "r = %+.3f.%s\n\n"),
                    h6b$r[i_con],
                    if (bigger)
                      " It is the largest of the three and it is not evidence."
                    else " It is not evidence."))
      }
    }
    # Nothing further to print for a feature with no rows, so move to the next
    # feature rather than falling through into the table-building code below.
    next
  }

  # The caption for this feature's table. Every table in this document carries
  # one, so that a table lifted out of the report still says what it shows and
  # which grouping it came from. The "%%" is not a typo: inside sprintf(), a
  # literal percent sign has to be written twice.
  cap <- sprintf(paste("%s %s: retributivists versus everyone else, Welch t",
                       "with Cohen's d and its 95%% CI, under the primary",
                       "ranking grouping"),
                 fd$feature, fd$feature_name)
  # print() is REQUIRED here, not decoration. This sits inside a for loop, where
  # R does not print a result automatically, and show_table() returns a kable
  # object (knitr's formatted-table object) rather than printing one itself. A
  # bare show_table() call here would build the table and throw it away, leaving
  # a heading with nothing under it.
  print(show_table(rows[, show_cols], cap))
  cat("\n")

  # A caution, where one is recorded. It says so when the rows under a feature
  # are not as independent of one another as a count of rows makes them look,
  # because they are built from overlapping items. It prints ABOVE the count,
  # not below it, so the reader holds the warning before reading the number it
  # qualifies.
  if (!is.na(fd$caution)) cat(sprintf("%s\n\n", fd$caution))

  # Reliability, but only where it is weak enough to matter. Everywhere else in
  # this document a reliability coefficient is printed beside every composite,
  # and promoting one composite to a named share of the evidence for a feature
  # must not lose that.
  #
  # The note prints ONLY when the alpha read back from 4.10 falls below .60, the
  # same floor 4.10 itself uses, so it is a statement about the number that came
  # back rather than a fixed claim about a particular scale. If alpha_of()
  # returned NA (R's marker for a missing value), the condition is false and no
  # note prints at all.
  if (!is.na(fd$alpha_watch)) {
    a_val <- alpha_of(fd$alpha_watch)
    if (!is.na(a_val) && a_val < .60) {
      cat(sprintf(paste("Reliability: `%s`, one of the %d rows above, has",
                        "Cronbach's alpha = %.2f. Cronbach's alpha measures",
                        "internal consistency, that is, how far a set of items",
                        "behaves like repeated measurements of one thing, and",
                        "4.10 flags anything below .60 as low.\n\n"),
                  fd$alpha_watch, nrow(rows), a_val))
    }
  }

  # A NEUTRAL COUNT, NOT A VERDICT. It reports which way the differences run and
  # how many clear the conventional p < .05 threshold, and stops there. What
  # that adds up to for the feature is an argument, and arguments belong in the
  # manuscript, written by the authors, not in text a script generated.
  #
  # The ifelse() scores each row in ITS OWN registered direction: a row
  # registered "less" counts when d is negative, a row registered "greater"
  # counts when d is positive. Every row here is currently "greater", but if a
  # "less" row is tagged with a feature later, this counts it the right way
  # round instead of backwards. na.rm = TRUE ignores NA, which is what a row
  # holds when its contrast could not be run at all.
  #
  # NOTE ON WHAT THAT DOES TO THE SENTENCE PRINTED BELOW. A row that could not
  # be run is dropped from this count and from n_sig, but it is still inside
  # nrow(rows), which is the total the sentence quotes. Such a row would
  # therefore read as one that simply did not run in the tested direction.
  # Whether that is wanted, or whether an unrunnable row should come out of the
  # total as well, is for the authors to settle.
  n_dir <- sum(ifelse(rows$alternative == "less", rows$d < 0, rows$d > 0),
               na.rm = TRUE)
  # How many reach the conventional one-sided p < .05. It counts p_dir, the
  # DIRECTIONAL p-value, so the count matches the test that was registered
  # rather than an undirected version of it.
  n_sig <- sum(rows$p_dir < .05, na.rm = TRUE)
  # The plain-English sentence below names "higher" as the tested direction.
  # That is true only while every row under this feature is registered
  # "greater". Checked rather than assumed: if a "less" row is ever tagged with
  # this feature, the direction-neutral wording prints instead of a sentence
  # that would be flatly wrong about what was tested.
  all_greater <- all(rows$alternative == "greater")
  # The pointer back to the caution is added only where there IS a caution above
  # to read. Otherwise it would send the reader hunting for a note that is not
  # on the page.
  caveat <- if (!is.na(fd$caution))
    " Read that count against the note above the table." else ""
  if (all_greater) {
    # Every row was tested in the "higher" direction, so the sentence can name
    # that direction and say plainly that it is the direction running against
    # the claim printed above.
    cat(sprintf(paste("Of the %d contrast rows under this feature, %d run with",
                      "the retributivists scoring HIGHER and %d reach",
                      "one-sided p < .05 in that direction. Higher is the",
                      "direction of the registered one-sided test, and it is",
                      "the direction that runs against the claim above.%s\n\n"),
                nrow(rows), n_dir, n_sig, caveat))
  } else {
    # A mixed set. Naming a single direction would be wrong, so the wording
    # stays direction-neutral and sends the reader to the spec in 9.3 for which
    # way each individual row was registered to run.
    cat(sprintf(paste("Of the %d contrast rows under this feature, %d run in",
                      "the direction of their own registered one-sided test",
                      "and %d reach one-sided p < .05 in that direction. The",
                      "rows here are not all registered in the same direction;",
                      "which way each points is in the spec in 9.3 and in the",
                      "exported CSV.%s\n\n"),
                nrow(rows), n_dir, n_sig, caveat))
  }
}

# === COVERAGE: WHAT IS NOT IN THE SIX FEATURES ===
# An index is only honest if it says what it leaves out. There are two ways a
# measure can be missing from the six sections above, and BOTH are printed here
# rather than left for a reader to discover by noticing a gap.
cat("### Coverage of the contrast set\n\n")

# (1) Contrast rows that belong to none of the six features. They are still
# tested, still registered and still reported in full in 9.4 to 9.8 and 9.15.
# They simply do not speak to one of the six claims. is.na() picks them out,
# because a row with no feature carries NA (R's marker for a missing value) in
# that column.
# Listing them keeps this section honest about being an INDEX rather than the
# whole of Phase 9.
unmapped <- feat_rows[is.na(feat_rows$feature), c("hypothesis", "outcome")]
cat(sprintf(paste("%d of the %d contrasts carry a feature. The remaining %d",
                  "are reported in 9.4 to 9.8 and 9.15 as usual, and are",
                  "listed here only so that nothing appears to have gone",
                  "missing.\n\n"),
            nrow(features_tab), nrow(feat_rows), nrow(unmapped)))
print(show_table(unmapped,
                 "Contrasts that belong to none of the six features"))
cat("\n")

# (2) The mirror-image problem: measures NAMED as belonging to a feature that
# the six sections above do not actually print under that feature. Each feature
# records its expected measures as one string of comma-separated names, so
# splitting on a comma plus any spaces that follow it turns that record into one
# row per measure.
#
# THREE OUTCOMES, KEPT DISTINCT. Simply asking whether the measure appears in
# contrast_spec$outcome would not be enough. That single test cannot tell "named
# but tested elsewhere" from "named but never computed", and it cannot see a
# measure filed under the WRONG feature at all:
#   MISMATCH   the spec has the row but tags it with a different feature, or
#              with none, so the mapping recorded here and the mapping the page
#              actually uses have come apart.
#   elsewhere  the measure exists in `d` but is not a two-group contrast. This
#              is the F2 case and it is expected; the pointer under the heading
#              says where it is tested instead.
#   NOT FOUND  no such column in `d`. A name has been recorded for a measure
#              this document does not build. Printed rather than fatal, so that
#              a measure named ahead of being built stays visible instead of
#              being silently dropped, and is never described as though it had
#              been tested.
exp_list <- strsplit(feature_defs$expected_outcomes, ",[[:space:]]*")
# One row per named measure. rep() repeats each feature code as many times as
# that feature named measures, and unlist() flattens the split-up pieces back
# into a single vector (a simple run of values), so the two line up.
expected <- data.frame(
  feature = rep(feature_defs$feature, lengths(exp_list)),
  measure = unlist(exp_list),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# Where each named measure sits in the spec, and which feature the spec tags it
# with. NA in either place is informative, and the status labels below turn each
# combination into words.
spec_i <- match(expected$measure, contrast_spec$outcome)
expected$spec_feature <- contrast_spec$feature[spec_i]
# TRUE only where the spec both HAS the row and tags it with the same feature
# that named it. Two details are load-bearing.
#
# First, this is computed as a logical (a plain TRUE/FALSE vector) BEFORE the
# status strings are built. The strings are then only labels for the reader, not
# the thing the check depends on, so rewording a message can never change which
# rows count as matched.
#
# Second, a spec row tagged NA returns NA from the comparison rather than FALSE,
# and NA would not behave as a failure. That is what the second is.na() catches,
# and it is why "or none" belongs in the mismatch message.
matched <- !is.na(spec_i) & !is.na(expected$spec_feature) &
  expected$spec_feature == expected$feature
expected$status <- ifelse(
  matched,
  "tested as a contrast under this feature",
  ifelse(is.na(spec_i),
         ifelse(expected$measure %in% names(d),
                "measured, but not a two-group contrast",
                "NOT FOUND: no such column in the data"),
         "MISMATCH: the spec tags this row with a different feature, or none"))
if (all(matched)) {
  # The clean case. It is stated out loud rather than left as silence, because
  # silence here is indistinguishable from the check never having run.
  cat("Every measure named for a feature is tested as a group contrast under",
      "that same feature.\n\n")
} else {
  # Something did not line up. The offending rows are printed with their status,
  # so the reader can see which of the three cases each one is instead of being
  # told only that a mismatch exists somewhere.
  cat(sprintf(paste("%d measure(s) named for a feature are not tested as a",
                    "group contrast under that feature. The status column says",
                    "which of the three cases each one is.\n\n"),
              sum(!matched)))
  print(show_table(expected[!matched, c("feature", "measure", "status")],
                   "Measures named for a feature but not a contrast under it"))
  cat("\n")
}

# === THE REPRINT CHECK ===
# This whole section rests on one claim: that it COPIES numbers rather than
# producing them. This is where that claim is tested.
#
# CIRCULARITY, AND WHY THE OBVIOUS CHECK IS NOT A CHECK. Comparing a copy with
# the object it was copied FROM cannot fail, and must never be mistaken for
# verification. `features_tab` is a subset of `contrasts_rank`, so looking its
# rows back up in `contrasts_rank` compares the object with itself. It would
# report a perfect match even if every single value in `contrasts_rank` had been
# overwritten somewhere between 9.3 and here.
#
# So this recomputes from scratch instead. welch_contrast() is called again on
# `d` for each row that carries a feature, using the same outcome column, the
# same grouping and the same one-sided direction the spec gave it back in 9.3.
# A Welch t-test compares two group means. It does not assume the two groups
# have the same variance, that is, the same amount of spread around their own
# mean. The fresh means, SDs and effect sizes are then compared against the ones
# reprinted above.
#
# This is the ONLY computation in the chunk. Its output is a single line, and no
# number it produces is reported anywhere. One Welch t-test per tagged row on
# the full sample costs nothing; a section that promises a check and runs none
# costs a great deal.
#
# all.equal() rather than == because these are floating-point numbers, the
# approximate decimals a computer stores. Two such values can be identical for
# every practical purpose and still differ in the very last bit, which == would
# call a mismatch. all.equal() tolerates a difference that small and nothing
# larger. isTRUE() is wrapped around it because all.equal() reports a difference
# as a description in words, not as FALSE.
if (nrow(features_tab) > 0) {
  recheck <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(features_tab)), function(i) {
    welch_contrast(d, features_tab$variable[i], features_tab$grouping[i],
                   alternative = features_tab$alternative[i],
                   label = features_tab$outcome[i])
  }))
  # All five quantities have to agree. Checking d alone would pass even if both
  # group means had shifted by the same amount, which is exactly the kind of
  # error worth catching.
  same_numbers <-
    isTRUE(all.equal(features_tab$M1,  recheck$M1))  &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(features_tab$SD1, recheck$SD1)) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(features_tab$M2,  recheck$M2))  &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(features_tab$SD2, recheck$SD2)) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(features_tab$d,   recheck$d))
  # Two whole sentences rather than one sentence with a phrase substituted into
  # it, so that the failure message reads as English written for a reader rather
  # than as a template with a word swapped into the middle of it.
  cat(if (same_numbers)
        sprintf(paste("Reprint check: the %d rows above reproduce exactly the",
                      "group means, spreads and effect sizes obtained by",
                      "running the same contrasts again from the data.\n\n"),
                nrow(features_tab))
      else
        sprintf(paste("Reprint check FAILED: the %d rows above do not match",
                      "the group means, spreads and effect sizes obtained by",
                      "running the same contrasts again from the data. Nothing",
                      "in this section should be used until that is",
                      "resolved.\n\n"),
                nrow(features_tab)))
}
```

## 9.17 Companion comparisons for the write-up of Part 3

The results of Phase 9 stand as reported above. The write-up of Part 3 needs a
few quantities that the sections above compute but never print or export, and a
few that no section above computes at all. This section supplies them. It
changes no result above and adds nothing to any registered family.

Six sets are produced, and their status differs from set to set.

- **A. How far the groupings agree.** Prereg 5.3 registers that we "report their
  pairwise agreement and the overlap among the groups they define", but it names
  no statistic. 5.5 prints two crosstabs and their raw agreement. Here every
  pair of groupings except the median split and the thirds, two cuts of one
  measure, gets its four cells, its raw agreement, the agreement expected by
  chance from the margins, and Cohen's kappa with a 95% interval. The duty to
  report is registered; the statistics are our choice. A also crosses the
  reduced, kept or raised grouping of 5.4b with the ranking, which is not
  registered.
- **B. Counts over the registered rows.** 9.12 and 9.12b count results over
  every row of the contrast set that each run includes (27; 25 under the
  sentencing ratio), which mixes the registered rows (21; 19 under the ratio)
  with the six E1 rows. Here the registered rows and the five E1 rows in their
  registered scorings are counted separately, and each run is scored on two
  rules: one-sided p < .05, the registered rule, and a 95% interval that
  excludes zero on the predicted side. Nothing is tested.
  These are counts of results already reported above.
- **C. H12 under the other three groupings, and among everyone else.** Prereg
  5.3 asks for the categorical analyses "(H11 to H21)" under the median split,
  the tertiles and the sentencing ratio. 9.2 ran H12 under the ranking only. The
  shares and the within-group correlations are run here on the retributive side
  of each other grouping, as registered. The shares among everyone else under
  the ranking are added for comparison, and are not registered; neither is the
  shark-decision row, which 9.2 reports beside the attitudes H12 lists.
- **D. The H15 shark decision under the other three groupings**, registered by
  the same sentence of 5.3. 9.6 and 9.9 ran it under the ranking and the
  continuous measures only. The share answering yes on each side is added.
- **E. H11 under the other three groupings**, registered by the same sentence.
  9.1 ran it under the ranking only. The same H1 to H10 functions run inside the
  retributive side of each grouping, and the results are summarised. The whole
  sample is run through the same summary as a reference column.
- **F. Punitiveness scored by its five parts, and the six-constituent hostility
  cluster, in the retributivist contrasts.** Not registered. 7.4 and 7.2b
  checked these two rescorings on the whole-sample tests only.

H12 names no direction for its correlations, so the two-sided p values are the
ones to report; the one-sided values 9.2 computes are kept beside them. D, E and
F keep the direction registered for each test they rerun. Apart from the
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment that `run_h1()` applies within each group's
twelve H1 correlations in E, which is the correction registered for H1 and
carried into H11, nothing here is corrected for multiplicity.

```{r phase9_part3_companions}
# === 9.17 COMPANION COMPARISONS FOR THE WRITE-UP OF PART 3 ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: six sets of summaries and reruns that the write-up of
# Part 3 needs. Produces P3_grouping_agreement,
# P3_sentence_direction_by_ranking, P3_scorecard, P3_rows_across_groupings,
# P3_H12_other_groupings, P3_H12_everyone_else, P3_H15_other_groupings,
# P3_H15_shares, P3_H11_other_groupings and P3_rescored_contrasts.
# PREREG: MIXED, and stated set by set below. A carries out the agreement
#         reporting prereg 5.3 registers, with statistics of our choosing. C, D
#         and E carry out prereg 5.3's "H11 to H21" under the other groupings.
#         B is a set of counts, not tests. NOT registered: the reduced, kept
#         or raised table in A, the everyone-else shares and the shark-decision
#         row in C, and all of F. Apart from the Benjamini-Hochberg
#         adjustment run_h1() applies within each group's twelve H1
#         correlations in E (as registered for H1, carried into H11), nothing
#         is corrected for multiplicity, and nothing enters a registered family.
# CONSUMES: d, d_retrib, d_other (Phase 9 opening); the grouping factors
#           grp_rank (5.1), grp_med and grp_tert (5.3) and grp_ratio (5.4),
#           and the variables they were cut from: retributivist (5.1),
#           retrib_medsplit and retrib_tertile (5.3), sentence_ratio and
#           is_high (5.4);
#           grp_ratio_dir (5.4b); overlap and overlap2 (5.5); h1_full (7.1)
#           and h10_full (8.7); contrast_spec, contrasts_rank, contrasts_med,
#           contrasts_tert, contrasts_ratio (9.3 to 9.11); cont_rel, cont_raw,
#           cont_ratio, cont_resid (9.9, 9.10); agreement (9.12); cq_contrasts
#           and cq_summary (9.12b); h12_spec and h12 (9.2); h15_logit (9.6);
#           h11_h1 to h11_h10 (9.1); p5_d (7.4); prop_ci(), cor_row(),
#           logit_reg(), run_contrast_set(), run_continuous_set(), run_h1() to
#           run_h10(), show_table().
# NOTHING HERE WRITES TO d. New columns live in p3_d, a private copy.
# NAMING: every object starts with p3_.
p3_d <- d

# --- A. How far the groupings agree about who is a retributivist ------------
# Each grouping becomes a 0/1 indicator of its retributive side: the ranking's
# retributivists, the high half of the median split, the top third, and the
# high sentencing ratio (did not reduce the sentence). The tertile indicator is
# NA (R's marker for a missing value) for the middle third, which that grouping
# leaves out. The ratio indicator is NA for the one participant with no ratio.
# Comparing a factor with a level name gives NA wherever the factor is NA, so
# those people stay missing rather than being counted on the non-retributive
# side.
p3_side <- data.frame(
  ranking = as.integer(d$grp_rank  == "Retributivist"),
  median  = as.integer(d$grp_med   == "High rel. retribution"),
  tertile = as.integer(d$grp_tert  == "Top third"),
  ratio   = as.integer(d$grp_ratio == "High sentencing ratio"))
p3_side_labels <- c(ranking = "Ranking (desert first)",
                    median  = "Median split on relative retribution",
                    tertile = "Top vs bottom third of relative retribution",
                    ratio   = "Sentencing ratio (no reduction vs reduction)")
# GUARDS: each indicator must match the variable its grouping was cut from in
# Phase 5, not merely the factor it was read off. A renamed factor level would
# otherwise make every comparison above FALSE, so the indicator would be 0 for
# everyone it classifies, and a check of the factor against itself would
# still pass.
#   ranking: the 0/1 retributivist flag the whole of Phase 9 is built on.
#   median:  retrib_medsplit, the strict ">" cut at the median (5.3).
#   thirds:  retrib_tertile, the three-level cut (5.3); the indicator is NA
#            for its middle third.
#   ratio:   is_high, the side of the ratio's median that 5.4 chose.
# identical(which(...), which(...)) compares the exact participants, and the
# last line confirms each indicator has people on both sides.
stopifnot(identical(which(p3_side$ranking == 1), which(d$retributivist == 1)),
          identical(p3_side$median, as.integer(d$retrib_medsplit)),
          identical(which(p3_side$tertile == 1), which(d$retrib_tertile == "Top third")),
          identical(which(p3_side$tertile == 0), which(d$retrib_tertile == "Bottom third")),
          identical(which(p3_side$ratio == 1), which(is_high)),
          all(vapply(p3_side, function(x) all(c(0L, 1L) %in% x), logical(1))))

#' Agreement between two groupings on the people both of them classify
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  a, b   names of two columns of p3_side.
#' RETURNS    one row: the four cells, raw agreement, the agreement expected by
#'            chance, and Cohen's kappa with its 95% interval.
#'
#' Raw agreement is the share of people the two groupings put on the same side.
#' Chance agreement is what that share would be if the two sorts were
#' unrelated, given how many people each puts on its retributive side: the
#' product of the two retributive shares plus the product of the two other
#' shares. Each grouping here puts between 39% and 54% of the people it
#' classifies on its retributive side, and each pair includes one near half,
#' so chance agreement is close to 50%, and raw agreement means little
#' without it.
#' Kappa is the distance above chance as a fraction of the most that distance
#' could be: (raw - chance) / (1 - chance). 0 is chance and 1 is perfect
#' agreement. The interval comes from psych::cohen.kappa, which uses the
#' large-sample variance of Fleiss, Cohen and Everitt (1969).
p3_agree <- function(a, b) {
  ok <- !is.na(p3_side[[a]]) & !is.na(p3_side[[b]])
  x <- p3_side[[a]][ok]
  y <- p3_side[[b]][ok]
  n11 <- sum(x == 1 & y == 1)   # retributive under both
  n10 <- sum(x == 1 & y == 0)   # retributive under the first only
  n01 <- sum(x == 0 & y == 1)   # retributive under the second only
  n00 <- sum(x == 0 & y == 0)   # retributive under neither
  n   <- length(x)
  po  <- (n11 + n00) / n
  pe  <- mean(x) * mean(y) + (1 - mean(x)) * (1 - mean(y))
  # The 2 x 2 table of counts, rows = first grouping, columns = second, with the
  # retributive side first in both. psych::cohen.kappa reads a square table of
  # counts directly.
  tab <- matrix(c(n11, n01, n10, n00), nrow = 2,
                dimnames = list(first = c("retributive", "other"),
                                second = c("retributive", "other")))
  ck <- suppressWarnings(psych::cohen.kappa(tab))
  kap <- ck$confid["unweighted kappa", ]
  # GUARD: psych's estimate must equal the kappa computed by hand from po and pe.
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(kap["estimate"]), (po - pe) / (1 - pe),
                             tolerance = 1e-8)))
  data.frame(first = unname(p3_side_labels[a]), second = unname(p3_side_labels[b]),
             n = n, both_retributive = n11, first_only = n10,
             second_only = n01, neither = n00,
             agreement = po, chance_agreement = pe,
             kappa = unname(kap["estimate"]),
             kappa_lower = unname(kap["lower"]), kappa_upper = unname(kap["upper"]),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
# Every pair except median split x tertiles. The tertiles are two slices of the
# same median split (the top third lies inside the high half and the bottom
# third inside the low half), so on the people both classify they agree
# perfectly by construction and that pair says nothing.
p3_agreement <- rbind(p3_agree("ranking", "median"),
                      p3_agree("ranking", "ratio"),
                      p3_agree("median", "ratio"),
                      p3_agree("ranking", "tertile"),
                      p3_agree("tertile", "ratio"))
# GUARD: the first two rows must reproduce the raw agreement 5.5 prints from its
# own crosstabs, or the two sections are not describing the same groupings.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(p3_agreement$agreement[1],
                           sum(diag(overlap)) / sum(overlap))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(p3_agreement$agreement[2],
                           sum(diag(overlap2)) / sum(overlap2))))
TABLES[["P3_grouping_agreement"]] <- p3_agreement
show_table(p3_agreement, paste(
  "9.17A: agreement between the retributivist groupings. Raw agreement, the",
  "agreement expected by chance, and Cohen's kappa [95% CI]."))

# What the ranking's retributivists did with the second sentence, beside
# everyone else. 5.4b crosses the three-way grouping (reduced, kept, raised)
# with the ratio split only; this crosses it with the ranking. The share that
# did not reduce is read off the ranking x ratio cells above (retributive under
# both, for the retributivists; retributive under the ratio only, for everyone
# else), as a share of each ranking group, with an exact interval. NOT
# REGISTERED: the three-way grouping is 5.4b's descriptive split.
# The three directions are read straight off 5.4b's factor grp_ratio_dir, whose
# levels are, in order, reduced, no reduction, and increased; indexing by the
# level number relabels them without redefining them. A participant with no
# ratio is NA in the factor and stays NA here.
p3_dir <- c("Reduced", "Kept", "Raised")[as.integer(d$grp_ratio_dir)]
# GUARDS: each label must pick out exactly the ratios it names (a reordering of
# 5.4b's levels would otherwise swap two columns silently), and the two ranking
# groups selected by name below must be the factor's only two levels.
stopifnot(identical(which(p3_dir == "Reduced"), which(d$sentence_ratio < 1)),
          identical(which(p3_dir == "Kept"), which(d$sentence_ratio == 1)),
          identical(which(p3_dir == "Raised"), which(d$sentence_ratio > 1)),
          identical(levels(d$grp_rank), c("Retributivist", "Other")))
p3_dir_rows <- lapply(c("Retributivist", "Other"), function(g) {
  on <- !is.na(d$grp_rank) & d$grp_rank == g & !is.na(p3_dir)
  nr <- prop_ci(as.integer(p3_dir[on] != "Reduced"), "Did not reduce")
  data.frame(group = g, n = sum(on),
             reduced = sum(p3_dir[on] == "Reduced"),
             kept = sum(p3_dir[on] == "Kept"),
             raised = sum(p3_dir[on] == "Raised"),
             share_reduced = mean(p3_dir[on] == "Reduced"),
             share_kept = mean(p3_dir[on] == "Kept"),
             share_raised = mean(p3_dir[on] == "Raised"),
             share_not_reduced = nr$prop,
             not_reduced_ci_lower = nr$ci_lower,
             not_reduced_ci_upper = nr$ci_upper,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})
p3_dir_tab <- do.call(rbind, p3_dir_rows)
# GUARD: the two rows together hold everyone with a ratio and a ranking.
stopifnot(sum(p3_dir_tab$n) == sum(!is.na(p3_dir) & !is.na(d$grp_rank)))
# GUARD: the retributivists who did not reduce are exactly the ranking x ratio
# cell "retributive under both" above.
stopifnot(p3_dir_tab$kept[1] + p3_dir_tab$raised[1] ==
            p3_agreement$both_retributive[2])
TABLES[["P3_sentence_direction_by_ranking"]] <- p3_dir_tab
show_table(p3_dir_tab, paste(
  "9.17A: what each ranking group did with the second sentence. Descriptive;",
  "the share not reducing has an exact 95% CI."))

# --- B. Counts over the registered rows, kept apart from E1 -----------------
# Three row sets. The 21 registered rows (H13 to H21). The five E1 rows in their
# registered scorings (the two-item cognitive-reflection score, which drops the
# mislabelled lily-pad item, is an unregistered rescoring and is left out of
# this set). And every row each run includes (27, or 25 for the three runs
# built from the sentence), which is what 9.12 and 9.12b count, so the guard
# below can tie the two sections together.
p3_crt2_label <- contrast_spec$label[contrast_spec$outcome == "CRT_2item"]
p3_row_sets <- list(
  "Registered (H13 to H21)" = function(r) r$hypothesis %in% paste0("H", 13:21),
  "E1, registered scorings" = function(r) r$hypothesis == "E1" &
                                          r$outcome != p3_crt2_label,
  "All rows run (as counted in 9.12)" = function(r) rep(TRUE, nrow(r)))

#' Score one run of the contrast set
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  res        a result frame from run_contrast_set() or
#'                       run_continuous_set().
#'            est, lo, hi the columns holding the estimate and its 95% limits
#'                       ("d", "d_lower", "d_upper" for a grouping;
#'                       "beta", "ci_lower", "ci_upper" for a continuous run).
#'            run_label  a name for the run.
#' RETURNS    one row per row set: rows run, rows in the predicted direction,
#'            rows at one-sided p < .05, rows whose interval excludes zero on
#'            the predicted side, and the median absolute estimate.
#' The two rules part company whenever the two-sided p falls between .05 and
#' .10: the one-sided test then passes while the two-sided interval still
#' reaches zero. Both counts are kept so the text can say which it uses.
p3_score <- function(res, est, lo, hi, run_label) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(p3_row_sets), function(s) {
    r <- res[p3_row_sets[[s]](res) & !is.na(res[[est]]), ]
    pred   <- ifelse(r$alternative == "less", r[[est]] < 0, r[[est]] > 0)
    clears <- ifelse(r$alternative == "less", r[[hi]] < 0, r[[lo]] > 0)
    data.frame(run = run_label, row_set = s, n_rows = nrow(r),
               n_predicted_sign = sum(pred),
               n_one_sided_p05 = sum(r$p_dir < .05),
               n_interval_clears_zero = sum(clears),
               median_abs_estimate = median(abs(r[[est]])),
               statistic = est, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
}
p3_scorecard <- rbind(
  p3_score(contrasts_rank,  "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "Ranking (primary)"),
  p3_score(contrasts_med,   "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "Median split"),
  p3_score(contrasts_tert,  "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "Tertiles"),
  p3_score(contrasts_ratio, "d", "d_lower", "d_upper", "Sentencing ratio grouping"),
  p3_score(cq_contrasts,    "d", "d_lower", "d_upper",
           "Ranking, against deterrence- or incapacitation-first (not registered)"),
  p3_score(cont_rel,   "beta", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "Relative retribution, continuous"),
  p3_score(cont_raw,   "beta", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "Retribution subscale, continuous"),
  p3_score(cont_ratio, "beta", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "Sentencing ratio, continuous"),
  p3_score(cont_resid, "beta", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
           "Second sentence residualized on the first, continuous"))
# GUARD: over every row each grouping runs (27; 25 for the ratio), the four
# groupings must reproduce 9.12's counts and
# medians, and the ranking and the narrower comparison must reproduce 9.12b's
# interval counts. A mismatch means the row sets above are not the rows those
# sections counted.
p3_all <- p3_scorecard[p3_scorecard$row_set == "All rows run (as counted in 9.12)", ]
stopifnot(
  identical(as.integer(p3_all$n_predicted_sign[1:4]),
            as.integer(agreement$n_predicted_sign)),
  identical(as.integer(p3_all$n_one_sided_p05[1:4]),
            as.integer(agreement$n_directional_p05)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_all$median_abs_estimate[1:4], agreement$median_abs_d)),
  identical(as.integer(p3_all$n_interval_clears_zero[c(1, 5)]),
            as.integer(cq_summary$n_interval_clears_zero)))
TABLES[["P3_scorecard"]] <- p3_scorecard
show_table(p3_scorecard, paste(
  "9.17B: each run of the contrast set, counted over the registered rows, the",
  "five E1 rows in their registered scorings, and every row the run includes",
  "(27, or 25 for the three runs built from the sentence: the ratio grouping,",
  "and the ratio and the residualized second sentence as predictors). Counts of",
  "results above; nothing new is tested."))

# Row by row across the four groupings: whether each outcome reaches one-sided
# p < .05, and whether its interval clears zero, under each. A row the ratio
# grouping does not run (the two sentence-based rows) is NA there.
p3_groupings <- list("Ranking" = contrasts_rank, "Median split" = contrasts_med,
                     "Tertiles" = contrasts_tert,
                     "Sentencing ratio" = contrasts_ratio)
p3_rows <- data.frame(hypothesis = contrast_spec$hypothesis,
                      outcome = contrast_spec$label, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for (p3_g in names(p3_groupings)) {
  p3_r <- p3_groupings[[p3_g]][match(p3_rows$outcome, p3_groupings[[p3_g]]$outcome), ]
  p3_rows[[paste0("p05_", p3_g)]] <- p3_r$p_dir < .05
  p3_rows[[paste0("clears_", p3_g)]] <- ifelse(p3_r$alternative == "less",
                                               p3_r$d_upper < 0, p3_r$d_lower > 0)
}
p3_pcols <- grep("^p05_", names(p3_rows), value = TRUE)
p3_ccols <- grep("^clears_", names(p3_rows), value = TRUE)
p3_rows$n_groupings_run <- rowSums(!is.na(p3_rows[, p3_pcols]))
p3_rows$holds_p05_every_grouping_run <- rowSums(p3_rows[, p3_pcols], na.rm = TRUE) ==
  p3_rows$n_groupings_run
p3_rows$clears_every_grouping_run <- rowSums(p3_rows[, p3_ccols], na.rm = TRUE) ==
  p3_rows$n_groupings_run
TABLES[["P3_rows_across_groupings"]] <- p3_rows
show_table(p3_rows, "9.17B: each contrast under each grouping (one-sided p < .05; interval clears zero)")
p3_reg <- p3_rows[p3_rows$hypothesis %in% paste0("H", 13:21), ]
cat(sprintf(paste("\nOf the %d registered rows that all four groupings run, %d reach",
                  "one-sided p < .05 under all four and %d have an interval clear of",
                  "zero under all four.\n"),
            sum(p3_reg$n_groupings_run == 4),
            sum(p3_reg$n_groupings_run == 4 & p3_reg$holds_p05_every_grouping_run),
            sum(p3_reg$n_groupings_run == 4 & p3_reg$clears_every_grouping_run)))

# --- C. H12 on the retributive side of every grouping, and among others ------
# The same two halves as 9.2, packaged as a function so they can be run on any
# group. Endorsing means a score above 4; each share has an exact interval; each
# attitude is correlated with the eight-item punitiveness scale inside the group.
# cor_row() is called with "greater" exactly as in 9.2, so the one-sided p it
# returns matches 9.2's, and its two-sided p comes back in p_two alongside.
p3_h12_run <- function(sub, grouping_label) {
  shares <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h12_spec)), function(i)
    prop_ci(as.integer(sub[[h12_spec$var[i]]] > 4), h12_spec$label[i])))
  shares <- rbind(shares, prop_ci(sub$shark_kill, "Putting the shark to death (yes)"))
  cors <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h12_spec)), function(i)
    cor_row(sub, "punitiveness", h12_spec$var[i], alternative = "greater",
            label_x = "Punitiveness (self-report)", label_y = h12_spec$label[i])))
  cors <- rbind(cors, cor_row(sub, "punitiveness", "shark_kill",
                              alternative = "greater",
                              label_x = "Punitiveness (self-report)",
                              label_y = "Putting the shark to death (yes)"))
  out <- merge(shares, cors[, c("y", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_dir", "p_two")],
               by.x = "measure", by.y = "y", suffixes = c("_share", "_r"))
  names(out) <- c("attitude", "n", "k_endorsing", "share", "share_ci_lower",
                  "share_ci_upper", "r_with_punitiveness", "r_ci_lower",
                  "r_ci_upper", "p_one_sided", "p_two_sided")
  out$grouping <- grouping_label
  out[order(-out$share), c("grouping", setdiff(names(out), "grouping"))]
}
p3_sub <- list(
  "Ranking (desert first)" = d_retrib,
  "Median split: high half" = d[!is.na(d$grp_med) & d$grp_med == "High rel. retribution", ],
  "Tertiles: top third" = d[!is.na(d$grp_tert) & d$grp_tert == "Top third", ],
  "Sentencing ratio: did not reduce" =
    d[!is.na(d$grp_ratio) & d$grp_ratio == "High sentencing ratio", ])
p3_h12 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(p3_sub), function(g) p3_h12_run(p3_sub[[g]], g)))
rownames(p3_h12) <- NULL
# GUARD: the ranking rows must reproduce 9.2's shares, correlations and
# two-sided p. The row count is checked first, so a label that stopped
# matching cannot leave two empty vectors to compare (all.equal() calls two
# empty vectors equal). The p values are compared on the log scale: on the
# raw scale the largest p would swamp an error in the very small ones.
p3_h12_rank <- p3_h12[p3_h12$grouping == "Ranking (desert first)", ]
p3_h12_chk <- h12[match(p3_h12_rank$attitude, h12$attitude), ]
stopifnot(nrow(p3_h12_rank) == nrow(h12), !anyNA(p3_h12_chk$share))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(p3_h12_rank$share, p3_h12_chk$share)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(p3_h12_rank$r_with_punitiveness,
                           p3_h12_chk$r_with_punitiveness)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(log(p3_h12_rank$p_two_sided), log(p3_h12_chk$p_two_sided))))
TABLES[["P3_H12_other_groupings"]] <- p3_h12
show_table(p3_h12, paste(
  "9.17C: H12 on the retributive side of each grouping. Shares above the",
  "midpoint with exact CIs; r with punitiveness inside the group, one- and",
  "two-sided p. The ranking rows reprint 9.2."))

# The shares among everyone else under the ranking (n = 577). NOT REGISTERED:
# H12 concerns retributivists only. The registered comparison of the same
# measures between the groups is the set of mean differences in H13, H15 and
# H20. These shares are descriptive, and no difference in shares is tested.
p3_h12_other <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(h12_spec)), function(i)
  prop_ci(as.integer(d_other[[h12_spec$var[i]]] > 4), h12_spec$label[i])))
p3_h12_other <- rbind(p3_h12_other,
                      prop_ci(d_other$shark_kill, "Putting the shark to death (yes)"))
names(p3_h12_other) <- c("attitude", "n", "k_endorsing", "share",
                         "share_ci_lower", "share_ci_upper")
TABLES[["P3_H12_everyone_else"]] <- p3_h12_other
show_table(p3_h12_other, paste(
  "9.17C: the same shares among everyone else under the ranking (n = 577).",
  "Descriptive; not registered."))

# --- D. The H15 shark decision under every grouping --------------------------
# A logistic regression of the yes/no decision on a 0/1 indicator of the
# retributive side, one-sided "greater", exactly as 9.6 runs it for the ranking.
# Each grouping uses only the people it classifies (the tertiles drop the middle
# third).
p3_d$side_rank  <- p3_side$ranking
p3_d$side_med   <- p3_side$median
p3_d$side_tert  <- p3_side$tertile
p3_d$side_ratio <- p3_side$ratio
p3_h15 <- rbind(
  logit_reg(p3_d, "shark_kill", "side_rank", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Ranking (desert first)"),
  logit_reg(p3_d, "shark_kill", "side_med", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Median split on relative retribution"),
  logit_reg(p3_d, "shark_kill", "side_tert", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Top vs bottom third of relative retribution"),
  logit_reg(p3_d, "shark_kill", "side_ratio", alternative = "greater",
            label = "Sentencing ratio (no reduction vs reduction)"))
# logit_reg() writes its label into a column named `outcome`. Here the label is
# the grouping, so that column is renamed and the outcome named explicitly.
names(p3_h15)[names(p3_h15) == "outcome"] <- "grouping"
p3_h15$outcome <- "Put the shark to death (yes/no)"
# GUARD: the ranking row must reproduce 9.6.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(p3_h15$OR[1], h15_logit$OR)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(p3_h15$p_dir[1], h15_logit$p_dir)))
TABLES[["P3_H15_other_groupings"]] <- p3_h15
show_table(p3_h15[, c("grouping", "n", "b", "OR", "OR_lower", "OR_upper", "z",
                      "p_dir", "p_two")], paste(
  "9.17D: the H15 shark decision under each grouping (logistic regression,",
  "one-sided). The first row reprints 9.6."))
# The share saying yes on each side of each grouping, with exact intervals.
p3_h15_shares <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(p3_side), function(g) rbind(
  cbind(grouping = unname(p3_side_labels[g]), side = "Retributive side",
        prop_ci(d$shark_kill[!is.na(p3_side[[g]]) & p3_side[[g]] == 1], "yes")),
  cbind(grouping = unname(p3_side_labels[g]), side = "Other side",
        prop_ci(d$shark_kill[!is.na(p3_side[[g]]) & p3_side[[g]] == 0], "yes")))))
TABLES[["P3_H15_shares"]] <- p3_h15_shares
show_table(p3_h15_shares, "9.17D: share saying yes to putting the shark to death, by grouping and side")

# --- E. H11 inside the retributive side of every grouping -------------------
# The same functions as 9.1, called on each retributive side. Each run is boiled
# down to the numbers the write-up reports, in long form: one row per quantity.
# The ranking is run too, and the guard checks that the summary reproduces 9.1,
# so the other three groupings are read off the same machinery. The whole sample
# is run as well, as the reference column for Table S2; its guard checks it
# against the Phase 7 and 8 objects (h1_full, 7.1; h10_full, 8.7).
#
# WHAT EACH QUANTITY READS (each test keeps its registered direction):
#   H1_*   the twelve correlations with punitiveness; the count significant
#          uses the one-sided p after the BH adjustment within the group.
#   H2_*, H10_*  Steiger's difference between two correlations with
#          punitiveness, Zou interval, one-sided p.
#   H3_*   share of the 66 intercorrelations above zero, the first
#          eigenvalue's share of variance, and the mean intercorrelation.
#   H4_*   row 1 of run_h4()$tests: the single proportionality item against
#          the midpoint of 4, one-sided "less" (so p near 1 = the reverse).
#   H5_d   paired d, punishing beyond the crime minus below the harm.
#   H6_*   r and alpha of the two halves of just deserts (two-sided), and the
#          CFA's CFI and RMSEA, NA when the model did not return fit indices.
#   H7_*   the six limits with revenge (rows 1-6, one-sided) and with just
#          deserts (rows 7-12, two-sided).
#   H8_*   the six limits with punitiveness, one-sided.
#   H9_*   row 1 of run_h9(): just deserts minus revenge, paired d.
p3_h11_summary <- function(sub, grouping_label) {
  h1 <- run_h1(sub); h2 <- run_h2(sub); h3 <- run_h3(sub); h4 <- run_h4(sub)
  h5 <- run_h5(sub); h6 <- suppressWarnings(run_h6(sub)); h7 <- run_h7(sub)
  h8 <- run_h8(sub); h9 <- run_h9(sub); h10 <- run_h10(sub)
  # run_h7 stacks the revenge side (rows 1 to 6, one-sided) above the
  # just-deserts side (rows 7 to 12, two-sided, since that side predicts no
  # relation).
  rev <- h7[1:6, ]; jd <- h7[7:12, ]
  fm <- h6$fit_measures
  v <- c(
    H1_n_positive_of_12   = sum(h1$r > 0),
    H1_n_BH_significant   = sum(h1$p_BH_one_sided < .05),
    H1_median_r           = median(h1$r),
    H1_min_r              = min(h1$r),
    H1_max_r              = max(h1$r),
    H2_diff               = h2$diff, H2_diff_lower = h2$diff_lower,
    H2_diff_upper         = h2$diff_upper, H2_z = h2$z, H2_p_one_sided = h2$p,
    H3_share_positive     = h3$share_positive,
    H3_first_eigen_share  = h3$var_explained_1,
    H3_mean_r             = h3$mean_r,
    H4_item_mean          = h4$tests$mean[1], H4_item_d = h4$tests$d[1],
    H4_item_p_one_sided   = h4$tests$p_dir[1],
    H5_d                  = h5$d[1], H5_p_one_sided = h5$p_dir[1],
    H6_r                  = h6$cor$r, H6_r_lower = h6$cor$ci_lower,
    H6_r_upper            = h6$cor$ci_upper, H6_alpha = h6$alpha_two_parts,
    H6_cfi                = if (is.null(fm)) NA_real_ else unname(fm[["cfi"]]),
    H6_rmsea              = if (is.null(fm)) NA_real_ else unname(fm[["rmsea"]]),
    H7_revenge_n_p05_of_6 = sum(rev$p_directional < .05),
    H7_revenge_median_r   = median(rev$r),
    H7_jd_n_positive_of_6 = sum(jd$r > 0),
    H7_jd_n_two_sided_p05 = sum(jd$p_two < .05),
    H7_jd_median_r        = median(jd$r),
    H8_n_p05_of_6         = sum(h8$p_one_sided < .05),
    H8_median_r           = median(h8$r),
    H9_jd_vs_revenge_d    = h9$d[1], H9_p_one_sided = h9$p_dir[1],
    H10_diff              = h10$diff, H10_diff_lower = h10$diff_lower,
    H10_diff_upper        = h10$diff_upper, H10_z = h10$z,
    H10_p_one_sided       = h10$p)
  data.frame(grouping = grouping_label, n = nrow(sub), quantity = names(v),
             value = unname(v), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
p3_h11 <- rbind(p3_h11_summary(d, "Whole sample"),
                do.call(rbind, lapply(names(p3_sub), function(g)
                  p3_h11_summary(p3_sub[[g]], g))))
rownames(p3_h11) <- NULL
# GUARD: the ranking summary must reproduce the H11 objects of 9.1, and the
# whole-sample summary the Phase 7 and 8 objects. p3_q() insists on exactly one
# match, so a label that stopped matching stops the knit instead of passing.
p3_q <- function(g, q) {
  v <- p3_h11$value[p3_h11$grouping == g & p3_h11$quantity == q]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
stopifnot(
  p3_q("Whole sample", "H1_n_positive_of_12") == sum(h1_full$r > 0),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_q("Whole sample", "H10_diff"), h10_full$diff)),
  p3_q("Ranking (desert first)", "H1_n_positive_of_12") == sum(h11_h1$r > 0),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_q("Ranking (desert first)", "H2_diff"), h11_h2$diff)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_q("Ranking (desert first)", "H10_diff"), h11_h10$diff)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_q("Ranking (desert first)", "H9_jd_vs_revenge_d"), h11_h9$d[1])),
  isTRUE(all.equal(p3_q("Ranking (desert first)", "H6_r"), h11_h6$cor$r)))
TABLES[["P3_H11_other_groupings"]] <- p3_h11
show_table(tidyr::pivot_wider(p3_h11[, c("grouping", "quantity", "value")],
                              names_from = grouping, values_from = value),
           paste("9.17E: H1 to H10 in the whole sample and inside the retributive",
                 "side of each grouping (H11). The whole-sample column reprints",
                 "Phases 7 and 8; the ranking column reprints 9.1."))

# --- F. The two rescorings in the retributivist contrasts -------------------
# NOT REGISTERED. 7.4 scores punitiveness by its five parts with equal weight
# (and six parts with the sentence), and 7.2b adds harsh prison conditions to
# the hostile-aggression cluster as a sixth constituent. Both were checked there
# on the whole-sample tests only. Here they go through the same contrast
# machinery as the registered scores, beside them, under every grouping and
# both continuous predictors. The six-part punitiveness score contains the
# sentence, so like the registered full index it is not run under the ratio.
# p5_d is 7.4's private copy of d, which carries punit_parts5 and punit_parts6;
# hostile_agg6 is already in d (4.9b). A SEPARATE spec is used, so the frozen
# contrast_spec is not touched.
stopifnot(all(c("punit_parts5", "punit_parts6", "hostile_agg6") %in% names(p5_d)))
p3_spec_rescored <- data.frame(
  outcome = c("hostile_agg", "hostile_agg6", "punitiveness", "punit_parts5",
              "punitiveness_full", "punit_parts6"),
  label = c("Hostile-aggression cluster, registered five constituents (z)",
            "Hostile-aggression cluster, six constituents (z)",
            "Punitiveness, registered eight-item scale",
            "Punitiveness, five parts weighted equally",
            "Punitiveness, registered full index (with the sentence)",
            "Punitiveness, six parts weighted equally (with the sentence)"),
  hypothesis = c("H13", "H13", "H21", "H21", "H21", "H21"),
  alternative = "greater",
  sentence_based = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  feature = NA_character_, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#' Run the rescored spec under one grouping
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  gcol    a grouping column of p5_d ("grp_rank", "grp_med", ...).
#'            glabel  a name for the run.
#'            drop    TRUE for the sentencing ratio, which may not be crossed
#'                    with a score that contains the sentence.
#' RETURNS    one row per score: group sizes, d with its 95% interval, and
#'            the one-sided p.
p3_resc_group <- function(gcol, glabel, drop) {
  r <- run_contrast_set(p5_d, gcol, spec = p3_spec_rescored, drop_sentence_based = drop)
  data.frame(run = glabel, outcome = r$outcome, n1 = r$n1, n2 = r$n2,
             estimate = r$d, lower = r$d_lower, upper = r$d_upper,
             p_one_sided = r$p_dir, statistic = "d", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
#' Run the rescored spec with one continuous predictor
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  pred    the predictor column ("retribution_rel" or "retribution").
#'            plabel  a name for the run.
#' RETURNS    one row per score: n, the standardized slope with its 95%
#'            interval, and the one-sided p, in the same columns as above.
p3_resc_cont <- function(pred, plabel) {
  r <- run_continuous_set(p5_d, pred, spec = p3_spec_rescored)
  data.frame(run = plabel, outcome = r$outcome, n1 = r$n, n2 = NA_integer_,
             estimate = r$beta, lower = r$ci_lower, upper = r$ci_upper,
             p_one_sided = r$p_dir, statistic = "beta", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
p3_rescored <- rbind(
  p3_resc_group("grp_rank",  "Ranking (primary)", FALSE),
  p3_resc_group("grp_med",   "Median split", FALSE),
  p3_resc_group("grp_tert",  "Tertiles", FALSE),
  p3_resc_group("grp_ratio", "Sentencing ratio grouping", TRUE),
  p3_resc_cont("retribution_rel", "Relative retribution, continuous"),
  p3_resc_cont("retribution", "Retribution subscale, continuous"))
# GUARD: every registered score's estimate must reproduce the registered run,
# or the rescored rows beside them are not comparable. The five-constituent
# cluster and the eight-item scale are checked under all six runs; the full
# index, which the ratio does not run, under the other five.
#' Does a registered score's row here equal the registered run?
#'
#' ARGUMENTS  run      the run name used in p3_rescored.
#'            reg      the registered result frame (contrasts_rank, cont_rel, ...).
#'            lab_new  the score's label in p3_spec_rescored.
#'            lab_old  the same score's label in contrast_spec.
#' RETURNS    TRUE when the two estimates agree. Each lookup must find exactly
#'            one value; two empty lookups would otherwise count as equal.
p3_chk <- function(run, reg, lab_new, lab_old) {
  a <- p3_rescored$estimate[p3_rescored$run == run & p3_rescored$outcome == lab_new]
  b <- reg[reg$outcome == lab_old, if ("d" %in% names(reg)) "d" else "beta"]
  stopifnot(length(a) == 1, length(b) == 1)
  isTRUE(all.equal(a, b))
}
p3_reg_pairs <- list(
  c("Hostile-aggression cluster, registered five constituents (z)",
    "Hostile-aggression cluster (z)"),
  c("Punitiveness, registered eight-item scale", "Punitiveness (self-report, 8 items)"))
for (p3_pr in p3_reg_pairs) stopifnot(
  p3_chk("Ranking (primary)", contrasts_rank, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]),
  p3_chk("Median split", contrasts_med, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]),
  p3_chk("Tertiles", contrasts_tert, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]),
  p3_chk("Sentencing ratio grouping", contrasts_ratio, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]),
  p3_chk("Relative retribution, continuous", cont_rel, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]),
  p3_chk("Retribution subscale, continuous", cont_raw, p3_pr[1], p3_pr[2]))
p3_full <- c("Punitiveness, registered full index (with the sentence)",
             "Punitiveness (full index, + sentence)")
stopifnot(
  p3_chk("Ranking (primary)", contrasts_rank, p3_full[1], p3_full[2]),
  p3_chk("Median split", contrasts_med, p3_full[1], p3_full[2]),
  p3_chk("Tertiles", contrasts_tert, p3_full[1], p3_full[2]),
  p3_chk("Relative retribution, continuous", cont_rel, p3_full[1], p3_full[2]),
  p3_chk("Retribution subscale, continuous", cont_raw, p3_full[1], p3_full[2]))
TABLES[["P3_rescored_contrasts"]] <- p3_rescored
show_table(p3_rescored, paste(
  "9.17F: the registered scores and their rescorings, under every grouping and",
  "both continuous predictors. One-sided p; not registered."))
```

## 9.18 Political orientation and prosecution leaning as moderators (prereg 6.6)

Prereg 6.6 lists "political orientation and the prosecution-defense leaning as
moderators" among the exploratory analyses, which "are not corrected as a
confirmatory family". It names no outcome, no model and no direction. A
moderator is a variable that changes the strength of a relationship. The
question here is whether the link between retributivism and punitiveness is
stronger or weaker depending on a person's politics, or on which side of a
criminal trial they identify with.

The eight moderation models are carried over unchanged from Phase 6.3 of
`03_supplementary_analyses.Rmd`, where they were first specified, so that the
numbers reported come from this document, the analysis of record. Four sets are
produced, and each says what it adds to 03.

- **A. The two moderators.** Their descriptives, the raw answer counts behind
  them, and their correlation with each other. The correlation is new; 03
  printed only n, mean and SD, and the counts of the two leaning items.
- **B. Zero-order correlations** of each moderator with six variables:
  punitiveness, relative retribution, the sentencing ratio, the hostile
  aggression cluster, the first sentence, and revenge. A zero-order correlation
  is the plain correlation between two variables, with nothing held constant.
  These are 03's twelve correlations.
- **C. Eight moderation models.** Each regresses an outcome on a retributivism
  measure, a moderator, and their product. The coefficient on the product, the
  interaction, is the moderation test. 03 reported each interaction's
  coefficient, standard error, t and p, and each model's R-squared. Added here:
  the interaction's 95% interval, the R-squared change it brings, the two other
  coefficients, and the slope of the retributivism measure at three levels of
  the moderator (one standard deviation below its mean, at its mean, and one
  above), so that a reader can see what each interaction means. The slopes are
  computed for all eight models, not only for those whose interaction reached
  p < .05.
- **D. The moderators by retributivist group**, under the four registered
  groupings, built with this document's grouping factors (Phase 5) and its Welch
  contrast (0.3). This replaces 03's version (its 6.4), which differed in three
  ways: its median split sent the participants tied at the median to the high
  side (476 against 472), where 5.3 here sends them to the low side (470
  against 478); its d used the pooled standard deviation with a normal-theory
  interval, where welch_contrast() uses the unpooled one with a noncentral-t
  interval; and it left out the tertiles. The political-orientation row under
  the median split therefore does not match 03's.
