**What is registered.** The prosecution-leaning rows of D are H18, which is
registered as a one-sided prediction ("Retributivists side more with the
prosecution than the defense") under all four groupings (prereg 5.3), and
which 9.7, 9.10 and 9.11 report that way. D repeats them two-sided only so that
they sit beside political orientation, and a guard checks that they match. Nothing
else here is registered as a test. The registration predicts no direction for
the moderation models, the correlations, or the group differences in political
orientation, so every p value in this section is two-sided. Nothing is
corrected for multiplicity, and nothing enters a registered family.

```{r phase9_moderators_vars}
# === 9.18A THE TWO MODERATORS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: checks the two moderator columns built earlier in the
# document, prints their descriptives and raw answer counts, and correlates
# them with each other. Produces `mod_desc` (exported as MOD_descriptives),
# `mod_counts` (MOD_response_counts) and `mod_between` (MOD_between).
# PREREG: 5.13 names the measures; 6.6 asks for them as moderators.
#         Exploratory. The correlation between the two moderators is not in
#         03 and is description, not a registered test.
# CONSUMES: d$libcons (the alias 1.2 makes for the Qualtrics column
#           `lib/conserv`), d$leanPros (built in 4.8 from leanPros_1 and
#           leanPros_2), cor_row(), format_p(), show_table().
# NOTHING IN 9.18 WRITES TO d. The centred variables of 9.18C live in a data
# frame that exists only inside each model fit.
# NAMING: every object in 9.18 starts with mod_, and every export with MOD_.

# --- The two moderators, as the rest of the document already defines them ---
# Political orientation is the single liberal-conservative item. Prereg 5.13
# names it; the instrument scores it 1 = strongly liberal to 7 = strongly
# conservative, with anchor text on the two endpoints only. 1.2 copies the
# column to the plain name `libcons`, because the slash in `lib/conserv` would
# otherwise need backticks in every formula.
#
# Prosecution leaning is the mean of two items: whom the participant identifies
# with at a real trial (leanPros_1), and which role they would rather serve
# (leanPros_2). Each is answered 1 = prosecutor, 2 = defense attorney, 3 = about
# the same. 4.8 recodes each answer to +1 / -1 / 0, so the mean runs from -1
# (defense on both items) through 0 to +1 (prosecution on both), and higher
# means leaning toward the prosecution. 03 built the same score under the name
# pros_lean; this section uses 4.8's column, so there is one score, not two.

# GUARDS. The moderation models below are only as good as these two columns, so
# each is checked against its source before anything is fitted.
#   1. Every column this section reads exists.
#   2. libcons is still an exact copy of the raw item, and lies on 1 to 7.
#   3. leanPros, rebuilt here from the raw items by a DIFFERENT route (a lookup
#      vector rather than 4.8's case_when), matches 4.8's column exactly. Two
#      independent routes agreeing is what rules out a slip in either one,
#      such as the neutral answer and the defense answer being swapped.
#   4. leanPros takes only the five values a mean of two -1/0/+1 answers can
#      take.
stopifnot(all(c("libcons", "lib/conserv", "leanPros", "leanPros_1",
                "leanPros_2") %in% names(d)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(d$libcons), as.numeric(d[["lib/conserv"]]))),
          all(d$libcons %in% c(1:7, NA)))
# The lookup vector: its names are the answer codes as text, its values the
# signed scores. Indexing it by as.character(code) returns the score, and an
# unexpected code (or NA) returns NA rather than a wrong number.
mod_sign <- c("1" = 1, "2" = -1, "3" = 0)
mod_lean_check <- rowMeans(cbind(unname(mod_sign[as.character(d$leanPros_1)]),
                                 unname(mod_sign[as.character(d$leanPros_2)])),
                           na.rm = TRUE)
# rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) returns NaN ("not a number") for a row with nothing to
# average; set those to NA, as 4.8 does, so the comparison is like for like.
mod_lean_check[is.nan(mod_lean_check)] <- NA_real_
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(d$leanPros), mod_lean_check)),
          all(d$leanPros %in% c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, NA)))

# --- Descriptives ------------------------------------------------------------
# n, mean, SD (standard deviation, the usual measure of spread), median and the
# observed range of each moderator. The shares below, at and above the midpoint
# are added, because a sentence such as "the sample leaned slightly liberal" or
# "more participants leaned toward the prosecution than toward the defense" has
# to rest on them, not on the mean alone.
mod_desc_row <- function(x, label, low_label, mid_value, high_label) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  data.frame(moderator = label, n = length(x), M = mean(x), SD = stats::sd(x),
             Mdn = stats::median(x), min = min(x), max = max(x),
             pct_below_mid = 100 * mean(x < mid_value),
             pct_at_mid    = 100 * mean(x == mid_value),
             pct_above_mid = 100 * mean(x > mid_value),
             below_means = low_label, above_means = high_label,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
mod_desc <- rbind(
  # For political orientation the midpoint is 4, the unlabelled middle of the
  # 1 to 7 scale, so "below" is the liberal side and "above" the conservative.
  mod_desc_row(d$libcons, "Political orientation (1 = strongly liberal, 7 = strongly conservative)",
               "liberal (1 to 3)", 4, "conservative (5 to 7)"),
  # For prosecution leaning the midpoint is 0: "about the same" on both items,
  # or one item each way.
  mod_desc_row(d$leanPros, "Prosecution leaning (-1 = defense, +1 = prosecution)",
               "toward the defense", 0, "toward the prosecution"))
TABLES[["MOD_descriptives"]] <- mod_desc
show_table(mod_desc, "9.18A: the two moderators", digits = 2)

# --- Raw answer counts --------------------------------------------------------
# The answer counts behind each score, one row per answer. These are what a
# reader needs to judge whether a moderator has enough spread to moderate
# anything: a moderator on which nearly everyone gave the same answer cannot
# change the strength of a relationship, whatever its interaction coefficient
# says.
mod_count_rows <- function(x, item, labels) {
  tab <- table(factor(x, levels = as.numeric(names(labels))), useNA = "no")
  data.frame(item = item, value = as.numeric(names(tab)),
             answer = unname(labels[names(tab)]), n = as.integer(tab),
             pct = 100 * as.integer(tab) / sum(tab), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
mod_lean_labels <- c("1" = "prosecutor", "2" = "defense attorney", "3" = "about the same")
mod_counts <- rbind(
  mod_count_rows(d$libcons, "Political orientation",
                 c("1" = "strongly liberal", "2" = "", "3" = "", "4" = "",
                   "5" = "", "6" = "", "7" = "strongly conservative")),
  mod_count_rows(d$leanPros_1, "leanPros_1: whom do you identify with at a trial", mod_lean_labels),
  mod_count_rows(d$leanPros_2, "leanPros_2: which role would you rather serve", mod_lean_labels),
  mod_count_rows(d$leanPros, "Prosecution leaning (mean of the two, recoded)",
                 c("-1" = "defense on both", "-0.5" = "", "0" = "neutral or split",
                   "0.5" = "", "1" = "prosecution on both")))
# Each item's counts must add up to the number of people who answered it, or a
# code outside the expected set has been dropped silently by factor().
stopifnot(sum(mod_counts$n[mod_counts$item == "Political orientation"]) == sum(!is.na(d$libcons)),
          sum(mod_counts$n[startsWith(mod_counts$item, "leanPros_1")]) == sum(!is.na(d$leanPros_1)),
          sum(mod_counts$n[startsWith(mod_counts$item, "leanPros_2")]) == sum(!is.na(d$leanPros_2)),
          sum(mod_counts$n[startsWith(mod_counts$item, "Prosecution")]) == sum(!is.na(d$leanPros)))
TABLES[["MOD_response_counts"]] <- mod_counts
show_table(mod_counts, "9.18A: answer counts behind the two moderators", digits = 1)

# --- How far the two moderators overlap --------------------------------------
# If conservatives were also, almost to a person, the ones who sided with the
# prosecution, the two sets of models in 9.18C would be two views of one
# moderator rather than two moderators. Their correlation says how far that is
# so. Two-sided; description, not a registered test.
mod_between <- cor_row(d, "libcons", "leanPros", alternative = "two.sided",
                       label_x = "Political orientation (conservative)",
                       label_y = "Prosecution leaning")
TABLES[["MOD_between"]] <- mod_between
cat(sprintf("Political orientation with prosecution leaning: r = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f], n = %d, two-sided p %s\n",
            mod_between$r, mod_between$ci_lower, mod_between$ci_upper,
            mod_between$n, format_p(mod_between$p_two)))
```

```{r phase9_moderators_correlations}
# === 9.18B ZERO-ORDER CORRELATIONS OF EACH MODERATOR ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: correlates each moderator with six variables and
# produces `mod_cors` (exported as MOD_correlations). Also defines the display
# labels `mod_vars` and `mod_mods`, which 9.18C and 9.18D reuse.
# PREREG: 6.6, exploratory. Twelve correlations, two-sided, UNADJUSTED. 6.6
#         declares no family for them, and they are reported as context for
#         the interactions in 9.18C, not as tests.
# CONSUMES: d; cor_row() and get_cor_ci() (0.3); show_table().
#
# WHY THESE COME FIRST. The interactions in 9.18C say how the slope of a
# retributivism measure changes across a moderator. These correlations give the
# plain relation of each moderator with the same variables, so that each
# interaction can be read beside the relations it modifies.
#
# The six variables are 03's, unchanged:
#   punitiveness     the registered 8-item self-report scale (4.2), which
#                    contains no part of the sentence.
#   retribution_rel  relative retribution (5.2): the retribution subscale minus
#                    the mean of the other goals.
#   sentence_ratio   second sentence over first (5.4).
#   hostile_agg      the registered five-member hostile aggression cluster (4.9).
#   Sentence1_z      the first sentence, standardized within vignette (3.2).
#                    Within-vignette, because the three crimes differ in
#                    severity, so raw years are not comparable across them.
#   revenge          the revenge composite (4.3).
# Some of the six overlap: the hostile aggression cluster contains revenge, and
# the sentencing ratio and the first sentence are both built from the first
# sentence. That does no harm here, because each row correlates a moderator with
# ONE of the six; no row relates two of them to each other.
mod_vars <- c(punitiveness    = "Punitiveness (8-item scale)",
              retribution_rel = "Relative retribution",
              sentence_ratio  = "Sentencing ratio",
              hostile_agg     = "Hostile aggression cluster",
              Sentence1_z     = "First sentence (z within vignette)",
              revenge         = "Revenge")
mod_mods <- c(libcons  = "Political orientation (conservative)",
              leanPros = "Prosecution leaning")
# A variable that failed to build would give a row of NAs from cor_row() and a
# table that looks like a null finding. Stop instead.
stopifnot(all(c(names(mod_vars), names(mod_mods)) %in% names(d)))

mod_cors <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mod_mods), function(m) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mod_vars), function(v) {
    cor_row(d, m, v, alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = mod_mods[[m]], label_y = mod_vars[[v]])
  }))
}))
# p_dir equals p_two for a two-sided call, so only one is kept, under a name
# that says which it is. `alternative` is constant and is dropped too.
mod_cors <- mod_cors[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")]
names(mod_cors)[1:2] <- c("moderator", "variable")

# GUARDS. Every row must have run (no NA r, n of at least 30). Then each row's
# r is recomputed with the document's other correlation helper, get_cor_ci(),
# on the column names looked up FROM THE ROW'S OWN LABELS. So the check fails if
# a label was attached to the wrong pair of columns, as well as if the two
# routines disagree.
stopifnot(!anyNA(mod_cors$r), all(mod_cors$n >= 30))
mod_chk <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(mod_cors)), function(i) {
  m <- names(mod_mods)[match(mod_cors$moderator[i], mod_mods)]
  v <- names(mod_vars)[match(mod_cors$variable[i], mod_vars)]
  unname(get_cor_ci(m, v, d)["r"])
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(mod_chk, mod_cors$r)))

TABLES[["MOD_correlations"]] <- mod_cors
show_table(mod_cors, paste("9.18B: zero-order correlations of each moderator",
                           "(two-sided, unadjusted; 95% CI)"))
```

```{r phase9_moderators_models}
# === 9.18C THE EIGHT MODERATION MODELS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: fits eight regressions of the form
#   outcome ~ predictor + moderator + predictor x moderator
# and reports the interaction from each, with the slope of the predictor at
# three levels of the moderator. Produces `mod_results` (exported as
# MOD_interactions) and `mod_slopes` (MOD_simple_slopes).
# PREREG: 6.6, "political orientation and the prosecution-defense leaning as
#         moderators". Exploratory. The registration names no outcome, model
#         or direction; the grid below is 03's (Phase 6.3), unchanged. Every p
#         value in both tables is two-sided. The interval, the R-squared
#         change, the two other coefficients and the simple slopes are
#         additions to 03, made for every model.
# CONSUMES: d; the predictors retribution_rel (5.2) and sentence_ratio (5.4);
#           the outcomes punitiveness (4.2), hostile_agg (4.9) and Sentence1_z
#           (3.2); the moderators libcons (1.2) and leanPros (4.8), checked in
#           9.18A; the labels mod_vars and mod_mods (9.18B); format_p(),
#           show_table().
#
# EIGHT INTERACTIONS, NO CORRECTION ACROSS THEM. This is the largest set of
# tests in the section and the most tempting place to apply a correction, so
# the reason is stated here. 6.6 places these analyses outside both registered
# families, and the eight models were never declared a family of their own.
# Correcting them here would mean choosing a family after seeing the data, and
# the adjusted p it produced would be one more choice made after the fact
# rather than a control on error. They are read as exploratory, alongside the
# coefficient, its interval and the slopes.
#
# WHAT AN INTERACTION COEFFICIENT MEANS HERE. In outcome ~ x * m, the
# coefficient on x:m is how much the slope of x changes for each one-unit step
# up the moderator. With political orientation, one unit is one point on the
# 1 to 7 scale. With prosecution leaning, one unit is half the scale's width,
# the whole way from neutral (0) to prosecution on both items (+1). So the two
# moderators' coefficients are not on a common footing and should not be
# compared by size. The slopes at -1 SD, the mean and +1 SD put them on one.

# --- The grid ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Written out row by row rather than generated by crossing every predictor with
# every outcome. Writing it out keeps the pairings that must never appear
# visible and checkable: an automatic expand.grid() would produce them.
#
# Relative retribution predicts three outcomes. The sentencing ratio predicts
# only the 8-item punitiveness scale. Prereg 5.3 and 5.11 require the
# sentence-free scale wherever the ratio appears together with punitiveness;
# giving the ratio no hostile-aggression model was 03's choice, kept here.
mod_specs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~y,             ~x,                ~m,
  "punitiveness", "retribution_rel", "libcons",
  "punitiveness", "retribution_rel", "leanPros",
  "hostile_agg",  "retribution_rel", "libcons",
  "hostile_agg",  "retribution_rel", "leanPros",
  "Sentence1_z",  "retribution_rel", "libcons",
  "Sentence1_z",  "retribution_rel", "leanPros",
  "punitiveness", "sentence_ratio",  "libcons",
  "punitiveness", "sentence_ratio",  "leanPros"
)
# HAZARD, and the guard that enforces it. There is deliberately no model of the
# first sentence on the sentencing ratio. The ratio is Sentence2 / Sentence1, so
# such a model would regress the first sentence on a quantity built from
# itself, and would find a relation whatever people believed. Swapping
# `punitiveness` for punitiveness_full in the two ratio rows would do the same
# thing by a back door, since the full index contains Sentence1_z. The check
# below stops the knit if anyone adds either pairing.
stopifnot(!any(mod_specs$x == "sentence_ratio" &
               mod_specs$y %in% c("Sentence1", "Sentence1_z", "Sentence2",
                                  "sentence_resid", "punitiveness_full")),
          nrow(mod_specs) == 8,
          all(unlist(mod_specs) %in% names(d)))

mod_labels <- c(mod_vars, mod_mods)

# --- One model --------------------------------------------------------------
# ARGUMENTS  y, x, m: column names of the outcome, the predictor and the
#            moderator.
# RETURNS    a list with `row`, a one-row data frame for the interaction table,
#            and `slopes`, a three-row data frame for the simple slopes table.
# Reads d and writes nothing to it.
mod_fit <- function(y, x, m) {
  # LISTWISE on the three model variables: a participant missing any of them is
  # left out of this model, and only this one. Fitting on one common set of
  # people means the coefficients all describe the same participants, and it
  # is what makes the n in the table meaningful. In practice only the one
  # participant with no sentencing ratio (whose first sentence was zero) drops
  # out, from the two ratio models.
  sub <- d[stats::complete.cases(d[, c(y, x, m)]), c(y, x, m)]
  # 30 complete cases is a floor for a four-parameter model, not a power
  # threshold. Every model here has over 900.
  stopifnot(nrow(sub) >= 30)

  # MEAN-CENTRING, within this model's own participants. Each predictor has its
  # mean subtracted, so 0 now means "average". Centring does NOT change the
  # interaction coefficient, its standard error or its p value; guard 1 below
  # checks all three on every model. What it changes are the two other
  # coefficients. In a model with a product term, the coefficient on x is the
  # slope of x when m is 0. Uncentred, that would be the slope of retributivism
  # for someone with political orientation 0, a value off the 1 to 7 scale.
  # Centred, it is the slope at the sample's mean orientation, a value that
  # exists. `md` is local to this function, so the centred columns never reach
  # d.
  md <- data.frame(y = sub[[y]],
                   x_c = sub[[x]] - mean(sub[[x]]),
                   m_c = sub[[m]] - mean(sub[[m]]))
  fit     <- stats::lm(y ~ x_c * m_c, data = md)   # expands to x_c + m_c + x_c:m_c
  fit_add <- stats::lm(y ~ x_c + m_c, data = md)   # the same model without the product
  co <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  ci <- stats::confint(fit, level = 0.95)
  df_res <- fit$df.residual
  b  <- co["x_c:m_c", "Estimate"]
  se <- co["x_c:m_c", "Std. Error"]
  tv <- co["x_c:m_c", "t value"]
  pv <- co["x_c:m_c", "Pr(>|t|)"]

  # GUARDS on this model.
  #   1. The uncentred model gives the same interaction coefficient, standard
  #      error and p value, to within rounding, as the comment above claims.
  #      Row 4 of an `a ~ b * c` fit is the b:c term.
  #   2. lm()'s p is the two-sided p for this t on these degrees of freedom.
  #   3. The F test for adding the product term to the additive model (anova)
  #      gives the same p as the interaction's t test, since for one added term
  #      F = t squared. This also checks the R-squared change reported below.
  raw    <- stats::lm(stats::as.formula(sprintf("%s ~ %s * %s", y, x, m)), data = sub)
  raw_co <- summary(raw)$coefficients
  stopifnot(grepl(":", rownames(raw_co)[4]),
            isTRUE(all.equal(unname(raw_co[4, c("Estimate", "Std. Error", "Pr(>|t|)")]),
                             c(b, se, pv), tolerance = 1e-8)),
            isTRUE(all.equal(pv, 2 * stats::pt(-abs(tv), df_res))),
            isTRUE(all.equal(stats::anova(fit_add, fit)[2, "Pr(>F)"], pv)))

  r2     <- summary(fit)$r.squared
  r2_add <- summary(fit_add)$r.squared

  row <- data.frame(
    outcome = mod_labels[[y]], predictor = mod_labels[[x]], moderator = mod_labels[[m]],
    n = nrow(sub), df = df_res,
    # The interaction: how much the predictor's slope changes per unit of the
    # moderator, with its 95% confidence interval (the range of values the data
    # leave plausible), t, and two-sided p.
    b_interaction = b, se = se,
    ci_lower = ci["x_c:m_c", 1], ci_upper = ci["x_c:m_c", 2],
    t = tv, p_two = pv,
    # R-squared change: the share of the outcome's variance the product term
    # explains beyond the two predictors on their own. It is the interaction's
    # effect size, on a scale shared by all eight models.
    R2 = r2, R2_change = r2 - r2_add,
    # The two other coefficients, each at the MEAN of the other variable
    # (that is what centring bought). b_predictor is the slope of retributivism
    # for a participant of average orientation or leaning; b_moderator the
    # reverse. Their p values are two-sided, like every p here. Kept for
    # interpretation; the interaction is the test.
    b_predictor = co["x_c", "Estimate"], p_two_predictor = co["x_c", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    b_moderator = co["m_c", "Estimate"], p_two_moderator = co["m_c", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # --- Simple slopes ----------------------------------------------------------
  # The slope of the predictor at three values of the moderator: one standard
  # deviation below its mean, at its mean, and one above. This is what turns an
  # interaction coefficient into a sentence: "among more conservative
  # participants, retributivism was more strongly related to punitiveness".
  #
  # The slope at moderator value m0 (centred) is b_x + b_xm * m0. Its variance
  # comes from the model's covariance matrix V, which holds each coefficient's
  # sampling variance and how pairs of coefficients vary together:
  #   Var = V[x, x] + m0^2 * V[xm, xm] + 2 * m0 * V[x, xm].
  # The covariance term matters: leaving it out would give the wrong standard
  # error whenever the two coefficients' errors are correlated.
  V   <- stats::vcov(fit)
  sdm <- stats::sd(sub[[m]])
  slopes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(-1, 0, 1), function(k) {
    m0 <- k * sdm
    est <- co["x_c", "Estimate"] + b * m0
    sev <- sqrt(V["x_c", "x_c"] + m0^2 * V["x_c:m_c", "x_c:m_c"] +
                2 * m0 * V["x_c", "x_c:m_c"])
    # GUARD, by a second route. Re-centre the moderator AT the probe value and
    # refit: the coefficient on x in that model is the slope at m0, and its
    # standard error is the slope's standard error. The refit uses none of the
    # formula above, so agreement at -1 SD and +1 SD, where both covariance
    # terms carry weight, shows those cells were read correctly.
    chk <- summary(stats::lm(y ~ x_c * I(m_c - m0), data = md))$coefficients
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(chk["x_c", c("Estimate", "Std. Error")]),
                               c(est, sev))))
    tt  <- est / sev
    data.frame(outcome = mod_labels[[y]], predictor = mod_labels[[x]],
               moderator = mod_labels[[m]],
               at = c("-1 SD", "mean", "+1 SD")[k + 2],
               # The moderator value the slope is evaluated at, on its own
               # scale, so a reader can see what "-1 SD" means in answers.
               moderator_value = mean(sub[[m]]) + m0,
               slope = est, se = sev,
               ci_lower = est - stats::qt(.975, df_res) * sev,
               ci_upper = est + stats::qt(.975, df_res) * sev,
               t = tt, p_two = 2 * stats::pt(-abs(tt), df_res),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  }))
  # GUARD: the slope at the mean must be the centred model's b_predictor, by
  # construction.
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(slopes$slope[2], row$b_predictor)),
            isTRUE(all.equal(slopes$se[2], co["x_c", "Std. Error"])))
  # Flag a probe value that lies outside the answers anyone gave. A slope there
  # would describe a participant who does not exist in the sample. With these
  # two moderators the +/-1 SD values are expected to fall inside the range;
  # the flag makes it visible if they do not.
  slopes$inside_range <- slopes$moderator_value >= min(sub[[m]]) &
                         slopes$moderator_value <= max(sub[[m]])
  list(row = row, slopes = slopes)
}

mod_out     <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(mod_specs)), function(i)
  mod_fit(mod_specs$y[i], mod_specs$x[i], mod_specs$m[i]))
mod_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mod_out, `[[`, "row"))
mod_slopes  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mod_out, `[[`, "slopes"))
stopifnot(nrow(mod_results) == 8, nrow(mod_slopes) == 24, !anyNA(mod_results$p_two))
if (!all(mod_slopes$inside_range))
  cat("NOTE: some +/-1 SD probe values lie outside the observed range; see inside_range.\n")

TABLES[["MOD_interactions"]]  <- mod_results
TABLES[["MOD_simple_slopes"]] <- mod_slopes
show_table(mod_results[, c("outcome", "predictor", "moderator", "n", "b_interaction",
                           "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "t", "df", "p_two",
                           "R2_change")],
           "9.18C: interaction terms (two-sided p, uncorrected)")
show_table(mod_slopes[, c("outcome", "predictor", "moderator", "at",
                          "moderator_value", "slope", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
                          "p_two")],
           "9.18C: slope of the predictor at three levels of the moderator (two-sided p)")

# One line per model, in words, for reading the report without the tables.
for (i in seq_len(nrow(mod_results))) {
  r <- mod_results[i, ]
  cat(sprintf("%-36s ~ %-22s x %-37s b = %7.3f [%7.3f, %7.3f], t(%d) = %6.2f, two-sided p %s, dR2 = %.4f\n",
              r$outcome, r$predictor, r$moderator, r$b_interaction, r$ci_lower,
              r$ci_upper, r$df, r$t, format_p(r$p_two), r$R2_change))
}
# The count of interactions at two-sided p < .05, printed as a count and
# nothing more. If no moderation existed anywhere, eight tests at .05 would be
# expected to give about 0.4 such results. The eight tests share predictors,
# moderators and outcomes, so they are not independent, and the count is
# description, not a test of anything.
cat(sprintf("\nInteractions at two-sided p < .05: %d of %d (uncorrected).\n",
            sum(mod_results$p_two < .05), nrow(mod_results)))
```

```{r phase9_moderators_groups}
# === 9.18D THE MODERATORS BY RETRIBUTIVIST GROUP ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: compares the retributive and the other side of each
# registered grouping on the two moderators. Produces `mod_grp` (exported as
# MOD_by_grouping).
# PREREG: the prosecution-leaning rows are H18, registered one-sided under all
#         four groupings (prereg 2.3, 5.3) and reported that way in 9.7, 9.10
#         and 9.11; here they are two-sided, and the guard below ties them to
#         those rows. The political-orientation rows are not registered as
#         tests; they are description. Two-sided throughout.
# CONSUMES: d; grp_rank (5.1), grp_med and grp_tert (5.3), grp_ratio (5.4);
#           welch_contrast() (0.3); contrasts_rank (9.3), contrasts_ratio
#           (9.10), contrasts_med and contrasts_tert (9.11); mod_mods (9.18B);
#           show_table().
#
# WHY THIS TABLE. It shows whether the moderators themselves differ between the
# retributive side of each grouping and the other side. If retributivists are
# more conservative, then part of what the retributivist contrasts of 9.3 to
# 9.11 pick up is shared with political orientation. Nothing here adjusts for
# that; it is description.
#
# The sentencing-ratio grouping IS included. The circularity rule of prereg 5.3
# keeps the ratio away from outcomes built from the sentence, and neither
# moderator contains any part of it.
#
# SIGN CONVENTION. welch_contrast() subtracts the second factor level from the
# first, and every grouping factor puts the retributive side first (Phase 5).
# So a positive d means the retributive side is MORE CONSERVATIVE, or leans
# MORE TOWARD THE PROSECUTION.
mod_groupings <- c(grp_rank  = "Ranking (retribution first)",
                   grp_med   = "Median split on relative retribution",
                   grp_tert  = "Top vs bottom third of relative retribution",
                   grp_ratio = "Sentencing ratio (no reduction vs reduction)")
stopifnot(all(names(mod_groupings) %in% names(d)))
mod_grp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mod_groupings), function(g) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mod_mods), function(v) {
    row <- welch_contrast(d, v, g, alternative = "two.sided", label = mod_mods[[v]])
    row$grouping <- mod_groupings[[g]]
    row
  }))
}))
mod_grp <- mod_grp[, c("grouping", "outcome", "n1", "n2", "M1", "SD1", "M2", "SD2",
                       "t", "df", "p_two", "d", "d_lower", "d_upper")]
stopifnot(!anyNA(mod_grp$d))

# GUARD. Each prosecution-leaning row here is the same Welch test as H18 under
# the same grouping, run two-sided instead of one-sided. Its t, df, two-sided p
# and d must therefore match the H18 row of that grouping's contrast set
# exactly. A mismatch would mean one of the two had been run on a different
# variable or a different grouping.
mod_h18_sets <- list(grp_rank = contrasts_rank, grp_med = contrasts_med,
                     grp_tert = contrasts_tert, grp_ratio = contrasts_ratio)
for (g in names(mod_h18_sets)) {
  h18  <- mod_h18_sets[[g]][mod_h18_sets[[g]]$hypothesis == "H18", ]
  mine <- mod_grp[mod_grp$grouping == mod_groupings[[g]] &
                  mod_grp$outcome == mod_mods[["leanPros"]], ]
  stopifnot(nrow(h18) == 1, nrow(mine) == 1,
            isTRUE(all.equal(c(h18$t, h18$df, h18$p_two, h18$d),
                             c(mine$t, mine$df, mine$p_two, mine$d))))
}

TABLES[["MOD_by_grouping"]] <- mod_grp
show_table(mod_grp, paste("9.18D: the moderators by retributivist group",
                          "(two-sided p; M1 = retributive side; the",
                          "prosecution-leaning rows are H18, tested one-sided in 9.7, 9.10 and 9.11)"))
```

## 9.19 The scorings the paper reports (not registered)

The paper's main text reports scorings that differ from the registration or
settle a choice it left open, and compares the retributivists with a narrower
group than the registration does. The co-authors settled these after the
analyses above were run (the last of them on 27 September 2026), so none of
them is registered. Every registered analysis above stands as it is, and the
Supplementary Materials report it.

- **Desert theory.** The registration scores desert from the four purpose items,
  Retribution_1 to Retribution_4 (prereg 5.4). The paper's desert-theory score
  uses the first five, adding Retribution_5, "The state has a duty to punish its
  criminals". Items 1 to 5 state support for punishing because of the offense;
  items 6 and 7 give rationales for it (repaying a debt, removing an unfair
  advantage) and stay out. Every PAPER_ export calls it "Desert theory"; the
  registered four-item score is "Desert (registered, items 1-4)" and the
  registered composite (desert averaged with the three-item proportionality
  component) is "Just deserts (registered)".
- **Just deserts, as the paper scores it.** The plain mean of the desert-theory
  score and the proportionality principle item, both on the 1 to 7 scale, so
  that H9 can compare its mean with revenge's. The paper reports H7, H9 and H10,
  and their repeats among the retributivists (H11), against desert theory and
  against this score (9.19G). The registered composite is not used here: its
  three proportionality items do not form one component (see H6 in 8.3 and
  8.3b), and prereg 5.4 provides that the two parts of just deserts are not
  forced into one score if they do not hold together.
- **H6 through the principle and the severity index.** The registration tests
  H6 on the three-item proportionality component. The paper states it as the
  correlation of desert theory with the proportionality principle (the direct
  item) against its correlation with the severity index (the two departure
  items), which 8.3b already reports for the four purpose items.
- **Punitiveness is its six components weighted equally.** Prereg 5.2 names the
  six components of punitiveness (support for more punishment, rejection of
  parsimony, three-strikes laws, life without parole, the death penalty, and
  the first sentence) and two versions built from them, the eight-item scale
  and the full index, without saying how the components are weighted or
  assigning the tests to either version. The runs above use the eight-item
  scale. The paper, in both studies, standardizes each of the six components
  (the five attitude components are each the mean of their items; the sentence
  is standardized within vignette) and averages them, so each carries a sixth
  of the weight: 7.4's six-part score. Where the sentence, or a measure built
  from it, is on the other side of an analysis (the sentencing ratio, its
  grouping, and the residualized second sentence), the six-part score would put
  the sentence on both sides, as prereg 5.11 forbids; there the paper uses the
  five attitude components, each standardized and then averaged (7.4's
  standardized five-part score). 9.19F reruns the paper's analyses on the
  registered scores, the full index (the eight-item scale and the sentence,
  each standardized, then averaged, so the sentence carries half the weight)
  with the eight-item scale on the sentence side, for the Supplementary
  Materials.
- **The two-item cognitive reflection score leads.** The registered score counts
  three items; the third (the lily-pad item) had its answer slider labelled in
  minutes. The contrast set already carries the two-item score (9.3), so nothing
  is recomputed for it; the counts in 9.19D use it in place of the three-item
  score.
- **The comparison group.** The registered contrasts compare the retributivists
  with every other participant. The main text compares them with the
  participants who ranked deterrence or incapacitation first (9.12b), leaving
  out those who ranked rehabilitation first, the stricter comparison. 9.19D runs
  both.

Revenge keeps its four registered items, and the hostile aggression cluster
keeps its registered form. The three items Study 1 used are kept as a rescoring
(`revenge3`) for the Supplementary Materials. Relative retribution, the primary
continuous measure, keeps all seven items as registered. The exploratory
moderator models of 9.18 (Table S23) are rerun with punitiveness scored as the
paper scores it in 9.19H.

Nothing here writes to `d`. The rescored columns live in `pa_d`, a copy of `d` in
which exactly four columns are replaced, so that the hypothesis functions of
Phase 7 and 8 and the contrast functions of Phase 9, which read columns by name,
run unchanged on the paper's scorings: `deserved` and `just_deserts` carry desert
theory, `punitiveness_full` carries the six-part score and `punitiveness` the
standardized five-part score. Every export starts with PAPER_. Every p value
keeps the direction and sidedness of the registered test it reruns, unless a row
says otherwise. Where a result depends on the choice of punitiveness measure,
the five-part version is exported beside the six-part one.

```{r phase9_paper_scorings}
# === 9.19A THE PAPER'S SCORINGS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: builds `pa_d`, a copy of `d` in which four columns are
# rescored (desert and just deserts carry desert theory; the two punitiveness
# columns carry the paper's six-part and standardized five-part scores), checks
# that nothing else differs, sets the labels every PAPER_ export uses for these
# scores and a relabelled copy of the contrast specification, and reports the
# reliability of the paper's scores beside the registered ones. Produces
# `pa_d`, `pa_spec`, `pa_old_full`, `pa_old_sr`, `pa_reliability` (exported as
# PAPER_reliability), `pa_tiers` (PAPER_retribution_tiers) and `pa_scores`
# (PAPER_person_scores).
# PREREG: NOT REGISTERED. The registered scorings are prereg 5.2 (punitiveness:
#         the eight-item scale, and the full index), 5.3 (the seven-item
#         retribution subscale) and 5.4 (desert = Retribution_1 to _4; just
#         deserts = desert with the proportionality component). Those scorings
#         stay in `d` and every registered result above is computed from them.
#         The paper's scorings were settled by the co-authors after the
#         registered analyses were run (the punitiveness weighting on 27 Sep
#         2026). Revenge (revenge_1 to _4, prereg 5.4) and the hostile
#         aggression cluster (prereg 2.1) are used as registered.
# CONSUMES: d; zmean() (0.3); p5_d with punit_parts6, punit_parts5z and
#           punit_parts5, and p5_rel (7.4); rv_d (8.7b); the retribution tiers
#           deserved_soft and retribution_hard (4.3b); alpha_table (4.10);
#           contrast_spec (9.3); cor_row(), show_table().
#
# WHY A COPY WITH REPLACED COLUMNS, NOT NEW FUNCTIONS. run_h1() to run_h10(),
# run_contrast_set() and run_continuous_set() read their inputs by column name
# ("deserved", "just_deserts", "punitiveness", "punitiveness_full"). Replacing
# those columns in a copy lets the same functions, already checked above,
# produce the paper's versions. Writing new functions would create a second
# implementation of every test, and two implementations can drift apart.
#
# DANGER: `pa_d` must never be used for a registered result. Its `deserved` and
# `just_deserts` columns carry desert theory, its `punitiveness_full` column the
# six-part score and its `punitiveness` column the standardized five-part
# score, all under the registered names. That is the point of it here, and the
# reason nothing outside 9.19 reads it. The column NAMES therefore say nothing
# about the scores in pa_d; the labels PA_LAB and PA_LAB_SR below do, and every
# PAPER_ export carries those labels.

# --- The paper's desert-theory score, and Study 1's revenge items ---------------
# Each is the mean of its items. No item in either set is reverse-keyed (4.1
# and 4.3 score them as they stand), and every item was required, so no row is
# missing; the checks below confirm both. The three-item revenge score is not a
# paper scoring: it is kept so the Supplementary Materials can show what
# setting revenge_4 aside would change.
pa_ret_items <- paste0("Retribution_", 1:5)
pa_rev_items <- paste0("revenge_", 1:3)
stopifnot(all(c(pa_ret_items, pa_rev_items) %in% names(d)),
          !anyNA(d[, c(pa_ret_items, pa_rev_items)]))
pa_retribution_items <- rowMeans(d[, pa_ret_items])
pa_revenge3          <- rowMeans(d[, pa_rev_items])

# --- The punitiveness measures the paper uses ---------------------------------
# PA_PUNIT: the six components weighted equally. Each of the five attitude
# components (support for more punishment, 2 items; rejection of parsimony, 2;
# three-strikes laws, 2; life without parole, 1; the death penalty, 1; each the
# mean of its items, reverse-coded where 4.2 reverse-codes them) and the first
# sentence (standardized within vignette) is standardized across the sample,
# and punitiveness is their mean, so each carries a sixth of the weight. This
# is 7.4's punit_parts6, reused rather than rebuilt.
# PA_PUNIT_SR: where the sentence, or a measure built from it, is on the other
# side of an analysis (the sentencing ratio, its grouping, the residualized
# second sentence), the six-part score would put the sentence on both sides,
# which prereg 5.11 forbids. There the paper uses the five attitude components,
# EACH STANDARDIZED, then averaged: 7.4's punit_parts5z. It is not 7.4's
# punit_parts5, which averages the five raw part scores and so lets the parts
# with a wider spread count for more.
# Both scores go into pa_d under the registered column names, so that the
# registered functions read them (see WHY A COPY above). The registered scores
# are kept as pa_old_full and pa_old_sr for 9.19F, which reruns the paper's
# analyses on them.
PA_PUNIT    <- "punitiveness_full"   # in pa_d: the six-part score
PA_PUNIT_SR <- "punitiveness"        # in pa_d: the standardized five-part score
PA_LAB    <- "Punitiveness (six components)"
PA_LAB_SR <- "Punitiveness (five attitude components)"
stopifnot(all(c(PA_PUNIT, PA_PUNIT_SR) %in% names(d)))
# GUARDS on the two scores.
#   1. 7.4's copy holds the same participants in the same order, so its columns
#      can be carried across row for row, and neither score is missing.
#   2. The six-part score agrees with the registered full index at r = .945 and
#      with the eight-item scale at .972 (the values the co-authors were shown
#      before choosing it); a different score, or a misaligned row order, would
#      not reproduce both.
#   3. The standardized five-part score agrees with the eight-item scale at
#      about .99 (the two differ only in how the five components are weighted)
#      and with 7.4's plain five-part mean at nearly 1.
stopifnot(identical(p5_d$ResponseId, d$ResponseId),
          !anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts6), !anyNA(p5_d$punit_parts5z))
pa_six  <- p5_d$punit_parts6
pa_five <- p5_d$punit_parts5z
stopifnot(round(stats::cor(pa_six, d$punitiveness_full), 3) == 0.945,
          round(stats::cor(pa_six, d$punitiveness), 3) == 0.972,
          round(stats::cor(pa_five, d$punitiveness), 2) == 0.99,
          stats::cor(pa_five, p5_d$punit_parts5) > 0.99)
pa_old_full <- d$punitiveness_full
pa_old_sr   <- d$punitiveness

# --- The labels every PAPER_ export uses -----------------------------------------
# Set once, so that no export can carry one score under another's name.
PA_DT         <- "Desert theory"                     # Retribution_1 to _5
PA_DESERT_REG <- "Desert (registered, items 1-4)"    # d$deserved
PA_JD_REG     <- "Just deserts (registered)"         # d$just_deserts
PA_JD         <- "Just deserts"                      # 9.19G: desert theory + principle

# --- The copy --------------------------------------------------------------------
pa_d <- d
pa_d$retribution_items <- pa_retribution_items
pa_d$revenge3          <- pa_revenge3
# The two columns the registered functions read for desert and just deserts,
# carrying desert theory: the paper uses the five items alone where the
# registration uses either (9.19G adds the paper's just-deserts score in a
# second copy).
pa_d$deserved     <- pa_retribution_items
pa_d$just_deserts <- pa_retribution_items
# The two punitiveness columns, carrying the paper's two scores.
pa_d$punitiveness_full <- pa_six
pa_d$punitiveness      <- pa_five

# GUARDS.
#   1. The copy differs from d in exactly the four replaced columns (plus the
#      two it adds). A slip that changed a fifth column, revenge or the cluster
#      above all, would move results that are meant to stay registered.
#   2. The three-item revenge equals the revenge_123 rescoring 8.7b built
#      independently, and the four registered items average to d$revenge, the
#      revenge every analysis in 9.19 uses.
pa_changed <- names(d)[!vapply(names(d), function(v)
  isTRUE(all.equal(d[[v]], pa_d[[v]])), logical(1))]
stopifnot(setequal(pa_changed, c("deserved", "just_deserts", "punitiveness",
                                 "punitiveness_full")),
          setequal(setdiff(names(pa_d), names(d)), c("retribution_items", "revenge3")))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_revenge3, rv_d$revenge_123)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(rowMeans(d[, paste0("revenge_", 1:4)]), d$revenge)),
          identical(pa_d$revenge, d$revenge), identical(pa_d$hostile_agg, d$hostile_agg),
          identical(pa_d$Sentence1_z, d$Sentence1_z),
          identical(pa_d$sentence_ratio, d$sentence_ratio))

# --- The contrast specification with the paper's punitiveness labels -------------
# run_contrast_set() and run_continuous_set() label each row from the spec. On
# pa_d the two H21 rows read the paper's scores, so they must carry the paper's
# labels. pa_spec is contrast_spec with those two labels changed and nothing
# else: the rows, their order, directions and sentence_based flags are the
# registered ones (the six-part score contains the sentence, like the full
# index, so it keeps that row's flag and drops out under the ratio grouping).
# contrast_spec itself is not touched.
pa_spec <- contrast_spec
pa_spec$label[pa_spec$outcome == "punitiveness"]      <- PA_LAB_SR
pa_spec$label[pa_spec$outcome == "punitiveness_full"] <- PA_LAB
# GUARD: the copy differs from the registered spec in those two labels only.
stopifnot(identical(pa_spec[, setdiff(names(pa_spec), "label")],
                    contrast_spec[, setdiff(names(contrast_spec), "label")]),
          sum(pa_spec$label != contrast_spec$label) == 2,
          pa_spec$sentence_based[pa_spec$outcome == "punitiveness_full"],
          !pa_spec$sentence_based[pa_spec$outcome == "punitiveness"])

# --- Reliability -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Cronbach's alpha, and McDonald's omega where a one-factor model is identified
# (three or more items; the same rule as compute_composite()). Computed here
# rather than through compute_composite(), which would append rows to the
# registered reliability table after 4.10 has already exported it.
pa_rel_row <- function(label, items) {
  x <- d[, items]
  a <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::alpha(x, check.keys = FALSE,
                                                      warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha))
  o <- if (length(items) >= 3) tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(
    psych::omega(x, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)), error = function(e) NA_real_)
    else NA_real_
  s <- rowMeans(x)
  data.frame(score = label, k = length(items), items = paste(items, collapse = ", "),
             alpha = a, omega = o, M = mean(s), SD = stats::sd(s),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
pa_reliability <- rbind(
  pa_rel_row("Desert theory (paper): Retribution_1 to _5", pa_ret_items),
  pa_rel_row("Retribution subscale, all seven (registered, prereg 5.3)",
             paste0("Retribution_", 1:7)),
  pa_rel_row("Desert (registered, items 1-4), prereg 5.4",
             paste0("Retribution_", 1:4)),
  pa_rel_row("Positive retribution: Retribution_2 and _5 (require, duty)",
             paste0("Retribution_", c(2, 5))),
  pa_rel_row("Negative retribution: Retribution_1, _3, _4 (right, restored, deserve)",
             paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 3, 4))),
  pa_rel_row("Rationales: Retribution_6 and _7 (debt, unfair advantage)",
             paste0("Retribution_", 6:7)),
  pa_rel_row("Revenge (paper, as registered): revenge_1 to _4", paste0("revenge_", 1:4)),
  pa_rel_row("Revenge, Study 1's three items (rescoring): revenge_1 to _3", pa_rev_items))
# The hostile aggression cluster, as 4.9 computes a cluster's reliability: over
# its five members, each standardized. The paper uses the registered cluster;
# the version built with the three-item revenge is the rescoring's. The
# punitiveness index (the eight items and the sentence, each standardized, as
# nine parts) keeps its registered row in 4.10's table (alpha_table).
pa_clu_alpha <- function(rev) suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::alpha(
  as.data.frame(scale(cbind(d$hatred, rev, d$degradation, d$suffering, d$prisonviol))),
  check.keys = FALSE, warnings = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha))
pa_clu_omega <- function(rev) tryCatch(suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(psych::omega(
  as.data.frame(scale(cbind(d$hatred, rev, d$degradation, d$suffering, d$prisonviol))),
  nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)), error = function(e) NA_real_)
pa_reliability <- rbind(pa_reliability, data.frame(
  score = c("Hostile aggression cluster with three-item revenge (rescoring)",
            "Hostile aggression cluster (paper, as registered)"),
  k = 5, items = "hatred, revenge, degradation, suffering, prison violence (each standardized)",
  alpha = c(pa_clu_alpha(pa_revenge3), pa_clu_alpha(d$revenge)),
  omega = c(pa_clu_omega(pa_revenge3), pa_clu_omega(d$revenge)),
  M = NA_real_, SD = NA_real_, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
# GUARD: the registered cluster's alpha reproduces 4.10's table.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  pa_reliability$alpha[pa_reliability$score == "Hostile aggression cluster (paper, as registered)"],
  alpha_table$alpha[alpha_table$composite == "hostile aggression cluster"])))
# The paper's two punitiveness scores, as 7.4 scores them: alpha over the
# standardized parts (the scores average standardized parts, so their
# reliability is that of the standardized parts); omega is not computed for
# them, as 7.4 does not. M and SD are of the score itself, which averages
# standardized parts and so has a mean of about 0.
# The five parts are 7.4's p5_parts, standardized here as the two scores
# standardize them.
# The alpha of each score is the alpha of the parts exactly as the score
# averages them: every part standardized across the sample, the sentence
# included (its within-vignette z-score is standardized once more, as zmean()
# does when it builds the six-part score).
# GUARDS: the standardized parts average to the five-component score, and with
# the standardized sentence to the six-component score, so each row describes
# the score the paper uses.
pa_parts_z <- as.data.frame(scale(p5_parts))
pa_sent_z  <- as.numeric(scale(d$Sentence1_z))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(rowMeans(pa_parts_z), pa_five)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(rowMeans(data.frame(pa_parts_z, s = pa_sent_z)), pa_six)))
pa_reliability <- rbind(pa_reliability, data.frame(
  score = c(paste0(PA_LAB, " (paper): five components and the sentence, each standardized"),
            paste0(PA_LAB_SR, " (paper, sentence side): each standardized")),
  k = c(6, 5),
  items = c("punish more, parsimony rejected, three strikes, life without parole, death penalty, Sentence1_z",
            "punish more, parsimony rejected, three strikes, life without parole, death penalty"),
  alpha = c(p5_alpha(data.frame(pa_parts_z, s = pa_sent_z)), p5_alpha(pa_parts_z)),
  omega = NA_real_, M = c(mean(pa_six), mean(pa_five)),
  SD = c(stats::sd(pa_six), stats::sd(pa_five)), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
# GUARD: the six-component alpha is the one the attenuation check in 7.6 uses.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_reliability$alpha[pa_reliability$k == 6 & grepl("^Punitiveness", pa_reliability$score)],
                           ds_a_six)))
TABLES[["PAPER_reliability"]] <- pa_reliability
show_table(pa_reliability[, c("score", "k", "alpha", "omega", "M", "SD")],
           "9.19A: reliability of the paper's scores, beside the registered ones")

# The one-line check the co-authors asked for: do the positive and the negative
# forms of retribution go together? The two tiers are 4.3b's composites,
# retribution_hard (items 2 and 5) and deserved_soft (items 1, 3 and 4). Desert
# theory is also correlated with revenge, as the paper scores it (four items)
# and as Study 1's three items.
# GUARD: each tier is the mean of the items its label names.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(d$retribution_hard, rowMeans(d[, paste0("Retribution_", c(2, 5))]))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(d$deserved_soft, rowMeans(d[, paste0("Retribution_", c(1, 3, 4))]))))
pa_tiers <- rbind(
  cor_row(d, "retribution_hard", "deserved_soft", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Positive retribution (items 2, 5)",
          label_y = "Negative retribution (items 1, 3, 4)"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "deserved", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT,
          label_y = paste0(PA_DESERT_REG, "; part-whole, not a finding")),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "revenge", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Revenge (four items)"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "revenge3", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Revenge, three items (rescoring)"))
# `deserved` in pa_d is desert theory, so the part-whole row is taken against
# the registered column in d instead.
pa_tiers[2, c("r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two", "p_dir")] <- cor_row(
  data.frame(a = pa_retribution_items, b = d$deserved), "a", "b",
  alternative = "two.sided")[, c("r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two", "p_dir")]
TABLES[["PAPER_retribution_tiers"]] <- pa_tiers
show_table(pa_tiers[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")],
           "9.19A: how the forms of retribution, and revenge, go together (two-sided)")

# --- The paper's scores, participant by participant --------------------------
# One row per participant with the paper's four scores, keyed by ResponseId,
# for 04_two_study_figures.Rmd, which reads the scored dataset (where these
# scores are not, because `d` is never rescored) and draws the paper's figures.
# NOT REGISTERED. The just-deserts score is built in 9.19G and added there.
pa_scores <- data.frame(ResponseId = d$ResponseId,
                        punit_six = pa_six, punit_five_z = pa_five,
                        desert_theory = pa_retribution_items,
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(pa_scores), !anyDuplicated(pa_scores$ResponseId))
```

```{r phase9_paper_part1}
# === 9.19B PART 1 ON THE PAPER'S SCORINGS: H1, H2, E2, H3 ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reruns H1, H2 and E2 with the six-part score as
# punitiveness (and, for the Supplement, with the standardized five-part
# score), and H3, which does not involve punitiveness. None of these tests
# involves desert or just deserts, so on pa_d they differ from the registered
# runs only in the punitiveness score; the guards prove it. Produces PAPER_H1
# (six-part score), PAPER_H1_self_report (five-part score; the name is kept
# for the sentence-free score), PAPER_H2, PAPER_H2_self_report, PAPER_E2,
# PAPER_H3_summary, PAPER_H3_eigenvalues and PAPER_H3_loadings.
# PREREG: the tests are registered (6.3, with sidedness from 6.8: H1 one-sided
#         with BH across the twelve; H2 Steiger one-sided; H3 as in 7.3); the
#         punitiveness scores are not.
# CONSUMES: pa_d, PA_PUNIT, PA_PUNIT_SR, PA_LAB, PA_LAB_SR (9.19A); p5_d
#           (7.4); run_h1(), run_h2(), run_h3() (7.0); h3_full (7.3).
pa_h1    <- run_h1(pa_d, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h1_sr <- run_h1(pa_d, punit = PA_PUNIT_SR)
pa_h2    <- run_h2(pa_d, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h2_sr <- run_h2(pa_d, punit = PA_PUNIT_SR)
pa_h3    <- run_h3(pa_d)
# E2 as 9.15 runs it (one-sided, hostile solidarity greater), on the six-part
# score.
pa_e2 <- steiger_overlap(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, "solidarity_hostile", "solidarity_durk",
                         alternative = "greater",
                         label = "r(punitiveness, hostile solidarity) > r(punitiveness, Durkheimian solidarity)")

# GUARDS: pa_d differs from d only in desert, just deserts and the two
# punitiveness columns, and these tests read no desert column, so the same
# functions run on 7.4's copy of d (p5_d, which differs from d only in the part
# scores it adds) with the part scores named as punitiveness must give the same
# answers. Therefore
#   1. H1 on each score reproduces the run on p5_d's column, row for row (the
#      correlations and the BH-adjusted p values);
#   2. H2 on each score, and E2 on the six-part score, reproduce the same runs
#      on p5_d;
#   3. the H3 correlation matrix is 7.3's.
# 9.19F runs the same calls with the registered scores restored, and there they
# reproduce 7.1, 7.2 and 9.15.
pa_same_h1 <- function(a, b) {
  m <- match(a$y, b$y)
  !anyNA(m) && isTRUE(all.equal(a$r, b$r[m])) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(a$p_BH_one_sided, b$p_BH_one_sided[m]))
}
stopifnot(pa_same_h1(pa_h1, run_h1(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts6")),
          pa_same_h1(pa_h1_sr, run_h1(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts5z")),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h2$diff, run_h2(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts6")$diff)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h2_sr$z, run_h2(p5_d, punit = "punit_parts5z")$z)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_e2$diff, steiger_overlap(p5_d, "punit_parts6", "solidarity_hostile",
                                                       "solidarity_durk", alternative = "greater",
                                                       label = "")$diff)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h3$cor_matrix, h3_full$cor_matrix)))

TABLES[["PAPER_H1"]]             <- pa_h1
TABLES[["PAPER_H1_self_report"]] <- pa_h1_sr
TABLES[["PAPER_H2"]]             <- pa_h2
TABLES[["PAPER_H2_self_report"]] <- pa_h2_sr
TABLES[["PAPER_E2"]]             <- pa_e2
show_table(pa_h1[, c("y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_one_sided",
                     "p_BH_one_sided")],
           "9.19B: H1 on the six-part score (one-sided, BH across the twelve)")
show_table(rbind(cbind(punitiveness = PA_LAB, pa_h2),
                 cbind(punitiveness = PA_LAB_SR, pa_h2_sr)),
           "9.19B: H2 on each punitiveness score (one-sided)")
show_table(pa_e2, "9.19B: E2 on the six-part score (one-sided)")

# H3 as 7.3 reports it: the share of the 66 intercorrelations that are
# positive, their range, the eigenvalues, and a one-factor EFA. Identical to
# 7.3 (guard 4 above); exported under the PAPER_ name so the write-up reads
# every Part 1 number from one family of files.
pa_off <- pa_h3$cor_matrix[upper.tri(pa_h3$cor_matrix)]
pa_h3_summary <- data.frame(
  n_pairs = pa_h3$n_pairs, n_positive = sum(pa_off > 0), r_min = min(pa_off),
  r_max = max(pa_off), mean_r = pa_h3$mean_r,
  eigen_1 = pa_h3$eigenvalues[1], share_1 = pa_h3$var_explained_1,
  eigen_2 = pa_h3$eigenvalues[2], share_2 = pa_h3$eigenvalues[2] / sum(pa_h3$eigenvalues),
  n_eigen_gt1 = pa_h3$n_eigen_gt1,
  efa_var_explained = if (is.null(pa_h3$fa)) NA_real_ else pa_h3$fa$Vaccounted[2, 1],
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pa_h3_eigen <- data.frame(component = seq_along(pa_h3$eigenvalues),
                          eigenvalue = pa_h3$eigenvalues,
                          proportion = pa_h3$eigenvalues / sum(pa_h3$eigenvalues))
pa_h3_load <- data.frame(correlate = rownames(pa_h3$fa$loadings),
                         loading = as.numeric(pa_h3$fa$loadings[, 1]),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pa_h3_load <- pa_h3_load[order(-pa_h3_load$loading), ]
TABLES[["PAPER_H3_summary"]]     <- pa_h3_summary
TABLES[["PAPER_H3_eigenvalues"]] <- pa_h3_eigen
TABLES[["PAPER_H3_loadings"]]    <- pa_h3_load
show_table(pa_h3_summary, "9.19B: H3 (the registered correlates)")
```

```{r phase9_paper_part2}
# === 9.19C PART 2 ON THE PAPER'S SCORINGS: H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, AND THEIR COMPANIONS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: states H6 through the proportionality principle and the
# severity index, and reruns H7, H9 and H10 with desert theory in place of just
# deserts (revenge as registered) and H8 on the six-part score; then reruns the
# companion analyses the Part 2 text uses: each goal against the limits, and
# the sentencing ratio against desert theory, revenge and punitiveness (the
# standardized five-part score, since the ratio is built from the sentence).
# For the Supplement, H10 is also run with Study 1's three revenge items. 9.19G
# repeats H7, H9 and H10 against the paper's just-deserts score. Produces
# PAPER_H6, PAPER_H6_cors, PAPER_H7, PAPER_H8, PAPER_H9, PAPER_H10,
# PAPER_H10_cors, PAPER_goals_by_limits, PAPER_ratio_continuous,
# PAPER_ratio_cors and PAPER_ratio_steiger.
# PREREG: H7, H8, H9 and H10 are registered tests (6.4), run here on scorings
#         that are not; H6 stated this way is not registered (the registered H6
#         is in 8.3); the companions are not registered. Sidedness follows each
#         registered test; H10 is also given two-sided.
# CONSUMES: pa_d, pa_spec, pa_revenge3, pa_retribution_items, pa_five, PA_PUNIT,
#           PA_PUNIT_SR and the PA_ labels (9.19A); p5_d (7.4); run_h7(),
#           run_h8(), run_h9(), run_h10(), paired_test(), steiger_overlap(),
#           cor_row(), cont_reg() (0.3, 7.0); h9_full, h10_full (8.6, 8.7);
#           run_continuous_set() (9.9); cont_ratio (9.10);
#           TABLES$P2_goals_by_limits (8.9B).

# --- H6: desert theory against the principle and against severity -------------
# Two correlations that share desert theory, compared with Steiger's test for
# dependent overlapping correlations. Two-sided: the registration
# predicted that the two halves of just deserts would not hold together, which
# names no direction for this comparison. Punitiveness is set beside it, as in
# 8.3b.
pa_h6 <- rbind(
  cbind(pair = PA_DT,
        steiger_overlap(pa_d, "retribution_items", "severity_index",
                        "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
                        label = "r(desert theory, severity index) vs r(desert theory, principle)")),
  cbind(pair = PA_LAB,
        steiger_overlap(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, "severity_index",
                        "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
                        label = "r(punitiveness, severity index) vs r(punitiveness, principle)")))
pa_h6_cors <- rbind(
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Proportionality principle"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "severity_index", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Severity index"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "severity_1", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "severity_1 alone (punish more than the crime)"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "severity_2_R", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "severity_2 reversed alone (reject punishing less)"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "retribution_items", "proportionality_jd", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Registered proportionality component"),
  cor_row(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, "severity_1", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_LAB, label_y = "severity_1 alone (punish more than the crime)"),
  cor_row(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, "severity_2_R", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_LAB, label_y = "severity_2 reversed alone (reject punishing less)"))
# GUARD: the Steiger rows carry the same correlations as the plain rows.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h6$r_jk[1], pa_h6_cors$r[2])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h6$r_jh[1], pa_h6_cors$r[1])))
TABLES[["PAPER_H6"]]      <- pa_h6
TABLES[["PAPER_H6_cors"]] <- pa_h6_cors
show_table(pa_h6_cors[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")],
           "9.19C: what desert theory and punitiveness track (two-sided)")
show_table(pa_h6[, c("pair", "r_jk", "r_jh", "r_kh", "diff", "diff_lower",
                     "diff_upper", "z", "p")],
           "9.19C: severity index against principle, for each score (Steiger, two-sided)")

# --- H7, H8, H9, H10 ----------------------------------------------------------------
# H8 correlates each limit measure with punitiveness (one-sided); on the
# six-part score here. None of its six limit measures involves revenge or
# desert.
pa_h8    <- run_h8(pa_d, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h8$y  <- PA_LAB   # run_h8() labels its column "self-report"
TABLES[["PAPER_H8"]] <- pa_h8
# run_h7() correlates each limit measure with `revenge` (one-sided, greater) and
# with `just_deserts` (two-sided), which in pa_d are the registered revenge and
# desert theory.
pa_h7 <- run_h7(pa_d)
# H9: desert theory against revenge, paired and one-sided in H9's direction
# (run_h9() on pa_d would return two identical rows, because desert and just
# deserts are both desert theory there).
pa_h9 <- paired_test(pa_d, "retribution_items", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
                     label = "Desert theory vs revenge")
# H10 in the registered direction (revenge more closely tied to punitiveness,
# one-sided), and two-sided, since on these scorings the two correlations are
# close and a reader may want the test of a difference in either direction.
pa_h10_run <- function(data, punit, who, rev = "revenge", tag = "") rbind(
  cbind(punitiveness = who, sidedness = paste0("one-sided, registered direction", tag),
        steiger_overlap(data, punit, rev, "retribution_items",
                        alternative = "greater",
                        label = "r(punitiveness, revenge) > r(punitiveness, desert theory)")),
  cbind(punitiveness = who, sidedness = paste0("two-sided", tag),
        steiger_overlap(data, punit, rev, "retribution_items",
                        alternative = "two.sided",
                        label = "r(punitiveness, revenge) vs r(punitiveness, desert theory)")))
pa_h10 <- rbind(pa_h10_run(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, PA_LAB),
                pa_h10_run(pa_d, PA_PUNIT_SR, PA_LAB_SR),
                # Rescoring for the Supplement: Study 1's three revenge items.
                pa_h10_run(pa_d, PA_PUNIT, PA_LAB, "revenge3", ", three-item revenge (rescoring)"),
                pa_h10_run(pa_d, PA_PUNIT_SR, PA_LAB_SR, "revenge3",
                           ", three-item revenge (rescoring)"))
# GUARDS: the Steiger test reads the scores it names (revenge is the registered
# four-item score); and the same functions, run again on d, still return the
# registered H9 and H10, so nothing in 9.19 has disturbed them.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h10$r_jk[1], cor(pa_d[[PA_PUNIT]], d$revenge))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h10$r_jh[1], cor(pa_d[[PA_PUNIT]], pa_retribution_items))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h10$r_jk[5], cor(pa_d[[PA_PUNIT]], pa_revenge3))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(run_h10(d)$diff, h10_full$diff)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(run_h9(d)$d, h9_full$d)))
# run_h7() labels its two rivals "Revenge" and "Just deserts"; on pa_d the
# second is desert theory, and the export says so. `lab` names the score in
# the just_deserts column (9.19G passes the paper's just-deserts label).
pa_relabel_h7 <- function(x, lab = PA_DT) {
  stopifnot(setequal(unique(x$y), c("Revenge", "Just deserts")))
  x$y <- ifelse(x$y == "Revenge", "Revenge", lab)
  x
}
pa_h7 <- pa_relabel_h7(pa_h7)
# GUARD: the revenge half of H7 is the registered run (revenge is registered),
# row for row.
pa_h7_reg <- run_h7(d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h7$r[pa_h7$y == "Revenge"], pa_h7_reg$r[pa_h7_reg$y == "Revenge"])))
TABLES[["PAPER_H7"]]  <- pa_h7
TABLES[["PAPER_H9"]]  <- pa_h9
TABLES[["PAPER_H10"]] <- pa_h10
# Each side of H10 with its own 95% interval, for the text: punitiveness (both
# scores) with desert theory, revenge, and Study 1's three revenge items, in the
# whole sample and among retributivists. Two-sided intervals, as everywhere.
# `labs` names the two punitiveness columns; 9.19F passes the registered
# scores' labels.
pa_h10_cors_run <- function(data, who, labs = c(PA_LAB, PA_LAB_SR)) do.call(rbind, lapply(c(PA_PUNIT, PA_PUNIT_SR), function(pu) {
  lab <- ifelse(pu == PA_PUNIT, labs[1], labs[2])
  tmp <- data.frame(p = data[[pu]], ret = data$retribution_items, rev = data$revenge,
                    rev3 = data$revenge3)
  cbind(sample = who, rbind(
    cor_row(tmp, "p", "ret",  alternative = "two.sided", label_x = lab, label_y = PA_DT),
    cor_row(tmp, "p", "rev",  alternative = "two.sided", label_x = lab, label_y = "Revenge"),
    cor_row(tmp, "p", "rev3", alternative = "two.sided", label_x = lab,
            label_y = "Revenge, three items (rescoring)")))
}))
pa_h10_cors <- pa_h10_cors_run(pa_d, "Whole sample")
# GUARD: the whole-sample rows carry the correlations the Steiger rows compare.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h10_cors$r[1:2], c(pa_h10$r_jh[1], pa_h10$r_jk[1]))))
TABLES[["PAPER_H10_cors"]] <- pa_h10_cors
show_table(pa_h7[, intersect(c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper",
                               "p_directional", "p_two", "alternative"), names(pa_h7))],
           "9.19C: H7, the limits against revenge (one-sided) and desert theory (two-sided)")
show_table(pa_h9[, c("comparison", "n", "M1", "M2", "t", "df", "p_dir", "d",
                     "d_lower", "d_upper")],
           "9.19C: H9, desert theory against revenge (paired, one-sided)")
show_table(pa_h10[, c("punitiveness", "sidedness", "r_jk", "r_jh", "r_kh", "diff", "diff_lower",
                      "diff_upper", "z", "p")],
           "9.19C: H10, revenge against desert theory as correlates of punitiveness")

# --- Each goal against the limits ----------------------------------------------------
# 8.9B's table with desert theory in desert's place. Two-sided; not
# registered. Deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation do not change and are
# kept for the comparison the text draws.
pa_d$parsimony_pair <- rowMeans(pa_d[, c("parsimony_1", "parsimony_2")])
pa_goals  <- c(retribution_items = PA_DT, deterrence = "Deterrence",
               incapacitation = "Incapacitation", rehabilitation = "Rehabilitation")
pa_limits <- c(parsimony_pair = "Parsimony (2 items)",
               parsimony_2 = "Parsimony principle item alone",
               proportionality_principle = "Proportionality principle item alone")
pa_goal_lim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pa_goals), function(g)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pa_limits), function(l)
    cor_row(pa_d, g, l, alternative = "two.sided",
            label_x = unname(pa_goals[g]), label_y = unname(pa_limits[l]))))))
# GUARD: the three goals that do not change match 8.9B's table.
pa_p2 <- TABLES[["P2_goals_by_limits"]]
pa_chk <- merge(pa_goal_lim[pa_goal_lim$x != pa_goals[["retribution_items"]], c("x", "y", "r")],
                pa_p2[, c("x", "y", "r")], by = c("x", "y"))
stopifnot(nrow(pa_chk) == 9, isTRUE(all.equal(pa_chk$r.x, pa_chk$r.y)))
TABLES[["PAPER_goals_by_limits"]] <- pa_goal_lim
show_table(pa_goal_lim[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")],
           "9.19C: each goal against the limits (two-sided; not registered)")

# --- The sentencing ratio ---------------------------------------------------------------
# The registered analysis of the ratio as a continuous score (9.10) regresses
# each outcome on the ratio. Its outcomes involve neither desert nor just
# deserts; the one outcome that reads a rescored column is punitiveness (H21),
# which here is the standardized five-part score, because the ratio is built
# from the sentence and the six-part score contains it (prereg 5.11; the
# sentence-based H21 row drops out, as registered). Every other row reproduces
# 9.10 exactly (guard below). It is exported under the PAPER_ name so the
# write-up reads one family of files. The ratio's plain correlations with
# desert theory, revenge, the principle and punitiveness, and the Steiger
# comparisons the text draws, follow.
pa_cont_ratio <- run_continuous_set(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", spec = pa_spec,
                                    drop_sentence_based = TRUE)
pa_ratio_cors <- rbind(
  cor_row(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "retribution_items", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Sentencing ratio", label_y = PA_DT),
  cor_row(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "revenge", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Sentencing ratio", label_y = "Revenge"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Sentencing ratio", label_y = "Proportionality principle"),
  cor_row(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", PA_PUNIT_SR, alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Sentencing ratio", label_y = PA_LAB_SR),
  cor_row(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "revenge3", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = "Sentencing ratio", label_y = "Revenge, three items (rescoring)"))
pa_ratio_st <- rbind(
  cbind(pair = "Desert theory vs proportionality principle",
        steiger_overlap(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "retribution_items",
                        "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided", label = "ratio")),
  cbind(pair = "Desert theory vs revenge",
        steiger_overlap(pa_d, "sentence_ratio", "retribution_items", "revenge",
                        alternative = "two.sided", label = "ratio")))
# GUARDS.
#   1. Every row but punitiveness is the registered run, row for row, and the
#      rows are the registered rows in the registered order.
#   2. The punitiveness row is the same regression on 7.4's standardized
#      five-part score (p5_d), and no row carries the six-part score.
pa_is_p <- pa_cont_ratio$outcome == PA_LAB_SR
stopifnot(sum(pa_is_p) == 1, !any(pa_cont_ratio$outcome == PA_LAB),
          identical(pa_cont_ratio$hypothesis, cont_ratio$hypothesis),
          identical(pa_cont_ratio$outcome[!pa_is_p], cont_ratio$outcome[!pa_is_p]),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_cont_ratio$beta[!pa_is_p], cont_ratio$beta[!pa_is_p])),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_cont_ratio$beta[pa_is_p],
                           cont_reg(p5_d, "punit_parts5z", "sentence_ratio",
                                    alternative = "greater")$beta)))
TABLES[["PAPER_ratio_continuous"]] <- pa_cont_ratio
TABLES[["PAPER_ratio_cors"]]       <- pa_ratio_cors
TABLES[["PAPER_ratio_steiger"]]    <- pa_ratio_st
show_table(pa_ratio_cors[, c("x", "y", "n", "r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_two")],
           "9.19C: the sentencing ratio against each score (two-sided)")
```

```{r phase9_paper_part3}
# === 9.19D PART 3 ON THE PAPER'S SCORINGS: H11, H12 AND THE CONTRASTS ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: reruns, on pa_d, the whole-sample hypotheses inside the
# retributivist group (H11) and on the retributive side of every grouping; the
# H12 correlations with the six-part score; the contrast set under the four
# registered groupings, against the deterrence- and incapacitation-first
# participants (the main text's comparison), and with the four continuous
# predictors; and the 9.17B counts over them. The contrast outcomes involve
# neither desert nor just deserts; the only outcomes that read a rescored
# column are the two H21 rows, which carry the paper's two punitiveness scores
# (the six-part score drops out wherever the run is built from the sentence,
# as the full index does). Every other row reproduces its registered
# counterpart row for row (guard below). The paper's other choices there are
# which rows it counts (punitiveness once, the two-item reflection score) and
# which comparison group it reports. Produces PAPER_H11_H1, _H2, _H3, _H6,
# _H6_steiger, _H7, _H8, _H9, _H10 and _H10_cors; PAPER_H11_groupings;
# PAPER_H12_cors; PAPER_contrasts_rank, _med, _tert, _ratio and
# _vs_deter_incap; PAPER_cont_rel, _raw, _ratio and _resid; PAPER_scorecard,
# PAPER_rows_across_groupings, PAPER_shark_vs_deter_incap and
# PAPER_H12_shares_vs_deter_incap.
# PREREG: the tests are registered (prereg 5.3, 6.5: H11 to H21 under the four
#         groupings and the continuous measures, one-sided in each row's
#         direction); the scorings are not. The comparison with the deterrence-
#         and incapacitation-first participants is not registered (9.12b).
# CONSUMES: pa_d, pa_spec, PA_PUNIT, PA_PUNIT_SR and the PA_ labels (9.19A);
#           p5_d (7.4); pa_relabel_h7(), pa_h10_run(), pa_h10_cors_run(),
#           pa_cont_ratio (9.19C); run_h1() to run_h8(),
#           paired_test(), steiger_overlap(), cor_row(), prop_ci() (0.3, 7.0);
#           run_contrast_set(), run_continuous_set(), contrast_spec (9.3);
#           h12_spec, h12 (9.2); d_retrib, h11_h1, h11_h3 (9.1); cq_d (9.12b);
#           p3_h12_other (9.17C);
#           p3_row_sets, p3_scorecard (9.17B); p3_sub (9.17C); the registered
#           contrasts_* and cont_* objects for the guards.

# --- H11: the whole-sample hypotheses inside the retributivist group -------------
pa_retrib <- pa_d[!is.na(pa_d$retributivist) & pa_d$retributivist == 1, ]
stopifnot(nrow(pa_retrib) == nrow(d_retrib))
pa_h11_h1  <- run_h1(pa_retrib, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h11_h2  <- run_h2(pa_retrib, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h11_h8  <- run_h8(pa_retrib, punit = PA_PUNIT)
pa_h11_h8$y <- PA_LAB   # run_h8() labels its column "self-report"
pa_h11_h3  <- run_h3(pa_retrib)
pa_h11_h7  <- pa_relabel_h7(run_h7(pa_retrib))
pa_h11_h9  <- paired_test(pa_retrib, "retribution_items", "revenge", alternative = "greater",
                          label = "Desert theory vs revenge, retributivists")
pa_h11_h10 <- rbind(pa_h10_run(pa_retrib, PA_PUNIT, PA_LAB),
                    pa_h10_run(pa_retrib, PA_PUNIT_SR, PA_LAB_SR))
pa_h11_h6 <- rbind(
  cor_row(pa_retrib, "retribution_items", "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Proportionality principle"),
  cor_row(pa_retrib, "retribution_items", "severity_index", alternative = "two.sided",
          label_x = PA_DT, label_y = "Severity index"))
pa_h11_h6_st <- steiger_overlap(pa_retrib, "retribution_items", "severity_index",
                                "proportionality_principle", alternative = "two.sided",
                                label = "retributivists: severity index vs principle")
# H3 inside the group: the share of positive intercorrelations, their range, and
# the first eigenvalue with its share of the variance (the figure the H11 table
# reports for every hypothesis). H3 reads none of the rescored columns, so it is
# 9.1's run (guard below).
pa_off11 <- pa_h11_h3$cor_matrix[upper.tri(pa_h11_h3$cor_matrix)]
pa_h11_h3_sum <- data.frame(n_pairs = pa_h11_h3$n_pairs, n_positive = sum(pa_off11 > 0),
                            r_min = min(pa_off11), r_max = max(pa_off11),
                            eigen_1 = pa_h11_h3$eigenvalues[1],
                            share_1 = pa_h11_h3$var_explained_1)
# GUARDS: the group is 9.1's retributivists, the same people in the same
# order; H1 inside the group reproduces the same run on 7.4's copy (p5_d) with
# the six-part score, row for row; and H3 inside the group is 9.1's.
pa_p5_retrib <- p5_d[!is.na(p5_d$retributivist) & p5_d$retributivist == 1, ]
stopifnot(identical(pa_retrib$ResponseId, d_retrib$ResponseId),
          pa_same_h1(pa_h11_h1, run_h1(pa_p5_retrib, punit = "punit_parts6")),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h11_h3$cor_matrix, h11_h3$cor_matrix)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(pa_h11_h3$var_explained_1, h11_h3$var_explained_1)))
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H1"]]  <- pa_h11_h1
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H2"]]  <- pa_h11_h2
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H3"]]  <- pa_h11_h3_sum
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H6"]]  <- pa_h11_h6
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H6_steiger"]] <- pa_h11_h6_st
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H7"]]  <- pa_h11_h7
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H8"]]  <- pa_h11_h8
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H9"]]  <- pa_h11_h9
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H10"]] <- pa_h11_h10
pa_h11_h10_cors <- pa_h10_cors_run(pa_retrib, "Retributivists")
TABLES[["PAPER_H11_H10_cors"]] <- pa_h11_h10_cors
show_table(pa_h11_h10[, c("punitiveness", "sidedness", "r_jk", "r_jh", "diff", "diff_lower",
                          "diff_upper", "z", "p")],
           "9.19D: H10 inside the retributivist group, on the paper's scorings")

# --- H11 on the retributive side of every grouping (9.17E, on the paper's scorings) --
# 9.17E's summary of H1 to H10, with the six-part score as punitiveness, H6
# stated through the principle and the severity index, desert theory in place
# of just deserts, and H10 also two-sided. H3, H4, H5 and H8's limits involve
# none of the rescored columns, but they are included so that each column of
# the table is complete. The whole sample is the reference. H3's
# first-component share is included for the table's H3 row. The quantities
# named H7_desert_theory_ are H7's second half, the limits against desert
# theory.
# PUNITIVENESS UNDER THE RATIO GROUPING IS THE STANDARDIZED FIVE-PART SCORE.
# The ratio grouping is cut from the sentence, so the six-part score, which
# contains the sentence, would put it on both sides (prereg 5.3, 5.11); 9.17E
# uses the eight-item scale there for the same reason.
# ARGUMENTS  sub, grouping_label; punit  the punitiveness column; lab  the
#            label the export gives that column (by default the paper's label
```
