```{r phase9_paper_moderators}
                           mod_slopes[rep(pa_same_rows, each = 3), ], check.attributes = FALSE)))
for (i in which(!pa_same_rows)) {
  y_vec <- if (pa_mod_specs$y[i] == "punitiveness_full") pa_six else pa_five
  fit_chk <- stats::lm(y_vec ~ d[[pa_mod_specs$x[i]]] * d[[pa_mod_specs$m[i]]])
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(stats::coef(fit_chk)[4]), pa_mod_results$b_interaction[i])),
            pa_mod_results$outcome[i] == if (pa_mod_specs$y[i] == "punitiveness_full") PA_LAB else PA_LAB_SR)
}
TABLES[["PAPER_MOD_interactions"]]  <- pa_mod_results
TABLES[["PAPER_MOD_simple_slopes"]] <- pa_mod_slopes
show_table(pa_mod_results[, c("outcome", "predictor", "moderator", "n", "b_interaction",
                              "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "t", "df", "p_two", "R2_change")],
           "9.19H: Table S23's interactions with the paper's punitiveness (two-sided p, uncorrected)")
```

# PHASE 10: EXPORT

Everything the analysis produced now leaves the document: the result tables, the
figures, and the cleaned and scored dataset. No new analysis is run here. This
phase exists so that a reader, a co-author or a journal's replication checker
can pick up the outputs as ordinary files, without re-running a line of this
code.

## 10.1 Result tables

Every table built anywhere above was collected into `TABLES` as it was made.
This section writes them all out as CSV files in one pass, and prints the list
of filenames it wrote, so the report itself records what left the building.

```{r phase10_tables}
# === EXPORT EVERY RESULT TABLE ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: writes one CSV per entry of TABLES into
# output/tables/, records the paths in `written` for the summary in 10.4, and
# removes the files of retired exports (RETIRED_TABLES, 9.19F).
#
# WHY THE NAMES MATTER SO MUCH. The NAME each table was given at the moment it
# was assigned IS its filename: TABLES[["H1_correlations"]] becomes
# output/tables/H1_correlations.csv. That is why the names chosen back in Phases
# 1 to 9 are descriptive and stable. Rename an entry and this loop silently
# writes a differently-named export instead, while the old file sits there
# unchanged. Any manuscript or downstream script pointing at the old name then
# reads a stale copy and reports numbers from a previous run.
written <- character(0)
for (nm in names(TABLES)) {
  obj <- TABLES[[nm]]
  # A NULL entry means an optional analysis did not run (a missing package, a
  # model that failed to converge). Skip it rather than writing an empty file:
  # an empty CSV on disk looks like a result of zero rows, which is a different
  # and much more misleading thing than no file at all.
  if (is.null(obj)) next
  path <- file.path(OUT_TABLES, paste0(nm, ".csv"))
  # tryCatch so that one unwritable table -- a matrix-backed object, a file
  # locked open in Excel -- does not abort the export of the other forty. The
  # failure is not hidden: it shows up as a missing filename in the manifest
  # printed below, which is the list a reader checks against.
  ok <- tryCatch({ readr::write_csv(as.data.frame(obj), path); TRUE },
                 error = function(e) FALSE)
  if (ok) written <- c(written, path)
}
# RETIRED EXPORTS. A table that an earlier knit wrote under a name this
# document no longer uses would otherwise stay in output/tables/ with its old
# contents, and a reader or script could take it for a current result (see
# WHY THE NAMES MATTER above). RETIRED_TABLES (9.19F) lists those names; their
# files are removed here, and each removal is printed. GUARD: no retired name
# is also a current table.
stopifnot(!any(RETIRED_TABLES %in% names(TABLES)))
for (nm in RETIRED_TABLES) {
  path <- file.path(OUT_TABLES, paste0(nm, ".csv"))
  if (file.exists(path) && file.remove(path)) cat(sprintf("Removed retired table %s\n", basename(path)))
}
# The manifest: how many files were written, and their names. This is the
# receipt for the export, and it is what makes a silent failure above visible.
cat(sprintf("Wrote %d result tables to %s/\n\n", length(written), OUT_TABLES))
print(data.frame(table_file = basename(written)), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 10.2 Figures

The figures were saved to disk at the moment each one was drawn, so there is
nothing left to write here. This section only lists them back, so the report
carries a record of which image files belong to this run.

```{r phase10_figures}
# === FIGURE MANIFEST ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: lists the figure files this run produced. It writes
# nothing. Each figure was already saved to disk at the point it was drawn, and
# FIGURES collected one path per ggsave/png() call through Phases 7 and 9.
#
# WHY LIST THEM AT ALL. Without this list, a reader looking at
# output/figures/ cannot tell which images came from this run and which are
# leftovers from an earlier one.
if (length(FIGURES)) {
  cat(sprintf("Wrote %d figures to %s/\n\n", length(FIGURES), OUT_FIGURES))
  print(data.frame(figure_file = basename(FIGURES)), row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  # Said out loud rather than left blank. A silent gap here could equally mean
  # the figures failed or that the manifest itself failed.
  cat("No figures were written.\n")
}
```

## 10.3 Cleaned and scored dataset

The dataset itself, after cleaning and scoring, saved in two formats. This is
the file the companion language-analysis document reads, and the file anyone
re-checking this analysis would start from.

```{r phase10_data}
# === EXPORT THE CLEANED, SCORED DATASET ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: writes the scored data frame (a rectangular table of
# rows and columns) as both CSV and RDS into data/cleaned/, plus a copy of the
# reliability table. This export is the input to the companion NLP document,
# which is why the three open-ended text columns are carried through untouched.
#
# Drop the twelve raw split-vignette columns. Phase 1.4 already coalesced them
# into Sentence1, Sentence2 and the two open-ends, and each of the twelve is
# two-thirds empty by construction, because each participant saw only one of the
# three vignette blocks.
#
# WHY THAT MATTERS: keeping them in the export invites a later analysis to reach
# for Sentence1_V2_1 and work, silently and without any error, on a third of the
# sample. The anchored ^ (match only at the start of the name) and the [123]
# class (match only those three digits) keep the pattern from catching the
# coalesced columns themselves.
drop_cols <- grep("^(Sentence1|Sentence2|Sentence_OpenEnd1|Sentence_OpenEnd2)_V[123]",
                  names(d), value = TRUE)
d_export <- d[, setdiff(names(d), drop_cols)]

# Both formats on purpose, because each one does something the other cannot.
# The CSV is plain text, portable, and readable by the Python side of the
# pipeline. The RDS keeps R's own types -- crucially the ORDER of the levels of
# the factors grp_rank, grp_med, grp_tert and grp_ratio. A factor is R's type
# for a categorical variable, and it remembers which category comes first.
#
# HAZARD: a round trip through CSV would reduce those factors to plain text and
# re-sort the categories alphabetically. That would flip which group counts as
# group 1, and with it the sign convention that every contrast in Phase 9
# depends on. A positive d would come to mean the opposite of what it means
# here. The RDS is what prevents that.
csv_path <- file.path(OUT_DATA, "retribution_scored.csv")
rds_path <- file.path(OUT_DATA, "retribution_scored.rds")
readr::write_csv(d_export, csv_path)
saveRDS(d_export, rds_path)

# Print the shape and the two paths, so the report records exactly how many rows
# and columns went out and where they went.
cat(sprintf("Cleaned dataset written: %d rows x %d columns\n",
            nrow(d_export), ncol(d_export)))
cat(sprintf("  %s\n  %s\n", csv_path, rds_path))

# The reliability table travels WITH the dataset as well as with the result
# tables. That duplication is deliberate. Anyone who picks up the scored file on
# its own then has the Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega for every composite
# in it, without having to re-knit this document to find them. Both are measures
# of internal consistency: how far a set of items behaves like repeated
# measurements of one thing.
readr::write_csv(alpha_table_out, file.path(OUT_DATA, "reliability_table.csv"))
cat(sprintf("  %s\n", file.path(OUT_DATA, "reliability_table.csv")))
```

## 10.4 Analysis summary and session info

A closing summary of what this run actually did, followed by the exact software
versions it did it with. Both are printed so that the knitted report is
self-contained: a reader can see the sample size, the counts and the package
versions without opening anything else.

```{r phase10_summary}
# === RUN SUMMARY ===
# WHAT THIS CHUNK DOES: prints a short summary of the run that just finished.
#
# Every number here is READ BACK from the objects the run produced -- nrow(d),
# n_raw from the exclusion funnel, the length of `written` and of FIGURES --
# rather than typed in by hand. That is the whole point. A hand-typed summary
# drifts away from the analysis the first time anything changes, and then
# confidently reports a sample size the document no longer has.
cat("========================================================================\n")
cat("RETRIBUTION STUDY — MAIN ANALYSIS COMPLETE\n")
cat("========================================================================\n\n")
# The headline counts: how many people are in the analysis, how many were in the
# raw file before exclusions, and how many of the analytic sample count as
# retributivists under the primary ranking definition.
cat(sprintf("Analytic sample:        N = %d (from %d raw responses)\n",
            nrow(d), n_raw))
cat(sprintf("Retributivists (rank):  n = %d (%.1f%%)\n",
            sum(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE),
            100 * mean(d$retributivist, na.rm = TRUE)))
cat(sprintf("Composites scored:      %d (alpha and omega reported for each)\n",
            nrow(alpha_table_out)))
cat(sprintf("Result tables written:  %d\n", length(written)))
cat(sprintf("Figures written:        %d\n\n", length(FIGURES)))

# A map of where each block of hypotheses was tested, so a reader chasing one
# hypothesis knows which phase to open.
cat("Hypotheses covered: H1-H3 (Phase 7), H4-H10 (Phase 8),\n")
cat("H11-H21 plus the continuous and sentencing-ratio reruns (Phase 9),\n")
cat("the E1/E2 exploratory extras, the prereg 6.6 moderators (9.18),\n")
cat("and the scorings the paper reports (9.19, not registered).\n\n")

# THIS RUN'S STATUS, STATED PLAINLY. Collection is finished, so per prereg 4.4
# this is THE confirmatory reading of the data, not a preview of one. That
# matters because a confirmatory reading cannot be revised after the fact
# without saying so.
#
# The shortfall is reported rather than glossed over: the target was 960 valid
# responses and 948 were realized, 12 short, or 1.25%. The power consequence is
# given as a number rather than as reassurance -- the smallest correlation the
# study can detect moves from .090 to .091 (prereg 4.3).
cat("*** CONFIRMATORY RUN — FULL DATASET ***\n")
cat(sprintf("Analytic N = %d after the pre-registered exclusions (1015 raw).\n", nrow(d)))
cat("Collection is complete, so per prereg 4.4 this is THE confirmatory reading.\n")
cat("Target was 960 valid; realized 948 (12 short, 1.25%). Power impact is\n")
cat("negligible: smallest detectable r moves .090 -> .091 (prereg 4.3).\n")
cat("========================================================================\n")
```

```{r phase10_session}
# === SESSION INFO ===
# Package versions and the R build, printed so that the run can be reproduced
# from the knitted document alone. Someone re-running this in two years needs to
# know which versions produced these numbers, and this is what puts that record
# into the report itself.
#
# psych, lavaan and cocor are the three that matter most. McDonald's omega, the
# confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) fit indices (RMSEA, CFI, SRMR) and
# Steiger's test for dependent overlapping correlations can all shift slightly
# across major versions of those packages. A small disagreement between two runs
# is far more often a version difference than a real one.
sessionInfo()
```

---

## What is deliberately left for the companion documents

This document is the confirmatory analysis and nothing else. Two bodies of
work belong to companion documents, and each is listed here so that its absence
reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

  - **E3–E7, the language analysis of the open-ended responses** (prereg 6.7).
    The three open-ends (`Sentence_OpenEnd1`, `Sentence_OpenEnd2`, and
    `Q333` / `Priorit_Explain`) are carried through cleaning and exported with
    the scored data, but the model-ensemble facet scoring, the word-list and
    embedding checks, and the validation gates (ICC ≥ .60, facet-to-scale
    r ≥ .30) belong to the NLP pipeline, not to this document. ICC is the
    intraclass correlation, a measure of how far independent raters agree, and
    the gates are the thresholds a facet score must clear before it is used at
    all. E3 through E7 form **one exploratory family**, and Benjamini-Hochberg
    is applied within it (prereg 2.4, 6.7). Benjamini-Hochberg limits the false
    discovery rate, that is, the share of false claims among the results called
    significant. Some such control is needed because running many tests at once
    otherwise turns up findings by chance alone. Nothing in the language
    analysis is confirmatory.
  - **The semantic retributivism measure**, the fourth (exploratory) way of
    identifying retributivists, for the same reason: it depends on the facet
    scores being validated first. Using an unvalidated measure to define the
    groups would put an untested tool at the centre of the analysis.

The other exploratory analyses prereg 6.6 lists are in this document: E1 and
E2 (9.15), the factor structure of the correlates (with H3, in 7.3), political
orientation and prosecution-defense leaning as moderators (9.18), and the change
from the first to the second sentence as a function of retributivism, through
the sentencing ratio (5.4, 5.5 and 9.17A).
